issues.title: Turner Duckworth dips Maker's Mark's new identity in red wax
issues.summary: Five years after its last refresh, the Kentucky bourbon has gone back to the London agency for a global identity pressed, quite literally, from the very farm it comes from. If you love your bourbon as...
issues.author: Katy Cowan
issues.content_html:
Five years after its last refresh, the Kentucky bourbon has gone back to the London agency for a global identity pressed, quite literally, from the very farm it comes from.

If you love your bourbon as much as I do, then you'll know every bottle of Maker's Mark is still dipped in red wax by hand. It's a slow and messy process any creative can appreciate, especially in a year when Cambridge Dictionary named 'human' its word of 2026.

So it makes sense that the brand's new global identity would go down the same route. Turner Duckworth London has taken stalks of soft red winter wheat, rings of American oak and plants native to Star Hill Farm, the distillery's home in Loretto, Kentucky, and dipped and pressed each one into that same red wax. What came out of that is a set of fresh marks that sit at the heart of the brand. There's also an updated colour palette, new photography and custom typography that pays homage to the brand's family roots.

Sound familiar? That's because Turner Duckworth has been here before. We covered its first Maker's Mark identity in 2021, when the agency built a system around a graphic version of the famous drip. Five years later, the drawing has made way for the real thing. Why illustrate wax when you've got access to vats of it?

The typography has its own story, too. It's inspired by the handwriting of Margie Samuels, who founded Maker's Mark with her husband, Bill Samuels Sr, and who came up with the bottle, label and wax in the first place. It is Margie's wit that the brand has always traded on. Well, I never.

Now for a little history lesson. Bill famously burned the family's 170-year-old recipe to start afresh and come up with a more balanced bourbon. The couple chose Loretto for its proximity to water and grain growers. And Margie decided that every bottle must be hand-dipped – a strategy that literally made its mark. Maker's Mark calls this streak 'Perfectly Unreasonable', the name of its brand platform, and the new identity is designed to carry this idea consistently worldwide, in what the brand describes as a "modern, more minimal way".

"In a world increasingly driven by speed and automation, we still believe some things are worth making slowly, by hand," says Chloe Lloyd-Jones, vice president of global brand marketing, Maker's Mark. "We returned to Star Hill Farm, working with natural materials from the land and our signature red wax to create a visual identity that reflects the 'Perfectly Unreasonable' spirit behind our bourbon. The result gives us a powerful way to tell our story around the world, while creating experiences that feel personal and relevant in each market."

"My grandparents weren't thinking about 'branding' when they created Maker's Mark. They cared about a hand-made process in service to flavour and design that honours that vision," adds Rob Samuels, eighth-generation whisky maker and managing director. "That deeply personal approach created some of the most recognisable symbols in bourbon. This new and exceptional work brings that same intention forward, honouring what they created and ensuring Maker's Mark feels as personal and distinctive today as it did from the start."

The identity was launched on 17 November and is rolling out across digital, social, advertising and retail, as well as events and experiences. Parts of it have already appeared at events in the US and China and in out-of-home campaigns in Australia and the UK, with more markets to follow throughout 2027.

issues.title: &Walsh takes a bite out of the moon for Insomnia Cookies
issues.summary: Jessica Walsh and her team have given the late-night bakery's identity a refresh, and it's based on the very thing it's promised since it launched in 2003: a warm cookie at any hour. Milk and cookies...
issues.author: Katy Cowan
issues.content_html:
Jessica Walsh and her team have given the late-night bakery's identity a refresh, and it's based on the very thing it's promised since it launched in 2003: a warm cookie at any hour.

Milk and cookies is very much an American thing. I've never once been tempted to sneak down the stairs in the dead of night and snack on something delicious. It's just not in our culture. Nigella Lawson might, god bless her. I can picture her now in her silk dressing gown, the goddess that she is. But late-night treats are not for me. Seeing the new identity for Insomnia Cookies, though, might tempt me otherwise.

The heart of &Walsh's rebrand is a logo that looks good enough to eat, and it pays homage to the whole premise. Insomnia Cookies is a late-night bakery that Seth Berkowitz started from his University of Pennsylvania dorm room in 2003. It now has more than 375 bakeries across the US, Canada and the UK. Its original identity had a cookie moon. Genius. &Walsh has thankfully kept that but swapped the drawing for the real deal: a photograph of a melted chocolate chunk cookie, half-eaten into the shape of a crescent. Anyone suddenly think of "Half mooooon!" or is that just me?

Yes, it's a brave move, a photographic logo. Any designer will tell you they're awkward at small sizes and damn fussy in print, yet here we are. But have no fear, dear readers – &Walsh has a vector version in reserve for exactly those moments. Everywhere else, though, the cookie is on full show.

So why didn't they start from scratch? One would assume the importance of heritage, certainly. By Insomnia's own account, it created the warm cookie delivery category, and &Walsh set out to recommit to that rather than reinvent it. So whilst everyone else is chasing trends, the new strategy focuses on a single promise: 'Always Warm'. Gosh, my mouth is watering just thinking about it.

That brand promise suits Insomnia's purpose – turning up at your door at any unreasonable hour with something straight from the oven. It's why the agency didn't overcomplicate things or try and be clever. When you look at this refreshed logo, you get that instant promise. It's confident without trying too hard.

Around the moon is a system built on the hours Insomnia operates. There's a nice late-night purple palette (Premier Inn, anyone?), along with a run of cookie-dough browns. Typography by Julio Zukerman is rounded and chunky. Illustration is also by Julio and Simran Meshram. And there's a refreshed tone of voice throughout.

The new identity has been rolled out across campaigns, digital, newsletters, print and packaging, including pizza-style boxes that regulars will be familiar with.

Then there's Insomnia's menu, which rotates constantly. And every limited-time offer is another opportunity for the brand to show off its new look. To keep it all feeling like one brand, &Walsh designed a tiered system: most launches share the same warm, appetising photography and art direction, while a select few campaigns get a more graphic approach.

What's really interesting is the sheer volume of the work. Over six months, &Walsh produced more than five photography and video shoots to cover 12 campaigns, from the core range of cookies to seasonal specials. OK, now I want to know about seasonal specials. Photography was by Henry Hargreaves, while Charlotte Omnes and Daniella Khan handled food styling. Motion design is by Pedro Magalhães, Igor Fajardo and Marco Del Pra, and moving elements can be seen across the refresh. It looks so good you can almost see the heat coming off the freshly baked cookies.

"Every decision in this rebrand, the photo moon cookie, the photography, the rounded type, the colours, was built toward the same feeling: warm, late night and confident," says Carolina Vazquez, art director at &Walsh. "The goal was to make the brand feel fresh without losing what's always made it Insomnia."

Given how much I'll be playing GTA 6 over the coming weeks, I reckon I could be persuaded to enjoy a late-night cookie.

issues.title: It's official: creatives are using AI daily, but most aren't making extra money from it
issues.summary: Envato's second annual survey of more than 1,000 creatives finds that AI use has become routine, even if they don't always tell the client. But whether they're using it well remains an open question....
issues.author: Tom May
issues.content_html:
Envato's second annual survey of more than 1,000 creatives finds that AI use has become routine, even if they don't always tell the client. But whether they're using it well remains an open question.

This time last year, many creatives were rushing to adopt AI tools, but nervously. Twelve months later, things have changed a lot. That's according to Beyond the Hype: The State of AI in Creative Work, the second annual report from Envato, the creative asset and AI toolkit owned by Shutterstock.

Based on a survey of 1,033 creatives across 103 countries and territories, the report reveals what creatives are actually doing with AI. And two big things immediately grabbed my attention. Firstly, more than half of AI users have used it on key client work without telling their client. And secondly, while AI may save you time, most creatives aren't seeing that turn into actual money.

To unpack these findings and more, I spoke to Hichame Assi, president of Shutterstock, which includes Envato.

Why ask?

Envato first ran the survey in 2025, and Hichame says the reason was simple. The public conversation about AI didn't match what he was seeing from the working creatives who use Envato. "At face value, the narrative was all hype or doom," he recalls. "Yet in our community, creatives were quietly working AI into client jobs." So last year, Envato asked creatives how they were using it.

One finding from that first survey stayed with Hichame in particular. "Almost half were using AI every day, but only about a third felt really prepared for it. That gap felt worth keeping an eye on, so we came back to see what had changed."

So what has changed in the last 12 months? Well, quite a lot actually. For a start, today 87% of creatives use AI at work at least occasionally, and 58% use it every day.

"AI is now part of the daily routine for most creatives," says Hichame. "Daily use rose from 49% to 58%, and agentic tools, which we didn't even ask about last year, are now used regularly by more than a third of AI users. At the same time, active avoidance has grown from 3% to 8%, so not everyone is on board yet."

But while most creatives are using AI to help them in their work, that doesn't mean that AI is doing their work, at least not all of it.

The survey split people's creative work into six stages, from research and admin to editing. At five of the six stages, "directing [AI] closely" was the most common approach. The percentage of creatives who let AI work "with little input" never went above 11%, and at some stages, it dropped to 4%. As for generating assets, only 7% took a hands-off approach.

The fall of the prompt

For Hichame, the biggest surprise in this year's data concerned the skill that, only a year ago, everyone seemed to agree was essential: prompting.

"Last year, our respondents named prompting as a skills gap and predicted 'prompt engineer' as a new job," he recalls. "This year, though, creatives ranked it last of eight factors, at 19%." Taste and judgement came first, at 53%. Craft came second, at 49%, followed by the strength of the idea, at 39%.

So what's going on? Perhaps this is just a sign that models have got much better at understanding natural language and visual references. Consequently, the time when precise prompts were all-important is long gone.

"The tools are going to keep getting easier and more accessible, so knowing how to use them won't be what sets creatives apart," says Jessica Walsh, founder of New York studio &Walsh and one of the experts interviewed for the report. What will, in her view, is "being able to recognise great work when you see it [which is] not something you can prompt, or learn overnight."

A lack of rules

One thing that surprised me personally is that nearly six in 10 creatives who work in teams say they have no written AI policy. Even in organisations of 250 or more people, four in 10 say they've been given nothing in writing. As Hichame puts it: "The tools moved fast, and the rules didn't. Most are working it out as they go." Which brings us to a thorny question: should creatives disclose whether they've used AI in their work?

In practice, it seems, this has become a matter of personal judgement. More than half of AI users (53%) have used it on key client work without telling the client, and most don't see that as a problem. Only 7% felt uncomfortable staying quiet.

Hichame notes, though, that when there are rules in place, "creatives are more open with clients, with 47% always disclosing AI use, compared with 38% where there's no policy." Age can play a part, too: while only 40% of creatives always tell clients when they've used AI, that rises to 53% among those aged 50 and over.

What humans are for

One of the most commonly cited concerns about AI is that its output is bland and lacks soul. Yet when creatives discard AI-generated concepts, that's rarely the real reason. According to the report, one third (34%) do so because the concepts missed the brief or vision, and a similar number (32%) do so because of errors or low quality, such as garbled logos or glitchy video. Only 5% drop them because they lack feeling or soul.

What's just as interesting is what creatives keep. "The typical creative generates three to five AI concepts and keeps about two," notes Hichame. "Three in four keep half or fewer of their concepts." That, as he sees it, shows how important human creativity remains in the creative process. "Quality control is where humans make the difference," he says. "Knowing what the brief needs, seeing where an output falls short and choosing what makes the cut are judgement calls.

"Generating 10 options is easy," he adds. "Knowing which one is right is the skill, and it's one that creatives build over years."

Where's the money?

Here's another interesting question the report poses: is AI making creatives richer? The answer is: mostly not, or at least not yet.

"Half of creatives who use AI say it makes them faster," says Hichame. "But of those, only one in four report any financial upside. Another one in five earn about the same for less effort. For the rest, they gain time, not money."

This isn't, though, because people are cutting their rates: quite the reverse. "Of the freelancers and agency owners we asked, 40% raised their rates this year and only 6% cut them," he says. More to the point, more than a quarter of AI users (28%) now offer services they couldn't before, and 26% of those whose rates moved credited new services.

The conclusion in Hichame's mind is clear. "Getting better results from AI is the skill creatives most want to learn, at 45%, while creative direction sits near the bottom at 18%," he notes. Yet in the survey, the creatives who have raised their rates credited speed, reputation and creative direction ahead of AI skills. "This suggests people are chasing the skill the market isn't paying for, and ignoring the ones it is."

His advice? "Take the hours AI gives back and put them where clients pay," he says. "That means turning work around faster, investing in your own name and point of view, so your work is recognisable as yours, and sharpening your direction. Because three in four creatives already discard at least half of what AI produces, and that judgement is what sets you apart."

issues.title: Julie Legrand finds poetry in coffee pots, shells and other things you see every day
issues.summary: The French illustrator and screen printer turns objects from her kitchen and studio into bold, smudged, characteristically simple images. Julie Legrand's portfolio is full of things you've seen a thou...
issues.author: Ayla Angelos
issues.content_html:
The French illustrator and screen printer turns objects from her kitchen and studio into bold, smudged, characteristically simple images.

Julie Legrand's portfolio is full of things you've seen a thousand times and probably never stopped to really look at, let alone draw them. There's a moka pot drawn in a wobbly black line, a large-scale sunshine-yellow coffee pot on chocolatey brown, a hand holding a shell among pale blue crabs and whelks, and roses in all sorts of guises, from a yellow bloom with 'ROSA' scrawled underneath in her own lettering to a tomato-red one floating on cobalt blue. A few simple shapes, a handful of colours and the odd paper dot from a hole punch are all it takes to make a kitchen staple feel like a star. And it's all so cheerful and homely that we want to put the kettle on, and maybe pin a few of these to the fridge.

The illustrator and screen printer comes from the south of France. "I grew up in the mountains of the Hérault hinterland," she says, before studying illustration in Épinal, eastern France, and later printmaking in Galicia, Spain. Those roots led her to work with traditional techniques, and are perhaps a key reason why rural life and seaside imagery turn up again and again in her work.

When asked where she finds inspiration, she says: "Primarily from everyday life: objects I find in my kitchen or my studio." That's the sort of stuff we all have lying around at home. Her themes are always "rooted in the intimate and the mundane," and she adds: "I try to convey the memories and poetry associated with them." Since moving to Sète, the sea has crept into her work, including its plant life, mineral forms and inhabitants. "I like to interpret the landscape through the elements and forms that compose it, rather than by representing the landscape itself."

Once she has her inspiration in check, she moves on to her process. "I exhaust forms," she explains, "meaning I choose an object or subject and explore its variations, sometimes over the course of months." That explains why a coffee pot and rose each show up in so many guises. She starts with photos, sketches, and drawings she's happy with, then works in collage or with pens, pencils, rulers, and lettering templates, before digitising and editing. The handcrafted feel matters enormously to her, so the paper textures from her collages and the marks and smudges on her drawings all make it through. "Cleaning up a scan is the opposite of my approach," she says – and we're glad.

Recently, Julie created a pair of collages for the Slow Down Studio open call, featuring a stem of nodding bell-shaped flowers and a cream rose, both on brown. "It perfectly sums up what I enjoy doing right now: flowers, a subject I find delightful, combined with my signature stylistic approach," she says. And what is that approach, you might ask? Well: "simple, synthetic forms, a limited colour palette, including brown (my favourite colour), a mix of angles and curves and those small paper circles from my hole punch (one of my favourite tools)." Those little dots scatter around the edges like confetti, and she deliberately avoids over-editing the colours or saturation so the original scan's "authentic, handmade quality" can shine through.

As for what she hopes people take away from her work, Julie is refreshingly relaxed about it. "There isn't really a message, other than raising my audience's awareness of the poetry found in simple things," she says. She thinks the people who connect with her work appreciate its materiality and "see themselves reflected in the universal motifs I choose to depict."

Plenty is in the works for Julie, including a personal piece for an upcoming exhibition in Sète, plus fairs and markets in London, Marseille, Milan and Valencia in the coming months. She's also about to start a screen-printed book with the Berlin-based studio Le Raclet. And while we have you, she'd like us to know she's "looking to expand my commission work as much as possible (take note!)", with branding projects and press work at the top of her wishlist. "That would be amazing," she says.

issues.title: Tiffany & Co. Brings a Century of American Beauty to Crystal Bridges
issues.summary: From a 27-carat Arkansas diamond to intricate orchid brooches, Nature Adorned explores the relationship between nature, jewelry, and fine art.
issues.author: Misha Agostinelli
issues.content_html:
In 1926 in central Arkansas, an 11-year-old girl discovered what she assumed was just a “pretty rock”—it turned out to be a 27.21-carat diamond, which Tiffany & Co. ultimately acquired and dubbed the Arkansas Diamond. One hundred years later, that pretty rock has returned to its home state as a highlight of Nature Adorned: The Artistry of Tiffany & Co. and the American Imagination at Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas.

Discovered in Arkansas in 1926, the 27.21-carat Arkansas Diamond was acquired by Tiffany & Co. in 1946 and is among the largest diamonds ever found in the United States. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

The Arkansas Diamond is displayed alongside archival documents tracing the state’s diamond-mining history in Nature Adorned. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

The diamond’s acquisition reflects a longstanding Tiffany tradition. Under the leadership of George Frederick Kunz, the company’s first chief gemologist, Tiffany championed American gemstones at a time when European jewelers largely overlooked them. From sapphires sourced in Montana and tourmalines from Maine to emeralds from North Carolina, these stones reveal the geological diversity of the American landscape. The Arkansas Diamond is another example of that legacy.

An 1885–1895 Tiffany & Co. necklace features 30 multicolored American-mined tourmalines, a gemstone championed by the company’s first chief gemologist, George Frederick Kunz. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

A blue mineral specimen displayed against Carmen Herrera’s Cerulean illustrates the exhibition’s exploration of connections between natural formations and abstract art. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Bringing together gemstones and jewelry from The Tiffany Archives with works from the museum’s collection, Nature Adorned explores how the natural world has influenced both jewelry and fine art. Through unexpected pairings, the exhibition reveals shared approaches to color, form, and craftsmanship across different mediums.

Installation view of Nature Adorned at Crystal Bridges, where gemstones, jewelry, and works of American art are presented in conversation with one another. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

“This exhibition reveals the power of seeing The Tiffany Archives and Crystal Bridges’ collection in conversation,” says Jen Padgett, Crystal Bridges’ Windgate curator of craft. “Through this collaboration, we can highlight the remarkable creativity, attention to materials, and skilled making that have shaped American art and design across generations.”

Inside the exhibition, this conversation begins in the garden. George Paulding Farnham’s orchid brooches balance the fluidity of the natural world with the precision of cut gemstones. Diamonds, emeralds, and pink sapphires are delicately placed among gold and enamel, capturing the flowers with botanical accuracy.

George Paulding Farnham’s Tiger Orchid brooch (1889–1893) combines gold, sterling silver, diamonds, emeralds, pink sapphires, and enamel to capture the flower’s intricate details. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

Martin Johnson Heade’s Cattleya Orchid, Two Hummingbirds and a Beetle (ca. 1875–1890) reflects the same fascination with botanical detail found in Farnham’s orchid jewelry. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

The brooches reflect the paintings displayed alongside them, including Martin Johnson Heade’s Cattleya Orchid, Two Hummingbirds and a Beetle. The paintings share the same attention to organic form and detail, making the two distinct works feel like an extensions of one another—and of nature itself.

George Paulding Farnham’s orchid-inspired jewelry is displayed alongside works of American art in Nature Adorned, highlighting a shared interest in the natural world’s intricate forms. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Carmen Herrera’s Cerulean (1965) and Leon Polk Smith’s New Moon for August (1983) introduce a different interpretation of nature, where form is reduced to crisp edges and angles. The exhibition pairs these abstract works with faceted gemstones, drawing attention to the relationship between shape, line, and geometry.

A blue mineral specimen displayed against Carmen Herrera’s Cerulean illustrates the exhibition’s exploration of connections between natural formations and abstract art. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

While Herrera and Polk Smith focus on precision, Jean Schlumberger lets loose. His rubellite and turquoise necklace, Hedges and Flowers, along with his tanzanite brooch, Bird on a Rock, capture what he described as the “irregularity of the universe.” Instead of taming nature, Schlumberger allows its unpredictability to take the spotlight. Hope Gangloff’s Queen Jane Approximately echoes this organic approach through lively colors and patterns, creating a visual dialogue with the jewels.

Jean Schlumberger’s Hedges and Flowers necklace (1978–1987) combines gold, platinum, diamonds, rubellite tourmalines, and turquoise in an exuberant interpretation of the natural world. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

Schlumberger’s Hedges and Flowers necklace on display at Crystal Bridges, where its organic forms are presented in dialogue with works of American art. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Victoria Reynolds, Tiffany & Co.’s chief gemologist and vice president of high jewelry diamond and gemstone acquisition, describes the exhibition as a celebration of the company’s heritage, highlighting “the enduring influence of nature across generations of creativity.”

Jean Schlumberger’s Bird on a Rock brooch (1965) pairs a diamond-studded bird with a striking tanzanite gemstone, transforming a familiar natural subject into an imaginative piece of jewelry. Photography courtesy of Tiffany & Co. Archives.

Hope Gangloff’s Queen Jane Approximately (2011) uses expressive color and pattern to explore organic forms, echoing the playful approach to nature found in Jean Schlumberger’s jewelry. Photography courtesy of Crystal Bridges.

Nature Adorned: The Artistry of Tiffany & Co. and the American Imagination is on view through Mar. 29, 2027, at Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art in Bentonville, Arkansas.

issues.title: Carsten Höller’s Monumental Slides Bring Play to Mexico City
issues.summary: Four towering, functional slides connect different parts of Antara, where Sordo Madaleno’s latest expansion brings architecture, contemporary art, and public space together
issues.author: Design Milk Staff
issues.content_html:
Leaving the office through a 125-foot spiral slide might sound like something out of a dream, but it’s becoming a reality in Mexico City. Four monumental slides by artist Carsten Höller are the centerpiece of a major expansion at Antara, a mixed-use development designed by architecture firm Sordo Madaleno. The interactive installations bring an unexpected element of play to a destination that combines retail, hospitality, workplaces, and contemporary art.

Photography by Fernando Farfan

Titled Mexico City Slides (2026), the permanent installation is Höller’s largest slide project to date. The four spiraling structures range from 39 to 125 feet in height, with lengths extending from approximately 102 to 295 feet. Rather than functioning as standalone sculptures, they are integrated into the architecture, connecting different parts of the development while giving visitors a new way to move between them.

The slides descend from retail and dining spaces, offices occupied by Google, and the future Rosewood Mexico City hotel, converging at a common landing area. Their arrangement transforms what might otherwise be separate destinations into a shared experience, bringing people from different parts of the complex together in an unexpected way.

Photography by Fernando Farfan

“People sliding from a hotel, from offices, from restaurants, and from an art center are brought together in the air and land next to each other,” Höller explains. “They share the experience of being taken out of their usual form of being, into the unknown, dreamlike territory of simultaneous joy and fear.”

The installation is part of the latest chapter for Antara, which opened in 2006 on a former industrial site in Mexico City’s Colonia Granada neighborhood. Developed by SOMA and designed by Sordo Madaleno, the original project introduced an open-air retail concept that has since evolved into a larger destination for shopping, dining, and cultural programming.

Photography by Fernando Farfan

Twenty years later, the expansion places greater emphasis on the spaces between buildings and the ways visitors move through them. A new 26,000-square-foot public garden, landscaped pathways, and stepped terraces connect the development’s different components, creating places to gather beyond its commercial spaces.

Art plays a central role in that approach. SOMA’s nonprofit contemporary art foundation, Arte Abierto, will open a new location within Antara, Arte Abierto Polanco, in December 2026. Alongside Höller’s installation, the venue will present Now What (2026), an exhibition by Danish artist collective Superflex that examines the relationship between built environments and natural forces. Combining architecture, sculpture, and text, the exhibition explores how human systems of design and organization influence our relationship with the surrounding world.

Photography by Fernando Farfan

For SOMA president Javier Sordo Madaleno De Haro, the investment in publicly accessible space is fundamental to the development’s long-term value. “I’ve realized that the most valuable thing is not the capital gain of a building itself, but the value it brings to its surroundings,” he says. “Art and public space are how we create that value.”

The expansion also introduces more than 80 new retail brands and concepts, bringing Antara’s total to 260. A forthcoming 43-story tower will house Rosewood Mexico City, with 163 guest rooms and suites, restaurants, a spa, and an outdoor pool deck, along with office space for international companies.

Photography by Fernando Farfan

Yet the most distinctive addition may be the one that challenges how people typically navigate a building. By incorporating Höller’s slides directly into the architecture, Sordo Madaleno and SOMA have made art part of the development’s circulation, turning movement between spaces into an experience in its own right.

The new public spaces and gardens are now open, while Mexico City Slides and the Superflex exhibition are scheduled to open in December. Access to the slides will be free, offering visitors a decidedly unconventional way to experience the evolving development.

Photography by Fernando Farfan

issues.title: OMA Rethinks Retail Through Craft and Circular Design at Potato Head Bali
issues.summary: Designed by OMA, Potato Head's Good Times General Store brings Balinese craftsmanship, circular design, and interactive workshops to the traditional retail experience
issues.author: Murrye Bernard
issues.content_html:
What if a store invited visitors to consider not just what they’re buying, but how it’s made? At Desa Potato Head in Bali, the new Good Times General Store explores that question through architecture, craftsmanship, and circular design. Created in collaboration with OMA, Potato Head’s first permanent retail space shifts the focus from consumption to discovery, inviting visitors to engage with the materials and processes behind the products.

Photography by Sharon Angelia

Building on a partnership spanning more than a decade, OMA and Potato Head envisioned the store as an extension of the hospitality brand’s “Good Times, Do Good” philosophy.

“Rather than focusing solely on the display and sale of products, the design prioritizes experience, participation and interaction,” explains David Gianotten, OMA managing partner and architect.

Photography by Sharon Angelia

The architecture embraces a “contemporary-traditional” approach, bringing Balinese vernacular building techniques into a modern setting. An alang-alang thatch façade, made from locally sourced tropical grass, creates a textured outer layer, while rammed-earth walls made from local clay lend the interior a grounded, tactile quality. Bamboo appears throughout, including in the terrazzo flooring, where it’s used as an aggregate, and in the display elements.

“We wanted to reinterpret Balinese traditional architecture and craftsmanship in a contemporary way, rather than simply reproducing traditional forms or decorative elements,” says Ade Herkarisma, group head of architecture and development at Potato Head.

Photography by Sharon Angelia

Reclaimed and locally sourced materials bring natural variations in color, texture, and form. Instead of concealing these irregularities, the designers embraced them, letting the materials guide the assembly and detailing.

Photography by Sharon Angelia

Inside, the store unfolds across five interconnected bays, guiding visitors from finished products toward the processes behind their creation. The first showcases souvenirs and lifestyle objects by Indonesian craftspeople, while the second presents the Potato Head Collection, an apparel line inspired by Bali. The third introduces Wasted by Potato Head, a collaboration with British designer Max Lamb that transforms discarded materials into furniture and homewares.

Photography by Sharon Angelia

In the final two bays, visitors move from browsing to making. A working natural dye studio transforms food and plant waste into pigments used in workshops exploring dyeing, painting, and pattern-making. Beyond it, The Workshop features a wall of shredded HDPE plastic recovered from waste collectors across Bali and Java. The colorful fragments become part of the architecture, making the material’s previous life visible, while the surrounding space is dedicated to experimentation.

“While the first three bays focus on products and the stories behind them, the final two bays prioritize participation, inviting visitors to engage directly with materials and processes,” Gianotten explains.

Photography by Sharon Angelia

The store also connects to Desa Potato Head’s broader sustainability initiatives, including its Waste Lab and Follow the Waste Tour, which demonstrate how discarded materials can be recovered, processed, and transformed into new objects. For OMA, the project extends ideas explored in N*thing is Possible, a 2022 exhibition in Singapore examining the potential of zero-waste hospitality.

“Circularity therefore becomes something experiential rather than abstract,” says Gianotten.

Photography by Sharon Angelia

Designing around reclaimed resources required flexibility, especially around material consistency and availability. Rather than forcing materials into predetermined specifications, the team adapted the design to their natural characteristics and limitations.

“We discovered that circularity goes beyond material selection,” Herkarisma explains. “It is about rethinking how we design, build, operate, and engage people in the process of giving new value to resources that would otherwise be discarded.”

Photography by Sharon Angelia

At the Good Times General Store, the act of making is as visible as the finished product. By placing workshops alongside retail displays and allowing reclaimed materials to shape the architecture, OMA and Potato Head offer a model of shopping that encourages visitors to look more closely at what they consume—and what might otherwise be thrown away.

issues.title: The Best Tech Gifts for Design Enthusiasts
issues.summary: Thoughtfully designed technology that brings something unexpected to everyday life
issues.author: Design Milk Staff
issues.content_html:
Technology has become so thoroughly integrated into our lives that it’s easy to overlook the design behind it. But look beyond the specifications, and you’ll find plenty of objects worth paying attention to: a clock that uses light and sound to mark the passing hours, a digital frame that resembles a printed photograph, and a cassette-playing boombox that brings back the pleasure of physical controls.

For this year’s tech gift guide, we’ve selected 18 products that put as much thought into how they look and feel as what they do. Some embrace the past, others experiment with new technology, and a few make the everyday business of charging, organizing, and staying connected a little more enjoyable.

Photography courtesy of MoMA Design Store

SB214OS Bluetooth Boombox by Studebaker

The boombox is back, complete with oversized speakers, analog controls, and illuminated VU meters. Studebaker’s retro-inspired design brings the 1980s into the present with Bluetooth connectivity, a CD player, USB playback, and a cassette deck that can even record music. A rechargeable battery and built-in carrying handle make it easy to take the nostalgia wherever the party goes.

The SB214OS Bluetooth Boombox is available at store.moma.org for $250.

Photography courtesy of Polaroid

Mod Instant Camera by Polaroid

Polaroid’s Mod puts creative controls directly on the camera, inviting experimentation without the distraction of a smartphone screen. Dedicated physical controls make it easy to explore effects like double exposures, light painting, motion freeze, and split-shot compositions. It’s a refreshingly hands-on approach to photography that encourages a little spontaneity and plenty of happy accidents.

The Polaroid Mod Instant Camera is available at polaroid.com for $169.99.

Photography courtesy of Therabody

CryoTherm Palm by Therabody

Therabody takes a different approach to workout recovery with a device designed to fit between your hands. To help manage body heat during workouts, the handheld device uses temperature-controlled surfaces to cool both palms simultaneously, with additional heat and contrast therapy settings. Compact and cordless, it provides an alternative to ice baths and other more cumbersome temperature-based recovery equipment.

The CryoTherm Palm is available at therabody.com for $399.99.

Photography courtesy of Balmuda

The Clock by Balmuda

Inspired by traditional pocket watches, Balmuda’s The Clock reimagines how we experience time through light, sound, and movement. Its carved aluminum body houses 75 LEDs that create an animated display, while built-in speakers play ambient soundscapes designed for focus, relaxation, and sleep. With customizable alarms, app connectivity, and USB-C charging, it’s a thoughtful alternative to the conventional bedside clock.

The Clock is available at us.balmuda.com for $499 in Silver and $519 in Champagne.

Photography courtesy of Bang & Olufsen

Beoplay H100 Headphones by Bang & Olufsen

Bang & Olufsen’s Beoplay H100 headphones are undeniably a splurge, but they’re designed with longevity in mind. The Danish brand developed the H100 with replaceable components, including the ear cushions, headband, and batteries. The custom titanium drivers, soft leather detailing, and rich color options give them a distinctly luxurious feel, while advanced noise cancellation and immersive sound make the listening experience just as considered as the design. It’s an investment piece for someone who appreciates exceptional craftsmanship as much as great audio.

The Beoplay H100 Headphones are available at bang-olufsen.com for $2,200.

Photography courtesy of Warby Parker

Intelligent Eyewear by Warby Parker

Smart glasses are getting a stylish update thanks to Warby Parker’s collaboration with Google and Samsung. Available in three of the brand’s familiar silhouettes, the lightweight frames incorporate a camera, open-ear speakers, and Gemini AI for hands-free photography, calls, navigation, and more. Subtly translucent temples offer a glimpse of the technology inside without compromising the classic eyewear design. With prescription, nonprescription, reading, and sunglass options, they’re a surprisingly versatile gift.

Intelligent Eyewear is available for preorder at warbyparker.com, starting at $395.

Photography courtesy of Flowtica

Flowtica Scribe AI Recording Pen by Flowtica

What looks like an ordinary ballpoint pen has a few technological tricks up its sleeve. The Flowtica Scribe combines a functional writing instrument with an AI-powered voice recorder, allowing users to capture conversations while taking notes on paper the old-fashioned way. A companion app can transcribe recordings and turn them into summaries and action items, bringing digital convenience to a familiar analog tool. An optional vegan leather charging case gives the device a place to rest between meetings.

The Flowtica Scribe is available at flowtica.ai for $159.

Photography courtesy of Bellroy

Tech Kit by Bellroy

Anyone who’s ever untangled a mess of charging cables at the bottom of a bag will appreciate Bellroy’s thoughtfully designed Tech Kit. The small organizer opens flat to reveal a series of mesh pockets and elastic loops that keep chargers, cables, earbuds, and other tech essentials neatly in place. Its structured shape makes everything easy to see and access, while the streamlined exterior, made from recycled woven fabric, slips neatly into a backpack or carry-on. It’s a simple solution to one of travel’s most persistent little annoyances.

The Tech Kit is available at bellroy.com for $59–$69, depending on color.

Photography courtesy of Amazon

Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition by Amazon

Amazon’s latest Kindle redesign brings a more refined look and feel to the familiar e-reader. The Paperwhite Signature Edition pairs a sleek aluminum body with a 7-inch, glare-free display, adjustable warm lighting, and double-tap page turning. Waterproof construction and wireless charging make it an easy travel companion, while two finishes, Graphite and Seaglass Green, offer a choice between classic and colorful.

The Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is available at amazon.com for $250.

Photography courtesy of Daily Objects

Surge Foldaway 3-in-1 Wireless Charger by DailyObjects

Who says charging stations have to be boring? DailyObjects’ Surge Foldaway turns an everyday tech essential into a sculptural desktop accessory. Its adjustable design accommodates an iPhone, Apple Watch, and AirPods simultaneously, consolidating three charging spots into one tidy footprint. The bold Cosmic Orange finish adds a welcome pop of color, giving the accessory a presence even when the devices are elsewhere.

The Surge Foldaway 3-in-1 Wireless Charger is available at dailyobjects.us for $175.

Photography courtesy of ModRetro

Chromatic by ModRetro

A love letter to handheld gaming, ModRetro’s Chromatic brings the original Game Boy experience into the present with a few thoughtful upgrades. Its magnesium-alloy body houses a custom, pixel-perfect display designed to play original Game Boy and Game Boy Color cartridges. The colorful finishes include four translucent options that expose the internal hardware, turning the console’s components into part of its visual identity.

The Chromatic + Tetris Bundle is available at modretro.com starting at $199.

Photography courtesy of Shark

CryoGlow Plus LED Face Mask by Shark

Shark’s CryoGlow Plus combines two skincare technologies in a single wearable device: LED light therapy and under-eye cooling. Red, blue, and infrared lights power several treatment modes, while adjustable cooling pads help refresh tired eyes. The upgraded design offers improved LED coverage around the eyes and mouth, and the soft Pastel Berry finish makes this wearable gadget surprisingly stylish.

The CryoGlow Plus LED Face Mask is available at sharkninja.com for $379.99.

Photography courtesy of Mudita

Mudita Kompakt by Mudita

In a market crowded with phones competing for attention, the Mudita Kompakt is designed to demand less of it. Its minimalist design centers on a 4.3-inch E Ink display, favoring a restrained interface over colorful notifications and app-heavy screens. Essential features like calling, messaging, offline maps, and a camera remain, while a dedicated offline switch offers a physical way to disconnect.

The Mudita Kompakt is available at mudita.com for $399.

Photography courtesy of Birdfy

Feeder Wood by Birdfy

Who says smart technology has to look high-tech? Birdfy’s Feeder Wood combines the charm of a traditional wooden birdhouse with a built-in camera, letting bird lovers watch their feathered visitors up close. Made from FSC-certified wood, the solar-powered feeder captures 1080p video. Its companion app can identify more than 6,000 bird species, bringing a layer of digital discovery to an otherwise familiar backyard ritual.

The Feeder Wood is available at birdfy.com for $189.99.

Photography courtesy of Wallie

Wallie 10 Digital Photo Frame by Wallie

Wallie’s approach to the digital photo frame starts with a simple idea: make the screen look less like a screen. Its 10-inch color E Ink display gives photographs the appearance of printed images, while real wood construction and a choice of four finishes help it blend into a gallery wall or shelf arrangement. Rounded or square corners offer further customization, and a rechargeable battery eliminates the need for a visible power cord. Photos can be updated remotely through an app.

The Wallie 10 is available at shop.wallieframe.com for $299.

Photography courtesy of Eve

Eve Flare Portable Smart LED Lamp by Eve

With its simple spherical form, Eve Flare looks more like an illuminated object than a conventional lamp. The rechargeable, water-resistant light offers millions of customizable colors, with app and voice controls for setting the mood indoors or outside. Its wireless charging base and portable design mean it can move effortlessly from a bedside table to the patio, adding a little atmosphere wherever it lands.

The Eve Flare Portable Smart LED Lamp is available at apple.com for $99.95.

Photography courtesy of Best Buy

Retro Mechanical Keyboard N Edition by 8BitDo

8BitDo borrows the visual language of the original Nintendo Entertainment System for a mechanical keyboard that feels straight out of the 1980s. Chunky gray keys, red accents, and tactile mechanical switches establish the retro aesthetic, while an included joystick and two oversized programmable buttons bring arcade-style controls to the desktop. Bluetooth and wireless connectivity keep the throwback design compatible with contemporary setups.

The 8BitDo Retro Mechanical Keyboard N Edition is available at bestbuy.com for $79.99.

Photography courtesy of Orbitkey

Nest v2 by Orbitkey

Even the most organized desk tends to accumulate charging cables, adapters, and other small tech accessories. Orbitkey’s Nest v2 gives them a designated home in a compact storage box with adjustable dividers and a fabric-lined interior. The removable leather-covered lid doubles as a valet tray and 15W wireless charger, keeping everyday essentials within reach while concealing the clutter underneath.

The Nest v2 is available at orbitkey.com for $125.

issues.title: Fictional Project designs home in Kerala to feel "one with the landscape"
issues.summary: Curving ceilings sweep down to frame the two small gardens that flank this home in Kerala, India, designed by local studio Fictional Project. The post Fictional Project designs home in Kerala to feel "one with the landscape" appeared first on Dezeen .
issues.author: Jon Astbury
issues.content_html:
Curving ceilings sweep down to frame the two small gardens that flank this home in Kerala, India, designed by local architecture studio Fictional Project.

Named Interstitial Living, the home in the village of Adoor was designed for a family of four who wanted to feel connected to the outside, in particular the lush greenery surrounding the site.

This led Fictional Project to pull the home's built volume back to create space for two planted yards on either side, overlooked by the home's pared-back and open interiors.

Plans and photographs

    Plans and photographs

    "The residence is careful not to overpower, becoming one with the landscape," the studio told Dezeen.

    Interstitial Living is organised around a bedroom at its centre, which is housed within a cubic volume finished in cement plaster.

    A small window in this bedroom overlooks a potted tree within a cut-out in the floor of the adjacent living room, which faces the yard to the west through a row of full-height windows above a built-in timber bench.

    On the opposite side of the home, the kitchen overlooks the eastern yard through a row of windows above its countertops. Both these spaces are defined by the curving white-plastered ceilings overhead, which sweep down from the centre of the home.

    "The scale of the residence allows for intimate working spaces in the kitchen and a welcoming living room, all accentuated by the dynamic nature of the roof. The other spaces negotiate the private/public nature of the indoors," the studio explained.

    "The concavity of the roof creates a visual connection to the outdoors, becoming a marker that emerges from within the site."

    Read:

    Mango trees shade "restrained and calming" home in India by InLe architects

    "It breaks the rigidity of a traditional sloping roof, helping create fluid indoor spaces. Nothing here is built or conceived in isolation, but rather as interconnected systems," it added.

    The smaller first floor contains a second bedroom, bathroom and a study area, which overlook the living space below from a steel-framed landing and internal windows.

    While the internal finishes were kept minimal, the exterior of the home and its boundary walls were built using terracotta-toned textured blocks, which the studio described as introducing a sense of "groundedness and warmth".

    Other dwellings in Kerala recently featured on Dezeen include a home by InLe Architectsframed and shaded by two large mango trees and a farmhouse by Evolving Radical Aesthetics that is built into a hillside above a carved-out, open-air temple.

    The post Fictional Project designs home in Kerala to feel "one with the landscape" appeared first on Dezeen.

issues.title: Shigeru Ban unveils proposal for tent-like church in Rome
issues.summary: A cross-shaped roof will mark the San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex in Rome, Italy, which Japanese studio Shigeru Ban Architects is designing with local architect Vittorio Petrucci. The post Shigeru Ban unveils proposal for tent-like church in Rome appeared first on Dezeen .
issues.author: Lizzie Crook
issues.content_html:
A cross-shaped roof will mark the San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex in Rome, Italy, which Japanese studio Shigeru Ban Architects is designing with local architect Vittorio Petrucci.

The church will occupy a currently underused site in Ostia, a coastal neighbourhood for which the project is hoped to become an architectural landmark.

The San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex will be constructed with a frame of timber – Ban's signature material – with a deliberately simple form that is intended to evoke a fabric tent.

According to Shigeru Ban Architects and Petrucci, the overarching goal is for the church to help establish a greater sense of community and place in the area, which they describe as having a "fragmented urban fabric".

“We wanted to design a place of worship that also brings the whole community together," said Ban.

"The timber structure expresses the idea of a tent, a simple, welcoming form that connects people with one another and with their surroundings. Through this project, we hope architecture can help create a new sense of belonging in the neighbourhood."

Shigeru Ban Architects and Petrucci's proposal was the winning entry of a competition for the church.

It is one of five winning designs selected as part of the New Churches Programme – an initiative led by the local church district, the Diocese of Rome, and the Italian Episcopal Conference, an assembly of Catholic bishops, to provide permanent homes for parish communities in the region.

As part of the project, four new churches will be built, while one existing parish complex will be extended.

The San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex will be built on a raised public plaza, with various parish facilities, community spaces and a priest's residence embedded below.

Its key feature will be its angular roof, which is shaped like a cross but not immediately readable as one. This is modelled on a latent cross – a feature in sacred architecture, in which a cross shape is integrated in the spatial design, without being clearly visible.

Inside, the church will have a diamond-shaped plan, with large stained-glass windows positioned in the four cardinal directions. They will be triangular in shape and feature designs modelled on neighbourhood street art.

Read:

Shigeru Ban's Cardboard Cathedral was the most significant building of 2013

The project will be complete with a landscaped park, as well as various recreational and sports facilities, which the studios said will "create opportunities for social interaction and everyday activities".

The San Vincenzo de’ Paoli Church and Parish Complex is not the first church project by Ban. Among his others is the landmark Cardboard Cathedral in New Zealand, which is formed of 98 cardboard tubes combined with wood and polycarbonate. We named it the most significant building of 2013 in our list of the 25 most significant buildings of the 21st century.

Other Italian church proposals recently featured on Dezeen include Stefano Boeri Architetti's design for the Ambrosian Monastery in Milan, which will have a sail-like roof form.

issues.title: Waugh Thistleton Architects set to transform derelict bathing pavilion into Tracey Emin-backed studios and sauna
issues.summary: UK studio Waugh Thistleton Architects is set to transform the Edwardian Westbrook Pavilion in Margate, UK, into an arts centre for British artist Tracey Emin with a cafe, public sauna and changing rooms. The post Waugh Thistleton Architects set to transform derelict bathing pavilion into Tracey Emin-backed studios and sauna appeared first on Dezeen .
issues.author: Tom Ravenscroft
issues.content_html:
UK studio Waugh Thistleton Architects is set to transform the Edwardian Westbrook Pavilion in Margate, UK, into an arts centre for British artist Tracey Emin with a cafe, public sauna and changing rooms.

"The project will bring a much-loved seafront building back into use, combining its original purpose with new spaces for art, culture and the local community," said Waugh Thistleton Architects.

The studio recently won planning permission from the local council to convert the abandoned building, which Emin purchased in 2023, into a facility run by the Tracey Emin Foundation.

The project aims to return the building to its former use as a changing room for swimmers and as a tea room, when it originally opened in 1914.

"Originally opened in 1914, the building provided public changing facilities for sea-bathing and a tea room," said the studio.

"Following storm damage in the Great North Sea Storm of 1953, subsequent alterations detracted from its original Edwardian character," it continued.

"The renovated pavilion will accommodate artist studios, an art gallery, clubroom, cafe, sea-bathing changing facilities, a new sauna and refurbished public toilets, restoring its original role as a place for bathing and socialising by the sea."

Along with making the pavilion a building used by the public again, the studio aims to return the building's core to its Edwardian look by removing later additions. It will also add glazed facades to the wings on either side of the central pavilion.

The building will be topped by a rooftop terrace, while a public toilet on the site will be renovated.

Read:

Tate Modern opens largest ever exhibition of Tracey Emin's work

"The design draws on the proportions and character of the original building, removing later additions and reinstating lost features such as the historic belvederes which top the central tower structures," said the studio.

"The beachfront facade will see a new glazing system and colonnade to each of the building’s wings, with a new sheltered archway forming a new seating terrace at the building’s heart," it continued.

"The design seeks to reference the original architecture while providing contemporary needs of a public building. Where original features are references, these are distinguishable architecturally."

Emin is one of the UK's best-known living artists. We recently produced a video of a landmark exhibition of her work at Tate Modern.

Recent projects by Waugh Thistleton Architects include plans for the “tallest mass timber office building in the US”.

issues.title: If I See an Author Out to Lunch, Am I the Asshole for Approaching Them?
issues.summary: Hey there, howdy! Welcome back to the most marvelously drunken advice column on the planet. That’s right, it’s time for another stellar installment of Am I the Literary Asshole, a place where movers and shakers come to both move and
issues.author: Kristen Arnett
issues.content_html:
Hey there, howdy!

Welcome back to the most marvelously drunken advice column on the planet. That’s right, it’s time for another stellar installment of Am I the Literary Asshole, a place where movers and shakers come to both move and shake. I’m your host, Kristen Arnett, and it’s time for us to get down to business. That’s right, we’ve got a truckload of exciting quandaries awaiting us today, so I’d like to jump straight into things with some pomp and much circumstance.

Let’s get some icy cold martinis going and sip at them while we take a gander at our first question, shall we?

1) Is it in bad taste to approach authors in their “off” time? Say, perhaps, when they’re out to lunch or dinner and away from the hubbub of something like AWP or at a festival or after a reading? Thank you for your time!

I think we’ve answered a version of this question before, but I don’t think there’s anything wrong we’ve approaching it again for new readers to the column. And since I just got done hanging out at Texas Book Festival last weekend, I feel especially ready to chat.

This is going to play out much like it would in any other regular social situation. Before approaching the author in question, you must first read the room.

Is the person with their children? Are they on the phone? Are they carrying lots of bags, lugging around a giant suitcase, or are they in the middle of paying the check and/or talking to a waiter? Are they ordering coffee? Are they typing very furiously on their computer or speaking in whispers, privately, to another person? Are they kissing their partner or holding hands at a romantic dinner for two? Are they in a public restroom? If any of this is the case, I’d advise you to hold off. Wait.

But if the writer is just out and about and seems amenable to an interaction – maybe having a quick drink at the bar or perusing books at the local indie – I say go for it! There are always going to be some authors who are much more introverted (not everyone is as wildly extroverted as me), but a very polite and breezy introduction and a timely exit are going to be the key things to remember here.

It’s really nice to have your body of work recognized by someone who says they are a fan. I generally think people should err on the side of indulging in a friendly word if afforded the opportunity.

Hope this helps!

A martini is a beautiful thing and so are you! Let’s move on to our second question:

2) There is a woman at my job who reads on her break time. They’re the same kind of books that I’m into—think cozy fantasy—and I want to approach her. I’m worried that this could come across as inappropriate. I don’t want her to think I’m hitting on her.

I’m not sure why this kind of interaction would read as a romantic overture? They should have no problem with you asking them about what they’re reading. It’s a completely neutral topic for a work environment.

My reasoning here is that this is a person you’ve ostensibly talked to before. You both have jobs at the same company. It’s not a random interaction with a stranger.

It’s totally possible that in a casual every day scenario, this type of interaction could read as romantic and much less neutral. Example: if a person was sitting alone reading at a bar and you walked up to them and asked about their book? Sure, that could reasonably feel like a come on (even if it’s not) simply because 1) they’re a stranger and 2) the setting is a place where people often go to pick strangers up. But if it’s a fellow coworker, it should be perfectly reasonable to ask them about a book while they’re on break, especially if you’re also a fan of that author.

They might engage with your line of questioning or they might not. After all, it’s their break. Maybe they don’t want to use those precious minutes to talk with a coworker; they might just want to sit there and read. But you’ll never know if you don’t ask! And to me it seems like a great way to make a new friend. I wouldn’t worry.

Fingers crossed that you make a new break time reading buddy! Get out there and get to chatting.

So far, so great! I’ll pour us one last martini apiece and we’ll dive into our final question of the day:

3) I’m in a reading rut. For the past year I’ve been stuck on a very specific genre. These books rely on a formula and I know how each of them will end. I should read more “literary” books, but as soon as I sit down with one I blank. Is it bad to only read one type of book?

I don’t think there’s anything wrong with reading something that makes you happy. Maybe you’re just in a space right now where all your brain can handle are these books where you already know the outcome. The world is full of conflict and chaos. Having something safe, even if it’s just knowing how a book will end, can sometimes feel reassuring. It’s why people watch the same TV shows on repeat.

I do think it’s okay to question whether you should branch out and try new work, though. It seems you’ve already been doing that!

Keep reading the things you’re enjoying at the moment. If you turn reading into a chore it will start to feel like an unpaid job, so try and find ways to make it seem fun for yourself. As long you feel like you’re getting something from it, that’s what really matters.

Now, before we close out today, I had an email from the organizers of the trademarked Silent Book Club (in response to my last column about a club charging extravagant membership fees). I thought I’d share with you what they’ve informed me. I don’t know if the club in question was trademarked or not, but it’s good information to have, regardless:

Hi Kristen! I’m Guinevere, the cofounder and CEO of Silent Book Club. I saw your recent Lit Hub article about someone charging $100 a month for a Silent Book Club meetup and I was horrified. Silent Book Club does not allow local organizers to profit off of events—it violates the terms of our organizer agreement that grants volunteers a non-exclusive license to use our trademark.

For more than 10 years, we have prided ourselves on being a values-driven organization that creates welcoming, inclusive spaces for all readers. We host meetups in public locations to support local businesses, we do not partner with Amazon/Audible, and we donate a percentage of our annual profits to literary non-profits. We just wrapped up a Banned Books campaign that raised funds for the American Library Association.

If it is true that there is a Silent Book Club organizer charging $100 per month without our knowledge, they are in violation of our terms and we need to revoke their license.

And there you have it! If you are the anonymous person who submitted the question for our last column and have follow up information regarding this situation, please feel free to reach out to Guinevere directly.

Join me next time when I get answer more of your anonymous questions (send them here, please) and hopefully I get to share another round of martinis with you. So glad we’re friends!

Cordially,

Dad

__________________________

Are you worried you’re the literary asshole? Ask Kristen via email at AskKristen@lithub.com, or anonymously here.

issues.title: Meet the Winner of the 2026 National Book Award for Nonfiction
issues.summary: Meet the winner of the 2026 National Book Award for Nonfiction.
issues.author: Community
issues.content_html:
The National Book Awards have announced the winner of the 2026 National Book Award for Nonfiction: Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming by Abdelrahman ElGendy. See below for more about this title as well as the runners-up.

The Nonfiction category attracted some controversy this year when The New York Times suggested that Abdelrahman ElGendy doesn’t qualify for the award because he was residing in Europe at the time the book was submitted for consideration. The National Book Awards released a statement confirming that Abdelrahman ElGendy passed their eligibility checks:

“In the case of Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming, the publisher communicated to the Foundation that Abdelrahman ElGendy was a legal and tax-paying US resident who, in the context of arrests being made by ICE in 2025, fled the United States temporarily in concern for his safety. The organization made a determination based on the information shared with us that this satisfied the Foundation’s eligibility criteria.”

2026 National Book Award for Nonfiction Winner

Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming by Abdelrahman ElGendy

The National Book Awards judges’ citation: “In the space between violence and becoming there is something like a breath; Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming by Abdelrahman ElGendy inhabits that breath. Huna is a lyric testament to survival and resistance threaded through with a father-son story of love, endurance, resilience, and hope. Inspired by the Arab protest song ‘Sawfa Nabqua Huna (We Will Remain Here),’ this debut memoir is a phenomenal liberation story that resists all forces of authoritarian silencing and erasure with full-throated song.”

Here are the four runners-up that were on the shortlist for the 2026 National Book Award for Nonfiction, along with what critics and authors are saying about them.

2026 National Book Award for Nonfiction Runners-Up

The Midnight Special: The Secret Prison History of American Music by Colin Asher

“It’s a fog-piercing down-bound train of a book, better than it had to be… [A] multilayered indictment of America’s prison system, the largest in the world.” —The New York Times

“Asher does especially nimble work in portraying his subjects as three-dimensional figures while detailing how the record industry exploited their links to the prison system to profit off their music, often in ways that flattened their life narratives. This is illuminating.” ―Publishers Weekly

Let the Poets Govern: A Declaration of Freedom by Camonghne Felix

“In these fierce yet tender pages, Camonghne Felix reveals how imagination can become a form of governance—an instrument for creating a world rooted in care, community, and radical possibility.” —Michelle Alexander

“A few pages into Let the Poets Govern, you will want to read this book out loud to strangers on the street via bullhorn. Several chapters in, you’ll be pricing professional-grade stereo systems and asking friends if you can borrow their balcony for the weekend. The people need to hear what this poet has to say.” —Saeed Jones

Mother Tongue by Sara Nović

“Mother Tongue is one of the most powerful memoirs I have read in years, a book I defy anyone to read without being challenged or changed… A revelation and a reckoning.” —Nicole Chung

“Lucid and rigorously researched, Nović’s memoir offers a powerful critique of the systems that have marginalized deaf Americans across the decades. It’s a sobering must-read.”—Publishers Weekly

Spawning Season: An Experiment in Queer Parenthood by Joseph Osmundson

“A singular and deeply moving book. Osmundson has birthed a profound meditation on family and food, longing and loss, hope and grief, humans and salmon. In his story, we find a multitude of beautiful, complicated ways of imagining the future-and then working to build one.” —Ed Yong

“With Spawning Season, Joseph Osmundson offers us an intimate look at the way queer theory becomes written on the body and moves through the world. Spawning Season is a book that only a queer scientist could write, and a powerful exploration of the relationships between queer men and queer women, between white queers and queers of color. A powerful rejoinder to old notions about fatherhood, emotion, and masculinity, Spawning Season is a reminder that queer theory calls on us to not just transform society but also ourselves.” ―Chanda Prescod-Weinstein

More information about the National Book Award Finalists is available on their website.

issues.title: Best Romance Books of the Year
issues.summary: The best romance books of 2026 include genre-benders, queer romantasies, fake-dating rom-coms, and more.
issues.author: Emily Martin
issues.content_html:
As 2026 comes to a close and we officially enter cuffing season, it’s time for us to look back at the romance books that had our hearts pounding. Winter months are the perfect time to cuddle up with a love story (or five), so here are the best romance books of the year. Were all of these on your radar? Is there a must-read romance you have yet to discover? Read on to find out!

Die for Me by Shirlene Obuobi

What makes Shirlene Obuobi’s latest novel stand out as one of the best of the year is the way it expertly blends multiple genres in a fun and engaging way. Paranormal romance, psychological thriller, medical drama, gothic horror, urban fantasy… this story has it all. Sean is a 38 year-old interventional cardiologist who isn’t looking for love, but then she meets Julian. Julian is devastatingly charming, mysterious, and eleven years Sean’s junior. And by the time Sean falls hard for him, she realizes Julian is much more dangerous than he first appears.

The Bad Boyfriend Curse by Farah Heron

Fans of contemporary YA rom coms and fake dating stories need to pick up The Bad Boyfriend Curse, the absolute best YA romance of the year. Raised by a single mom, Meera has always believed that the women in her family are cursed to date men who will ultimately destroy their lives. To evade the curse, Meera spends her whole life playing it safe. Yet somehow Meera’s first date ends with an arrest and community service. Since being the “good girl” has gotten her nowhere, Meera decides she will “date” another bad boy to get back at her mom. But what happens when the bad boy she chooses isn’t so bad after all?

Bromantasy by Máire Roche

Life in the countryside suited best friends Juniper O’Reilly and Mo Elmthorn before Juniper was sentenced to a quest after a bar fight. At least the capable and considerate Mo offered to join him. Although the two embark on a quest to slay a dragon, when they discover the terrifying creature is a terrified child, they immediately reroute their efforts into protecting her. As they avoid dodgy heroes—and eat through their substantial cheese reserves—they begin to realize their platonic relationship is starting to develop a romantic flavor in Roche’s delightful queer cozy fantasy debut. —R. Nassor

One & Only by Maureen Goo

I like Maurene Goo’s YA novels, but I loved her first adult romance even more. Cassia Park comes from a long line of matchmakers, dating back hundreds of years to Korea. In her family, every woman has the ability to discover the name of each person’s true love. Cassia has known the name of her soulmate for almost 10 years, but she can’t find him, even with the help of private investigators. On the eve of her 40th birthday, she gives up her search momentarily and has a no-strings two-night stand with a handsome, younger guy. But then, she finds out his boss is…her soulmate. Love triangles rarely work for me in adult books, but this one is superb! —Alison Doherty

Daggerbound by T. Kingfisher

In a series that epitomizes everything that romantasy should be, the latest in the White Rat series is somehow the best book yet. Come for the ‘jaded warrior turning to mush for one particular person’ trope, stay for the giant sentient Pill Bug who definitely does “not eat human meat.” Truly, romantasy at its finest. T. Kingfisher is a master of the genre. —Rachel Brittain
