issues.title: Electric Lit’s Top 10 Poetry Collections of 2026
issues.summary: This year’s most interesting poetry collections keep circling one small word: we. In an era when we’re constantly sorted into us and them, these poets ask who does the sorting and what it costs. Is we a people, a piece of land, a family, a crowd, a database? And where does that leave the rest […] The post Electric Lit’s Top 10 Poetry Collections of 2026 appeared first on Electric Literature .
issues.author: Electric Literature
issues.content_html:
This year’s most interesting poetry collections keep circling one small word: we. In an era when we’re constantly sorted into us and them, these poets ask who does the sorting and what it costs. Is we a people, a piece of land, a family, a crowd, a database? And where does that leave the rest of us, trying to keep up?

Layli Long Soldier’s We (Wé) takes the question of we to its most elemental level. The Lakota word wé means blood, and Long Soldier uses it to explore family, nation, history, and language through poems, essays, and artwork. For Jake Skeets, we extends beyond people to the land and everything living on it. Horsesopens with 200 feral horses stuck in Arizona mud and unfurls into an elegy for a changing Navajo Nation. Fatimah Asghar’sDaughter of the Mountains asks what remains after exile, reckoning with estranged kin and the landscape of their ancestors in poems both funny and elegiac. In Assembled Audience, the ever-delightful Erika Meitner takes up the strange business of being together, on beaches and in airports, in mourning and in protest. William Lessard’s haunting /face turns patents for facial capture technology into unlikely poetry about what happens when a face becomes data. And Hieu Minh Nguyen’s Staying Still traces the distance between the people and places we long to belong to and the selves we’re trying to become.

So much about who counts as us is now decided by people and machines that don’t know us at all. Against all that flattening, these poems get stubbornly specific. Maybe we begins there, not in agreement or allegiance, but in the act of paying attention to what—and whom—we might otherwise overlook.
–Kelly Luce
Editor, The Commuter

Editor’s note: The following books were hand-selected by Electric Literature staff and interns, with the help of our community of contributors, readers, and friends of the organization. While books by current staff or board members are not eligible for consideration, we would like to informally recommend I Can Tell You the Version That Will Make You Take My Side by board member J Brooke, another collection we loved this year! The 10 titles below are presented alphabetically by title; they are not ranked.

/face by William Lessard

If there’s something slightly absurd about composing an ode to the misty beauty of landscape on a Macbook Pro while pausing intermittently to check Instagram, take a selfie, take a screenshot, /face pinpoints it. William Lessard’s poetry accomplishes the seemingly impossible feat of writing in the tradition of powerpoints, patent filings, and the whole chaos of social media-fueled data harvesting that defines so much of life in 2026. Lessard’s book is not so much filled with traditionally formed poems as with shocks to the idea of what constitutes poetry; with experiments in embracing the parts of modern life that seem unfit for art; and, in short, with an unashamed attempt at authenticity. Read Lessard’s meditations on /face in an EL interview . . . and read the book!
–Willem Marx, Associate Editor

America, A Love Storyby Camille T Dungy

In America, A Love Story, Camille T Dungy addresses the nation with the exasperated, clear-eyed intimacy of someone who knows its capacity to wound. Writing as a Black woman and mother, Dungy turns love into an interrogation, pushing away the easy comfort of a flag-waving tribute. Her poems move fluidly from strawberry fields tarped against frost to a father questioned on a roadside, from a grandmother’s willow switch to the sleepless, fragile early days of parenting. Love, through these poems, is an enduring tenderness for daughters, for soil and blooming lilacs, for the hard-won instinct to protect what is vulnerable. In Dungy’s hands, love is what keeps imagination alive when safety falters, an unflinching devotion that refuses to ignore danger while still demanding that America answer back.
–Shandela Contreras, Editorial Intern

Assembled Audience by Erika Meitner

In Assembled Audience, Erika Meitner looks straight at the conditions that make “staying present” feel like a moral demand: fracking, climate change, pandemic aftermath, gun violence, the erosion of reproductive rights. A peripatetic speaker moves from eschatology to a Hampton Inn, from Whitman-sized questions to Bud Light and dragonflies, making room for luck, wonder, and the strange comedy of being alive. Reading this collection, I was certainly reminded of the Whitmanesque impulse in “Song of Myself”—which is really the chorus of each other, the idea that to create and exist is to wonder, and that we celebrate our fractured world by relentlessly examining everything within it, finding interest even in the mundane. Meitner channels that expansive, defiant celebration into our own dizzying moment. In Meitner’s electric, unsentimental vision of all its gatherings, attention itself becomes a way of standing with others.
–Shandela Contreras, Editorial Intern

Daughters of the Mountainsby Fatimah Asghar

Unafraid of tackling the vastness of human experience from love to loss, Asghar asks how an exile can find their place in the world. What follows are meditative, at times humorous, and always introspective poems that embrace the complexities of lineage, environment, family, and nature in shaping and disrupting home and the self. If you’re a fan of poetry dealing with queerness, displacement, or searching for connection, there’s a lot to be said for Daughter of the Mountains.
–Rachel Maybee, Editorial Intern

Horsesby Jake Skeets

Beginning with the evocative image of 200 horses found dead in the mud of a former stock pond on Navajo land in Arizona, Navajo Nation Poet Laureate Jake Skeets faces down environmental apocalypse and dares to allow hope to blossom from grief. Queer, lyrical, and inextricable from Diné thought, Skeets’ poems span time and distance, blurring the artificial boundary set between people and place. This gorgeous, highly-anticipated second collection will leave readers marking Skeets as a poet to watch.
–Rachel Maybee, Editorial Intern

Maybe the Body by Asa Drake

In his introduction to EL’s interview with Asa Drake, Cameron Quan describes reading her gorgeous debut collection as not unlike “the experience of being cared for at a distance.” I, editor of that interview, rushed to read Drake’s book myself. Quan is right, a sense of care emanates from Drake’s words. Yet what continues to resonate now, as the year comes to a close and Drake’s book still lingers in my mind, is the way it demonstrates how to care. These poems tease out the crystalline threads that connect a self and a body, a body and a world, a place and a history, and in doing so, demonstrate a stunning capacity to observe. To observe this carefully is to care radically. Drake writes: “When I feed the animals / the rabbit stands up // so straight she falls over. / This is the part I want / you to know.” Maybe the Body is the kind of book that is both splash and ripple, sound and echo.
–Willem Marx, Associate Editor

Run It Back by Kortney Morrow

In Run it Back, Kortney Morrow’s debut poetry collection, nostalgia takes center stage. We float through a luminous remembrance of the early 2000s, a time when freedom felt inevitable and aspiration felt a mere breath away. Hope and heroics are the lifeblood of this collection, much like “the hero” (in this case, Lebron James) injects life into his community, uplifts the people, and they, in turn, become their own heroes. As a fellow Cleveland native, this collection was especially important to read; it is a tribute to the power of a place—and a people—that has long felt forgotten. Morrow reminds us, in this stunning and timely collection, that learning the past is the key to unlocking our future.
–Denne Michele Norris, Executive Director and Publisher

Staying Stillby Hieu Minh Nguyen

In Staying Still, Hieu Minh Nguyen treats remaining alive as an arduous, tender labor. Moving across packed dance floors, motel beds, and quiet doorways, these poems reckon with the isolation of queer boyhood, refugee inheritance, and the fraught bond between mother and son. There’s a gripping portrait of a boy secretly swaying in his mother’s floor-length dress before a mirror, discovering how beauty and shame can share the same hemline. Nguyen searches restlessly for an anchor, asking what it means to remain—in a body, a family, or a future—that has not always felt like home. Like the cover’s apartment windows glowing behind colored shades, these poems reveal how close we can be to one another while still remaining out of reach: turning small acts of attention (naming a landscape, sharing fruit, searching for the right color) into ways of keeping silence from taking over.
–Shandela Contreras, Editorial Intern

Tree of Knowledge by Victoria Chang

Victoria Chang’s latest collection is part art history course and part arboreal eulogy. Chang watches the eucalyptus across her street get cut down, then she continues to see cuts everywhere: in Picasso, in Joan Mitchell, in the Hilma af Klint paintings that give the book its title. At the center of the book is “Eureka,” a long poem about the California town that expelled its entire Chinese population in 1885. The color red runs through the poems, whether it’s paint, a body’s last few periods, and, in several poems, the actual ink itself.
–Kelly Luce, Editor, The Commuter

We (Wé)by Layli Long Soldier

In We (Wé), Layli Long Soldier takes we, meaning “first-person plural” in English, and wé, meaning “blood” in Lakota, and blends the two, looking closely at how language, as well as family, bear the communal meanings imparted by decades of shared experience. Likewise, Long Soldier blends artwork, essay, and poetry to emulate in-person spaces where knowledge is created and reinforced through mentorship and collaboration. History remains at the forefront of this unique, groundbreaking collection.
–Rachel Maybee, Editorial Intern

issues.content_html:
Stealing Space by Dayna Mahannah

The gas station’s fluorescent lights glowed as I waited for the vehicles to clear their pumps. When the lot had emptied, I abandoned the till. I roamed the aisles, straightening candy products and rearranging the Hungry Man sub sandwiches in the fridge. The security camera had a blind spot where I could wedge myself, right up against the counter. I snuck a Danish, the syrupy glaze clinging to the wrapper like mucus. I chewed fast, facing the wall, and stuffed the packaging in the coffee station trash.

After pretending to organize the chocolate bar display in front of the till, I swiped a Mr. Big off the shelf, tucking it under the edge of my work shirt, and pushed open the side exit into the garage. Light beamed into the defunct repair shop. Dust motes glimmered, floating in the dark like phosphorescent plankton. Then the door shut, severing the shaft of light. Petroleum wafted up from the concrete floor. Standing on the stoop, my skin hot despite the frigid shop, I tore through the serrated edge of the candy wrapper, scarfing the chewy mess. I jammed the yellow wrapper underneath used oil containers in the recycling drum.

Back inside the station, a cursory check out the window showed no customers gassing up. I flipped the Back in 5 Minutes sign on the front door, turned the lock, raced for the bathroom, and drove my fingers down my esophagus until everything pushed out into the open.

I’d started working at the gas station in June, just as grade 10 was petering off and the warmer Okanagan days were stretching out like a promise. That first year of high school my friends and I cemented ourselves together with secrets and sleepovers and the second-last season of The O.C. We broke loose in the summer, splintered into new alliances, graduated from gossiping about crushes to hooking up in the dark at bush parties. We experimented with tiny crimes like egging houses and stealing makeup from Zellers. I pulled my first all-nighter and showed up to my Saturday shift at the station, appalled at how great I felt. Hangovers didn’t catch up to 16-year-olds.

My boss, Kevin, owned the gas station, which stood on a busy corner in Westbank (now West Kelowna) where the old highway intersected the new highway that funneled people out of town. Kevin, curly-haired and stocky, must have been in his 30s—maybe even the same age I am now, 36. Really nice guy. Organized. Good-natured and even-keeled but took his business seriously. Always looked like he’d just polished off a great cup of coffee.

Kevin trained me behind the till. He taught me to make eye contact with every customer who drove into the lot. This helped prevent fill ‘n’ runs, since in 2006 you filled first, paid second. He told me that people were less likely to act on a bad intention when they felt acknowledged.

When a customer forgot their points card, we were to instruct them to bring the receipt on their next visit. Kevin showed me how to manually add points to a customer’s card by typing in the dollar total, scanning the points card, then deleting the amount from the computer. Using the clunky Knuckle Buster, we’d imprint the points card on carbon paper. Initial the customer’s receipt so they couldn’t double back for points. People didn’t forget their cards often, but they forgot them regularly.

The points system worked like most: spend money, rack up points, redeem for goods—slurpees, propane, firewood, fuel. On the counter next to the rack of wraparound sunglasses stood a turnstile bejewelled with shiny plastic gift cards glued to cardboard backings, their denominations printed in white in the top corner. Each rotation revealed a higher number.

$25.

$50.

$100.

“How long does it take to save up for something like that?” I had asked when Kevin explained that points could even be redeemed for gift cards.

A long time, was all he said.

To me, that meant years. A unit of time that adults measured life by. My social studies teacher talked about the world in years and it seemed so irrelevant that I skipped that class the most. I could see only as far ahead as the end of the next work schedule.

When grade 11 started that fall, I switched to evening and weekend shifts and often worked alone for hours at a time. I would show up for my shift at 4:00 PM. At 5:00 PM, my coworker Janice pulled a sweater over her uniform, lighter and cigarette in hand as she waved goodbye. The shift commenced in sales: Coke slushies and tanks of diesel to long-haul truckers, Lotto Max tickets and regular fuel to moms in Von Dutch trucker hats and frosted lip gloss. But there was the space between sales, too.

All that alone time.

Crispy Crunch.

Old Dutch BBQ chips.

At a low point, I gobbled one of the Hungry Mans, a sandwich more self-assured than I dreamed of being.

Grade 10 had been an excellent year for my eating disorder. I’d been so vigilant, eating privately within a restricted time frame, followed by an immediate purge. I became skinny enough that people started asking if I was okay. The goal was not to take up less space, but to accumulate space—between my thighs, between my stomach and waistband. Indiscriminate, space started to wedge itself between everything: me and other people, me and myself. The space was my secret. And all I wanted was more and more space.

Now, in grade 11, I was getting sloppy. I ate in less controlled environments: here at work, surrounded by food, where variables such as cleaning duties and paying customers disrupted the conditions necessary for my carefully orchestrated process. Over the winter, my body revolted. Chided by sandwich displays and endless rows of bright packaging, it sneaked and snatched and stuffed and swallowed. Then I’d ring in Paydays and Gold Rush tickets and cartons of Export A Gold, smiling at customers through the silent horror of the digestive process occurring in my body, the calories accumulating, absorbing, storing.

I’d lost control—every chip and Danish transmuting into extra flesh. Bubbling over the waistband of my Lululemon tights. The spaces that I coveted shrank. People stopped asking if I was okay. Still, my secret flourished.

Snow melted on sidewalks the day I took an imprint of a customer’s points card and entered the dollar amount into the computer. I did it twice—once to load the points onto their card. A second time, after they left, to load the same amount onto my own. I recall thinking that a double charge of the same figure could be called a mistake if it showed on the records. Which it wouldn’t—no imprint, no record. Only when a customer redeemed points did their card show up in the system.

Since I wasn’t totally reckless, I didn’t swipe points again for a long time. Instead, I ate. And I hid. And I hid and I ate. I felt just as nervous about the prospect of being caught sneaking points as I did being caught with my mouth muddied with chocolate. But the former transgression only made me feel guilty. The latter? Shame. My hunger had greater control over me than I had over it.

Swiping the points, however, felt deliberate, calculated. No sloppiness here. Another secret, but a case over which I held jurisdiction.

After a couple weeks, Kevin had still made no mention of the unaccounted-for points. He greeted me the same as usual each shift. A warm smile. Eye contact. Occasionally, a dad joke. When Kevin headed for the garage where he parked his car, I looked him in the eye and wished him a good night.

I began to match points on my own card every time a customer handed me their receipt from a day they had forgotten theirs. Twenty or, if I was lucky, 50 bucks a pop. But they didn’t forget often enough. The gift cards hung next to the till on their cardboard backings.

Free money.

Awaiting activation.

One day, I arrived at work and the skin on Kevin’s face looked taut, like he had a sunburn. He only offered a clipped, joyless ’lo as he stormed up to his office, door swinging shut behind him, the hollow thwomp of his footfalls on the stairs ebbing away. In his absence, the pervasive drone of the refrigerators hummed on.

Janice, my coworker, put a hand on her hip and gave a subtle nod to the closed door. Break-in, she said.

Janice had cropped brown hair shot through with silver. Big blue eyes. A voice characterized by sooty lungs. I liked Janice a lot. Someone had broken into the station in the middle of the night, she informed me, and stole the safe right out of the office. This, only weeks after a guy had driven off in his SUV with a full tank of gas, despite the prevention tactics Kevin had taught us.

Kevin was furious for a long time after that. Which meant he was quiet.

That didn’t stop me from loading points onto my card. Kevin was obviously preoccupied with bigger issues and, besides, it could hardly be called theft—they were just points. It was costing no one. I even stopped relying on the forgetfulness of customers. I learned that by using the “unpriced item” button, I could input any dollar amount onto the computer, swipe the points, then delete the item. No trace. I did this in random amounts—$53, $45, $62, $98—nearly every shift.

But no matter how I justified it to myself, I knew I was doing something wrong because I was hiding it. A good secret both legitimizes and requires loneliness. I had found a new way to create the space I craved.

It was a weekend, a Friday, I believe. The weather was still cool, but the first nudges of spring meant I could get away with skimpier clothes at night. I approached weekend parties with mounting fervor and the acerbic desperation of an insecure 16-year-old trying to be liked. The sun was setting, dusk moving in quick. I had just finished my shift. The new guy, a towering, dopey twenty-whatever, rang me through. He said something along the lines of nice when I unhooked a $100 gift card from the tall carousel next to the shelf of candy. A beep sounded as he scanned the gift card, typed a code to activate it. A ringing as the computer siphoned my points. He ran through my trove of goods: a bottle of Simply Orange juice to mix with the Bombay Sapphire I’d buy from a boot outside the liquor store later that night; a Red Bull, because my friends liked to do Jägerbombs. I threw in a tub of Dentyne Ice—the 60 pack—and a green BiC lighter—the big one—at the last minute. My purse was lined with half-used lighters and packs of gum, but the drinks alone seemed like too little. The amount had to be over $10, at least. My coworker subtracted the total from the freshly minted gift card and handed me the difference in cash—another loophole I’d known about. Eighty-something dollars. More than 90 would have seemed felonious.

The paper bills were thick and dry in my moist hand, and I felt flighty, terrified, avoiding even a wayward glance at the camera above the counter as I folded the cash and stuffed it into my wallet. Heat flooded my face as the zipper struggled over the bulge. I got it half-closed before shoving it in my pocket, waving goodbye to my coworker, and heading out to the lot where my mom waited in our turquoise Ford Windstar. My seatbelt clicked into place. Mom kissed my cheek. That night, I partied.

The next day, I went to my friend Zoë’s house. We listened to Kanye West’s new Graduation album in her basement after inhaling bowls of Ichiban noodles slathered with mayonnaise. I had spent all the money—between booze for me and my friends, a pack of Prime Times and snacks, 80-odd bucks didn’t last long. But it didn’t matter because it hadn’t cost me anything.

My phone rang. I recognized the number radiating from my all-black Samsung flip phone. I told Zoë I’d be right back and closed her bedroom door to take the call on the staircase. For a second, I considered running to the bathroom. Then I flipped the phone open.

Kevin’s voice sounded sing-songy on the other end, or at least it does in my memory. He had been going through the transaction records from the previous week. He said, I just want to know how you managed to collect enough points to get a $100 gift card.

Kevin had each employee’s points card number on file. I knew this, since Kevin himself had covered it in my training. I knew Kevin checked the records each week. I knew that, had I exercised more patience, I surely could have gotten away with my scheme simply by redeeming points at a different location. Looking back, this makes me wonder where my impatience as justification for willfully ignoring those facts ends, and where some unconscious desire to be found out starts sneaking in. I cringe at the cliché this begs: Was this a cry for help, a call for attention? Or something far more banal and just as likely, such as teenaged carelessness?

The lie bubbled up quick and hot, much like a great idea. It’s my grandpa’s card, I said into the phone. He’s had it for a long time, but he gave it to me a while ago because he doesn’t use it anymore.

Based on my training, I figured my grandpa had enough years on him to account for a bill’s worth of points. I didn’t bother doing the math back then, but it turns out that to collect the number of points necessary to redeem a $100 gift card, he would have had to have spent around $10,000. My grandpa drove a blue Chrysler LeBaron, not an 18-wheeler.

Okay, Kevin responded brightly. I just need a handwritten note from your grandfather explaining that. And I’d like to speak with him on the phone.

The noodles lurched in my stomach. I told Kevin I’d bring the note to my next shift. Then I said goodbye and snapped my phone shut as though it was about to end my life.

Silence followed first, then a shallow breath grating in my chest. My eyes slid from the pile of shoes on the linoleum to the frosted window framing the front door. Sound rushed up from my feet and over my head the way water moves when pencil-diving into a pool. The beat of “Stronger” thumped through the wall, filled the stairwell. I glanced at the closed bedroom door. I wanted to be back on my friend’s carpet, smoking weed and shouting along to Kanye.

I called my mom. She answered instantaneously, as she always did, as though expecting me to call. I told her what I’d done. She didn’t get mad or admonish me or even express surprise. Her voice remained steady, as though I had only asked if I could stay late at Zoë’s to finish homework. She told me to call Kevin back and apologize.

Just tell him the truth, she said. If I were you, I’d say, this is what happened; you can take the $100 off my paycheck. I’m so sorry and I’ll never do it again.

I often laugh off this quintessential way my mom gives advice—too simplistic, I think, lacking in nuance. Like every problem is so easily solved. At the time, no such critical lens shrouded my vision. A criminal’s clarity, perhaps. I told her I would, and hung up.

Alone again on the carpeted staircase, mayonnaise greasing my throat, full of sodium and fear and a mother’s advice, I called Kevin. The phone rang once.

I was lying, I told him. I didn’t use my grandpa’s card. I stole the points and used them to buy the gift card. You can take the $100 off my next paycheck and I’m really sorry and I will never do it again.

The words spewed from my mouth and left me feeling very close to how I felt after purging: relieved and disgusted.

It took 10 full Mississippis for Kevin to speak again. I stared at the translucent window above the pile of shoes, feeling strange. I hadn’t told anyone about the gift card, about stealing points. Not even my friends. Even though it’s the exact sort of secret that friends are supposed to share. The kind they’d be impressed by. Instead, I was telling this secret to my boss.

No longer all that alone on the staircase.

Dayna, Kevin finally said.

My name hung there like a sentence.

Then: That is the best thing you could have said to me. I was prepared to charge you to the full extent of the law.

A chunk of old paint from the banister loosened under my fingernail and floated to the carpet.

Kevin had it in mind to make an example out of me because he was fed up with people taking advantage of him. Fill ‘n’ runs. The robbery of the safe, which, he reminded me, wasn’t the first time. Constant petty theft. The money would be docked off my paycheck. I was to show up for my regular Sunday shift the following day, and I should come prepared to do some cleaning tasks that would not be fun. A little punishment, which was a relief, because though I didn’t know it then, penance lived in my bones. It’s no coincidence I also had an eating disorder. That I stole chocolate bars and, before they had time to digest into a lump in my conscience, purged myself clean.

The next morning, Janice stood behind the till.

Well, she said by way of greeting.

I walked around the counter and stuffed my sweater underneath.

I am really surprised. She crossed her arms. I wouldn’t have guessed you would do something like that.

Janice looked like she’d seen some shit. Now she was looking at me. I wanted to put my sweater back on.

For six hours, I hauled firewood stacks off the outdoor shelving unit, piled dusty four-litre bottles of windshield washer fluid and antifreeze onto the sidewalk, cleaned out the dirt and spiderwebs and insect gunk from the far corners. My knees dug into the concrete and it felt good. I ignored my thirst and my bladder, happy to have a pane of glass between me and the people I’d disappointed, even with Janice pursing her lips through it every so often. I hated the way she had looked at me, that she’d been so shocked. Didn’t she know this was how teenagers acted? She was the idiot for not expecting it.

Finally, the Windstar crunched through the lot and parked on the side. Pebbles fell from my knees as I stood, and Kevin popped out of the station to say I should meet him upstairs before I left. I signalled to my mom, holding up a couple fingers. Two minutes.

The office smelled like old bread. Light slanting through the blinds had a second-hand quality. Kevin sat in an office chair, elbows resting on his desk. To his right, I spotted a chalk-grey safe the size of a milk crate—the replacement. I sat opposite in a cheap computer chair, thinking about the theft prevention tactics, so I looked him in the eye but it was hard. The space we shared felt cramped. His eyes were clear and kind and I was a thief.

You realize I have to let you go, unfortunately, Kevin said. He was almost smiling, but in a way that assured me he wasn’t angry.

I nodded, but I had not realized that. Stupidly, I figured there was some sort of exception for semi-forthcoming delinquents.

The $100 will be deducted from your final paycheck, he continued. But I won’t mention this to anyone else. You can still put my name on your resumé and I’ll give you a good reference.

Kevin told me that my honesty counted for a lot. That I was a good kid, and he didn’t want this mistake to screw up my chances of getting another job.

A mistake.

Just a mistake.

My mistake, Kevin’s livelihood.

Thank you, I said. I could hear the remorse in my own voice, but my emotions surpassed that. All the space I’d cultivated around me deflated, shrank. Breathing came a little bit easier.

Then Kevin tapped his desk. Surely, I’d made more mistakes than stealing $100, he suggested.

Bits of sun struggled through the window slats and landed across his hands planted on the oak surface.

Is there anything else you’ve stolen from me? he asked, his face open, expectant. About how much, would you guess?

Vehicles whooshed by outside.

I’m not going to tell your parents, he continued. Just give me your best estimate and I’ll deduct that from your final paycheck, too.

My body started to twist, trying to hide itself. Had he seen me on the cameras, squirreling away chocolate bars? Had I been so obvious? Maybe he found the wrappers stuffed under the recycled motor oil jugs in the garage. That theft felt out of my control—the most humiliating thing to be. I hadn’t been trying to hide the stolen goods so much as I was hiding my eating disorder. And yet, it was more embarrassing to imagine that Kevin thought I had eaten so much junk food without throwing it up.

In any case, I don’t know if Kevin had evidence of any of this, or if he simply assumed that there must be more to it. I’d been stealing junk food for months. It was April now, and I could trace it back to the previous October, maybe even September.

Umm . . . I scrunched my face toward my nose, looked hard at the thin brown carpet. Maybe . . . another $100? Altogether?

He nodded. Okay, was all he said. Then he wrote it down on a notepad.

But it had definitely been more than that.

When Kevin held out his hand, I shook it.

When he looked me in the eye, I looked back.

A liar.

The lie stung the back of my throat, tasting like the packaged Danish did on the way up, sickly sweet and acidic. I could still taste the sugary burn after I waved my final goodbye to Janice at the till. It lingered after I climbed into the front seat of the Windstar, partially relieved to see my mom, beacon of honesty, who had saved me from some court-ordered punishment I wouldn’t allow myself to imagine, who would never know about the secondary theft. As I buckled my seatbelt, sunlight tilting onto the backs of my hands, she asked about my shift, how it had gone with Kevin. She didn’t yet know about the vile secret I held in my mouth—the kind of secret that tastes just as bad as a lie. She would only find out months later, when I became careless enough about hiding the traces of my bingeing and purging, when the space between things became too wide. Which makes me realize that it was never carelessness, but my way of calling for help without calling.

issues.content_html:
The Original Mother

The original mother brought out the toenail clippers and sat cross-legged in front of the La-Z-Boy, steadying her husband’s narrow foot with her left hand, his calloused heel wedged in her palm. His eyes were pointed at the TV. Jeopardy. “Who was it?” he asked. There had been a knock at the door a short while ago.

“A man.”

“Huh.”

“Selling fish from a pole,” the original mother said.

Her husband dug at his jaw. “Who is Vasco . . .” he said. “Vasco da Gama!”

“Is that his name?”

Her husband’s face fell. “Huh?”

“The man,” the original mother said, suddenly finding herself curious for anything that might shed light on the stranger that had come to their door. “Does he sell fish here often? Vasco?”

“Oh, right,” her husband said, concentrating on the next clue. “Sure.” He wriggled his toes. His ankle let out a frivolous little crack.

They lapsed into silence.

The original mother pursed her lips and tried to clip his gray toenails, but the hot ache in her old, arthritic fingers was too much to bear.

“Ah . . . oh! What is the Law of Reflection?” her husband said.

The original mother let her eyes go soft. Her husband’s toes grew indistinct. As she reckoned with the crude geometry of this latest defeat, another woman, her mirror image, brought out a second pair of toenail clippers, sat cross-legged before the La-Z-Boy, and steadied the husband’s other foot with her right hand.

The original mother’s husband jerked the legrest down and grasped both women by their wrists, shaking the toenail clippers from their hands. The mothers appraised each other and said, “Who are you?” Then they looked at their husband, gawking at them like a carp.

He tightened his grip and held on well past the evening news.

The second woman coughed harshly and then, quite astonishingly, crumpled in on herself, until a fox emerged from the folds of a uniform of a mother. “Get out of here,” her husband growled. The fox regarded the original mother before bolting out the door through the pet flap, unused since the beagle’s death, but the original mother hadn’t seen a thing. She’d made herself absent, her eyes shut tight to brace against the pain of her husband’s grip, but also to better heed her heart.

Remarkable, the way it beat!

The original mother’s older brother came to visit, the first time in nearly forty years, spurred by their younger sister’s coming-out message in their otherwise uneventful group chat on KakaoTalk. When he arrived, his shirttail got caught in the taxi’s door, the tiny wheels of his mean aluminum suitcase burst asunder over a crack, and he immediately stubbed his toe on the doorjamb. “Sister,” he said, between dramatic breaths and staring incredulously at the pet flap, “what is this? This American existence?”

The original mother knew why he had really come: to lay bare his love and resentment to the woman for whom he had long nursed a quiet crush, foolishly believing her to be nothing more than their younger sister’s best friend. It didn’t matter that he was old, that they were all old, the geometry of their ways long set fast. He had come to make a point. He would have the original mother drive him a short distance to the sister’s apartment, where he’d condemn her for the wickedness of homosexuality, disown her in the same breath, and then turn his frustrations on the original mother, enumerating all the ways American life had tarnished her character.

As the original mother cooked him a lavish meal, she flung open the windows to air the house so her husband wouldn’t carp about the smell of their “exotic” food encroaching on his enjoyment of Jeopardy. “My hands are dry, sister.” She gave her brother almond-scented hand lotion, envying the straightness of his fingers. “I’m thirsty,” he whined. She handed him a glass of cold water. “America has made you fatter than you should be.” The bean curd stew boiled furiously. The stuffed perilla leaves steamed into her face. Her brother proceeded to explain how she was to blame for, well, everything. He had an enlarged prostate and had developed an irrational fear of death, and even that was her fault. “I’m hungry. I’m hungry.” Just as she set down the bowl of rice, another hand, not her own, placed a bowl of rice beside it. It belonged to a woman who looked exactly like her. They stood at the table and appraised each other and said, “Who are you?” Then they looked at their brother, glaring incandescently at them like a lacquered scorpion.

“Ahn-nyah! Now, sister, what is this?” Her brother’s eyes narrowed as he ripped into her for such brazen chicanery. Only in America, he fumed, would a brother be served a dinner conjured by some kind of black magic, almost certainly purchased on Amazon. He shouted so loudly that the original mother’s husband had to crank up the TV.

Her brother shouted well past the evening news.

The second mother plugged her ears with her fingers, then puffed out her cheeks and emitted an uncanny whine. The sound was enough to stop the original mother’s brother mid-rant. As the air escaped the woman’s body, she crumpled in on herself, quite miraculously, until a fox emerged from the folds of a uniform of a mother. “Get out of here,” her brother growled. The original mother hadn’t seen a thing. She’d made herself absent, her eyes shut tight to brace against her brother’s words, but also to better heed her heart.

Remarkable, the way it beat!

The original mother once had a mother, and her mother a mother as well, the uniform of the original mother passing from one generation to the next.

Earlier, her son had called, but she wasn’t in the right mindset to answer, crushed, as she was, by the geometry of her exhaustion.

She should have answered, or at least called back. Now, an intrusive guilt keeps her awake long after the late-night news.

The original mother blinks into the dark, thinking. If her son had answered the door, he would have bought a fish from—what was his name again? She opens her mouth very slightly and focuses on the puckered shadow cast by the curtain, situating herself in the moment the name was spoken. Finally, it comes to her, bright as happiness: Vasco.

Her son, keen to avoid confrontation in any form and unwilling to risk seeming an inconvenience to anyone but his mother, would have taken one look at Vasco, spun a private story about his troubles, and bought a fish, because who went around selling fish like that? He would have carried it inside and left it in its taut plastic bag on the kitchen counter beside the instant coffee and her husband’s glazed donuts, where she would have had to contend with the fish’s pouting mouth and its eyes, gaping up at her in troubled amazement.

Her son’s birth had been a very difficult one.

The original mother eases out from under the sheets, pads past the extraordinary sounds of her husband’s snoring, past her brother’s faltering puffs and snorts, and pauses before the cheval mirror, an heirloom from her husband’s mother, and the only thing her brother allowed any measure of approval as he wended unbidden through every room, drumming his index finger against his lips. Even in the dark, she sees the woman standing on the other side who looks exactly like her. She is wholly present now, heeds her heart—remarkable, the way it beats!

She slips into the utility room and opens the drawer that only a mother would ever think to open, a drawer that only a mother would even know exists. From beneath a bright orange box of dryer sheets, she pulls out a uniform of a fox. She contorts into it, her joints and muscles screaming, thinking all the while, “When will it be done?”

It is done.

She will return before sunrise, before the morning news, to resume her duties as the original mother, of course. But until then, the night is hers. She darts through the pet flap—but not before appraising the woman in the mirror—and vanishes tenderly into the dark.

issues.summary: The author explores the life and legacy of his estranged father, from adoption and abandonment to his horrific experiences of the second world war When Haruki Murakami was a child living in Nishinomiya, Japan, his father announced they were getting rid of their cat. He put his son and the cat on his bike and cycled along the Shukugawa river to a beach 2km from their house. There, they put the box
issues.author: Fiona Sturges
issues.content_html:
The author explores the life and legacy of his estranged father, from adoption and abandonment to his horrific experiences of the second world war

When Haruki Murakami was a child living in Nishinomiya, Japan, his father announced they were getting rid of their cat. He put his son and the cat on his bike and cycled along the Shukugawa river to a beach 2km from their house. There, they put the box with the cat in it on the ground among some trees and cycled away “without a backward glance”. When they got home, they opened their door to find the cat they’d just left “greeting us with a friendly meow, its tail standing tall. It had beaten us home.”

Murakami always wondered how the cat got home so quickly, and why his father had wanted to banish her. These are just some of the unanswered questions that surface in Abandoning a Cat, an essay that first appeared in the New Yorker in 2019, and which is now being published as a book and audiobook. Translated by Philip Gabriel and read with gentle warmth by Kotaro Watanabe, it finds the author telling the story of Murakami Sr, from whom he was estranged for 20 years and who remained a mystery to him in his lifetime.

issues.title: The Hill by Harriet Clark review – distinctive debut of growing up with a mother in prison
issues.summary: This unusual portrait of a young girl whose prison visits are interweaved with her grandmother’s war-weary reminiscences rewards attention American author Harriet Clark’s first novel, partly inspired by her own life, is narrated by a girl whose mother is in prison. Suzanna is being raised by grandparents while her mother serves a life sentence for driving the getaway car for a botched bank robbery
issues.author: Sarah Moss
issues.content_html:
This unusual portrait of a young girl whose prison visits are interweaved with her grandmother’s war-weary reminiscences rewards attention

American author Harriet Clark’s first novel, partly inspired by her own life, is narrated by a girl whose mother is in prison. Suzanna is being raised by grandparents while her mother serves a life sentence for driving the getaway car for a botched bank robbery intended to fund revolutionary political activism. Although Suzanna refuses the narrative, in some ways this is a coming-of-age story, but with a protagonist whose overwhelming need is to go nowhere and change nothing.

The Hill is shaped by the tension between the novel’s need for a plot and Suzanna’s rejection of her own role in the Bildungsroman. Prison visits structure Suzanna’s life, their rituals and repetitions at once marking and resisting the passage of time. At first, her grandfather drives her from their shabby urban apartment to the hilltop prison and escorts her to the entrance to the children’s centre, where on a good day the prisoners are allowed to play with their children under close surveillance. Later, the grandfather dies, activities in the centre are restricted and Suzanna’s visits take increasingly constrained forms. Abjuring ordinary teenage activities, she takes the train towards the hill every Saturday, submits to searches, and follows rules about how to move and what and whom she may not touch.

Palestinian-Jewish author Hannah Lillith Assadi has won the National book award for fiction, one of the US’s most prestigious literary prizes, for her novel Paradiso 17.

Assadi’s third novel is a study of the psychic toll of displacement on migrants, through the tale of a Palestinian man who escaped the Nakba in 1948, when more than 700,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled from their homes by Israel. The story was inspired by her father, Sami Abdul-Fattah Al-Assadi, who fled the Nakba as a child with his family, before studying in Italy and moving to New York.

The two had much in common. They were not expert mathematicians; they prized physical intuition over mere competence; and they did not shy away from the moral and political implications o
issues.author: Luca Turin
issues.content_html:
Scientific discoveries are explained effortlessly in this portrait of a man whose research was driven by pure passion

Niels Bohr shares with Albert Einstein pride of place in the pantheon of 20th-century science. The two had much in common. They were not expert mathematicians; they prized physical intuition over mere competence; and they did not shy away from the moral and political implications of their work.

But Bohr differed from Einstein in one crucial respect: his extraordinary personality. In his gripping biography Philip Ball ensures we feel the intense pull of Bohr’s genius. Today he would probably be considered neurodivergent; he possessed a passion for physics that cast a spell on all who knew him. Solving problems is the raison d’etre of any scientist, but Bohr went far beyond that: having inaugurated quantum mechanics with his model of the atom in 1913, he simply would not give up until the rest of it was understood.

issues.title: Check out Phoebe Bridgers’ cosy festive cover of Adrianne Lenker’s ‘Anything’
issues.summary: Proceeds go to the Palestine Children's Relief Fund (PCRF) The post Check out Phoebe Bridgers’ cosy festive cover of Adrianne Lenker’s ‘Anything’ appeared first on NME .
issues.author: Tom Skinner
issues.content_html:
Phoebe Bridgers has shared a festive cover of Adrianne Lenker’s ‘Anything’ – you can listen to it below.

  • READ MORE: Phoebe Bridgers – ‘Lost Weekend’ review: indie’s poet laureate returns with a staggering, strange and stirring opus

The singer-songwriter’s new take on the Big Thief frontwoman’s 2020 solo song is the latest entry into her ever-growing Christmas catalogue. Proceeds from the track from both Bridgers and Lenker will benefit the Palestine Children’s Relief Fund (PCRF).

Bridgers’ cosy and intimate version remains faithful to the original, as she sings about spending the holidays with family: “Christmas Eve with your mother and sis/ Don’t wanna fight, but your mother insists/ Dog’s white teeth slice right through my fist/ Drive to the ER and they put me on risk.”

The cover was produced by Bridgers alongside her longtime collaborators Tony Berg and Ethan Gruska, as well as Jack Antonoff. All three are credited as producers on her third album ‘Lost Weekend’, which was released in August.

Listen to ‘Anything’ here:

Bridgers has previously marked the festive period with covers of Tom Waits’ ‘Day After Tomorrow’, yuletide classic ‘Have Yourself A Merry Little Christmas’, Merle Haggard’s ‘If We Make It Through December’, Simon & Garfunkel’s ‘7 O’Clock News/Silent Night’ (with Fiona Apple and The National’s Matt Berninger), and McCarthy Trenching’s ‘Christmas Song’ (with Jackson Browne).

She then took on The Handsome Family’s ‘So Much Wine’ in 2022, with proceeds going to the Los Angeles LGBT Center.

Boygenius also shared a charity Christmas version of Irish traditional ‘The Parting Glass’ with Ye Vagabonds in 2023, in tribute to the late Sinead O’Connor.

Speaking to NME in 2022, Bridgers explained: “I like fucked up holiday songs. I always have. I remember being so inspired when I went to Nashville and saw where Elvis had done his Christmas album and, because he’s a crazy person, he had to make it feel like Christmas in July.”

She added: “It’s also a cool thing to do for charity every year, and it’s fun. I like tradition.”

Meanwhile, Bridgers is set to kick off the UK leg of her 2026 ‘Lost Tour’ in Dublin next week. The run of dates also includes two shows at The O2 in London in December, ahead of further gigs across Europe. Next summer, Bridgers will return to the capital to headline All Points East in Victoria Park. Find any remaining tickets here.

The star has been announced on the line-up for Coachella 2027, too.

In other news, Phoebe Bridgers has earned seven Grammy nominations for next year’s ceremony, including Album Of The Year (‘Lost Weekend’) and Best Rock Song (‘Lost Boys’).

issues.title: Taylor Swift returns to country roots for first CMA Awards performance in 13 Years with ‘Our Song’ and ‘I Knew It, I Knew You’
issues.summary: Keith Urban also joined her for the performance, having toured with her when she was a teenager The post Taylor Swift returns to country roots for first CMA Awards performance in 13 Years with ‘Our Song’ and ‘I Knew It, I Knew You’ appeared first on NME .
issues.author: Liberty Dunworth
issues.content_html:
Taylor Swift returned to her country roots last night (Wednesday November 18) when she performed at the CMA Awards for the first time in 13 years.

  • READ MORE: Taylor Swift – ‘The Life Of A Showgirl’ review: magical when the songwriter just lets herself be

The performance marked the pop star’s first appearance at the awards since 2016, when she presented Garth Brooks with the Entertainer of the Year award. It also marked her first time performing on the CMAs stage since 2013, when she performed ‘Red’ with Vince Gill and Alison Krauss.

For last night’s performance, Swift sported some bejewelled cowboy boots and broke out her track ‘I Knew It, I Knew You’, which was written for the Toy Story 5 soundtrack. She began the set backstage and moved through the hallways – passing by country stars including Lainey Wilson, Eric Church, Brad Paisley and more – as she made her way to the stage.

There, she threw things back to her early material by breaking out ‘Our Song’ from her 2006 self-titled debut album, and was joined by Keith Urban. Swift previously opened for the country legend during the early days of her career before she brought him out as a surprise guest on her ‘1989 World Tour’ in 2015.

Urban also provided backing vocals for ‘That’s When’ and ‘We Were Happy’ on two ‘From The Vault’ tracks from ‘Fearless (Taylor’s Version)’, as well as covering her song ‘Lover’ on his 2019 tour.

Swift first attended the CMA Awards when she released her debut solo album in 2006, and went on to win the Horizon Award – celebrating significant growth – the following year.

In 2009 she became the youngest recipient of the Entertainer Of The Year trophy, and went on to win the award again in 2009. When she last performed at the ceremony in 2013, she also took home the Pinnacle Award, which celebrated unprecedented global success.

Swift’s latest CMAs appearance comes shortly after her being inducted into the Nashville Songwriters Hall Of Fame last month, and also saw her nominated for Single Of The Year with ‘I Knew It, I Knew You’. That award would ultimately go to Ella Langley’s huge hit ‘Choosin’ Texas’.

Earlier this week, Swift was announced as one of the nominees for the 2027 Grammys. She is up for six awards on the night, including both Song Of The Year and Best Song Written For Visual Media with ‘I Knew It, I Knew You’.

Her ‘The Fate of Ophelia’ is nominated for Record Of The Year, her latest album ‘The Life Of A Showgirl’ is shortlisted for Album Of The Year, and the title track she released with Sabrina Carpenter is up for Best Pop Duo/Group Performance. The Chris Lake remix of her track ‘Opalite’ is also nominated for Best Remixed Recording.

issues.title: Pierce Brosnan welcomes Robert Pattinson to James Bond role: “You are going to be magnificent”
issues.summary: “It has been a joy to watch you create a remarkable body of work and to go from strength to strength” The post Pierce Brosnan welcomes Robert Pattinson to James Bond role: “You are going to be magnificent” appeared first on NME .
issues.author: Liberty Dunworth
issues.content_html:
Pierce Brosnan shared a message welcoming Robert Pattinson to his new role as James Bond, and telling him that he is going to do a “magnificent” job.

  • READ MORE: ‘No Time To Die’ review: Daniel Craig’s surprisingly emotional final fling

Pattinson was announced as the new James Bond On Monday (November 16), after months of speculation – beating off competition from Jacob Elordi, Jack Lowden, Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor and Nicolas Hoult.

The new Bond film will be the first since Amazon took over the franchise last February, and is set to be directed by Dune’s Denis Villeneuve and feature a script written by Peaky Blinders creator Steven Knight.

With the casting, Pattinson is now the eighth actor to take on the role of the iconic British agent, taking over Daniel Craig, who said goodbye to Bond in 2021’s No Time To Die.

Now, Pierce Brosnan, who played Bond between 1995 and 2002, has shared his seal of approval for Pattinson being selected for the role, and shared a heartfelt message on Instagram wishing him the best.

View this post on Instagram

“Dear Robert, Welcome to the world of Bond,” he wrote, sharing a promo shot of the actor. “You are going to be magnificent.”

“I have fond memories of our time together making Remember Me,” Brosnan added, referring to the 2010 movie they starred in together. “It has been a joy to watch you create a remarkable body of work and to go from strength to strength. Enjoy the ride. Grá mor, Pierce.”

Brosnan is the second former Bond actor to share support for Pattinson following the news of his casting, with George Lazenby – who took on the role for 1969’s On Her Majesty’s Secret Service – also sharing a message.

“I hear they’ve announced the new James Bond @007… Robert, welcome to the most exclusive club in the world,” he said on X. “But remember to enjoy yourself. Let’s see if you’ll have ‘this never happened to the other fella’ moment. All the best mate, George xx”.

A little bit about how it feels to be cast as the new James Bond @007… pic.twitter.com/JSmS6pqAQg

— George Lazenby (@lazenbyofficial) November 18, 2026

Details about the next Bond film remain under wraps, although it is expected that the next film will be released in 2028.

After news broke of the casting, Pattinson shared: “James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime. To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement. I couldn’t be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.”

Both Brad Pitt and Florence Pugh have already expressed hopes to play the latest Bond villain. On the red carpet for The Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth, Pitt shared: “I’d like to do that. My man Javier [Bardem, who starred opposite him in F1] did it so well, it’s tall shoes but I’d take it on.”

“Sign me up for the villain. Get Denis Villeneuve on the flip phone, let’s go,” he added.

For Pugh, she revealed that she spoke to Villeneuve about the next Bond film after working together on Dune 3, and asked him if he was open to the idea of a villain who was “the size of 5’4’”.

It was previously revealed that Amazon boss Jeff Bezos was “heavily involved” in picking Pattinson for the role.

“By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing. But there was something special about Rob and his performance,” he said at the Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event this week. “It was immediately undebated. We all gravitated toward Rob.

“Initially, we were slightly biased against him just because he’s already so famous, like maybe we should have somebody more unknown, but in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond.”

issues.title: The College Kids Who Drove a Duck Across the Americas
issues.summary: In 1961, nine young Americans set out to promote international friendship. Their adventures survive in a remarkable collection of letters. The post The College Kids Who Drove a Duck Across the Americas appeared first on JSTOR Daily .
issues.author: April White
issues.content_html:
The DUKW was designed for war. The gray metal vehicle had six wheels, a rudder, and a propeller, an unlikely cross between a Jimmy deuce-and-a-half—as the standard GMC military truck was known—and a bulky metal scow. Between 1942 and 1945, more than 21,000 DUKWs came off the assembly lines in Michigan and Missouri. Called “ducks” by just about everyone, these land-water hybrids would carry troops and supplies to the beaches of Sicily and Normandy and countless other battle sites through World War II. Later they delivered the same cargo to the shores of Incheon, changing the tide of the Korean War.

And then in the summer of 1961, an aging DUKW from an Akron scrapyard became an unlikely symbol of peace in the midst of the Cold War.

“What I learn from this trip will make me appreciate life (especially with you) more.”

It was an adventure only a couple of college kids could dream up—a yearlong road trip across the Americas in a vehicle that had broken down five times on the drive from Ohio back home to New York. But “adventure was only part—a small part—of this trip,” Dan Twomey, one of nine men who participated in what they called Operation Americas, told a local newspaper. (The contingent also included his twin brother, Tom.)

For Twomey, who documented the odyssey in letters to his girlfriend Rosemarie Feuerbach, now shared by Drew University via JSTOR, the purpose was much bigger. The adventure was both a goodwill mission and a personal quest.

To the newspapers, Twomey explained that the goal was “friendship and understanding”—“meeting ordinary people, listening to their ideas and perhaps putting across the true American story was and is the sole purpose of this whole thing.”

“I think the fuller a person you are the more you can enjoy life.” Click on the letter to take a closer look. “I think the fuller a person you are the more you can enjoy life.” Click on the letter to take a closer look.

But to Feuerbach, Twomey confessed from Panama during a particularly challenging stretch of the trip that the “noble” reasons “really don’t mean as much.” “What I learn from this trip will make me appreciate life (especially with you) more,” he wrote. “I think the fuller a person you are the more you can enjoy life.”

Their journey kicked off in August 1961 with a media tour, including an interview on Today. Over the next several months, the men and their DUKW—which was christened El Pato Valiente (“The Valiant Duck”) and painted with a cheerful Donald Duck in a mortarboard—would cross the United States, zigzag through Mexico, and ping-pong around Central America before finding themselves seemingly stuck in Panama.

Along the way, the men spent much of their time visiting college campuses, where they played guitar, performed silly skits, and challenged students on the basketball court. But Twomey credited most of the trip’s successes—and most of its troubles—to the DUKW itself.

“One fellow slowed down to see the duck and the fellow in back was viewing the duck also, but didn’t slow down. Result—Bang!”Click on the letter to take a closer look. “One fellow slowed down to see the duck and the fellow in back was viewing the duck also, but didn’t slow down. Result—Bang!”Click on the letter to take a closer look. “One fellow slowed down to see the duck and the fellow in back was viewing the duck also, but didn’t slow down. Result—Bang!”Click on the letter to take a closer look. “One fellow slowed down to see the duck and the fellow in back was viewing the duck also, but didn’t slow down. Result—Bang!”Click on the letter to take a closer look.

Everywhere they went, the odd vehicle attracted curiosity. In Mexico City, the sight of a boat with wheels caused a traffic collision: “One fellow slowed down to see the duck and the fellow in back was viewing the duck also, but didn’t slow down. Result—Bang!” In Juchitán, Mexico, it attracted a mob. As the men navigated the DUKW through the rough, narrow back streets of the community’s poor neighborhoods, “we had a crowd of about 50 people following us,” Twomey wrote to Feuerbach. When they stopped at a basketball court for an impromptu game, “In about 10 minutes there was a crowd of two to three hundred watching. Many of the people cheered for us.” (The DUKW crew lost 38–34.) By the time they reached Guatemala in mid-October 1961, Twomey reported that “people, crowds, unusual happenings are so commonplace, I feel like I’m repeating myself.”

“We had a crowd of about 50 people following us.” Click on the letter to take a closer look. “We had a crowd of about 50 people following us.” Click on the letter to take a closer look.

Maintenance on the DUKW was also unfortunately commonplace. In the first two weeks of the trip alone, there was a brake issue in New Jersey, a flat tire in Indiana, and a busted fan belt in St. Louis. But the real trouble came just before Christmas, one hundred miles from Panama City, when a busted motor required the US Army to step in, towing the immobile vehicle to the Canal Zone.

The men, the machine, and their mascot, a German shepherd named Robin who had joined the crew in Texas, would stay much longer than they intended in Panama. They needed to raise more money, first to fix El Pato Valiente and then for boat passage to South America, bypassing the impenetrable Darién Gap. In theory their duck could swim, but they’d been warned the waters would be too rough. Eventually, though, the men became impatient and decided to set off across the Caribbean to the northern coast of Colombia.

Their planned five-day voyage was doomed almost from the beginning. “For the first few hours everything went o.k.,” Twomey wrote. “Then the rudder cable broke.” The men had to steer by hand as waves washed over the DUKW, swamping the new motor and washing the survival gear overboard. Everyone was seasick, even Robin. They continued to limp along for a couple of days. “Then it happened,” Twomey wrote.

Weekly Newsletter

" * " indicates required fields

“A loud noise told us something had gone wrong (broken) with our propeller,” he wrote. They beached the DUKW on an island off the coast of Panama, where it would stay for a week—delaying the men still further, but attracting ever more publicity to their travels. It even caught the attention of President Kennedy, who assured one frantic parent that the US government would help her stranded son, despite the administration’s previous misgivings about the trip. With help, the men eventually made their way to Colombia, spending another five months touring South America before returning to the United States.

More than 50 years later, Matt Twomey told the story of this more-than-an-adventure in a documentary titled Duck Diaries: A Cold War Quest for Friendship Across the Americas. In interviews and images, the film brings to life the amazing stories in the Drew University archives. And it provides a lovely coda to the tale: the filmmaker is the son of Dan Twomey and Rosemarie Feuerbach, who married a year after Dan’s return. When Dan Twomey passed away in 2024, his obituary noted that his time on the DUKW and the couple’s correspondence through Operation Americas had, as Twomey had hoped in 1962, “set the tone for a life full of adventures and global interest and inquiry.”

issues.title: The Stories That Make Thanksgiving
issues.summary: Turkey or Tofurkey? Stuffing or dressing? Whatever’s on your table, these Thanksgiving stories will satisfy your curiosity. The post The Stories That Make Thanksgiving appeared first on JSTOR Daily .
issues.author: The Editors
issues.content_html:
Americans are getting ready to celebrate Thanksgiving, the middle entry in the Halloween-Thanksgiving-Winter holidays trifecta. Plate up with some table talk about the origins of the holiday, the reason we eat turkey, and what really makes people so sleepy after the annual meal. Extra fixings: all stories contain free links to the supporting academic research on JSTOR. Happy Thanksgiving!

How Thanksgiving took shape

Quakers Against Thanksgiving

Livia Gershon November 24, 2025 In colonial America, government “thanksgivings” blurred faith and politics. For Quakers, rejecting them was an act of religious conviction.

Why the Pilgrims Were Actually Able to Survive

Peter C. Mancall November 28, 2019 If you were reading Bradford's version of events, you might think that the survival of the Pilgrims' settlements was often in danger.

Thanksgiving Has Been Reinvented Many Times

Matthew Wills November 1, 2019 From colonial times to the nineteenth century, Thanksgiving was very different from the holiday we know now.

The Modern Invention of Thanksgiving

Livia Gershon November 26, 2014 Thanksgiving as we know it was deliberately invented in the nineteenth century.

Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade: A History in Pictures

The Editors November 12, 2021 In 1927, the parade replaced live animals with helium balloons designed by puppeteer Tony Sarg.

Indigenous histories and living traditions

Translating Corn

Matthew Wills November 22, 2023 To most of the world, “corn” is “maize,” a word that comes from the Taíno mahizwas. Not for British colonists in North America, though.

Returning Corn, Beans, and Squash to Native American Farms

Christina Gish Hill November 24, 2020 Returning the “three sisters” to Native American farms nourishes people, land, and cultures.

How (Not) to Teach Kids about Native Cultures

Livia Gershon November 23, 2020 Even well-intentioned books for children can romanticize (or demonize) Native Americans. But better materials exist.

From turkey to tofu

Let’s Talk Turkey

Matthew Wills November 26, 2014 First of all, why the name "turkey?"

The Great American Turkey

Livia Gershon November 27, 2024 The turkey was semi-domesticated and kept in pens in the American Southwest some 2,000 years ago—but not for the reason you think.

Seven Things You Might Not Know About Cranberries

Matthew Wills November 21, 2018 They're red, tart, and mostly eaten at Thanksgiving. Love them or hate them, here are seven things you might not have known about the humble cranberry.

Vegetarian Thanksgiving Dates Back to the 1900s

Lina Zeldovich November 25, 2019 Tofu Turkey was created in 1990, but some Americans celebrated Thanksgiving with veggie dishes over a century ago.

The Real Joy of Mock Food

Livia Gershon November 8, 2019 "Wow, this really kind of tastes like turkey.”

Beyond the meal

Thanksgiving Is a Feast of Things Forgotten

Sarah McColl November 22, 2016 Thanksgiving is a feast so complex and semiotically dense that things are very often forgotten and rarely go according to plan.

What Does Thanksgiving Look Like in Prison?

Morgan Godvin November 23, 2021 Our American Prison Newspapers collection provides a peek at Thanksgiving celebrations in prisons throughout the decades.

Why Does Eating Food Make You Sleepy?

James MacDonald November 25, 2015 Your turkey is not to blame.

Synesthetic Adjectives Will Make You Eat Your Words

Chi Luu November 23, 2016 Fragrant. Sweet. Tangy. Certain synesthetic adjectives actually trigger cognitive simulations of eating.

It’s Time to Reinvent Food Waste!

Lori Miller Kase November 13, 2018 Startups worldwide convert refuse into energy, biomaterials, and more food.

A moment of gratitude

Eight Poems of Gratitude

The Editors November 23, 2020 Let us pause now and give thanks.

issues.title: The Great American Beer Wars
issues.summary: In the late nineteenth century, rival breweries slashed prices in a ruthless fight to dominate America's booming beer industry. The post The Great American Beer Wars appeared first on JSTOR Daily .
issues.author: Matthew Wills
issues.content_html:
Since wet grains ferment naturally in the presence of airborne yeasts, various forms of beer were likely discovered by multiple agriculturalists across the early farming regions of the world. The earliest archeological evidence of fermentation dates back 13,000 years. For thousands of years, beer was an artisanal product made at home, one that was sometimes safer to drink than the local water. Then the Industrial Revolution transformed beer into a mass-produced beverage.

German immigrants were largely responsible for bringing beer culture to the US. Anheuser-Busch, Pabst, Schlitz, Coors, and Yuengling, for instance, were all founded by German Americans. These giants of the industry today (minus Schlitz) emerged victorious from the wild and foamy “beer wars” of the late nineteenth century.

In one locally notorious case, a construction worker’s rented room collapsed from all the hoarded cheap beer he was storing against an inevitable price increase.

Historian Braden Neihart explores that ferocious competition in a case study of Rock Island, Illinois.

“Brewers fought constantly for market share on multiple fronts, through price dropping and undercutting each other with little concern for the immediate fallout. The end goal was survival, and the casualties along the way were the cost of sustaining business.”

In 1886, Rock Island’s three major local breweries produced a total of 80,000 barrels of beer. This was enough, Neihart figures, for an astonishing 800 beers per resident annually. Because this was well-above-average, the brewers were clearly finding additional markets in nearby towns like Moline as well as in Bettendorf and Davenport across the Mississippi in Iowa.

“Brewers operated within a fiercely capitalist market, restrained by few rules and characterized by high risk,” writes Neihart, noting that the competition was both homegrown and from big beer cities like Peoria, Chicago, and Milwaukee.

Locally, the Rock Island Brewing Company (RIBC) ended up buying its competitors, Atlantic Brewery, City Brewery, Rock Island Brewery, and Junge’s Bottling Works, by 1894. But then, in early 1895, Milwaukee-based Schlitz Brewing Company started rolling its barrels into town. On the road to becoming the nation’s largest beer producer, Schlitz dropped the price of its barrels from $6 to $4. The RIBC was forced to follow suit, though the price was ruinous for the company. The RIBC counterattacked with an advertising campaign to “Sustain Home Industry” and support local unions, which helped it weather the onslaught.

More to Explore

“Brewed with Blood”: The Coors Beercott of the 1970s

H.M.A. Leow June 12, 2026 An unusual coalition transformed a labor dispute into one of the longest-running consumer protests in US history.

Drinkers, on the other hand, celebrated; in one locally notorious case, a construction worker’s rented room collapsed from all the hoarded cheap beer he was storing against an inevitable price increase.

Another strategy was to challenge a competitor’s ingredients and hence impugn their purity. German immigrant brewers came with the tradition of the centuries-old Reinheitsgebot “purity order.” This stated that “beer” was to be made from water, barley, and hops. As a form of time-honored branding, this meant that if you added anything else, you could be called out for faking it.

Challenging the purity of ingredients still goes on, as Neihart notes. Anheuser-Busch spent $30 million during the 2019 Super Bowl boasting that its Bud Light was made from rice while Molson Coors’ products, Miller Lite and Coors Lite, were made from corn syrup. Molson Coors subsequently took Anheuser-Busch to court. The Court of Appeals, which hopefully didn’t have to do a taste test, said the companies were free to list each other’s ingredients.

Weekly Newsletter

" * " indicates required fields

But back to the turn-of-the-twentieth-century strife and competition. It all came to a sudden end with the onset of Prohibition in January 1920. The Eighteenth Amendment to the Constitution prohibited the “manufacture, sale, or transportation of intoxicating liquors.” The law crippled America’s robust beer industry and culture. Local brewers like the RIBC were driven out of business, but large factory producers had the wherewithal to pivot to legal “near-beers” and “soft drinks.”

The re-legalization of beer in 1933 left the field to the beer factories that had survived the dry years. Local beer-making didn’t really recover until the 1970s, when craft beer and the microbrewery movement began. These were in many ways a protest against the bland quaffs sold by the major players. More recent years have seen the rise of “nanobrewers”—very small operations producing beer for sale—because, like all those millennia ago, you can still brew beer at home.

issues.title: This colossal statue was a wonder of the ancient world – until 900 camels took it away
issues.summary: The giant statue of a god inspired awe in ancient travellers to the island of Rhodes, but it did not last long as a wonder before it came crashing down
issues.author: Jonny Wilkes
issues.content_html:
Along with a pyramid, a temple, a mausoleum, a lighthouse, a near-mythical garden and another statue, the Colossus of Rhodes earned its place as one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

The mighty bronze figure of the sun god Helios stood at 70 cubits high, or around 32 metres, making it the tallest statue of antiquity. It took 12 years to build, but would ultimately be the shortest-lived of the Seven Wonders as it lasted less than 60 years.

Constructing a colossus

The Greek island of Rhodes had grown into a prosperous trading hub in the Mediterranean Sea when, in 305 BC, it fell under attack by the military leader Demetrius, who was son of Antigonus, king of Macedonia and one of Alexander the Great’s generals.

A master of siege warfare, earning the title of Poliocetes (the Besieger), Demetrius nevertheless failed as the forces of Rhodes withstood the onslaught for a year. To celebrate this great victory, the Rhodians decided to build a statue to honour their patron god, Helios. It would be designed by the island’s preeminent sculptor, Chares of Lyndus, and reach an unprecedented size.

According to legend, the tools and weapons abandoned by their vanquished foe were melted down and sold to pay for the construction, while a siege tower was repurposed as scaffolding.

Accounts differ on the appearance of the Colossus, which was completed in c282 BC. In keeping with other depictions of Helios, it may have had one hand raised to shield its eyes from the Sun, while the other gripped a torch or a spear. It may have also had a crown of sunbeams on its head.

It has been commonly claimed that the legs straddled the entrance to the city’s harbour, so that ships could sail between them, but this would have been an impossible feat of engineering for the time, and was an embellishment from long after the Colossus had been destroyed.

  • Read more | It was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World – so why was it destroyed three times?

Fall of a god

In 226 BC, after less than six decades standing, the Colossus came crashing down when an earthquake hit Rhodes, causing the statue to snap at the knees. By then, it had already started to feature among must-see architectural marvels compiled by ancient travellers, which would become the definitive list of the Seven Wonders.

So important had it become in the Hellenistic world that rich and powerful patrons offered to pay for its rebuilding, including Ptolemy III, the Macedonian pharaoh of Egypt. After consulting the oracle of Delphi, though, the Rhodians believed they had offended Helios, so chose to leave the broken pieces of the Colossus scattered on the ground.

There they remained for centuries. The stones used inside the statue’s framework to weight it down, or the white marble of its pedestal, were likely repurposed for nearby construction projects over the years, such as the medieval fortress that stands in Rhodes to this day.

  • Read more | These are the 12 most underrated Roman sites in the world – how many have you visited?

The bronze body parts still attracted visitors, too. “Even as it lies, it excites our wonder and admiration,” wrote the historian Pliny the Elder. “Few people can clasp the thumb in their arms, and its fingers are larger than most statues.”

It was only in the mid-seventh century AD that Arabian forces raided the island and sold off the bronze for good, most likely to be melted down. It reportedly took 900 camel loads to shift it all.
