issues.title: A world of wealth: 12 of the richest people who ever lived
issues.summary: How do you weigh Genghis Khan’s empire against Elon Musk’s shares? Meet 12 people from world history whose fortunes reveal just how many ways there are to be rich
issues.author: Jonny Wilkes
issues.content_html:
When it comes to sifting through history’s uber-wealthy and deciding exactly who was rolling in the biggest pile of cash, a myriad of issues arise. One that stymies historians and economists is how to go about adjusting values across different epochs and different, even defunct, currencies.

Then there’s how to distinguish between personal wealth (essentially, how much money a person has stuffed under their mattress) and the worth of holdings, whether that is in assets, land or glittering treasures. This is especially tricky with sovereign leaders: their domain might bring in spectacular wealth, but that does not necessarily make it their money.

Is it possible to compare Elon Musk – who, in June 2026, made history when a rise in his shares temporarily made him the world’s first trillionaire – with Genghis Khan, who built a colossal empire filled with lucrative resources and industries?

Identifying the richest people in history, therefore, is fraught with difficulty and open to infinite interpretation. Regardless, there's no doubting that these rulers, businessmen and bankers all had the deepest of deep pockets.

Amenhotep III (Unknown–c1353 BC)

Egyptian pharaoh whose wealth is estimated in the trillions of US dollars, though his personal fortune is unknown.

The pharaohs of ancient Egypt were, to put it mildly, not embarrassed about flaunting their wealth. Standing tall above them all as the wealthiest was Amenhotep III of the 18th Dynasty, during the 14th century BC.

His reign witnessed a golden age both for Egyptian culture and political power. Diplomats and leaders from other nations would write to Amenhotep simply to ask him for gifts of gold, such was his reputation. There is no knowing the value of his domain, or personal fortune, but suffice to say that it ran into the trillions, and since he was deified as a god, all of Egypt’s glory was indeed his.

Marcus Licinius Crassus (c115 BC–53 BC)

Roman statesman and general worth approximately 200 million sesterces, according to Pliny the Elder.

While Marcus Licinius Crassus reached the top of Roman politics as one-third of the First Triumvirate, he is better known as “the richest man in Rome”.

As a general, he prospered thanks to proscriptions (the confiscation of property belonging to enemies of the state) and as a businessman, he was a ruthless estate agent and bought up many of the houses in Rome. One of his tricks was to set up his own fire brigade and offer to put out any houses that caught ablaze when the owners promised to sell it to him for slashed prices.

Crassus’s wealth is hard to gauge in modern terms, although Pliny the Elder claimed he had 200 million sesterces, which equated to the entire annual budget of the Roman Republic. Such was his reputation for lucre that a rumour spread after his death in 53 BC that his enemies had poured molten gold down his throat.

Augustus (63 BC–AD 14)

Roman emperor worth approximately US$4.6 trillion, based on his estimated share of the imperial economy.

Calculating the personal wealth of a historical ruler is enough to give historians and economists alike a headache, but the sums attached to Augustus are truly head-spinning.

Not only did he oversee the finances of a mighty empire, but, after defeating Mark Antony and Cleopatra, he took ownership over Egypt. To be clear, the land of the pharaohs did not just become part of the Roman world – it was a personal province of Augustus. Estimates about what this did to his wealth suggest that he owned one-fifth of the imperial economy, which has been translated into a modern-day value of $4.6 trillion (almost £3.5 trillion).

Wu Zetian (AD 624–705)

Empress of China who ruled an economy valued at approximately US$16 trillion.

On top of being the only female emperor in China’s history, Wu Zetian may well hold the title as the richest woman of all time.

Having ruled the Tang Dynasty alongside her husband and in the name of her sons for decades, in AD 690 she proclaimed her own Zhou Dynasty and acted as sole sovereign for 15 years. Under her efficient and brutal leadership, the empire expanded and the economy flourished with the tea and silk trades to western nations. In fact, while she was empress, China accounted for around 23 per cent of the global GDP, which has been estimated to be at the $16 trillion (almost £12 trillion) mark. For context, the richest woman today – Alice Walton, the heiress of Walmart – has a fortune 120 times smaller.

William the Conqueror (c1028–1087)

King of England worth approximately US$230 billion.

After seizing the English throne in 1066, the conquering Duke of Normandy set about confiscating vast swathes of land and bringing the resources of the country under his personal control. For the next 20 years, revenue poured in through rents, taxation and plundered treasures, and William the Conqueror protected his position and his purse with new castles, most famously the White Tower, the central fortification of the Tower of London.

Not content with accumulating wealth for himself alone, he also handed out huge sums to his allies. One relative, Alan Rufus, received such extravagant rewards for his military service in the Norman Conquest that his fortune ballooned to around $194 billion (almost £145 billion), just off the pace of William’s $230 billion (£170 billion).

Mansa Musa (c1280–c1337)

Ruler of the Mali Empire worth approximately US$400 billion, by a speculative estimate.

A name that crops up on every list of the historical rich is Mansa Musa.

In the first half of the 14th century, he presided over the pinnacle of the Mali Empire, a vast realm in West Africa rich in gold and salt, and strategically placed for trade routes. Mansa Musa is often credited as the richest person in history due to his dragon-sitting-on-a-treasure-sized piles of gold, with his mines supplying the Islamic world. Most famously, when he embarked on a hajj to Mecca in 1324, he travelled with 60,000 people and long caravans of slaves, dressed in Persian silk, each carrying gold bars.

According to accounts of his fabulous parades in Cairo, Mansa Musa handed out so much gold that it caused a major devaluation of the precious metal and a currency crisis that lasted years. A conservative estimate of his adjusted wealth is $400 billion (almost £300 billion), although many historians refuse to give a figure at all, instead claiming his wealth was beyond calculation.

Jakob Fugger (1459–1525)

German merchant and banker worth up to US$400 billion.

As the man behind the scenes and pulling the purse strings of medieval politics, Jakob Fugger was far wealthier than emperors, kings and popes.

Born in 1459 into a successful merchant family, he possessed a canny head for business and bookkeeping, shifting from Italian textiles to a more diverse portfolio. Most lucratively, he engaged in silver and copper mining, and tried his hand as a banker. Offering loans to the rich and powerful made him even richer and more powerful, with every deal negotiated bringing in assets and compounding wealth. He funded military campaigns, loaned to the Vatican and acted as chief financier of the Habsburgs, securing the position of Holy Roman Emperors.

On his death in 1525, he left a fortune of 2 million guilders; in today’s money Fugger the Rich may have been worth as much as $400 billion (£300 billion).

Heshen (1750–1799)

Chinese imperial official worth up to US$270 billion.

Heshen has been described as the most corrupt official in Chinese history.

As a favourite of the Qianlong Emperor in the 18th century, he gained control over ministerial posts and imperial revenue, which allowed him to steal funds and take bribes on an almost-industrial scale. At the same time, he built his own commercial empire of banks and pawnshops. During a revolt in 1796, he made sure the military campaign to put it down was prolonged so that he could pocket money being allocated to the army. It all came crashing down with the death of the emperor in 1799, with Heshen arrested and forced to put himself to death. His property was seized, valued at 1.1 billion taels of silver, or possibly as much as $270 billion (£200 billion) in today’s money.

Andrew Carnegie (1835–1919)

Scottish-American steel industrialist worth over US$300 billion before his major charitable gifts.

Andrew Carnegie made his fortune with steel.

Born to a poor family in Scotland and immigrating to the United States as a child, he built a career at the Pennsylvania Railroad Company before setting up the first steel plants in the country in the 1870s. By the time he sold Carnegie Steel in 1901, it was worth around two per cent of the entire US gross domestic product (GDP). While that fortune – adjusted to over $300 billion (£225 billion) – earns his place on this list, Carnegie did not die in 1919 as one of history’s wealthiest people. After retiring, he dedicated his life to philanthropic pursuits and gave way most of his money, espousing the mantra: “The man who dies thus rich dies disgraced.”

John D Rockefeller (1839–1937)

American oil industrialist worth well over US$300 billion.

The Rockefeller name is a bulwark of American business: throughout the 20th century, it became synonymous with wealth and success, thanks to its patriarchal figurehead. John D Rockefeller founded Standard Oil Company in 1870, correctly predicting the potential impact of oil on the modern world, and under his leadership, the company grew so powerful that it refined more than 90 per cent of all the oil in the United States. He held the monopoly on what was quickly becoming one of the most precious resources, accruing a fortune worth well over $300 billion (almost £225 billion) today.

In 1916, he was recognised as the first American to hit the magic ten figures to become a billionaire.

Henry Ford (1863–1947)

American automobile industrialist worth up to US$200 billion.

Henry Ford forever changed the world of the 20th century by making the automobile available to the mass market and revolutionising industrial practices through the introduction of assembly line production.

His Ford Motor Company, founded in 1903, unveiled the Model T and sold 15 million of them around the world over the next two decades (no car sold more until the Volkswagen Beetle). Needless to say, this made Ford a fabulous fortune. He joined the billionaire club in the 1920s, only a few years after John D Rockefeller, and by the time of this death in 1947 he had the equivalent of up to $200 billion (£150 billion) today. And, of course, Ford's company is still going strong.

Osman Ali Khan (1886–1967)

Nizam of Hyderabad worth upwards of US$200 billion.

Here’s how rich Osman Ali Khan was: he used the Jacob Diamond – a 184-carat masterpiece and one of the largest diamonds in the world – as a paperweight. During his 37-year reign as nizam (ruler) of the Indian state of Hyderabad (1911-48), he built his monumental wealth by issuing his own currency and controlling the world’s primary diamond mines, including where the Jacob and Koh-i-Noor were unearthed.

His private treasury was reportedly bursting with gold, silver and precious jewels, which would be worth upwards of $200 billion (almost £150 billion) today. No wonder the cover of a 1937 issue of Time magazine described him as “the richest man in the world”.

issues.title: Why stopping SSRIs can cause anxiety: A rebound in serotonin neuron activity may play a role
issues.summary: Stopping an SSRI may release serotonin neurons from the restraint they experience during treatment, triggering a rebound in activity. A mouse study links this rebound, along with hippocampal activation, to anxiety after discontinuation.
issues.author: Vladimir Hedrih
issues.content_html:
A study of male mice found that stopping treatment with the SSRI antidepressant paroxetine was associated with increased activity in two brain areas involved in anxiety, the dorsal raphe nucleus and the ventral hippocampus. These changes appeared two days after treatment ended, when the mice also showed elevated anxiety-like behavior. Five days after discontinuation, the anxiety-like behavior had subsided, but activation of serotonin-producing neurons in the dorsal raphe nucleus persisted. The paper was published in Neuropharmacology.

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, or SSRIs, are a widely used class of antidepressant medications. They are commonly prescribed to treat depression and some anxiety disorders. SSRIs work by blocking the reabsorption of serotonin, a neurotransmitter involved in regulating mood and other psychological processes, thereby increasing its availability in the brain.

However, abruptly stopping SSRI treatment can cause withdrawal-like symptoms, including increased anxiety, sleep disturbances, and unusual sensory experiences. These symptoms typically appear within a few days of discontinuation and can persist for several weeks or even longer. Animal studies have shown that stopping SSRI treatment can also produce behavioral changes resembling anxiety, including increased vigilance and avoidance of potentially threatening environments.

Previous research by the same team found that anxiety-like behavior in mice appeared two days after paroxetine was discontinued but had disappeared by five days, although disturbances in sleep and reduced weight gain lasted longer. Scientists believe that these effects may involve changes in the activity of brain circuits regulating anxiety, particularly those involving serotonin-producing neurons.

Study author Helen M. Collins of the University of Oxford and colleagues investigated how discontinuing paroxetine affects c-Fos immunoreactivity in a range of brain regions linked to anxiety. The protein c-Fos helps regulate gene expression and is produced in increased amounts in neurons after they become active, which makes it useful as a marker of recent neuronal activity. Researchers can detect this protein using antibodies, a technique known as c-Fos immunoreactivity, to identify neurons that have recently been activated.

The study was conducted on male mice that were seven weeks old at the start of the study. The mice were housed in groups of three littermates. The researchers studied only males because their previous research did not find evidence that discontinuing paroxetine increases anxiety in female mice.

Mice were randomly assigned to one of three groups of 12. For 12 days, two groups received daily injections of paroxetine (10 mg/kg) and one group received saline injections. Afterward, the saline group and one paroxetine group continued their treatments for another two or five days, while the third group, the discontinuation group, was switched from paroxetine to saline injections.

All mice were then tested on an elevated plus maze, a standard test of anxiety-like behavior in rodents. Ninety minutes later, six or seven randomly selected mice from each group were euthanized, and their brains were examined for signs of recent neuronal activity using c-Fos immunoreactivity. The behavioral results from these mice were reported in the team’s earlier paper.

Two days after paroxetine discontinuation, when the mice showed elevated anxiety-like behavior, neural activity was increased in the dorsal raphe nucleus and the ventral hippocampus compared with mice receiving saline. No such increases were found in other anxiety-related regions the researchers examined, including the median raphe nucleus, prefrontal cortex, amygdala, periaqueductal grey, and paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus.

In the dorsal raphe nucleus, the main source of serotonin for the forebrain, the increased activity occurred in serotonin-producing neurons, including a subgroup of neurons that produce both serotonin and glutamate. The authors suggest that stopping an SSRI may suddenly release serotonin neurons from the inhibition they experience during ongoing treatment, producing a rebound in their activity.

Five days after discontinuation, serotonin neurons in the dorsal raphe nucleus were still more active, but the mice no longer showed increased anxiety-like behavior. Activity in the ventral hippocampus and in the serotonin-glutamate neurons had also returned to normal by this point. The authors note that activation of serotonin neurons alone may therefore not be sufficient to produce anxiety, while ventral hippocampus activity followed the same time course as the anxiety-like behavior.

“These findings suggest that, under the current conditions, paroxetine discontinuation is associated with a short-lasting activation of anxiety-promoting circuitry limited to DRN 5-HT neurons [dorsal raphe nucleus neurons that produce serotonin] and the hippocampus. This circuitry may contribute to symptoms such as anxiety that are a feature of SSRI discontinuation syndrome,” the study authors concluded.

The study contributes to the scientific understanding of brain changes following SSRI discontinuation. However, it should be noted that the study was conducted on mice, not humans, and effects in humans might differ. The study also included only male mice, and the brain analyses involved six or seven mice per group, which may have limited the ability to detect subtle changes in other brain regions. In addition, c-Fos provides only a snapshot of recent neural activity, and the study cannot establish that the observed brain changes caused the anxiety-like behavior.

The paper, “Increased c-Fos immunoreactivity in anxiety-related brain regions following paroxetine discontinuation,” was authored by Helen M. Collins, L. Sophie Gullino, Cara Fuller, Raquel Pinacho, David M. Bannerman, and Trevor Sharp.

issues.title: Focused ultrasound aimed deep into the brain may ease delusions, pilot study suggests
issues.summary: Many people with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder experience delusions despite medication. A small sham-controlled study suggests that gentle, focused sound waves directed deep into the brain may temporarily dial down delusional symptoms without surgery.
issues.author: Eric W. Dolan
issues.content_html:
A small pilot trial suggests that aiming gentle, noninvasive sound waves deep into the brain may temporarily ease delusions in adults living with chronic psychosis. In a randomized comparison against a fake stimulation session, 10 outpatients who received 10 minutes of low-intensity focused ultrasound directed at a deep brain hub showed a moderate drop in delusion severity without experiencing serious side effects. The preliminary findings were published in npj Acoustics.

Schizophrenia and related conditions such as schizoaffective disorder are chronic psychiatric illnesses that alter how a person perceives reality, thinks, and relates to the world around them. Two hallmark psychotic symptoms are hallucinations, such as hearing voices when no one is speaking, and delusions, which are fixed beliefs that persist even when contradicted by everyday evidence. Standard antipsychotic medications quiet these symptoms for many patients, yet a substantial number continue to experience distressing delusions despite ongoing drug treatment.

Brain-imaging studies link psychosis to abnormal signaling along a deep loop of neural pathways connecting the cerebral cortex, the brain’s outer layer, with central relay structures called the striatum, the globus pallidus, and the thalamus. Tucked near the middle of the brain beneath the cortex sits the globus pallidus interna, a paired cluster of nerve cells within the basal ganglia that serves as a primary output gate sending dopamine-influenced signals to the thalamus. Beyond helping coordinate physical movement, this pathway helps filter incoming information so the brain can judge which everyday events deserve attention.

In a 2023 brain-imaging study conducted by members of the same research group, unmedicated patients experiencing a first episode of schizophrenia showed unusually heightened communication between the right anterior globus pallidus interna and the dorsal anterior cingulate gyrus, a frontal brain region involved in weighing what demands attention. Stronger signaling along that link tracked with worse psychotic symptoms and predicted how well patients responded to eight weeks of medication, pointing to the right globus pallidus interna as a candidate for brain stimulation.

Targeting a deep brain hub without incisions

Reaching a structure buried roughly six centimeters beneath the brain’s outer membrane has historically posed a steep technical challenge. Standard noninvasive neuromodulation tools, such as magnetic coils held against the scalp, mainly influence tissue near the brain’s surface, whereas modulating the globus pallidus interna without destroying tissue has traditionally required neurosurgery to implant electrodes, as done in movement disorders like Parkinson’s disease.

Low-intensity transcranial ultrasound stimulation works differently: a curved acoustic device rests against the scalp and transmits focused, relatively low-frequency ultrasound waves through the skull to converge on a narrow, elongated zone of deep tissue, temporarily shifting nerve cell excitability without incisions or tissue heating.

To test whether this noninvasive technique could influence psychotic symptoms by targeting the right globus pallidus interna, Wei Qi collaborated with senior colleagues Donald C. Goff and Shy Shoham at NYU Grossman School of Medicine. Goff is the Marvin Stern Professor of Psychiatry and vice chair for research in the Department of Psychiatry at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and directs the Nathan S. Kline Institute for Psychiatric Research, while Shoham is a professor in the Department of Neuroscience at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and co-director of its Tech4Health Institute.

“Many people with schizophrenia continue to have delusions despite antipsychotic medication, and there are few options for them once medications have failed,” Qi, a clinical assistant professor in the Department of Psychiatry at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and a psychiatrist and researcher at Rockland Psychiatric Center and the Nathan S. Kline Institute for Psychiatric Research, told PsyPost. “Brain imaging and decades of research in movement disorders point to the globus pallidus interna, a deep hub in a circuit thought to help the brain decide which experiences feel important. Until recently, the only way to reach such a deep target was surgery. Low-intensity focused ultrasound allowed us to test, without surgery, whether modulating this circuit could affect psychotic symptoms.”

Earlier human experiments laid the groundwork for testing this approach in psychosis. First, a 2021 brain-imaging study of healthy volunteers demonstrated that aiming low-intensity ultrasound at the left globus pallidus reduced blood-oxygenation signals linked to neural activity both inside that deep hub and across connected brain networks during stimulation.

More recently, a clinical trial of adults with mood, anxiety, and trauma disorders found that focused ultrasound lowered activity in the left amygdala compared to a sham procedure, and a three-week course of repeated sessions produced moderate-to-large drops in depression, anxiety, trauma symptoms, and overall emotional distress. Only two previous studies had tested ultrasound stimulation in schizophrenia, one reporting an immediate drop in hallucinations after targeting other striatal areas in three patients and the other targeting the outer prefrontal cortex for social withdrawal and blunted emotion, leaving the right globus pallidus interna unexplored.

How the randomized crossover trial worked

Before treating patients, the engineering team calibrated their custom 350-kilohertz ultrasound device in a water tank and across the temple bone of two human skull specimens. Although passing through skull bone absorbed 83 to 88 percent of the acoustic intensity, the beam maintained a cigar-shaped focal zone measuring 5.6 millimeters wide by 27.5 millimeters long. Introducing the skull shifted the beam’s focus by an average of one millimeter, and estimated pressure and heating inside the brain remained well within international safety limits.

The researchers registered the trial on ClinicalTrials.gov in November 2022 ahead of recruitment, made the full protocol and analysis plan available on the registry alongside publicly posted analysis code, and kept individual patient records restricted to protect medical privacy. Designed as an initial pilot study to assess safety, tolerability, and preliminary symptom signals, the trial screened 15 adults and enrolled 11 outpatients aged 18 to 55 with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder and at least moderate psychotic symptoms between May 2023 and January 2024.

One volunteer withdrew after an initial brain scan, leaving 10 participants who completed every stage of the study. Those 10 participants had an average age of 37.5 years, were split evenly between men and women, and included four African American, three Asian, one Caucasian, and two adults who identified as mixed race or another category.

Before enrolling, every participant had to pass a psychiatrist’s evaluation of decision-making capacity and score 100 percent on a 10-item quiz covering the study’s procedures, risks, and alternatives. Six participants were taking stable doses of antipsychotic medication (paliperidone, aripiprazole, quetiapine, or haloperidol), and four had been off antipsychotic drugs for at least four weeks; all 10 maintained that pre-enrollment status throughout the trial.

Using a randomized crossover design, each volunteer attended two sessions spaced one week apart: one active ultrasound session and one sham session, delivered in random order so that neither the participants nor the clinical raters knew which session was active. Each participant first underwent a structural MRI scan to map their individual brain anatomy. During the visits, foam blocks held the seated participant’s head steady while optical tracking cameras monitored reflective markers on both the head and the ultrasound device in real time. Coupled to the scalp with ultrasound gel and a water-filled membrane, the device was aimed directly at the right globus pallidus interna.

During the 10-minute active session, the system delivered brief ultrasound pulses in ten cycles of 30 seconds on and 30 seconds off, actively transmitting sound for 5 percent of each 30-second window. During the sham session, the equipment ran at identical settings, but an air layer inside the water cushion blocked the ultrasound waves from entering the skull.

Participants completed brief questionnaires rating delusions and auditory hallucinations at six points around each visit: beforehand, during stimulation, immediately afterward, one hour later, one day later, and seven days later. They also took the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, a short screening test of memory and thinking skills, before and one hour after each session, while clinicians tracked physical and psychiatric side effects and suicidal thoughts through day seven. Resting-state functional MRI scans were collected before and after each session as well, though technical issues later prevented those brain scans from being analyzed.

Moderate reductions in delusions and an unexpected delay

Across all post-baseline assessments combined, delusion scores declined by an average of 1.2 points after active ultrasound stimulation, compared with a 0.4-point average increase after sham stimulation, against session-baseline averages ranging from roughly 12 to 16 points. In the primary statistical model accounting for assessment timing and session order, active ultrasound was associated with an estimated 1.56-point greater reduction in delusion scores than sham, corresponding to a moderate effect size (Cohen’s d = 0.68). At the individual level, symptom trajectories varied considerably from person to person across the two-week crossover sequence.

“The difference between real and sham stimulation was moderate in size and statistically robust for a study this small,” Qi noted. “Still, with only 10 participants, the estimate is imprecise, and the benefit beyond the first days is unknown. Larger, longer trials are needed to know how big and how lasting the effect really is.”

Changes in auditory hallucination ratings across the post-baseline assessments were not statistically significant between active ultrasound and sham, in contrast to the immediate drop reported in the earlier three-patient trial targeting other regions of the striatum. Differences on the cognitive test one hour after stimulation fell just short of statistical significance, with scores rising an average of 0.2 points after real ultrasound and dipping 1.0 point after sham.

After finishing the study, six of the 10 participants accurately guessed which session was real, a rate not statistically distinguishable from chance, and follow-up checks indicated that guessing accurately was unrelated to delusion change. Evaluated descriptively rather than through a formal statistical test because of the small sample, session-baseline scores also showed no consistent pattern of carryover from one week to the next.

No serious adverse events occurred in either condition. Seven of the 10 participants reported at least one mild, temporary symptom increase after active ultrasound, while all 10 reported at least one side effect after sham stimulation. Reported complaints included brief fatigue, headache, mild stomach discomfort, and minor upticks in delusions or hallucinations, along with a single moderate report of feeling detached from surroundings after a sham session.

Asked what the average person should take from the trial, Qi said, “It’s an encouraging first step, but it is not yet a treatment.”

An exploratory analysis of individual time points hinted at an unexpected temporal pattern, although the pilot trial was not designed to confirm effects at isolated days. Rather than peaking during the 10-minute stimulation and fading right away, the estimated gap in delusion reduction between active and sham sessions stood at 1.90 points one day afterward and widened to 2.70 points seven days afterward. However, the day-one difference did not reach statistical significance even before adjustment, and none of the five post-baseline comparisons remained statistically significant after adjusting for multiple testing.

To explain that gradual pattern, the authors propose that pulsed ultrasound may initiate lasting neuroplastic adjustments in glutamate-related signaling within the right globus pallidus interna and its connected cortical loop, consolidating over days until the brain’s tendency to assign undue importance to everyday experiences, known as aberrant salience, subsides. They note that durable responses have appeared in other ultrasound studies of deep brain hubs, including a 2024 clinical study of chronic pain where a single session targeting a pain-processing region eased pain through day seven, and a 2023 case report on severe treatment-resistant depression where deep-brain ultrasound preceded remission lasting up to 44 days.

“Seeing an effect on psychosis wasn’t a surprise, because that was our hypothesis,” Qi explained. “The pattern was surprising. We expected an immediate effect that would fade, as with many forms of brain stimulation.”

“Instead, the improvement seemed to build over the following days,” Qi added. “That suggests ultrasound may trigger lasting changes in how the circuit adapts, rather than acting like an on/off switch.”

Caveats and next steps for ultrasound research

There are a few things to keep in mind when weighing these early findings. Testing a single 10-minute session in 10 outpatients over one week makes this a preliminary proof-of-concept study rather than confirmation of clinical efficacy. The authors note that the statistical effect size for delusions (0.68) is comparable to the 0.47 average reported across placebo-controlled trials of antipsychotic medications, yet the brief questionnaire used at the six check-ins was built to track moment-to-moment fluctuations rather than clinically meaningful recovery. As a result, it remains uncertain how much an average 1.56-point drop on a roughly 12-to-16-point baseline translates into noticeable relief in daily life.

Qi also drew a line between the experimental technique and treatments already in clinics. “This is not a cure, and it’s not a replacement for medication; all participants stayed on their usual treatment,” Qi emphasized. “It is also different from the high-intensity focused ultrasound approved for tremor, which destroys a small area of tissue.”

“Our approach uses much lower energy to change brain activity temporarily,” Qi continued. “Finally, this treatment isn’t available outside research. It is not ready for clinical use.”

Several technical hurdles also limit what the pilot data can establish about how the stimulation worked. Because technical problems rendered the resting-state functional MRI scans uninterpretable, the researchers could not confirm that the ultrasound beam altered neural activity inside the right globus pallidus interna as intended. Acoustic dosing was also calibrated using two human skull specimens rather than tailored to each volunteer’s skull thickness, which can affect how much sound energy reaches deep tissue. In addition, blinding was checked only with a two-choice guess at the end of the study; with six of 10 participants guessing accurately, expectation effects cannot be excluded, and the authors state that the trial should not be considered fully double-blinded.

“We aim to run a larger trial with repeated sessions and longer follow-up, to test how durable and reproducible the effect is,” Qi stated. “We also want to measure how ultrasound changes the underlying circuits involved in delusions using functional MRI.”

Looking back on the pilot trial, Qi credited the interdisciplinary partnership behind the study, adding, “This study was a team effort across psychiatry, engineering, and statistics, and I’m grateful to my co-authors, our participants, and the funding foundations (Doris Duke Fund and Brain & Behavior Research Foundation) for their support.”

The study, “Transcranial ultrasound stimulation of the right globus pallidus interna in schizophrenia: A randomized, sham-controlled pilot study,” was authored by Wei Qi, Alon Gilad, Michele Santacatterina, Spencer Brinker, Gillian Capichioni, Fumika Ando, Shy Shoham, and Donald C. Goff.

issues.title: Mindfulness therapy alters brain waves in major depressive disorder
issues.summary: Combining mindfulness therapy with standard antidepressant medication reduces depression symptoms while simultaneously altering the brain's electrical activity. A new study reveals how cognitive training shifts specific brain waves to help patients better regulate their emotions.
issues.author: Karina Petrova
issues.content_html:
Combining mindfulness training with standard antidepressant medication reduces depression symptoms more effectively than medication alone while simultaneously altering electrical activity in the brain. The new research, published in the journal Mindfulness, reveals that adding cognitive therapy centered on awareness to a patient’s routine care leads to distinct shifts in brain waves associated with emotional regulation.

Major depressive disorder involves persistent low mood, loss of interest in daily activities, and physical or cognitive changes that can severely disrupt a person’s life. The condition is associated with altered functional connections in the brain, particularly in networks responsible for processing emotions and self-referential thoughts. Standard treatments often include medications like antidepressants, but a large portion of patients do not experience full relief from these drugs alone. To improve outcomes, clinicians sometimes supplement medication with additional psychological therapies.

One such intervention is mindfulness-based cognitive therapy. This group-based psychosocial treatment combines meditation practices, such as deep breathing and guided body scans, with cognitive behavioral strategies designed to break patterns of negative thinking. The therapy aims to help patients observe their thoughts without judgment, which may prevent the spiral of rumination that often leads to a relapse of depressive symptoms.

Lead researcher Seyed Ruhollah Hosseini of Ferdowsi University of Mashhad in Iran and colleagues conducted the study to explore how this therapeutic combination affects the brain’s underlying electrical networks. While behavioral improvements from mindfulness are well documented, the neurobiological changes driving those benefits are less understood. The research team sought to map the specific brain wave changes that occur when mindfulness techniques are layered onto standard pharmacological care.

The researchers recruited 66 women diagnosed with major depressive disorder who were seeking treatment at psychiatric clinics. All participants were prescribed a standard daily dose of the antidepressant citalopram. The researchers then randomly assigned the women to one of two groups.

One group received only their usual medication and standard psychiatric monitoring. The second group received the same medication but also attended an eight-week mindfulness-based cognitive therapy program. This program involved weekly two-hour group sessions led by certified psychotherapists, alongside daily home meditation practice using audio recordings.

To track clinical progress, the research team administered the Beck Depression Inventory-II, a standard questionnaire evaluating depression severity, before and after the eight-week period. They also recorded the participants’ brain waves using an electroencephalogram, a test that detects electrical activity in the brain using small sensors placed on the scalp. The participants rested with their eyes closed during the recording to capture their baseline brain activity.

By analyzing the electroencephalogram data, the researchers could look at different frequencies of brain waves, such as theta, alpha, and beta waves, which correspond to different mental states. They used a specialized software program called exact low-resolution electromagnetic tomography. This software estimates where electrical signals originate within the brain’s three-dimensional structure based on the surface recordings.

Both groups experienced a reduction in their depression symptoms over the eight weeks. At the start of the study, participants in both groups scored an average of around 28 on the depression scale, indicating moderate to severe symptoms. By the end of the trial, the group receiving only medication saw their average score drop to about 13.

The women who participated in the mindfulness therapy reported a steeper decline in their depression scores, dropping to an average of 11.6. Statistical analysis confirmed that the addition of the mindfulness program had a robust effect on reducing depressive symptoms beyond the benefits of the medication alone.

The brain wave data revealed distinct neurological differences between the two groups after the treatment period. The women in the mindfulness group showed a decrease in theta wave activity in areas of the brain likely corresponding to the left insula. The insula is a deep brain structure heavily involved in processing emotions and bodily sensations, a function often disrupted in depression.

The mindfulness group also displayed an increase in upper alpha wave activity across several regions of the right hemisphere, including areas of the frontal and parietal lobes. Alpha waves are typically associated with a relaxed, resting state. Increased alpha activity in these regions may reflect a calming of overly active emotional responses and a normalization of brain rhythms.

Additionally, the researchers observed an increase in low beta wave activity in the mindfulness group, again localized to areas suggesting the involvement of the left insula. Beta waves are often linked to active, focused cognitive processing. The researchers suggest that the left insula helps integrate bodily states with cognitive and emotional experiences.

The combination of these electrical changes points to a neurological reorganization following mindfulness training. By altering activity in areas related to bodily awareness and emotional regulation, the therapy may help patients better manage their psychological distress.

The study relied on a relatively basic electroencephalogram setup with 19 electrodes on the scalp, which provides a limited spatial resolution of brain activity. Because of this limitation, the specific brain regions identified by the software, such as the insula, are only probabilistic estimates rather than definitive anatomical locations. The researchers noted that these structural identifications remain suggestive.

Confirming these specific brain regions will require future studies using high-density electrode arrays or functional magnetic resonance imaging. The research was also conducted exclusively on women, meaning the results may not apply to men or non-binary individuals experiencing depression. The study also lacked participant blinding, a common issue in psychological interventions.

Participants in the study knew which treatment group they were in, which can sometimes influence how people report their own symptoms on questionnaires. Future investigations will need to follow participants over a longer period to see if the brain wave alterations and mood improvements hold up months or years after the mindfulness program ends. Incorporating objective clinician ratings alongside self-reported scales could also strengthen the reliability of the clinical outcomes.

The study, “Can Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy Change the Cortical Electrical Activity of the Brain in Major Depressive Disorder?,” was authored by Seyed Ruhollah Hosseini, Nikzad Ghanbari, Maryam Shamsaei, and Elaheh Kardan Ghabel.

issues.title: Deep Work in a Messy Workspace Is Like Sleeping at an Airport
issues.summary: Trying to do deep work in a distracting workspace is like trying to sleep at an airport. The activity is possible. The environment keeps fighting you. I contrast that with a quiet, comfortable place, where rest comes more naturally. What does your workspace make easy, and what does it make difficult? The benefit I’m after […]
issues.author: Thanh Pham
issues.content_html:
Trying to do deep work in a distracting workspace is like trying to sleep at an airport. The activity is possible. The environment keeps fighting you. I contrast that with a quiet, comfortable place, where rest comes more naturally.

What does your workspace make easy, and what does it make difficult?

The benefit I’m after is more reliable focus. Consistent focus is a system. I identify the meaningful work, design an environment that supports it, and reduce incoming interruptions. The goal is to make focus the default.

Three outcomes, three small tasks, three maintenance tasks

On a busy day I plan with a method I call 3-3-3.

Three major outcomes. These are the results that would make the day count.

Three smaller tasks. Give each one a slot next to the bigger outcomes.

Three maintenance tasks. Email, meetings, and upkeep belong in the plan. The method gives them a bounded place alongside meaningful progress.

The constraints force prioritization before the day fills itself. Make a worksheet with three slots in each category. This is my planning practice, and finishing all nine is not the assignment. Quick heads-up on the name. My 3-3-3 means categories of tasks. Three hours of deep work is a separate idea, so use these labels.

Decide, then experiment

Does testing a new AI tool feel like work? It can be a sophisticated form of procrastination. I do this. Testing tools and following AI updates can feel productive while the actual deliverable waits. I have not solved it for good.

My boundary is plain. I write down the major outcomes, the smaller tasks, and the maintenance tasks first. Once those commitments are complete, I give myself permission to experiment.

Name the deliverable your next AI session should advance. Or explicitly label the session as exploration.

Related example. I spent about 10 minutes helping someone define what organized meant for a cluttered Documents folder. The list covered naming conventions, active projects, inactive projects, archives, and deletion criteria. I gave those rules to Claude Cowork and gave it access to the folder. It organized thousands of files and folders within minutes. That scale and that timing are my anecdotal report.

The useful preparation was clarifying the decisions. Write a short file-organization policy before an AI-assisted cleanup. Back up the folder, test a small folder first, and approve any deletion yourself. I’m recommending those safeguards on top of what happened.

Save, bookmark, close, break, reopen

I reset my digital workspace between tasks instead of carrying every open window into the next assignment. I save the work. References worth keeping become bookmarks rather than permanent visual reminders. I close the apps and browser tabs, take a short break, and open only what the next task requires.

I typically work with two to four tabs because of this habit. That number is a side effect. Try the sequence on the next task you complete.

A four-lever checklist

I audit focus environments through four levers.

Visual. Clear the clutter in front of you. Facing a blank wall is one example from a session.

Auditory. Reduce distracting sounds. Music without lyrics is worth a test. See what it does to your focus, and keep the choice personal.

Digital. Close unnecessary applications. Closing email is one example.

Social. Create a signal that discourages interruptions. A door sign does this. Headphones can too.

Use friction on purpose across all four. Distractions get harder to reach. Meaningful work gets easier to start.

Which lever is weakest for you? Fix that one first.

Ten to fifteen minutes of news

A person in a workshop worried they would miss the news. Worried you’ll miss something if it isn’t on your start page? That fear makes sense to me. Stay informed inside a boundary.

Move news out of the browser’s default view and into a routine, about 10 to 15 minutes in the morning. Replace a news-heavy start page with a neutral page and schedule the short check. The habit stays. It loses the chance to interrupt every browsing session.

Client email can be the work

Another participant asked how to classify client correspondence. Responding to customers can be essential work. Judge that by the role and the outcome. Ask whether unlimited inbox time crowds out other valuable responsibilities.

Set communication windows that fit your client commitments. Protect a separate block for delivery or business development.

Notifications off, then a short list back on

My detox starts with notifications off. Then I restore the ones worth receiving. Match the exceptions to real communication responsibilities. The lesson is selective access. Stay reachable for the communication that is actually your responsibility.

I add friction on top when I need it. Do Not Disturb on the phone and the computer. The phone goes in another room. No dedicated email app on the phone. Browser access stays available, and the extra steps make casual checking less appealing.

Remove one unnecessary notification today. Tomorrow, pick one interruption source and either remove it or add friction.

Find one distraction your environment makes too easy. A notification sound, visual movement, or a repeated interruption. Change that default today.

issues.title: I Thought I Had About 200 Screenshots. The Count Was 361.
issues.summary: I was in the middle of a live class when I tried to guess one month of screenshots. 150 to 200 files. The archive goes back to 2014, so you’d think I’d have a feel for it. I asked the assistant to count. It came back with 361. I didn’t sort them myself. I told […]
issues.author: Thanh Pham
issues.content_html:
I was in the middle of a live class when I tried to guess one month of screenshots. 150 to 200 files. The archive goes back to 2014, so you’d think I’d have a feel for it.

I asked the assistant to count. It came back with 361.

I didn’t sort them myself. I told it to inspect each image, give every file a descriptive name, and move it into a monthly folder. Then I went back to teaching. Renamed screenshots started showing up in the organized folder while class was still going. At the point I checked, the task was still running. I never verified that all 361 were done.

Have you ever been that wrong about a pile you look at all the time?

The target I organize around is finding what I need within seconds. The question I care about is whether I can reliably find this later. AI lets me shift the effort from filing everything by hand to defining how retrieval should work.

Duplicate the folder first

Screenshots are where I start. You can duplicate the folder and watch what the assistant does.

The instructions stay short. Group the screenshots into YYYY-MM folders. Inspect what each image contains. Rename each file with the date, then three to five keywords that describe the picture. Keep that date format identical every time. The keywords keep the filename useful when you browse the folder with no assistant open.

In class, the assistant interpreted the picture itself.

Run the first pass on a copy. Begin with default permissions. Observe what comes back. Expand access only once you understand the workflow. Preserve a backup. If something is going to be deleted, you approve it. Then compare the output with the originals on that first batch.

Screenshots can still contain sensitive information. A clean test still leaves prompt injection and data exposure in play. I’m no security researcher. Local file access is a separate question from local processing and from privacy. I demonstrated that folder access in Claude Cowork and in a Codex desktop app. Check current features and permissions before you copy the setup.

Let it execute, then repeat it at 5 p.m.

The step past chatting is a bounded task the assistant carries out.

I gave a desktop assistant one selected folder. It could read the files, create files, rename screenshots, and move them. I stopped explaining the system and delegated the execution.

Try it on one low-risk folder. Ask for an inventory before any renames or moves. Read what it lists. Then decide what it may change.

A cleanup you never repeat just waits for the next backlog. After the screenshot rules were in place, I created a daily 5 p.m. task to sort new screenshots with that same structure. I created that scheduled task in Claude Cowork during the class, and I said the app needed to remain open. Review the first few runs yourself.

Build the index, then ask something you already know

I’ve kept a long-standing note archive in Evernote. In that class I had the assistant turn it into a library I could search. It reported extracting 1,700 notes from 22 notebooks and creating an index. I was looking at Markdown notes and indexes. Those counts are the assistant’s report from the demo. I did not validate every note.

I opened a fresh task and asked for a summary of my December 2025 weekly reviews. It located the relevant material and summarized it within seconds. The speed was my observation from the room. I never ran it as a benchmark. I also have not independently checked every attachment or every sentence of that summary.

It held locations and metadata. The assistant consulted the index, then opened the source notes needed to answer. Build that map once. Consult it before you open a stack of documents.

Export one notebook. Ask for a table of contents of the folder. Test it with three questions whose answers you already know.

One category, on purpose

Where do you lose the most time looking for things?

Participants kept coming back to the same problem. Information scattered across multiple locations. I’m not naming anyone.

Pick one category you regularly struggle to retrieve. Meeting notes, screenshots, files, photos, or email. Gather a safe working copy, and decide the one trusted location for that material. Write down what successful retrieval looks like. A focused retrieval problem gives the first workflow a purpose you can test.

Email and photos need a slower start. Confirm the export, the access you are granting, and the privacy requirements. Direct folder access is something you verify for each app.

One suggestion, and I did not verify this one live. A small sample of your sent email can become a writing-voice profile. Redact it, and remove other people’s personal details. Read the profile it writes. Test the profile on an unsent draft. Leave the rest of the mailbox alone. Approve anything before it is sent.

Do this on a copy, this week

Duplicate one month of screenshots. Point Claude Cowork at that copy. Stay on default permissions. Ask for an inventory before it changes any names or locations. On a small batch, group the files into YYYY-MM folders, inspect each image, and rename the file with the date plus three to five keywords. Compare the batch with your originals. Keep the backup. You approve any deletion.

One copy. If the batch holds up, then you can talk about a second folder.

issues.title: A 5 a.m. Alarm Didn’t Fix My Mornings
issues.summary: I tried waking up at 5 a.m. When that meant too little sleep, I could manage a few good hours, and then I crashed. The rest of the day was a struggle. Brooks naturally wakes early. I’m no sleep doctor, and I won’t turn his schedule or mine into a credential. Build a good start […]
issues.author: Thanh Pham
issues.content_html:
I tried waking up at 5 a.m. When that meant too little sleep, I could manage a few good hours, and then I crashed. The rest of the day was a struggle.

Brooks naturally wakes early. I’m no sleep doctor, and I won’t turn his schedule or mine into a credential. Build a good start to your day around your sleep needs.

What actually sat between me and meaningful work was the preparation. Sorting email. Checking the calendar. Reviewing meeting history. Deciding where to start. I was doing all of that before I had touched anything that mattered. Now an agent assembles the context, and I begin the day with a direction.

Inbox triage can be the only reason for an early start. Hand that sorting to an agent and the administrative reason for the early alarm can disappear. A later start tells me that reason was gone. It does not tell me how much additional sleep came with it.

Hand the night-before plan to an agent

I still plan the night before. I used to do the whole pass myself. At 9 p.m. the repetitive part now runs as an AI workflow.

The agent reviews unfinished tasks. It inspects tomorrow’s calendar. It compares both against my goals for the next 30 days. From that, it proposes one thing to do first the next morning, then secondary options.

I kept the benefit of planning ahead. The preparation is what I delegated. The agent recommends. I decide.

Already doing some version of this by hand? Turn that evening checklist into a repeatable instruction. Give it the same inputs: unfinished tasks, tomorrow’s calendar, and your goals for the next 30 days. Ask for a single first priority and a short list of backups. Read the proposal before you adopt it.

Replace the inbox scan with a brief

Do you open email to figure out what your day is?

I stopped using the morning inbox scan as my launcher. An agent reviews email, calendar commitments, and relevant meeting history before I start, then surfaces the day’s priorities and the messages that need attention. I want a clear starting point and a short reply list. That’s the brief.

This is a workflow you configure. Connect only information sources you have approved. While you are still establishing whether you can trust it, check the brief against the originals.

One question before you start

AI can prepare my priorities. I still choose them.

Brooks warns that agents can gravitate toward tasks with due dates and overlook important work that is not urgent. A clean brief can still be aimed at the nearest deadline.

I let the agent assemble the options. Then I check the proposed first task. What important, non-urgent work is missing? If the top item only clears a deadline, I start with the work that advances a meaningful goal.

Flip the script

I used to ask for a personalized workflow and hope a generic prompt captured how I work. Now I flip the script. The agent asks me four to six targeted questions before it proposes a solution. Those questions reveal the context it was missing.

Paste this in before you ask for the brief:

“Before designing my morning brief, ask me four to six questions about my goals, schedule, information sources, and notification preferences.”

Answer them. Then look at what it proposes.

Two delivery windows

My updates arrive in two windows, and the rest of the morning stays quiet. A short morning brief carries priorities and essential information. Around 11 a.m. I get the fuller pass: email replies, follow-ups, and relationship news. The agent gathers in the background. My morning stays available for focused work.

11 a.m. fits me. Put your fuller delivery after your first focused block. Collection can run whenever. Interruption should wait.

The later window is where relationship news shows up. My agent reviews public updates about people I know and includes the relevant bits. A personal note, if one is warranted, is one I write and send myself. Monitoring on one side. The human note on mine.

Want to try a smaller version? Use public sources. Keep the pilot small. Decide yourself whether you respond and how.

Write the permissions down

My line is simple. Preparation can be automated. Actions that affect money or reputation require a human sign-off.

The agent can read relevant information and draft communications. Messages that go out under my name are ones I have personally reviewed. Finances stay read-only. Reputation-sensitive work stays read-only. Writes wait for manual approval. I send outbound messages myself, on purpose. I want the calmer morning and I want the final say on what I commit to.

Read access. List the email, calendar, and meeting history it may see. Mark finances and reputation-sensitive sources as read-only.

Drafting. Let it prepare priorities and draft replies. A draft still belongs to you.

Your approval. Money, commitments, and anything sent under your name wait until you say so.

Here’s the only move I’d make tonight. Identify one recurring morning preparation task. Just one. The email triage, the calendar check, the meeting-history review, or the decision about where to start. Hand that task to an agent with a clear instruction, and in the morning ask what important, non-urgent work it left out.

issues.title: Four Meetings, No Lunch, and the Dinner That Brought My Energy Back
issues.summary: Right before a vacation, I squeezed roughly four meetings into 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. Short breaks. No lunch. I finished depleted. Dinner that evening was with three friends I hadn’t seen in a while. On the walk home, I had energy I didn’t have at 3 p.m. I used to think recovery meant being […]
issues.author: Thanh Pham
issues.content_html:
Right before a vacation, I squeezed roughly four meetings into 11 a.m. to 3 p.m. Short breaks. No lunch. I finished depleted.

Dinner that evening was with three friends I hadn’t seen in a while. On the walk home, I had energy I didn’t have at 3 p.m.

I used to think recovery meant being alone or doing nothing. Time with the right people gave me energy back. I still needed the lunch I skipped. Food, sleep, and breaks belong in the day too. Name one relationship or social plan that leaves you more energized, and make room for it.

A full calendar can still exhaust you

I use a frame I call TEA: time, energy, and attention. You can manage time well and still end exhausted, because energy ran out.

Creative writing is where I notice it. I can sustain one strong writing session in a day. I can’t repeat that same session morning, afternoon, and evening.

An open slot tells me the time is free. My energy for a second writing session may already be gone.

The goal is meaningful work I can repeat. Before you fill tomorrow, find one demanding task sitting in a low-energy window and one recovery break that is missing.

Hero mode

Hero mode is simple. Demanding work goes in the window where I’m sharpest. Lately mine has been roughly 10 a.m. to noon.

List ten tasks you do most weeks. Label each H, M, or L for high, medium, or low energy. Are the H tasks landing while you’re sharp? An empty afternoon is a lousy home for deep work if that’s your dip. Move one high-energy task.

On a good window I can focus for about 90 minutes to two hours. That’s my experience. I’m no doctor.

Four energy layers

Sometimes the answer really is sleep. I still check four layers, so I fix the one that’s actually thin.

Physical energy. Sleep, movement, food, and recovery all sit here. Skipping lunch hit me on this layer.

Emotional energy. Stress, relationships, and emotional load. The four meetings took from this. Dinner with three friends gave some back.

Mental energy. Overload, ambiguity, and decisions.

Spiritual energy. Meaning, identity, and alignment with what you care about. Religion might be part of that for you. I use this layer as a coaching frame on my own weeks.

Choose the biggest bottleneck and write one small improvement for this week.

Two leaks I keep paying for

New AI tools excite me and overload me. The pace of change, the pile of tools, the stimulation of trying things. A tool can be useful and still cost attention. Is your AI exploration helping you finish meaningful work, or adding mental load? I deal with that overload myself.

Ambiguity is the quieter leak. No finish line, and I tweak and rearrange after the useful progress has slowed. I struggle with this. Defining done is an energy decision and a project decision.

Pick one lingering project and write what done looks like before you touch it again. If AI is part of that project, write the finish line before you experiment further.

Ask the last three days

Before I design a week, I audit the last three days with three questions.

When did I feel sharpest?

What drained me more than I expected?

What gave me energy back?

I look at physical energy, concentration, and emotional steadiness. You can finish a lot and still be flat. Treat the answers as a gut check, then plan for the person those three days described. Ignore the imaginary you who is equally focused all day.

Write the answers in a note before your next planning session.

Recovery menu

A break is easier when the choice is already made. I keep a recovery menu where I can see it.

Two minutes. I get up and fetch a glass of water. I’m away from the screen.

Ten minutes. I walk.

Twenty minutes. I take a longer walk, away from the workspace.

I want movement, a screen break, and a change of environment. Your menu should match what restores you. People kept asking what a break should be, so I made a menu. Some people keep theirs as a desktop background.

Make a two-minute option, a ten-minute option, and a twenty-minute option. Keep the menu visible. Test one default this week.

Mine is a ten-minute walk after lunch. Familiar route. No phone, no headphones, no audio. I call it my Daily Reset. I tried to hold an evening walk and my evenings were often booked, so the habit wouldn’t stick. I moved it to midday.

I grew up with the Dutch practice of uitwaaien, and the lunch walk is my version of that. I stop taking information in. I come back to the desk more able to focus. Try one device-free walk after lunch and notice how you feel when you sit down again.

Two lists

Write what occupied most of the last three days. Write the values that matter most to you. Look at both.

Does the second list show up anywhere in the first?

Work and bills can own a lot of hours. Let them. What you care about still needs a deliberate spot, including a value like quality time. That dinner was a small block of it, and it restored me. Schedule one small action for a value that has been living on leftovers.

Five days

Rate your energy from 1 to 10 at a few points each day, for five days. Find the strongest window. Put one important, demanding task in it. Add one recovery ritual and keep it.

Then write an Energy Blueprint: your biggest energy bottleneck, and one commitment you can remove, renegotiate, or buffer.

Tonight, answer those three questions in a note. Tomorrow, put the thing that gave you energy back on the calendar.

issues.title: My 2019 Annual Review
issues.summary: Another year complete. Here’s a quick recap of 2019, which also happened to be one of the craziest years of my life. As always, this Annual Review will answer three questions. What went well this year? What didn’t go so well this year? What did I learn? Before we begin, it is worth noting that […]
issues.author: James Clear
issues.content_html:
Another year complete. Here’s a quick recap of 2019, which also happened to be one of the craziest years of my life.

As always, this Annual Review will answer three questions.

  1. What went well this year?
  2. What didn’t go so well this year?
  3. What did I learn?

Before we begin, it is worth noting that every Annual Review is a personal process. This is simply an overview of what my year looked like, not advice for how you should live your life. (That said, you are always welcome to use this general format for your own Annual Review.)

1. What went well this year?

I had a lot to celebrate this year.

Book sales.Atomic Habits launched in October 2018, which meant that 2019 was the first full calendar year it had been available. I came in with big aspirations, but I think it’s fair to say that book sales have outpaced my expectations.

As of December 2019:

  • Over 1.3 million copies sold worldwide
  • 12 consecutive months on the New York Times bestseller list
  • 4.8/5 stars on Amazon with over 1,800 reviews
  • 4.8/5 stars on Audible with over 25,000 ratings
  • Over 15 national TV segments in the United States, Canada, and Australia
  • Translated into 40+ languages

This has been a wild ride to say the least.

Of course, the greatest reward has been hearing from readers. It seems like nearly every day someone tells me that Atomic Habits helped them lose weight or start a business or make some positive change in their life. People are finding real value in the ideas and it feels great to produce something useful.

3-2-1 Newsletter. My new project for 2019 was launching the 3-2-1 newsletter, which shares 3 ideas from me, 2 quotes from others, and 1 question to ponder each week. I had been struggling to write consistently during the first half of the year (discussed below) and this new format offered something I knew I could stick with despite a busy schedule. (Sometimes I have to take my own medicine and scale my habits down.)

I didn’t realize it at the time, but it turns out to have been a good idea. I feel good because I’m producing new work each week and the response from subscribers has been quite favorable. Many readers tell me it’s the only newsletter they actually read as soon as it hits their inbox.

Audience growth. I didn’t write many new articles this year, but thanks to the buzz generated by Atomic Habits and the momentum of the 3-2-1 newsletter, audience growth remained strong.

Here’s what the year looked like:

  • 5 new articles published this year (fewest ever; discussed in next section)
  • 353,970 new email subscribers in 2019
  • 586,638 total email subscribers as of December 31, 2019
  • 10,848,250 unique visitors in 2019
  • 47,308,712 total visitors since launching on November 12, 2012

Even after doing this for a few years, the scale of the internet still blows me away. I’m grateful to have the opportunity to share my work with so many people.

Twitter and Instagram. I didn’t put much energy into social media for a long time, but the web has evolved in the last five years and social media plays an important role now. This was the first year I put consistent effort into Twitter and Instagram, and it paid off. My audience doubled on both platforms this year. Feel free to join the fun and follow me on Twitter and on Instagram.

Travel. This was the craziest travel year of my life and, in all likelihood, the craziest I will ever have. I spent a total of 158 nights away from home this year, which means I spent 43% of the year not sleeping in my own bed. It’s a pace I will probably (hopefully?) never match again.

Here’s the rundown…

18 states (0 new) – Arizona, California (5x!), Colorado (2x), Florida (2x), Georgia, Hawaii, Illinois (2x), Indiana (3x), Maryland, Nebraska (2x), Nevada, New York (5x!), Ohio, Pennsylvania (3x), Tennessee (2x), Texas (2x), Utah, and Virginia.

14 countries (7 new) – Australia (2x!), Canada (2x), Croatia, Denmark, Greece, England, Iceland, Ireland, Japan, Malaysia, Singapore, Spain, Sweden, and the United Arab Emirates.

While I love traveling, I did feel a bit guilty about the number of flights I took this year and the resulting pollution. In response, I decided to buy carbon offsets not only to cover my flights, but also to be entirely carbon neutral for 2019. I bought mine through Project Wren, and it wasn’t nearly as expensive as I expected.

New restaurants. Whenever I travel to a new city, I like to ask for restaurant recommendations on Twitter. Oh man, did you all set me up this year. I had so many great meals thanks to reader suggestions.

I feel compelled to repay you all by sharing some of my favorites (in no order):

  • Los Angeles, CA — fundamental LA
  • Denver, CO — Mercantile Provisions
  • Honolulu, HI — Marukame Udon
  • New York, NY — Manhatta (my meal of the year)
  • Philadelphia, PA — Zahav (runner up)
  • Melbourne, Australia — Chin Chin
  • Sydney, Australia — NOMAD
  • Sydney, Australia — Mr. Wong
  • Toronto, Canada — PAI
  • Dubrovnik, Croatia — Pantarul
  • Dubrovnik, Croatia — Taj Mahal
  • London, England — Nopi
  • London, England — Dishoom
  • Athens, Greece — Atitamos
  • Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia — Village Park Restaurant
  • Singapore — Artichoke
  • Singapore — Maxwell Food Court
  • Madrid, Spain — El Charrua
  • Madrid, Spain — Ten Con Ten

For more ideas (including specific dishes), check out my full list of recommended restaurants.

Speaking. I delivered 31 paid keynote speeches in 2019. This is far and away the most I’ve ever given in a calendar year. Obviously, this is tied directly to the success of Atomic Habits, but I’ve improved my speaking skills as well. My biggest takeaway is that if you write about a topic for years and are forced to clarify your thinking in a well-structured book, then speaking about that topic for one hour becomes much easier to do. (Note: If you’d like me to speak at your company or event, you can submit a request here.)

2. What didn’t go so well this year?

Many wonderful things happened in 2019, but I suffered plenty of growing pains as well.

Writing. For years, my business was built on the consistency of my writing. I published a new article every Monday and Thursday from 2012 to 2015. From 2016 to 2018, I spent most of my time writing Atomic Habits. Overall, those six years were filled with writing.

Then 2019 arrived and the book began to sell far and wide. My attention shifted to promotion mode: interviews, speeches, book signings. It was all great, but there was very little time left for writing. Honestly, I probably wrote more words on Twitter last year than in new articles.

Thankfully, I began to course correct during the second half of the year by writing the 3-2-1 newsletter (as mentioned previously). We’ll see what things look like in 2020, but if I’m going to write another book at some point, I will need to carve out more time to write.

Weightlifting. Everything has a tradeoff. It turns out that it is hard to maintain consistency in the gym when you are on the road for nearly half the year. In 2019, I completed 91 workouts for an average of 7.6 per month, which is better than nothing, but a steep drop off from previous years.

Workouts per month in 2019:

  • January – 16
  • February – 6
  • March – 4
  • April – 8
  • May – 4
  • June – 2(!)
  • July – 12
  • August – 8
  • September – 9
  • October – 15
  • November – 1(!)
  • December – 6

When looking at these numbers, the thing that sticks out to me is that my worst months were the months I had lots of international travel (March, June, and November). I’ll need a better plan for exercising in foreign locations in the future.

Given how inconsistent things were, I didn’t bother with max lifts this year and just did rep work most days. As a result, my best lifts of the year were:

  • Back Squat – 330 lbs (150 kg) for 5 rep
  • Bench Press – 245 lbs (111 kg) for 5 rep
  • Deadlift – 415 lbs (188 kg) for 5 rep

This marks the second year in a row when I failed to hit an all-time PR in any major lift. Admittedly, it’s unlikely you’re going to reach a personal best every year anyway, but nonetheless I have a lot of catching up to do in the gym in 2020.

Email. I joked earlier this year that my email response time is either 3 minutes or 3 months. Problem is… it’s not really a joke. I’m terrible at answering email. Honestly, this wouldn’t bother me except for one reason: it bothers other people.

My poor email response times came back to burn me multiple times this year. Sometimes it was a missed opportunity due to a delayed reply. Other times people became annoyed or frustrated, or thought I was intentionally ignoring them.

I’m not sure the best way to handle this. I get more email than I can manage and answering emails is certainly not as important as writing the next article or book. And yet, people expect responses within a day or two. One thing is for sure, I’ll probably need a new email approach in 2020.

3. What did I learn this year?

Some of my major lessons from this year include:

Move fast. The importance of moving fast was clarified for me over the last year. The original release date for Atomic Habits was set for March 2019. I pushed to move the date forward six months to October 2018 because I didn’t want to miss out on holiday sales around Christmas. My publishing team agreed, everyone worked their tails off, and we had a fabulous launch in October.

What happened next was even more important: The book was available in January when everyone was thinking about New Year’s Resolutions. As a result, Atomic Habits jumped out to a very strong start during the fall and winter. By the time we arrived at the original launch date in March, we had already sold nearly 500,000 copies.

In this case, the difference between waiting and acting was massive. We all know exactly what would have happened if we had waited: time would have flown by, somehow planning the launch would have expanded to fill all of that time, and six months of sales would have vanished.

Growing up takes time. For the last three years my business has been stuck in that awkward pre-teen stage where one minute it acts like a full-fledged adult and the next minute you realize it’s covered in pimples and doesn’t know how to control all four limbs at the same time.

But in 2019—maybe!—it turned a corner. The to-do list is still endless, but that’s what running a business is like. It does feel like I’m starting to find my footing, however. The strategy is becoming more clear. The products are gaining a foothold. The fog is lifting ever-so-slightly. I have spent nearly a decade as a full-time entrepreneur, but I’m finally uncovering a clear roadmap of what the future of the business looks like.

A life well-lived is a life well-edited. My biggest area of growth this year was prioritization. I had to become much better at saying no— and I’m still not very good at it!

In short: Prune away the inessential. Pour yourself into what remains.

That’s it! As always, thanks for reading. Happy New Year! 1
