issues.title: A University of Florida Professor Stopped Fighting AI in His Classroom: A Peer-Reviewed Study Followed
issues.summary: When Dr. Brian Harfe first noticed that AI tools could answer his essay prompts better than most of his students, he did not panic. He redesigned the assignment. That decision, made in a large-enrollment course at the University of Florida, has since become the subject of a peer-reviewed study published in TechTrends in 2026. What […] The post A University of Florida Professor Stopped Fighting AI
issues.author: Grammarly
issues.content_html:
When Dr. Brian Harfe first noticed that AI tools could answer his essay prompts better than most of his students, he did not panic. He redesigned the assignment.

That decision, made in a large-enrollment course at the University of Florida, has since become the subject of a peer-reviewed study published in TechTrends in 2026. What started as one professor’s practical response to a fast-moving problem is now a data-backed framework for how institutions can approach AI in student writing.

The problem with how we have been measuring AI use

Most institutions trying to get a handle on student AI use have landed on two approaches: surveys and AI detectors. Both fall short in predictable ways.

Self-reported survey data is shaped by what students think their instructors want to hear. Students who see AI use as acceptable tend to over-report it; those who fear academic penalties tend to under-report it. Even honest responses run into a memory problem. Few students can accurately reconstruct how much of a final draft came from a chatbot versus their own editing across multiple writing sessions.

AI detectors have a different problem. They work probabilistically, assessing whether text is likely to be AI-generated rather than confirming whether it actually is. None currently achieve 100% accuracy, and most do not tell you how much of a document is AI-generated or which parts. Just a verdict on the whole, which treats writing as a product rather than a process.

Institutions are left with plenty of anxiety about student AI use and very little reliable data about what students are actually doing.

A different approach to the assignment itself

Dr. Harfe’s response was not to add surveillance. It was to change what the assignment asked students to do.

In his University of Florida course titled “Can We Design Better Humans? Should We?”, he redesigned the final essay around AI rather than removing it. Students were required to begin with a fully AI-generated draft, then revise it to reflect their own views on human cloning and genetic engineering. The final submission had to represent the student’s perspective. How much of the AI draft they kept, changed, or discarded was up to them.

That design did something the traditional essay could not: It removed the incentive to hide AI use. Students were not penalized for leaning on the draft or rewarded for avoiding it. The question shifted from whether they used AI to what they actually did with it.

To track that objectively, Dr. Harfe used Grammarly Authorship, a writing transparency tool that tracks the origin of text. Unlike AI detectors, Authorship does not deal in probability. It records provenance, identifying whether each word was typed by a human, copied from an AI tool, or pulled from another source.

Students submitted their Authorship reports alongside their essays, and Dr. Harfe could use the tool’s replay feature to watch how each submission evolved from AI draft to finished product.

What 310 essays revealed

The resulting dataset, 310 essays from students across seven colleges and more than 100 declared majors, is the foundation of the study, Quantitative Analysis of Generative AI Text Usage and Identification of Factors Influencing Text Choice, that Harfe co-authored with Aaron Thomas of the University of Florida’s Information Technology department. It is among the first studies to track student AI use at the word level across a large, diverse undergraduate cohort.

Three findings stand out.

  1. Engagement shows up in the data. Students who wrote more of their own text took significantly longer to complete the assignment. The correlation was strong and consistent. Time-on-task tracked closely with how much students actually revised, which suggests that when an assignment is built to require genuine engagement, the data reflects it.
  2. Discipline influences editing behavior. STEM students produced more human-generated text than non-STEM students, even though both groups were equally likely to agree with the AI draft’s position on the topic. Subject-matter familiarity alone does not explain the gap. It’s an open question that the researchers have flagged for further study.
  3. Academic standing predicted revision depth. Students who performed above their semester- and major-matched peers revised AI-generated text more extensively. The pattern held across every discipline in the dataset. The tendency to push back on a draft appears to reflect broader academic habits more than discipline-specific knowledge.

On average, students kept about 76% of the AI-generated draft in their final submissions. The roughly 5% who genuinely disagreed with the AI’s position edited far more heavily, which reinforces the assignment’s central logic: Students who have something to say added more of their own writing.

The graph below shows that students with higher academic standing revised AI-generated text more extensively, across every major in the dataset. Each dot represents one student.

Figure reproduced from Harfe & Thomas (2026), “Quantitative Analysis of Generative AI Text Usage and Identification of Factors Influencing Text Choice,” TechTrends. [https://doi.org/10.1007/s11528-026-01182-5] Licensed under CC BY 4.0.

What this means for instructors and institutions

Dr. Harfe’s course is not a template to be copied wholesale. The topic, the student population, and the tool were all choices made in a specific context. But the logic underneath them travels.

Building AI into an assignment rather than designing around it changes the dynamic for students and instructors alike. It is no longer a game of cat and mouse, and instead focuses on the reflection of AI use across the writing process. That’s a more productive conversation, and it’s one that traditional essay design cannot reliably start.

Word-level transparency makes that conversation possible to have with data behind it. Where AI detectors deliver verdicts, Authorship delivers a record. That distinction matters for instructors trying to understand what is happening in their courses and for administrators building AI policies that need to hold up over time.

One of the more persistent worries in higher ed right now is that students will simply hand their thinking over to AI entirely. The data here pushes back on that harder than a usage statistic can. Students in Harfe’s course had explicit, written permission to submit a 100% AI-generated essay and receive full credit. The assignment instructions stated that directly. The only additional requirement was a reflection essay explaining their choices. Despite that, only two of 310 students made no edits to the AI draft. The rest engaged. The students who engaged most deeply were also the strongest academic performers. They did not just happen to engage; they chose to, even though they had every reason not to.

That is worth sitting with. It does not resolve every concern about AI in academic writing, but it does suggest that assignment design has more leverage than most institutions have given it credit for.

“It’s really important to show students what AI can be used for: the good, the bad, the ugly, and then let them make decisions on when and how they should use it in their future lives. Grammarly Authorship is a tool that facilitates that process for faculty in a more collaborative way with students.”

— Dr. Brian Harfe, Professor and Associate Provost, University of Florida

The peer-reviewed study “Quantitative Analysis of Generative AI Text Usage and Identification of Factors Influencing Text Choice” was published in TechTrends in April 2026. Read the full study.

issues.title: Why the holiday season is the best time to start earning points and miles
issues.summary: If you haven't ventured into earning credit card rewards yet, this holiday season is the perfect time to get started.
issues.author: Olivia Mittak
issues.content_html:
The holidays can be an expensive time of year, but they also present an opportunity to earn valuable points and miles on purchases you're already planning to make.

Whether you're booking holiday travel, buying gifts or stocking up on groceries for family gatherings, using the right rewards credit card can help you earn points and miles toward future trips.

Here at TPG, we've used points and miles to reach dream destinations, cover last-minute travel plans and make it easier to visit friends and family.

Here's how your holiday expenses can help you unlock great travel opportunities.

Related: Getting started with points, miles and credit cards to travel

Earning a welcome bonus

Rewards credit cards almost always extend a welcome offer to new cardholders. These welcome offers are the best and easiest way to earn a huge stash of points or miles. Most cards require that you meet a certain spend threshold in order to earn the welcome bonus.

Your holiday spending can cover a large portion of a card's spending requirement or even get you to the finish line. Some great welcome offers that you might be able to earn with the help of end-of-year purchases include:

  • Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (see rates and fees): Earn 75,000 bonus points after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.
  • Capital One Venture Rewards Credit Card: Earn 75,000 bonus miles after spending $4,000 on purchases within the first three months from account opening. Plus, receive a $300 credit to use on hotel and vacation rentals booked through Capital One Travel in the first cardholder year.
  • Citi Strata Premier® Card (see rates and fees): Earn 60,000 bonus points after spending $4,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.
  • Chase Freedom Flex® (see rates and fees): Earn a $200 bonus after spending $500 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.
  • Chase Freedom Unlimited® (see rates and fees): Earn a $200 bonus after spending $500 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

Just make sure you're sticking to your existing budget rather than spending extra solely to earn a bonus.

What are these welcome bonuses actually worth?

One of my favorite things about points and miles is that their value fluctuates depending on what you redeem them for. If you want to hunt for extremely high-value redemptions that are impossible to afford with just cash, you can.

Or, if you'd rather use your rewards for simple redemptions that get you where you want or need to be, that works, too.

In order to maximize the value of your points and miles, we recommend transferring them to your card's airline and hotel transfer partners. Each month, TPG releases valuations for every issuer's rewards currency. If you're curious about the value of the rewards you'll earn with the above welcome bonuses, check out our valuations page.

With the exception of the two Freedom cards, all the welcome offers mentioned will net you at least $1,000 in value, based on our November 2026 valuations.

The right bonus categories can earn you a lot of rewards

When it's time to head to the grocery store for Christmas dinner or to open your wallet for holiday gifts, you want to have the right card in hand to pay with. Rewards cards generally come with bonus categories that earn multiple points or miles per dollar spent.

For example, a card that earns elevated rewards at grocery stores could be especially useful when shopping for holiday meals, while a card with an online shopping bonus category could help you earn more on gifts.

Through Dec. 31, you can earn 5 points per dollar spent (or 5% cash back) at grocery stores with the Chase Freedom Flex, on up to $1,500 in spending (activation required). That makes this card a great choice for your holiday grocery purchases.

If you strategically plan your holiday shopping to max out that $1,500 in spending, you'd earn 7,500 bonus Chase Ultimate Rewards points, which is worth about $154, according to our November 2026 valuations. The Freedom Flex is a favorite card of mine because of how powerful its quarterly categories can be.

If you're shopping with a merchant that isn't covered by any of your cards' bonus categories, use a card that earns more than 1 point or mile per dollar spent on general purchases.

A couple of great examples include the Chase Freedom Unlimited and the Capital One Venture Rewards. The Freedom Unlimited earns 1.5 points per dollar spent on all nonbonus spending, while the Venture Rewards earns 2 miles per dollar spent on all purchases.

Shopping portals and issuer offers can earn you even more

Before checking out, it's worth seeing whether your credit card issuer has an offer for the retailer you're shopping with.

Issuers such as American Express, Chase and Capital One extend offers to existing cardholders. These offers generally give cardholders the opportunity to earn bonus cash back, points or miles in exchange for spending with a specific merchant.

During the holiday season, it's important to check your card often for these opportunities. Offers can vary per card, and some issuers may target a cardholder with a specific offer, so you should always monitor them yourself.

These offers can be combined with deals from shopping portals like Rakuten and Rove. Rakuten is a favorite of mine since I can earn American Express Membership Rewards points through it, even if I'm not paying with an Amex card. Of course, you can't earn Membership Rewards points through Rakuten without a Membership Rewards card, but it's a great perk for eligible Amex cardmembers.

A few years ago I purchased a new LG TV during Black Friday through Rakuten. That purchase earned me an additional 30,000 Membership Rewards points, showing just how valuable a well-timed shopping portal promotion can be. That's enough points to cover round-trip economy flights within the U.S.

If you don't hold an eligible Amex card, you can also now earn Bilt Points through Rakuten.

Aside from Rakuten, individual card issuers and airlines also offer online shopping portals that can help you earn your preferred rewards. Overall, if you have any holiday purchases to make, you could be leaving a huge chunk of rewards on the table by skipping out on issuer offers and shopping portals.

Bottom line

Holiday shopping can be a great opportunity to start earning points and miles balance or work on your stash.

By combining rewards credit cards, eligible issuer offers and shopping portals, you could earn valuable rewards to put toward travel in 2027 and beyond. Just make sure you're spending within your budget and paying your credit card balance in full to avoid interest charges that could outweigh the rewards you earn.

Using points and miles, many TPG staffers have been able to take dreamworthy trips to everywhere from underrated wineries in Slovenia to the beaches of Hawaii.

With a little work, you can take these kinds of trips without breaking the bank, too.

issues.title: Black Friday deal alert: 50% off all NCL cruises, free unlimited open bar and more
issues.summary: Norwegian Cruise Line is offering 50% off all cruises this Black Friday season. Here's how to book this deal before it ends.
issues.author: Gabrielle Bernardini
issues.content_html:
What better way to kick off the holiday season than by planning your next vacation?

Whether you're looking to bask in the sun on a tropical Caribbean getaway or explore glaciers along Alaska's mesmerizing coastline, Norwegian Cruise Line is offering a noteworthy Black Friday deal you don't want to miss.

NCL is offering 50% off all sailings* — nearly 350 destinations — regardless of itinerary or ship. This lucrative cruise deal lets families, couples or even solo travelers make their dream vacation plans a reality and map out an itinerary well within their budget.

In addition to this Black Friday promotional discount, guests can enjoy an unlimited open bar, shore excursion credits and much more.

Keep reading to find out how you can save money and get more than $2,000 in value on your next cruise booking with this Black Friday deal.

NCL Black Friday 2026 deal details

NCL's 50% off Black Friday deal* applies to all cruises and is available to book for sailings through 2028. To browse sailings for this promotion, visit NCL.com and filter by destination, port of departure, ship and duration to narrow down your perfect itinerary.

Plus, as an added bonus, this promotion can be combined with NCL's "Free at Sea" package. Delivering more than $2,000 in value, guests can enjoy benefits such as an unlimited open bar, specialty dining, shore excursion credits and Wi-Fi.

This all-inclusive package is great for guests who want to take advantage of key cruise perks without paying a la carte for additional benefits.

And, as if this Black Friday deal couldn't get any better, on select sailings, kids sail for free. This is a great perk for families looking to travel at a greater cost-saving value.

Note that fare prices shown are in U.S. dollars on a per-person basis and include taxes, fees and port expenses.

Choose your perfect getaway: Explore NCL's itineraries

With nearly 350 destinations to choose from, including sailings to the Bahamas, Alaska, Europe and the Caribbean, there is no shortage of adventures and options to choose from.

For instance, you could book a four-day getaway to the Bahamas, departing from Orlando, Florida (Port Canaveral) and stopping at Nassau and NCL's private island, Great Stirrup Cay.

The Bahamian oasis is now home to a 6-acre private water park that features 19 waterslides, cliff jumps, a lazy river and more. Great Tides Waterpark opened in September 2026 and gives guests flexibility to choose their own adventure.

If a full day of thrills isn't for you, guests can also opt to relax and enjoy the Great Life Lagoon, a 28,000-square-foot pool. For families or couples looking for a quick vacation, this could be the perfect option.

For those wanting to explore several European countries — without the hassle and additional out-of-pocket cost of booking trains, flights or hotel rooms — guests can embark on a nine-day Eurotrip starting from London and cruising to ports in France, Germany, Belgium and Denmark.

This can be a nice option for couples, those traveling with friends or even families.

As a mom of a two-year-old, it can be challenging (and stressful) to navigate trekking across Europe with a toddler. I like that cruising takes the guesswork off of meal plans, nap times and travel between countries.

Plus, unlike other cruise lines, Norwegian is known for its "freestyle cruising," which means there are no enforced dress codes or assigned dining times. As a toddler mom, I like that NCL gives guests the flexibility to book the vacation they want.

Related: The 5 best destinations you can visit on a Norwegian Cruise Line ship

Black Friday NCL promotion includes the new Prima Class ship

If cruising on a megaship is not your style, NCL offers a resort-like ship class known as the Prima Class. These smaller, more upscale ships feature a more modern aesthetic, larger outdoor areas and elevated experiences.

In March, NCL's newest ship, Norwegian Luna, set sail to destinations in the Caribbean, the Bahamas and Bermuda. This ship has signature Prima Class touches, such as Indulge Food Hall and Cagney's Steakhouse, as well as some must-try additions, including the authentic Thai restaurant Sukhothai.

Standout ship attractions include the Aqua Slidecoaster, the world's first hybrid waterslide and roller coaster, waterfront infinity pools, kids' splash pad, adults-only pool area, game room, and so much more.

Basically, the new Norwegian Luna will make it hard for guests to decide to even leave the ship.

If exploring destinations and being one of the first to set sail on a new ship is enticing, NCL is also extending this promotion to its recently unveiled ship, Norwegian Aura. The biggest ship in Norwegian's fleet will set sail in April 2027 and will feature more expansive spaces, waterslides and attractions around every corner. Itineraries for this ship include ports in the Caribbean, Greek isles, Italy and Spain.

With this 50% off Black Friday deal*, now is a great time to book your 2027 or even your 2028 travel plans and experience these brand-new cruise ships.

Book and earn even more rewards

Whether you're planning to take advantage of this Black Friday deal or book an NCL cruise, be sure to check out the company's Latitudes Rewards program. This loyalty program is free to join and lets cruisers earn rewards and get access to exclusive discounts, onboard experiences and more.

Members can earn 1 point for every cruise night, and 1 additional point per night for reserving select rooms or when booking with a Latitudes Rewards insider offer.

As you reach a certain threshold of points, you can unlock new status tiers, which may include specialty offers, cabin upgrades, dining benefits and more.

Related: Norwegian Cruise Line's Latitudes Rewards loyalty program guide

Bottom line

NCL is an award-winning cruise line that offers itineraries for all types of travelers, giving action-packed thrill-seekers or guests seeking a relaxing, elevated sailing experience the flexibility to book a cruise that matches their vacation aesthetic.

And if you want to save (possibly thousands of dollars) on your 2027 or 2028 travel plans, now is the time to book with NCL and receive 50% off all cruises*.

So, what are you waiting for?

issues.title: Cheaper rides, double miles: How to save on your Thanksgiving trip to the airport
issues.summary: Save on Thanksgiving airport rides with Uber, Lyft and Blacklane deals, plus bonus Delta, United and credit card rewards.
issues.author: Ben Smithson
issues.content_html:
The busy Thanksgiving travel season is just about to kick off as millions take flight around the country. You can expect crowded terminals, long security lines and potentially surge-priced rides to and from the airport.

The good news is that major ride-hailing players Uber, Lyft and Blacklane all have launched Thanksgiving offers, including one that is exclusive to our TPG members.

Here's how to make the most of your holiday ride transport.

Related: Here's what Thanksgiving foods you can bring in your carry-on and what has to be checked

Uber: Up to 30% off if you get stuck with a bad seat

Through Nov. 30, Uber is running a promotion called "From Bad Seats to Better Rides." If you get squeezed into a middle seat with no armrest or end up in the last row by the lavatory, you could receive up to 30% off your Uber ride home from the airport.

To take part, register your flight and seat details on Uber's Thanksgiving promotion page. Uber provides several examples of undesirable seats but has not published a complete list of what qualifies as undesirable. Individual savings vary, and terms apply, so check the offer added to your Uber account before booking. In our testing, you will not be required to submit a boarding pass or an image of your undesirable seat to receive a discount.

TPG tip: Link your Delta SkyMiles and Uber accounts and select Delta as your earning partner before you travel. You will earn 1 mile per eligible dollar on UberX airport rides, 2 miles per eligible dollar on Uber XL, Uber Comfort, Uber Black and Uber SUV rides and 3 miles per eligible dollar on Uber Reserve rides in the U.S. Note that taxes, fees, mandatory charges and tips do not earn miles.

Related: From Starbucks to Uber: Airline and hotel partnerships that earn points and miles

More ways to save with Uber this holiday season

Uber One Member Days run through Dec. 1, where Uber says members can unlock up to $500 in savings across rides, deliveries, hotels and other offers. Some deals are targeted, so check your email and your Uber app to see if you are eligible, but offers may include:

  • 20% off two premium airport rides: Eligible members can save up to $26 per ride on up to two Uber Black, Black SUV, Premier, Premier SUV, Elite or Elite SUV airport rides from Nov. 24 to 30.
  • 15% back on hotels: Eligible hotel bookings made through Uber during Member Days earn 15% back in Uber One credits, which can be used on future rides and Uber Eats orders after check-in.
  • Marriott Bonvoy sweepstakes: Uber One members with linked Marriott Bonvoy accounts earn 1 entry per qualifying Uber ride or Uber Eats order. More than 1,000 winners will share 30 million Marriott Bonvoy bonus points, with a top prize of 1 million points.
  • Delta sweepstakes: Members with linked Delta SkyMiles accounts earn entries for qualifying Uber rides and Uber Eats orders. More than 1,000 winners will receive Delta Gift Cards, with a top prize of $10,000.

No purchase is necessary to enter either sweepstakes.

TPG tip: Link your Marriott Bonvoy and Uber accounts and select Marriott as your earning partner. You will earn 3 Marriott Bonvoy points per eligible dollar on Uber XL, Uber Comfort, Uber Black and Uber SUV rides in the U.S., including those booked with Reserve and 2 points per eligible dollar on UberX rides booked with Reserve. Members who have not linked the two accounts can also earn 1,000 bonus points for linking by Nov. 24, plus another 1,000 points after completing an eligible premium or Reserve ride by the same date.

You can link both Delta and Marriott to Uber, but only one can be selected as the earning partner for a ride at a time, so choose which currency is more useful to you.

Related: Marriott announces Uber partnership changes: The good, the bad and the totally worthless

Lyft: Double United miles on scheduled airport rides

United MileagePlus members can earn 8 United miles per eligible dollar on scheduled airport rides with Lyft through Nov. 30, twice the standard rate of 4 miles per dollar. Link your MileagePlus and Lyft accounts and select United as your active rewards partner before booking.

The offer applies to eligible rides requested, completed and paid for in the U.S. or Puerto Rico.

Make sure you schedule your ride in advance, because unscheduled airport rides only earn 3 miles per eligible dollar, while most standard personal rides earn 1 mile per eligible dollar.

Note that taxes, fees, tolls and tips do not earn miles.

TPG tip: Shift your rewards up a gear by paying with the Chase Sapphire Reserve® (see rates and fees) or Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card (see rates and fees), and you will earn 5 total Chase Ultimate Rewards points per dollar on qualifying Lyft purchases through Sept. 30, 2027. Both cards earn 1 point per dollar on purchases outside their bonus categories.

Sapphire Reserve cardholders also receive a $10 monthly in-app Lyft credit through Sept. 30, 2027. Unused credit expires at the end of each calendar month.

Related: How to easily earn extra rewards on Lyft rides

Blacklane: An exclusive offer for TPG members

If you would rather avoid a crowded airport pickup zone, why not treat yourself to Blacklane? The global luxury chauffeur service operates in more than 500 cities across more than 60 countries, and its fixed prices include standard taxes, tolls, tips and fees.

TPG members can currently receive an exclusive $80 credit toward two chauffeur journeys in the U.S. To claim it, sign in to or create a TPG account through the TPG Member Offers page, then click through to Blacklane from the offer.

TPG tip: Bilt members can redeem Bilt Cash toward Blacklane rides each calendar year: up to $50 for Blue and Silver members, $100 for Gold members and $150 for Platinum members. Blacklane rides booked through Bilt also earn 1 Bilt Point per dollar.

Related: No surge, no scramble: Why I loved using Blacklane for my latest airport transfer

Bottom line

Thanksgiving airport rides can be expensive, but this holiday season you may be able to reduce the cost and/or increase your rewards.

Uber's bad-seat offer is the most straightforward discount if your aircraft seat qualifies and is a fun and lighthearted way to reward those whose seat allocation is unfortunate. Uber One members should also check their accounts for targeted airport and hotel offers, while the Lyft promotion is an easy way to earn double United miles on a ride many travelers will book anyway.

Link your loyalty accounts, select the right earning partner and check your card benefits before traveling to ensure a happy and rewarding holiday.

issues.title: Frontier's GoWild All You Can Fly pass is back with no blackout dates and earlier booking
issues.summary: Frontier Airlines has released its latest GoWild All You Can Fly pass and it's better than before, with no blackout dates and an earlier booking window.
issues.author: Eric Rosen
issues.content_html:
It's here! Frontier Airlines is now offering its GoWild All You Can Fly Pass for 2027, letting travelers take to the skies at a deep discount for an entire year (and potentially longer).

Here are all the details.

GoWild All You Can Fly Pass pricing

For a limited time, flyers can purchase a GoWild Pass good through 2027 for just $399. Members of the airline's Discount Den can score the pass for $349.

While that's not quite as good as some offers we've seen in past years (but better than some in other years), it can add up to significant savings if you fly the airline a lot. You must be a Frontier Miles member to purchase one.

Keep in mind that passholders pay $0.01 in airfare plus applicable taxes, fees and charges at the time of booking, so the pass gets you out of the regular airfare, but you're still on the hook for taxes and fees as well as other charges for things like optional seat selection and bags. While taxes on domestic legs are low, international ones can incur $60-$110 each way, depending on the destination.

Sneak peek: Frontier's new first-class seats are finally on sale, set for March debut

Multiple passholders can book travel at the same time, but you can't mix and match passholders with non-passholders on the same reservation.

Likewise, different types of fares can be combined each way on itineraries as long as all passengers hold a valid GoWild Pass at the time of booking and the primary passenger holds a Discount Den membership if Discount Den fares are selected.

Autorenewal

One other big caveat: GoWild passes autorenew, so if you want to cancel when your current pass expires, you'll need to contact the airline to do so. Your renewal date will be stated in your confirmation email when purchasing the pass.

Where can you fly?

The GoWild Pass is valid for flights to over 100 destinations across Frontier's route network, including both domestic gateways and international cities in Mexico, the Caribbean and Central America. The airline's route network changes frequently, though, so stay on top of it to make sure your route will be in service when it's time to book.

Travel dates

Travel begins after purchase (meaning as soon as today) and is available through Dec. 31, 2027, meaning potentially over a full year of flying.

There are no blackout dates, like we've seen in some past instances, but on peak dates, you can expect to pay $59-$199 extra per segment.

Peak dates for 2027 include:

  • Jan. 1-3, 14, 15, 18
  • Feb. 11-2, 15
  • Mar. 12-14, 19-21, 26-29
  • Apr. 2-4
  • May 27-28, 31
  • July 1-5
  • Sept. 2-3, 6
  • Oct. 7-8, 11
  • Nov. 23-24, 27-29
  • Dec. 18-24, 26-31

The booking window

Here's the kicker: Standard bookings for eligible GoWild fares begin a day before departure for domestic flights and 10 days before departure for international flights. If your return flight is outside that window, then you'll have to try to make an additional booking when the window opens for that flight.

If you do want to book more in advance than that, however, you can pay an additional charge to do so, though this can vary based on the date and the route.

Also keep in mind that just because a seat is open on the flight you want does not mean it's eligible for a GoWild booking.

Earning miles

You can earn Frontier Miles on the purchase of the pass as well as any extras, like seat assignments, bag fees or priority boarding that you purchase.

Elite status

If you hold elite status with Frontier, you are still eligible for your benefits, including free seats and bags, so that can be a great way to save on optional fees that non-elites have to pay.

Bottom line

All-you-can-fly airline passes are a rarity these days and come with lots of limitations. Frontier Airlines' GoWild All You Can Fly Pass is no exception.

Still, if you fly the airline a lot, have flexibility (and a bit of spontaneity) in your plans and don't need a ton of extra amenities like preferred seats or checked bags, these fares can be a good way to save a bit on flights you'd be taking anyway ... or perhaps some fun last-minute fares you wouldn't be able to take advantage of otherwise.

issues.content_html:
Most memorial museums stay put in the house of the person they remember. This one moved out.

It was founded in 1968 in the Tashkent house where Abdulla Avloni (1878–1934) had lived with his family from 1910 until his death. Avloni was one of the Jadids, the Muslim reformers who believed Central Asia could be renewed through new-method schools, newspapers and the theatre. He opened schools, wrote their textbooks, published the newspaper Shuhrat and, in 1913, gathered the Turon theatre troupe.

In 1993 the museum left the house for the institute that carries Avloni's name, where teachers from all over Uzbekistan now come to brush up their skills. Without its original walls, it relies on things to bring him close: his desk, typewriter and candlestick, his bookcase and wardrobe, even his clothes, arranged in a reconstruction of his study.

Around them are early twentieth-century books and newspapers in Arabic script, printed in Tashkent, Kazan, Orenburg, Baku and Istanbul, and a small stage that recalls the Turon troupe. The most surprising corner is a tall red display in the middle of the hall, where Avloni and fellow reformers such as Mahmudkhoja Behbudi, brought to life with artificial intelligence, look out at visitors and present passages from their writings. Walk around to the back and there is a mirror with the words "Zamonamiz jadidi", "a Jadid of our time". Whoever looks into it becomes, for a moment, the newest member of the movement.

The museum is also the only one from Uzbekistan in the UMAC Worldwide Database of University Museums and Collections.

issues.content_html:
Unlike most surviving Cham towers that crown dramatic hilltops, Binh Lam Tower rises almost unexpectedly from the flat, verdant plains of a quiet lowland village.

Constructed around the late tenth to early eleventh century, this 20-meter brick sanctuary serves as a vital architectural bridge, catching the art form mid-evolution between the delicate, lyrical features of the My Son A1 style and the grand, spear-like forms of classic Binh Dinh towers.

Its weathered facade features slender vertical pilasters, mini-temple false doors, and faint relief carvings of the mythical bird-god Garuda. Beyond its standing brickwork, Binh Lam hides deep subterranean secrets: archaeological digs uncovered vast foundations of a once-extensive religious complex, alongside stone Nagas and relief sculptures.

Furthermore, the tower once formed the eastern heart of ancient Thi Nai Citadel, positioned along river channels leading to the historical port—making this lowland monument a crucial physical anchor to Champa's lost naval and architectural empire.

issues.content_html:
The National Underground Railroad Freedom Center, located in Cincinnati along the banks of the Ohio River makes a solemn statement about the lives that were lived enslaved in the early history of the United States, and the many heroic men and women who played important roles in the Underground Railroad movement, which helped to bring an end to African slavery in the United States. Referred to as a "museum of conscience", The Freedom Center is dedicated to exploring the struggle to abolish human enslavement. During the era when the Underground Railroad was active, Cincinnati was a major gateway across the Ohio River where freedom seekers escaped from southern slave states to the northern states or Canada, making the Center's location rather significant.

Having opened its doors in 2004, the Freedom Center uses immersive exhibits across multiple floors to convey an account that is simultaneously rich in the cultural traditions of the enslaved, as well as steeped in the violence and tragedies that were endured. The histories are told through a combination of permanent and traveling exhibits that utilize storytelling, film, artwork, hands-on activities and more.

Perhaps one of the most impressive and prominent displays at the center is an authentic, 19th-century reconstructed slave pen that was obtained from a farm in Kentucky. It stands as America's only remaining, pristinely preserved slave pen and stands as a stark reminder of the atrocious conditions that were endured.

The pen, originally built somewhere around 1830 by a wealthy Kentucky farmer, runaway slave catcher, and slave trader, was used as a holding facility for captured and purchased enslaved men, women and children. It was discovered, quite by accident in 1998 when a farmer, who was preparing to demolish an old barn on his property, discovered that the barn had been built up around this old pen, thus protecting and preserving (and hiding) the slave pen for more than 100 years.

During its unfortunate years of use, enslaved people would be kept in the pen, often for months, until the slave trader accumulated a large enough "stock" to march them further south to be sold. These forced marches would often cover upwards of 750 miles. Conditions in these pens would be brutal, offering no sanitation, lighting or warmth. As many as 65 enslaved people would often be housed in this small pen. Also very moving is the memorial room dedicated to the Transatlantic Slave Trade, as well as the Freedom's Eternal Flame Terrace which overlooks the Ohio River and the city skyline.

The National Underground Railroad Freedom Center is a beautiful and meaningful tribute to the human right for freedom, and to the brave men, women and children who stood up to the inhuman treatment of themselves and of others; and to those who continue to fight for the cause of freedom through out the world today.

issues.content_html:
Above the village of Kalnik in northern Croatia, the walls of Veliki Kalnik Castle rise from a jagged rocky ridge. Built across several levels, the medieval stronghold follows the natural contours of the rock, making its surviving towers and walls appear to grow out of the mountain.

First documented in 1243, the castle is best known for a story involving King Béla IV of Hungary and Croatia. According to local legend, the king took refuge here during the Mongol invasion of the 13th century. As the siege dragged on and supplies dwindled, villagers kept the defenders fed with plums.

The grateful king is said to have rewarded his rescuers with noble status. They became known as the kalnički šljivari—the “plum nobles of Kalnik.” This tale remains part of the region’s identity, connecting an imposing fortress with an unexpectedly humble fruit.

The ruins visible today developed over centuries. Their towers, fragments of walls, and elevated viewpoints reveal how the builders used the steep terrain as part of the castle’s defenses. From the heights, the view opens across the villages, fields, and wooded hills below.

issues.title: Why this Tokyo photographer sold everything and started over with manual-focus lenses
issues.summary: Marcel shares the Sony a7R V and manual-focus Voigtländer and Zeiss primes he built after selling everything, plus the lessons his grandfather taught him.
issues.author: Mathew Anderson
issues.content_html:
Marcel shares the Sony a7R V and manual-focus Voigtländer and Zeiss primes he built after selling everything, plus the lessons his grandfather taught him.

Meet Marcel

Home base: Tokyo, Japan

This week, we head to Tokyo to chat with forum member Vamp898-ng , a photographer whose love of the craft traces back to watching his grandfather shoot eagles in flight from a mountain trail, steadying a 500mm lens in an era before image stabilization.

Over 22 years, Marcel has cycled through gear obsessions and eventually sold everything to start over – arriving at a setup built almost entirely around manual-focus primes from Voigtländer and Zeiss for his Sony a7R V. His big question for much of his photography: what photos would he want to show his grandchildren someday?

Our What’s in your bag? community spotlight series features readers sharing their favorite gear and photography, including from past DReview collaborators. See below for what today’s guest has to share.

Have your photography featured on the DPReview homepage! Find out how.

What’s in Marcel’s bag

Favorite camera(s):Sony a7R V

“The a7R V has a lot of room for cropping, so I don’t have to use zoom lenses or large tele. It has a big, comfortable grip and a large, high-resolution EVF, which is perfect for fast and precise manual focus.”

Favorite lens(s): “All of my lenses are from either Voigtländer or Zeiss. If I leave the house without knowing what is going to happen, I will have the following with me:

  • Voigtländer APO-LANTAR 50mm F2 (mounted on the camera)
  • Voigtländer APO-LANTHAR 35mm F2
  • Voigtländer Nokton 75mm F1.5

If I know the shooting conditions beforehand, I take the Zeiss Sonnar 135mm F2.8 (C/Y).

I only have one accessory: the Voigtländer VM-E Close Focus Adapter II. I love it because it enables me to use all M-Mount lenses, like the Zeiss C Sonnar 50mm F1.5, which was love at first sight for me.”

What got you started, and how long have you been a photographer?

“My Grandfather was a photographer, and I was the first (and only) of his grandchildren who showed interest in his work. He taught me with a Zeiss Ikon Icarex 35 and a Tessar 50mm F2.8, promising I would get that camera if my photos got good enough. It was fully analog, so no battery, not even a light meter. I had to use a Zeiss Ikon Ikophot to meter the light, and he even wanted me to guess the shutter speed for the aperture I wanted before measuring, because relying on the light meter was simply too slow.

While many people today think of analog photography as a way to slow down intentionally, they probably think of a rangefinder. He taught me how to get as fast as possible with that camera. “The subject might not wait for you”. It was an SLR; it can shoot fast if the photographer knows how to, and he wanted me to pull it off.

After roughly three months, he deemed me worthy to get the whole set. The Icarex, the Tessar 50mm F2.8, the Ikophot, and a nice book called Mit der Kamera auf du by Alexander Spoerl to continue learning. It’s an amazing book whose tricks I still use today.”

How has your photography changed since you started?

“As soon as I got my first job (16 years ago), I had a co-worker who was a travel photographer with years of experience. He showed me amazing images from India and Ireland. As someone just getting his first job, world travel with a full-frame SLR (he used the original Canon EOS 5D) was an unthinkable dream.

Then I got into gear wars, comparing 100% crops of lenses and cameras over and over again, looking for the best comparison tool. This is probably the darkest era for me personally because I spent more time researching than shooting.

I started realizing that what I do didn’t feel right to me when I was working with a portrait photographer who told me, “You have to get better-looking models,” after showing him a photo of my girlfriend.

That single sentence changed a lot for me because, even though there are a lot of famous exceptions, he wasn’t wrong. I soon realized that this was not what I wanted to do. I sold everything I owned and started again. With a set of fully manual, fixed-focal-length lenses, taking photos purely of what I wanted to photograph.”

What’s so special about Voigtländer?

“Cosina Co., Ltd. (the company that makes Voigtländer and a lot of Zeiss lenses) is not getting enough love, and it seems people have a hard time understanding their lens lineups (like the difference between Nokton (Vintage), Nokton Classic and so on) and sometimes end up with a lens they are not happy with, even though the lens does exactly what it was built for.

Cosina is the only maker brave enough to offer the same lens in different versions. All their products are handmade in Japan with insane, full-metal build quality. As far as I know, they are also the only maker that does not artificially inflate prices based on gray imports and currency exchange rates. They are a small, traditional lens maker who works out of a love for lenses and photography.”

What places of interest do you shoot?

“One thing that felt unique to me was shooting the Formula E Race in Berlin. I stumbled into that by accident. I noticed you couldn’t buy tickets for the press stand, and I just wanted to know how you get into these stands (I did not intend to shoot there), and they looked at my SIGMA Sports 120-300mm F2.8, whispered to each other, and then put a band on my wrist and told me to get in.

Because I had a SIGMA SD Quattro at that point whose AF was absolutely not up for the job, I remembered what I learned from my grandfather and shot the whole race in MF.”

What have you learned?

“As I am shooting with manual lenses only, fast, precise MF is of utmost importance. I disabled the MF assist (the focus loupe that triggers as soon as you turn the focus wheel) because it slows me down. You lose control over framing; if the subject moves, you can’t refocus, as all you see is a magnified blurry mess, and so on.

Choose the lenses you want to use, then find a body to attach them to. And always think about how you want to use a lens. Do you really want a lens with harsh bokeh that is razor-sharp edge-to-edge for wide-open portrait shots? If not, be brave enough to choose the lens with the bokeh you prefer, even if it might not be as sharp on a test chart.

Don’t know what lenses you might want to use? Start with one that has the focal length roughly equal to your sensor diagonal. You’ll eventually end up owning most focal lengths anyway, so it doesn’t really matter which you’ll start with. If you ask me, I’d always recommend a used full-frame camera with a 50mm lens.”

Marcel really enjoyed participating in this spotlight article and would love to hear what you think of his photography and to answer any of your questions in the comments below.

issues.title: Capture One adds wired tethering for the Hasselblad X2D II 100C
issues.summary: The feature follows July’s native Raw support and requires X2D II 100C firmware 1.4.15.7 and Capture One 16.9.1.
issues.author: Dale Baskin
issues.content_html:
The feature follows July’s native Raw support and requires X2D II 100C firmware 1.4.15.7 and Capture One 16.9.1.

Hasselblad has released firmware version 1.4.15.7 for the X2D II 100C, adding support for wired tethered shooting in Capture One. Tethering is available in Capture One 16.9.1 for desktop and Capture One Mobile 4.3.0. This marks the second stage of a partnership the two companies announced in July.

What the update adds

With the camera connected via USB, each 100MP frame appears in Capture One at full resolution as soon as it’s captured, so focus and exposure can be checked while it is still live. Capture One’s full editing toolset is available while shooting, and adjustments applied to the first frame carry over to subsequent captures.

“You pick up your camera, you plug in, and it just works,” said Capture One chief executive Rafael Orta.

This release only adds tethered shooting for the X2D II 100C. The X2D 100C and CFV 100C digital back, which gained native Raw support in Capture One in July, weren’t included in today’s announcement.

A complicated history

Historically, Hasselblad support had been missing from Capture One, a result of the old rivalry between Hasselblad and Phase One, Capture One’s former parent company, which competed for the same medium format customers.

That changed in July, when Capture One added native support for Hasselblad’s .3FR Raw files in version 16.8.3, covering the X2D II 100C, X2D 100C and CFV 100C, along with dedicated lens profiles for XCD lenses. At the time, the companies said tethering would follow later in 2026.

Bronius Rudnickas, Hasselblad’s global marketing manager, said tethering was one of the top requests from photographers after the collaboration was announced.

Availability

Firmware 1.4.15.7 for the X2D II 100C is available now for download from Hasselblad. Tethering support is available in Capture One 16.9.1 and Capture One Mobile 4.3.0. Capture One is also offering Hasselblad camera owners a 90-day trial of the software.

issues.title: National Geographic reveals its Pictures of the Year 2026, from spawning moray eels to a Greenland shark under the ice
issues.summary: Chosen from more than a million images, this year’s 25 selections range from a six-month solarigraph over an ancient Peruvian observatory to a camera trap on a Kenyan riverbank.
issues.author: Dale Baskin
issues.content_html:
Chosen from more than a million images, this year’s 25 selections range from a six-month solarigraph over an ancient Peruvian observatory to a camera trap on a Kenyan riverbank.

If there’s one name that’s synonymous with great photography, it’s National Geographic, which has just announced its Pictures of the Year for 2026.

National Geographic’s editors sifted through more than a million images captured by its photographers to arrive at the 25 that make up this year’s selection. That ratio alone says a lot about what it takes for a photo to make the cut. But in National Geographic’s tradition, these aren’t just great images; the publication emphasizes that they reflect the patience and dedication its photographers bring to its visual storytelling.

This year’s selections cover a wide spectrum, from the first-ever images of eels spawning in the wild, to a climber suspended from a sea cliff in Spain moments after a total solar eclipse, to Kiliii Yüyan’s encounter with a Greenland shark in the sub-freezing waters near Kulusuk in East Greenland.

Many of the images are as notable for how they were made as for what’s in them. Diego López Calvín used solarigraphy, a single continuous exposure lasting six months, to trace the sun’s path between the solstices over Peru’s ancient Chankillo observatory. Will Burrard-Lucas hid a camera trap on a remote riverbank in Kenya’s Masai Mara, and Prakash Matada mounted a fisheye lens on a telescoping pole to photograph a troop of endangered golden langurs at close range.

National Geographic’s editor-in-chief, Nathan Lump, suggested the selections are also a response to a changing photography landscape, citing the value of documenting reality. “Together, these images remind us how much there is still to discover about our planet, and that the deeply human work of documenting what’s real is more valuable than ever in a time when fakes are everywhere,” he said.

Below are a few of our favorites from National Geographic’s Pictures of the Year 2026. All 25 images will appear in the December issue of National Geographic and can be seen now on the National Geographic website. [Editor’s note: National Geographic requires users to register for a free account to view the full set of images.]

A Greenland shark, the oldest vertebrate on Earth, swims underneath the meter-thick sea ice near the village of Kulusuk in East Greenland, as diver Philipp Oppermann watches. This shark came up from the depths into the shallows at night to follow the scent of a Greenlander’s bait, frozen ringed seal. This photograph was made March 17, 2026, in early spring, when the sea ice remains strong and the visibility of the water is spectacular, over 50m (165ft).

A crack of rifle fire marks the finale of a performance of tbourida, a Moroccan equestrian tradition in which a team of riders act out a cavalry charge. Women are gradually gaining a foothold in the centuries-old sport. At the festival pictured here, all-female brigades represented two of the 140 competing troupes.

Climber Chris Sharma dangles from a completely horizontal limestone face in the moments after August’s total solar eclipse in Spain.

Apparent path of the sun as seen from the western observation point at the Chankillo Solar Observatory in Casma (Ancash), Peru. The six-month-long continuous exposure (solarigraphy) taken between June 21 and December 21, 2025, accurately shows the sun’s path, with the winter and summer solstices located at the ends of the structure outlined by the silhouette of the towers.

Deep in Kenya’s Masai Mara, a reserve bordering the northern edge of the Serengeti, photographer Will Burrard-Lucas worked with a team of rangers to hide a camera trap high on a riverbank and waited for action. The images that came back revealed something extraordinary. The secluded crossing turned out to be a high-traffic wildlife thoroughfare. Among the passersby: a pair of slinking lions, unusual visitors here.

A pair of Abbott’s moray eels (Gymnothorax eurostus) reaching the pinnacle of their spawning run, three-tenths of a second after leaving the cover of coral. The male on the left is just releasing the jaw of the female, with both eels sending gametes into the water. Kagoshima Prefecture, Japan.

A curious troop of Gee’s golden langurs – named for a naturalist who documented them in the 1950s peer into a fisheye lens that Prakash Matada affixed to a telescoping pole. The endangered canopy dwellers here have formed a rare bond with humans and proved anything but camera-shy, gazing at their own reflections.

issues.summary: The post Freewell and Dunna Did It launch ultra-slim modular filter system for photographers and filmmakers appeared first on Digital Photography School . It was authored by Sime . We missed the launch of this one, but the pricing is GREAT right now, so thought we’d share for the guys at Freewell x Dunna Did It (and he certainly did, these look great!) A new locking filter system from Freewell and
issues.author: Sime
issues.content_html:
The post Freewell and Dunna Did It launch ultra-slim modular filter system for photographers and filmmakers appeared first on Digital Photography School. It was authored by Sime.

We missed the launch of this one, but the pricing is GREAT right now, so thought we’d share for the guys at Freewell x Dunna Did It (and he certainly did, these look great!)

A new locking filter system from Freewell and photographer and filmmaker Dunna Did It combines magnetic attachment with a mechanical locking mechanism, allowing photographers to share filters across lenses with different thread sizes.

Freewell has teamed up with photographer, filmmaker and YouTube creator Dunna Did It to launch a new modular camera filter system designed to make switching filters between lenses quicker and easier.

The Dunna Did It × Freewell Ultra-Slim Locking Filter System uses a combination of magnetic attachment and a mechanical locking mechanism. Rather than needing a separate set of filters for every lens, photographers can use a single collection of filters across lenses with thread sizes ranging from 49mm to 95mm, simply by changing the base ring.

The system is available in two configurations: a Videography Kit aimed at filmmakers and hybrid creators, and a Photography Kit designed primarily for still photographers.

One filter system for multiple lenses

Anyone with a growing collection of lenses will know that filter sizes can quickly become a bit of a headache. Even when lenses have similar focal lengths, their filter thread sizes can vary, potentially leaving you with multiple versions of the same ND or polarising filter.

Freewell’s new system aims to address that problem by separating the filter itself from the lens mounting ring.

A dedicated base ring attaches to each lens, with the filters then transferred between compatible rings. Magnets help guide the filter into position, before a short clockwise turn engages the mechanical lock.

The system supports ten filter thread sizes: 49mm, 55mm, 58mm, 62mm, 67mm, 72mm, 77mm, 82mm, 86mm and 95mm.

There are a few other interesting details worth noting:

  • Ultra-slim design: The fixed ND filters measure just 2.95mm thick and weigh 18.4g, helping minimise additional bulk and weight, particularly useful for handheld and gimbal-based video work.
  • Magnetic attachment with mechanical locking: Magnets help position the filter, while a short clockwise twist locks it in place.
  • Colour accuracy: Freewell says the filters are designed to minimise colour shifts, helping maintain natural-looking skin tones, greens and skies.
  • Stackable filters: Compatible filters can be used individually or stacked to combine different effects, including exposure control, reflection reduction and diffusion.

Two kits for different creative needs

The system launches with two kits, each offering a different selection of filters.

Videography Kit

Designed with filmmakers and hybrid shooters in mind, the Videography Kit includes:

  • ND4 (2-stop)
  • ND8 (3-stop)
  • ND16 (4-stop)
  • ND32 (5-stop)
  • Glow Mist 1/4

The kit also includes a selected base ring, protective caps (including one with built-in reference targets) and a fitted carry case.

The range of ND filters provides exposure control across different lighting conditions, while the Glow Mist filter adds a diffusion option for video and still photography.

Photography Kit

The Photography Kit takes a slightly different approach, with a selection of filters aimed at everyday photography and longer exposures.

It includes:

  • UV filter
  • ND64 (6-stop)
  • ND1000 (10-stop)
  • CPL (circular polariser)
  • Glow Mist 1/8

As with the Videography Kit, it comes with a selected base ring, protective caps and a fitted carry case.

The combination covers lens protection, reflection control, long exposures and a touch of diffusion without requiring multiple filter systems.

Developed in collaboration with Dunna Did It

The system was developed over nearly a year in collaboration with Dunna Did It, a photographer, filmmaker and music producer based on Vancouver Island, British Columbia.

With an audience of more than 440,000 YouTube subscribers, Dunna regularly creates photography and video content, including gear reviews and tutorials.

The collaboration focused on refining the physical design and practical workflow of the system, including its locking mechanism, overall profile and ease of use when moving between lenses.

Pricing and availability

The Dunna Did It × Freewell Ultra-Slim Locking Filter System launched online on 26 August 2026.

Both the Photography Kit and Videography Kit have a launch price of US$299.99, reduced from the regular retail price of US$349.99.

Customers choose a base ring to suit their existing lens, with additional ring sizes available for use across the rest of their lens collection.

For more information, visit the Freewell product page or watch Dunna’s product introduction video on YouTube.

issues.author: Sime
issues.content_html:
The post Is it still photography if you’re only using your phone? appeared first on Digital Photography School. It was authored by Sime.

Yes.

That’s as simple as the answer need be, but that’s not the point of this article.

Another Godox press release (Those guys are busy!) and again, we’ve not had a chance to play with one of these so you’ll need to do your own research, but Godox have just announced the Smartphone Xenon Flash A2, and their tagline is “Your phone, now a pro camera” which isn’t exactly factual, but also, the definition of “pro camera” is very loose.

The thing to keep in mind with ANY small light source is that its going to be harsh – there’s stuff you can do about it, though. You can diffuse it, bounce it (though a small light like the A2 might not give quite enough output to do much there) but even things like bouncing it off a close wall or even a sheet of paper in a pinch – use what you have, experiment.

I love the idea of small portable lights, this one is certainly an interesting addition to your phone photography – maybe worth giving a try, it’s certainly a good starter to your photography lighting journey.

Here’s the Godox Press Release (With a little bit of my own ramble)

Smartphone Photography, Now With More Zap

Phone cameras keep getting better, but low light, backlighting and mixed lighting can still make them sweat. Enter the Godox A2: proper pro-style lighting for your phone, with more control over your light and a lot more room to play.

Its short, punchy burst of xenon light freezes motion in its tracks, which is great for action shots and stylized looks.

Xenon Flash: Bring Your Subject to Life

Go bold with direct flash, or add a subtle lift to a backlit portrait. With a guide number of roughly 15 (ISO 100, metres), the A2 has plenty of oomph for close-range shots. When flash is your main light, that quick burst also helps freeze movement. *For best results, keep the A2 within 2 m of your subject. Want more power or wider coverage? Pair Godox’s upcoming smartphone wireless flash trigger (sold separately) with Godox speedlights or outdoor flashes.

TTL and Manual Modes: Stay Spontaneous, Get Precise

Fast and flawless when the moment’s fleeting, or hands-on when you want to flex your creative muscles. TTL and Manual modes have you covered both ways.

High-Speed Sync: Find Your Balance

Why banish that bright background when it can star in the story? With high-speed sync up to 1/8000s, the A2 lets you control ambient exposure while lighting your subject. Balance a face against a sunlit scene, or go for a faster shutter speed to keep the action crisp.

Bi-Color LED: True Color for Everyday Stories

Truer colors and flattering skin tones make portrait videos look natural and beautifully textured. Low light or indoors, the results feel authentic and ready to share. Your content doesn’t just look good, it feels right, and it’s always social-media ready.

Godox Camera App: Your Look, at Your Fingertips

Find your look right on your screen. Built on Godox’s TTL know-how, the Godox Camera app keeps exposure simple in Auto (A) mode, with Natural, Even and Contrast flash effects to try out. Feeling fussy? Switch to Manual (M) mode and tweak shutter speed and flash output yourself. Bluetooth with NFC-assisted setup lets you adjust flash and LED settings wirelessly, on or off camera.

Dual-Side Magnetic Mounting: Snap On, Explore New Angles

The A2’s dual magnetic design isn’t just for the back of your phone. Snap it to any metal surface or pop it on a stand and you’re ready to roll. On the front, the magnetic ring lets you attach accessories to shape the light exactly how you like. Simple, flexible and always creative.

Magnetic Accessories: Change the Light, Set the Mood

Go moodier and more dramatic with optional extras like a honeycomb grid, barndoors or a snoot to aim your light and tame the spill. Add a touch of warmth with a full CTO magnetic filter. *For best results, use the A2 off-camera with light-shaping accessories.

Compact. Magnetic. More Ways to Light.

Pro flash power in a palm-sized body. Pocketable, portable and happy to go anywhere you do.

Four Colors, A Style of Your Own

The A2 brings pro lighting to your phone in four distinctive colors. Pick a finish that suits your everyday style, and make your kit as personal as the photos you take.

issues.author: Sime
issues.content_html:
The post Do people still print their photographs? appeared first on Digital Photography School. It was authored by Sime.

The guys at Godox sent across a press release (A few weeks back now I’m sorry as I’ve been a little ‘offline’) for their then new Godox Portable Colour Photo Printer, the P100. And it got me thinking, even at a simple, easy to use level of printing like this little guy, who is still printing out their photographs?

We celebrated my dad’s life recently, and at the wake my brother had printed out a couple hundred photographs that showed the life and times of dad and those he cared about. There’s something very real about having a print you can hold in your hand, nothing to log in to, no computers to boot up, just a square of paper and your memories.

Before we share this press release, here’s a challenge: In the next couple of months, aim to have one of your photographs printed, and to take that one step further, I was just listening to a clip from a podcast (You can see it here) Print Swap, what a great idea, print one of your images and send it to someone – to have and to hold.

Right, the Godox P100, it’s not an A3 Epson printing onto some beautiful Canson Rag, but it’s WITH YOU, you can print images and have them. (I’ve been grabbing frames with the beautiful FujiFilm Instax Mini 99 which prints a little 45x62mm photo)

On with our press release, please keep in mind we have not tested the P100 ourselves.

Godox Introduces P100 Portable Color Photo Printer

Godox has announced the P100 Portable Color Photo Printer, a compact dye-sublimation printer designed to turn digital images into physical prints wherever you are.

The P100 uses 300 dpi high-precision dye-sublimation printing, with 1,256 printhead heating elements and support for 16.7 million colours. According to Godox, the combination is designed to produce smooth colour gradations, fine detail and vivid colour reproduction.

Each print also receives an automatic protective overcoat, helping protect the finished photo from dust, water, fingerprints, fading and everyday abrasion.

Print and personalise from your phone

The P100 connects to the Godox Cam APP via Bluetooth, while NFC tap-to-connect provides another quick way to pair the printer.

From within the app, users can capture and print photos directly, or work with images already on their device. Creative options include filters, frames, stickers and templates, along with tools for creating ID photos and collages.

The app also allows users to check remaining paper and battery levels, making it easier to keep track of the printer’s status.

Designed to travel

With its compact design and lightweight construction, the P100 is intended to be easy to take along to parties, family gatherings, housewarmings and other everyday occasions.

Rather than leaving photos sitting on a phone or buried in a cloud library, the P100 gives users a simple way to turn them into physical prints that can be displayed, collected, added to a scrapbook or shared with friends and family.

Automatic protection

The P100’s automatic lamination process adds a protective overcoat to every finished print. Godox says this helps protect prints against dust, water, fingerprints, fading and everyday abrasion, as well as humid conditions.

The process happens automatically after printing, so there is no additional lamination step for the user.

All-in-one cartridge

The P100 uses an all-in-one photo paper cartridge, designed to make replacing the printing supplies quick and straightforward.

Combined with wireless connectivity and the Godox Cam APP, the system is designed to keep the process from capturing a photo to holding the finished print as simple as possible.

A physical home for digital memories

The P100 is ultimately aimed at something increasingly familiar in photography: we take plenty of photos, but relatively few ever make it off our phones.

By combining portable dye-sublimation printing with a range of simple editing and personalisation tools, Godox says the P100 is designed to make printing those images easier, whether you’re sharing them with friends at a gathering or simply putting a favourite photograph somewhere you’ll actually see it.

The Godox P100 Portable Color Photo Printer is now part of Godox’s expanding range of photography accessories.

You can get them online for around $200 Aussie, do a Google and see what you can find!

Don’t forget, PRINT YOUR WORK.

issues.title: Iconic and Independent: New York Studio School's MFA Program
issues.summary: NYSS is now accepting applications from independent thinkers and experimenters in the arts.
issues.author: New York Studio School
issues.content_html:
What does it mean to give art the time and attention it requires? Since its founding in 1964, the New York Studio School (NYSS) has pursued this question through an approach to art education grounded in sustained studio practice, rigorous inquiry, and the conviction that artists develop through the ongoing process of making, looking, and thinking.

Located at 8 West 8th Street in Greenwich Village, the School occupies a building with a rich history in American art. Founded by artist and educator Mercedes Matter, NYSS carries forward a tradition of independent thinking and experimentation, offering an environment where artists can challenge assumptions, investigate fundamental questions, and develop their work through direct engagement with materials and ideas.

The School’s full-time, two-year Master of Fine Arts (MFA) program is a 60-credit degree centered on intensive, individual studio practice in drawing, painting, sculpture, and art history. Rather than prescribing a single artistic direction, the program provides students with the time, space, and mentorship to pursue their own questions and cultivate their own distinctive artistic language.

At the heart of the New York Studio School MFA program is the relationship between individual practice and collective exchange. Students are assigned private or semi-private studio spaces and select two core faculty artists to serve as their atelier mentors. Through studio visits, group critiques, and ongoing dialogue with faculty and peers, students are encouraged to examine their work from multiple perspectives while developing the confidence and critical awareness to move their practice forward.

The curriculum combines independent studio work with intensive two-week Marathons, drawing courses, Critical Studies seminars, and encounters with visiting artists. The School’s renowned Evening Lecture Series and Exhibitions further connect students to a broad community of artists, writers, historians, and thinkers. Drawing remains a foundational component of the program, informing the study of painting and sculpture and encouraging deeper attention to perception, form, space, and material.

Students in the MFA program are encouraged to engage with the histories of art while questioning established conventions, exploring the relationships between representation and abstraction, and discovering new possibilities through sustained experimentation. The goal is to support the development of an independent, thoughtful, and resilient artistic practice. The MFA program’s second year culminates with a thesis project and exhibition in the School’s historic galleries, connecting a new generation of artists with a building that has been part of New York’s cultural life for more than a century.

For artists seeking a demanding, immersive environment in which to deepen their work, the New York Studio School offers an education built around the essential questions of art-making, and the time, community, and commitment needed to pursue them.

Applications are now open for Fall 2027 admission. For full consideration for admission and financial aid, apply by the Priority Deadline: January 15 .

Learn more about the MFA program and apply at nyss.org.

issues.title: Recovering Edward Said’s Voice
issues.summary: Moustafa Bayoumi on a new documentary about the legendary Palestinian critic and activist; plus, can contemporary art make us laugh?
issues.author: Hyperallergic
issues.content_html:
For decades, the word “Palestinian” conjured a very specific image in the minds of many intellectuals and members of the public: the commanding presence of Edward Said, credited with no less than revolutionizing our collective understanding of the dynamics of oppression. Now, as Israel’s genocide in Gaza continues, Said’s legacy is not just urgent, but also, in some spaces, the target of censorship . Today, author Moustafa Bayoumi, who studied under the late critic, activist, and professor at Columbia University, pens a thoughtful review of Edward Said: Between Worlds (2026), a new documentary by Maiken Baird whose audio consists almost entirely of Said’s own words. “To recover Said’s voice is to rediscover some of the most compelling arguments that have been made for Palestinian liberation,” Bayoumi writes.

Can contemporary art make us laugh (and not just when we’re making fun of it)? Greta Rainbow visits a New York exhibition that’s all about embracing humor in art, and somewhere between Brian Belott's absurdist fan-embedded assemblages and Ebecho Muslimova’s delightfully transgressive depictions, she learns a thing or two about her own funny bone.

—Valentina Di Liscia, senior editor

Edward Said Speaks More Urgently Than Ever

In their (still brilliant) 1990 experimental film Introduction to the End of an Argument, filmmakers Jayce Salloum and Elia Suleiman splice together troves of found footage about Palestinians and Israelis. The result is an exquisite mash-up of Hollywood cartoons and political clichés, a comic pastiche illustrating the common bond between Orientalism and zombies. Both just won’t die. | Moustafa Bayoumi
