issues.title: Georgia O'Keeffe Painting Found in NYC Closet Sells for $4.9M
issues.summary: Calls to exclude Russia from Venice Architecture Biennale, Public Art Fund announces 2027 program, and more in today's art news.
issues.author: Phillip Pyle
issues.content_html:
Welcome to our roundup of daily art news, featuring top stories and timely updates handpicked by Hyperallergic’s writers and editors. Have a news tip? Get in touch with us .

Long-Lost Georgia O'Keeffe Painting Found in Closet Breaks Estimates

Georgia O’Keeffe’s “Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I” (1930), which was rediscovered in the back of an East Village closet where it was stored for four decades, fetched $4.9 million at Christie’s 20th-Century Evening Sale last night, November 18, surpassing its $2-3 estimate. Read Hyperallergic Staff Writer Rhea Nayyar’s report detailing the fascinating backstory behind the painting, created just one year after the artist's first visit to New Mexico.

EU Countries Call to Exclude Russia From Architecture Biennale

Days before the close of this year’s Venice Biennale, 10 European Union countries are demanding that the European Commission exclude Russia from the 2027 architecture biennale. “In light of the current geopolitical realities … there should be no room for ‘normalisation’ of Russia’s participation in international sporting and cultural events, as long as there is no just and lasting peace in Ukraine,” reads a letter signed by representatives in Poland, Austria, Croatia, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Germany, Latvia, Lithuania, and Sweden, according to Rapporteur.

Public Art Fund Announces 2027 Program

Ahead of its 50th anniversary next year, Public Art Fund has announced its 2027 exhibition program. The organization will continue its longstanding bus shelter series with I Happen to Like New York, which will transform 700 JCDecaux shelters across New York, Chicago, and Boston with the works of 19 artists, including Nicole Eisenman, Louis Fratino, and Toyin Ojih Odutola. New outdoor public sculptures from Ugo Rondinone, Lotus Kang, and Firelei Báez, a photo series from Catherine Opie, and a first-of-its-kind participatory performance by Jeremy Dweller round out Public Art Fund's 2027 offerings.

More in Today’s News:

  • Brooklyn artist Julia Jo's "One Fell Swoop" (2026) will be offered at Christie’s evening sale tomorrow, November 19, to benefit the Coalition for the Homeless. The New York-based nonprofit has supported unhoused individuals and families in the city through food, clothing, housing, job training, and youth programs since its founding in 1981. "One Fell Swoop" is estimated to fetch between $30,000 and $50,000.
  • Two months before the closing of Ana Mendieta at London’s Tate Modern, the Museum of Modern Art has announced it will present the first retrospective on the late Cuban-American artist in the United States in over 20 years.
  • Leading feminist conceptual artist Eleanor Antin has sued her dealer Richard Saltoun , who operates galleries in New York, London, and Rome, over his alleged withholding of at least 179 works.
  • After this month’s “blue wave,” President Donald Trump will soon have to contend with a Democrat-majority Congress ready to investigate his culture war tirades against institutions including the National Portrait Gallery, the Smithsonian, and the Kennedy Center.
  • This week, the City of Sydney in Australia awarded 40 artists $25,000 “no strings attached” grants in a new initiative aimed at preventing the city from losing “its local storytellers and creative soul.”
  • Five works, including 15th-century illuminated manuscripts and 18th-20th century inscribed crosses, were repatriated to Ethiopia following a ceremony in London today, November 18, as part of a new partnership between the Toledo Museum of Art in Ohio and the Ethiopian Heritage Authority.

issues.title: Is My Art Funny to You?
issues.summary: A sprawling exhibition across two New York campus galleries explores humor in contemporary art, imploring us to take seriously the jokes artists made and preserved in time.
issues.author: Greta Rainbow
issues.content_html:
Genuine laughter — involuntary, unplanned — is rare. Called “Duchenne laughter” after a 19th-century neurologist, the gesture is bodily, sometimes to a repulsive degree. But most of the time, we laugh because we feel that we should — that it would behoove us socially. In a talk at the Aspen AIR Festival this year, poet and psychoanalyst Nuar Alsadir described eliciting Duchenne laughter as an attempt “to strip away the layers of socialization and the false self.” While laughter “flies under the radar because of our associations to it as being joyful,” when you dig deeper, it’s “usually coming from some kind of conflict in the unconscious.”

What to make of art that makes us laugh? (Or at least desperately wants to?) Does This Taste Funny?: Humor in Contemporary Art, a sprawling exhibition across at Lehman College Art Gallery in the Bronx and The Gallery at Heimbold Visual Arts Center at Sarah Lawrence in Bronxville, proposes comedy as a potent artistic device. Co-curators Melissa Brown, artist and professor of art at Lehman College, and John O’Connor, chair of the Visual and Studio Arts program at Sarah Lawrence, use humor’s various tones — absurd, cringe, slapstick, ironic — as organizing principles to present the work of 41 artists. From museum-collection heavy hitters like Ray Johnson and Cindy Sherman, to established cartoonists Roz Chast and Aline Kominsky-Crumb, to contemporary rising stars such as Ebecho Muslimova, Does This Taste Funny? implores us to take seriously the jokes artists made and preserved in time.

Humor is “an emotional response that’s a little bit like a sneak attack,” Brown said in an interview with Hyperallergic. “It causes you to think about things in a way that is not led by a press release, not predetermined by art history. There’s something that’s very, very personal about it.” Indeed, humor tends to be anti-didactic. You either guffaw or giggle, or you don’t. Alsadir would say that what you find funny or not provides information about your psychic state — what does it say about me that I chuckled sympathetically at Jill Danenberg’s 2024 accordion book Underground Comic, detailing trials and tribulations between veganism and feminism, while my mouth refused to curl for Tony Matelli’s “Veg Man” (2008), a droopily vegetal bronze figure?

The participatory nature of humor means this show is uniquely invested in perception, and in provoking a certain response. As at an open mic, I felt the pressure of bearing witness, aware of my role as an audience member with the power to deem certain works successful or not by producing that ever-elusive involuntary laugh. This semester, O’Connor is teaching an undergraduate class on taking laughter seriously: He tasked his students with making small sculptures, their only instruction to try to be “the funniest in the class.” The winning piece, according to votes cast via smiley-face stickers on a table outside the gallery, is a realistic bust of Professor O’Connor with a No. 2 pencil stuck halfway up his nose. Second place was a reference to a meme O’Connor still doesn’t quite understand.

The oldest featured work in Does This Taste Funny? is Karl Wirsum’s drawing “Untitled (Study for Blue Tattoo)” (1964), featuring a classic Sailor Jerry star design on the tongue of a woman sporting a perfect mid-century housewife hairdo. Getting the reference is important to appreciating a good joke beyond the most base level of someone farting or slipping on a banana peel (which, to get psychoanalytic again, we laugh at to mask our own shame). Brown and O’Connor’s curation is never insidery or niche to the canon, but they are aware of the quality of funniness changing over time.

Some of O’Connor’s students recognized River Phoenix in Ray Johnson’s mail-art collage; more were taken by Jeremy Couillard’s “Escape from Lavender Island” (2023), an open-world video game simulation featuring deep-fried animation aesthetics and relatably tragic dialogue from the depths of neoliberal hell (“While he ate he would watch film classics on an overpriced streaming service and sometimes cry.”)

“Absurdism ends up being pretty timeless,” Brown said. “Using ridiculously absurd materials to make work that doesn’t connect necessarily to a political moment or a socioeconomic issue, it represents this irreverent attitude towards art-making.” And apparently that’s what appeals to Gen Z, who are inundated with visual content, yet perhaps still seeking a response to contemporary life that truly resonates.

Brown, who has been teaching at Lehman for 20 years, wants artists to find their idiosyncratic voice. If being funny comes naturally, maybe that’s the tack they should take.

“There’s such a tendency for imitation out there. You can easily become a version of something that exists, and that is no longer considered a bad thing,” she said. “I'm interested in trying to find, ‘What's your really weird way of approaching that?’”

Take Kristen Mills’s “It IS Cake” (2026), a filmic parody of the Netflix baking contest series Is It Cake? using entirely brown cardboard, displayed in the gallery on a screen within a faux kitchen made of the same plainly bland material. Installed nearby is puppet theater ephemera that does directly respond to a political moment: John Vasquez Mejias’s “The Puerto Rican War” (2026), which expands his novelette about revolutionaries fighting colonialism in 1950. The Puerto Ricans’ demands aren’t funny, but some of the depictions of American incompetence are.

Does This Taste Funny? reminds us of humor as a tool, as a way to frame whatever it is that we hope to communicate. Life is not always joyful, but it should at least be emotional. At Sarah Lawrence, I watched Robert DeJesus’s surreal video “The Survey” (2024), starring a talking Olmec head who speaks only when there are no corroborative witnesses. I didn’t laugh. Later in the day, turning a corner on the grounds of Lehman College, I was suddenly confronted with the stone statue, whose onscreen lips I’d just seen move. I audibly snorted.

issues.title: Guadalupe Maravilla to Offer Midnight Mass Sound Bath at St. John the Divine Cathedral
issues.summary: His Creative Time project will offer eight sound baths during its run, as well as other programming.
issues.author: Maximilíano Durón
issues.content_html:
As part of his forthcoming Creative Time commission at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine, artist Guadalupe Maravilla will offer a bevy of programming beginning December 18.

Titled Consejos de las Estrellas and presented in collaboration with the Clemente Soto Vélez Cultural and Educational Center, the project comprises a sculptural installation that will “serve as a healing instrument and a place to find warmth and belonging when the holidays deepen the feeling of absence,” as Maravilla told ARTnews when the project was announced in October.

Core to Maravilla’s sculptures is their ability to be activated for sound baths, and Consejos de las Estrellas will offer eight sound baths during its run. Two of them will be staged in tandem with two winter holidays: a Christmas Eve Midnight Mass sound bath, beginning at 11:59 p.m. on December 24, and New Year Cleansing sound bath on January 9. The latter event will be proceeded by an herbal cleansing workshop by Herban Cura, which describes itself as a “healing justice herbalism and ecology school,” per its website.

A cancer survivor himself, Maravilla has long held sound baths specifically for the cancer community and he will offer two at St. John the Divine that will bookend this part of the programming. The first of these, on December 18, will be specifically for cancer survivors, healthcare workers, and caregivers and realized in partnership with the Mount Sinai Tisch Cancer Center. The final one will be staged on February 4, which is also World Cancer Day.

Consejos de las Estrellas will also feature performances by artist-collaborators who will activate Maravilla’s installation. They are Holland Andrews (January 22), Tersora Garcia and Camillo Godoy (January 29), and Jesús Hilario-Reyes (February 6). Maravilla will hold an artist conversation and Tarot reading on January 14.

Additionally, there will be a Three Kings Eve celebration and procession on the afternoon of January 5 with puppeteers from Teatro Sea. The project also will serve as a mutual aid hub, collecting food, clothing, and toy donations during its open hours, Wednesday to Sunday.

Consejos de las Estrellas will be open at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine in New York’s Morningside Heights neighborhood from December 17 to February 7. Opening hours will be Wednesdays to Fridays from 2 p.m. to 8 p.m. and Saturdays and Sundays from 12 p.m. to 7 p.m.; the project will be closed from December 31–January 2. Full details for the accompanying programming, which is free and open to the public, can be found on Creative Time’s website.

issues.title: Art World Advice Columnists Chen & Lampert Answered Questions as Old as Time
issues.summary: Among them: Do mean people in the art world actually like art?
issues.author: Andy Battaglia
issues.content_html:
The disquieting question of how to be human in the art world came in for special consideration during a talk with advice columnists Chen & Lampert during Art Week NYC, a citywide festival organized by ARTnews, Artforum, and Art in America.

Together, Howie Chen and Andrew Lampert talked about their individual and collective efforts as artists, curators, and incomparable visionaries whose recurring “Hard Truths” advice columns and accompanying “Hard Choices” interactive quizzes are highlights of every issue of Art of America. Since their debut in 2019, the two writers have mulled pressing questions—can senior citizens be sage social-media ambassadors for museums in need of street cred? should a jilted artist keep applying for grants? is our advice helpful?—while dishing out wisdom for the ages.

At their talk on Friday, November 13 at the PMC Studio in Midtown Manhattan, Chen & Lampert reminisced about fielding queries from the past as well as their trip to Las Vegas for a 2025 essay titled “Art and Ecstatic Ambience in Las Vegas’s Neon Vortex.” (A little taste of that, for old time’s sake: “Some writers go on Hajj to Marfa to feel the minimalist wind blow sand into their eyes, while others schlep Brooklinen tote bags as they chase biennials across small European cities. Being earnest art-world advice columnists, we prefer to explore more democratic forms of visual culture—the kind that ribaldly stages a two-hour revue called The Empire Strips Back: A Burlesque Parody.”)

As watchable in the video of their talk above, Chen & Lampert also addressed questions solicited from A.i.A. readers on the fly—among them: “Do mean people in the art world actually like art? If not, what is their motivation?”

issues.title: Laura Hoptman Wins CCS Bard’s 2027 Audrey Irmas Award for Curatorial Excellence
issues.summary: Hoptman will receive $25,000 and will be honored at CCS Bard’s spring gala in April
issues.author: Anne Doran
issues.content_html:
The Center for Curatorial Studies at Bard College (CCS Bard) has given its 2027 Audrey Irmas Award for Curatorial Excellence to Laura Hoptman, executive director of New York’s Drawing Center. She will receive $25,000 and will be honored at CCS Bard’s spring gala in April.

Hoptman joined the Drawing Center in 2018 following eight years as a curator in the department of painting and sculpture at the Museum of Modern Art (MoMA). While at MoMA, she oversaw major traveling exhibitions devoted to Isa Genzken (2013) and Bruce Conner (2016), as well as the museum’s hotly debated survey of contemporary painting, “The Forever Now” (2014–2015).

After beginning her career as an assistant curator at the Bronx Museum, Hoptman worked as an assistant curator in MoMA’s department of drawings from 1996 to 2002. In 2003 she guest-curated “Drawing Now: Eight Propositions,” featuring more than 200 representational works by 26 contemporary artists, at MoMA QNS, and in 2004 she was director of the 54th Carnegie International in Pittsburgh. Between 2006 and 2010 she was senior curator at the New Museum in New York, where she co-organized “Unmonumental: The Object in the 21st Century” (2007–2008) and “The Generational: Younger than Jesus” (2009).

The Audrey Irmas Award has been given annually since 1998 and recognizes “groundbreaking visionaries in the curatorial field,” according to a press release. Past recipients include Adriano Pedrosa, Connie Butler, Carolyn Christov-Bakargiev, Thelma Golden, and Okwui Enwezor.

“Laura’s longstanding curatorial practice has furthered new art historical analysis and international recognition of drawing as a creative medium and social practice,” said CCS Bard executive director Tom Eccles in a statement. “Her international projects have reexamined the legacies of an array of artists through new and creative frameworks. What is often forgotten is how consistently Laura has demonstrated a boldness and bravery in championing artists across many institutional structures.”

issues.title: Sotheby’s New York Impressionist and Modern Art Sale Rakes in $777.8 M., Italian Exhibition Ordered to Remove Fascist Imagery, and More: Morning Links for November 19, 2026
issues.summary: Here's what we're reading this morning.
issues.author: Hikmat Mohammed
issues.content_html:
To receive Morning Links in your inbox every weekday, sign up for our Breakfast with ARTnews newsletter.

Good Morning!

  • It was an evening of superlatives at Sotheby’s, whose two auctions of Impressionist and modern art in New York last night raked in $777.8 million in total.
  • Italian lawmakers have ordered the removal of imagery containing fascist references from an exhibition in Rome marking the centenary of far-right politician Pino Rauti.
  • The collective Artists 4 Artists Miami is calling for an “Art Basel Boycott” that asks the public to refrain from participating in the forthcoming Miami Art Week’s major fairs.

The Headlines

SOTHEBY’S SUPERLATIVES. It was an evening of superlatives at Sotheby’s, whose two auctions of Impressionist and modern art in New York last night raked in a total of $777.8 million, reports ARTnews. The lump sum is the highest for a single night at the auction house, surpassing the $706 million it achieved a year ago at the same time. The highlights from the evening included the unexpected sale of a tiny Claude Monet with a wild backstory, There was also Vincent van Gogh’s Châtaigniers en fleurs (1890), which sold to dealer William Acquavella for $190.4 million with fees, after a week dominated by a Nazi-era restitution dispute. The sum was more than Sotheby’s bargained for and beat the artist’s previous record by just over 62 percent, marking a clear victory for the auction house. But there were hitches, including a Remedios Varo drawing that failed to sell, and three lots were withdrawn while the sale was in progress.

ROUTING OUT PINO RAUTI. Italian lawmakers have ordered the removal of imagery containing fascist references from an exhibition in Rome marking the centenary of far-right politician Pino Rauti, who died in 2012, reports Reuters. The exhibit at the Palazzo Valdina complex, sponsored by the Italian culture ministry, has caused an uproar in Italy, where Rauti is remembered for joining Benito Mussolini’s Nazi-collaborating government during World War II and later becoming a leader of the neo-fascist Italian Social Movement (MSI). The controversial content, which was reportedly removed by Wednesday, included a photograph of Rauti beneath a flag bearing a Celtic cross linked to neo-fascism, while the figure of Mussolini was also given pride of place. Rauti never denounced his past, but that didn’t stop him from being voted into Italy’s lower house of parliament for five terms, until 1992. The order to take down parts of the exhibition was sparked by demands from left-leaning members of parliament, who called the whole endeavor “a disgrace.”

The Digest

Artists 4 Artists Miami is gathering steam for an “Art Basel Boycott” that calls on the public to refrain from participating in the forthcoming Miami Art Week. [The Art Newspaper]

Benin may be the first country to benefit from new legislation in France designed to facilitate the return of artworks looted during the colonial era, and has formally made a request for 35 items, which are housed in the Musée du quai Branly. [Le Monde]

Jeff Koons’ decision to sell parts of his collection at Christie’s this week makes art critic Jerry Saltz sick, and here’s why. [New York Magazine]

The medieval “Ugly Duchess” portrait by Quentin Metsys hanging in London’s National Gallery may depict a famously homely “Old Woman,” but she was not meant to be alone: the companion piece to the painting features a man, and it is heading to auction at Christie’s next month, where it may fetch as much as $10.5 million. [Artnet News]

Phillips names new senior leadership in Asia, and other industry moves. [ARTnews]

The Kicker

BACKWARDS BEAUTY. One might be tempted to think that current beauty standards were whipped into the collective consciousness via modern mass media, but a new study confirms the source goes much further back and can be found glaringly apparent in historic paintings. Research published in Proceedings of the Royal Society Banalyzes hundreds of paintings throughout history to demonstrate how Western beauty standards for women have evolved away from the curvy female ideal to straighter and androgynous silhouettes over the past 300 years, reports the Times of London. Authors of the study examined paintings of upper-class women in Western paintings from 1650 to 1950, and asked over 1,500 people to judge them for things like waist-to-hip ratio. Little surprise: Women’s bodies tended to move from the hourglass shape once deemed the ideal beauty associated with fertility to a straighter, “more tubular” silhouette. To Jeanne Bovet, co-author of the study, the artworks are seen as “cognitive fossils,” or relics of vanished societies and their values. “People have always paid attention to appearance,” said Bovet. “And usually it’s because they have wanted to send a signal.” It seems to have worked.

issues.title: Hand-Marbled Papers Ground Sylvain Lefebvre’s Surreal Landscapes
issues.summary: 'Journeys Into the Unseen Forest' embraces the paradox of natural balance. Do stories and artists like this matter to you? The article Hand-Marbled Papers Ground Sylvain Lefebvre’s Surreal Landscapes appeared first on Colossal .
issues.author: Kate Mothes
issues.content_html:
Enormous trees dominate dreamlike wooded landscapes in the mixed-media paintings of Sylvain Lefebvre. A spectral form with dense, gnarly branches shelters a lounging woman in “The Quercus Corallium,” and a table alive with conversation nests beneath the canopy in “A Debat at Tea Time.”

The French artist’s Journeys Into the Unseen Forest at Rebecca Hossack Art Gallery comprises a series of almost fairytale-like tableaux. Collaged, hand-marbled papers beneath the delicate layers of oil paint represent the barely visible or unknown. And trees group closely in the background darken in the distance, while diminutive figures climb around and relax at the base of monumental trunks.

Summer 2026 marked France’s hottest ever documented since records began, during which rainfall was low and unprecedented wildfires raged. Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent, where the effects of the climate crisis are dramatic and impossible to ignore. In Journeys Into the Unseen Forest, Lefebvre delves into an imaginary realm where humans coexist harmoniously with flora and fauna, and old-growth sentinels harbor a wide range of life.

The artist says, “I wanted to put myself in the place of a forest and its trees by asking myself the following question: How is it that when we look at nature, whatever form it takes, it always appears balanced, while the trees that make it up can grow in such unbalanced ways… twisted, diagonally or horizontally, struggling to find their way towards the light?”

In “The Quercus Corallium,” a white tree glows like a sacred spirit, and in “The Polyphane Pachidermus,” one can imagine the canopy extending forever into the blue distance. “In the unseen forest, [Lefebvre] discovers species of trees that have never been seen before,” the gallery says. “They are completely plausible species that may exist somewhere in the few corners of the world that have not yet been discovered. Perhaps they are trees of the future.”

Journey Into the Unseen Forest continues through December 23 in London. See more on Lefebvre’s Instagram.

issues.title: Vhils and Marcelo Cidade Cloak a São Paulo Colonial Building in Silver Thermal Blankets
issues.summary: "2878" envelops a colonial-style building in silver thermal blankets typically used in emergencies. Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a Colossal Member today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article Vhils and Marcelo Cidade Cloak a São Paulo Colonial Building in Silver Thermal Blankets appeared first on Colossal .
issues.author: Grace Ebert
issues.content_html:
“A construction can remain standing while losing its place in the everyday experience of the city. Its address remains, but its presence no longer draws attention. In this sense, disappearance can begin before demolition,” says a statement about a recent collaboration between Alexandre Farto (a.k.a. Vhils) and Marcelo Cidade.

The monumental project at Rua Cardeal Arcoverde, 2878 in Pinheiros, São Paulo, is a meditation on this sentiment as it considers how architecture and the seemingly mundane fixtures of city life shape our understanding of a place. Titled “2878,” the site-specific installation envelops a colonial-style building in silver thermal blankets typically used in emergencies. A cornstarch glue binds the utilitarian material to the structure’s facade, revealing the arched windows and ornate patterns in relief.

Both drawing attention to the building and masking its real condition, the metallic blankets prompt questions about how we care for places and spaces. As passersby walk past, the installation mirrors their silhouettes as faint reflections, while the surface’s color and light shift depending on the time of day.

The collaborative intervention also evokes Christo and Jeanne-Claude’s “Wrapped Reichstag” and the early years of Andy Warhol’s Factory, in which silver paint and tin foil covered the walls of the artist’s New York studio. Warhol was interested in transience and the attention that comes with fame, concerns we see echoed and translated into broader conversations about public space, collective memory, and urban life in “2878.”

Find more from Vhils and Cidade on their Instagrams.

issues.title: Meticulously Detailed Animal Portraits by Thomas Cian Pop from the Page
issues.summary: "It has a lot to do with a desire to reconnect with everything that exists independently of human beings," the artist says. Do stories and artists like this matter to you? Become a Colossal Member today and support independent arts publishing for as little as $7 per month. The article Meticulously Detailed Animal Portraits by Thomas Cian Pop from the Page appeared first on Colossal .
issues.author: Kate Mothes
issues.content_html:
As if ready to swim right off of the page, Thomas Cian’s fish and other creatures are rendered in exquisite detail. Known for his realistic black-and-white portraits, the artist recently embarked on a series of hyperrealistic animal drawings in gouache and pencil. The new direction took him somewhat by surprise, as he realized one day he had been focusing much more on fauna than he had in years past.

“I think it has a lot to do with a desire to reconnect with everything that exists independently of human beings,” Cian tells Colossal. He felt compelled to get closer to what he describes as elemental raw matter, generated through eons of mysterious and fascinating evolutionary processes. “I think that’s what it comes down to: drawing something that hasn’t itself been designed by someone else.”

Cian’s technical aptitude is obvious, but for him, a work isn’t truly complete unless there’s another kind of investment. “For me, achieving a result I’m truly satisfied with is a considerable challenge because my approach is emotional long before it is descriptive,” he says. Truly understanding and sympathizing with a creature propels the process.

Light also plays an integral role in his deceptively simple monochrome approach: Cian highlights whatever the light touches and leaves everything else alone. A piece feels finished when “areas that remain black stop feeling black,” he says, balancing perception and technicality in equal measure.

The artist spends hours researching a subject before rendering it on paper, watching documentaries and browsing publications that give him a sense of their habitats and behaviors, but he resists working from printed images. Even the textures that, from a distance, may look realistic, are actually intuitive and imagined. “I never copy photographs,” Cian says. “I study the anatomy and then reconstruct it, sometimes exaggerating certain features, in a pose that allows me to feel as though I’m in the presence of that particular creature.”

See more on the artist’s Instagram.

The end of the year is quickly approaching, and you know what that means: gifting season is here.

Like clockwork, we’re back with a carefully curated, handy dandy gift guide to help you pick out the perfect presents for each name on your list. Organized by passions and personalities, our list has something special for everyone. So sit back, brew a cup of tea, and get scrolling! You’re about to have the breeziest holiday shopping yet.

As always, thank you for supporting Colossal.

For the Creative Professional

Visual thinkers understand the absolute joy of impeccably designed things. Treat the creative in your life to studio essentials that make the workday lighter and intriguing reads to keep the ideas flowing.

For the Maximalist

More is more! If bold colors, clashing patterns, and whimsical graphics are that special someone’s vibe, we’ve got the perfect accessories to complete their closet.

For the Nature Lover

We all know someone who feels the happiest among flora, fauna, and the great outdoors. Bring a bit of nature to them with a new pair of gardening gloves, fungi-inspired decor and puzzles, a guide to foraging for handmade inks, and plenty more.

For the Tasteful Host

Those with great taste often have a cozy home to match. Help your favorite host make their space even warmer with aesthetically-pleasing objects for cooking, gathering, and lingering just a bit longer.

For the Serial Hobbyist

Our exciting range of craft kits open up a world of possibilities for those who never seem to get tired of trying new hobbies. From hand loom weaving and embroidery to pressing flowers and growing herbs, there’s something new to try for everyone.

For the Budding Artist

What’s more important than encouraging those just beginning to explore their creative side? Surprise that little one with a big imagination with specially-crafted wooden toys, beautiful books, unique crayons, and beyond.

issues.title: Record-breaking $85.8 million Kandinsky leads Christie's November 2026 New York evening sale.
issues.summary: Russian painter Wassily Kandinsky ’s Betonte Ecken (Accentuated Corners) (1922–23), sold for $85.8 million with fees at Christie’s 20th-century evening sale in New York on November 17th, setting a new auction record for the artist. issues.author: Artsy Editorial
issues.content_html:
Russian painter Wassily Kandinsky’s Betonte Ecken(Accentuated Corners) (1922–23), sold for $85.8 million with fees at Christie’s 20th-century evening sale in New York on November 17th, setting a new auction record for the artist.

Bidding opened at $54 million, a price already about $10 million above Kandinsky's previous auction record of $44.8 million, set by Murnau mit Kirche II (1910) at Sotheby’s in 2023. Three bidders competed for the work, including art advisor Ralph DeLuca. Ultimately, Christie’s global president Alex Rotter won the painting for an anonymous client at a hammer price of $74 million.

The painting, estimated at $60 million to $80 million and backed by a third-party guarantee, was consigned by the Nahmad family, which purchased it at Sotheby's New York in 1986 for a hammer price of $1 million.

The nearly four-foot-square abstract composition, painted during Kandinsky’s early Bauhaus years, has a storied provenance. It was acquired in 1929 by Hilla Rebay, who became the Guggenheim Museum’s first director. She gave it to the museum in 1941. The Guggenheim deaccessioned it, along with dozens of other Kandinskys, at Sotheby’s in London in 1964. There it was sold to New York dealer Stephen Hahn before passing to Boston collectors Sandra and David Bakalar and then to the Nahmads.

The other star lot of auction night was Gustav Klimt’s Litzlbergkeller (1915–16), which sold for $82.3 million. It came into the sale as the highest-estimated lot of the evening. Together, the Kandinsky and the Klimt accounted for nearly 27 percent of the sale’s total of $626.6 million ($521 million at the hammer). The evening auction closed at the low end of its $511 million to $743 million estimate range. The sale itself was uneven and selective. Other lots included a group of seven small Jackson Pollock paintings, a 1915 Amedeo Modigliani portrait, and a Léger canvas, all of which went unsold. An 11-foot bronze horse by Fernando Botero, meanwhile, set an artist record at $5.2 million.

Kandinsky has had a strong year at auction. Born in Moscow in 1866, Kandinsky helped found the Blaue Reiter group, taught at the Bauhaus in Germany, and later had dozens of his works seized by the Nazis as “degenerate art” before he died in France in 1944. Earlier this October, Christie’s London sold the artist’s 1907 painting Das bunte Leben for £31,560,000 ($41.5 million).

issues.author: Artsy Editorial
issues.content_html:
Shopping for an art lover is hard. Shopping for yourself is harder: Even if you’ve been saving and wishlisting all year, it’s easy to be overwhelmed.

So we sorted our holiday gift list by collector type. Meet the Tiny Treasure Hunter, the Analog Enthusiast, the Dopamine Decorator, the Surrealist at Heart, and the Plant Parent: five collections for five art lover identities. Then we asked our team to pick one work from each that they’d gladly give, or keep for themselves. Here’s what they chose.

Marlon de Azambuja, Mundo, 2025

Instituto de Visión

Price: $1,500

From: The Tiny Treasure Hunter

Mundo, 2025
Marlon de Azambuja
Instituto de Visión

I’ve always loved tiny things, from dollhouse furniture to small dogs, so The Tiny Treasure Hunter is very much a collecting identity that resonates (and full disclosure, I helped curate it). It’s full of gems, like a beach scene painted on a slice of toast and a little gold ceramic alien who looks like E.T. But at the top of my wish list is Mundo (2025), a thumbprint-sized snail shell by Spanish Brazilian artist Marlon de Azambuja.

It’s made of concrete, the pale gray stuff of smooth sidewalks, yet it looks delicate and organic. The sculpture was recently featured in “Light Field,” de Azambuja’s fall exhibition at Instituto de Visión in New York, which explored how small interventions can transform our perception of space. Mundo does just that: At just over an inch and a half tall, it hangs on the wall like a tiny talisman, as if resting before slithering off.

I love shells of all sorts but snails bring me back to childhood—they’d emerge after it rained and we’d go looking for them to collect them. “Mundo” of course means “world,” and so I’m also reminded that snails appear in creation myths across cultures, symbols of renewal and the cycle of life. I love how this tiny sculpture can hold an entire world of meaning and still it’s just such a delight.

—Casey Lesser, director of editorial and content


Herman Leonard, Louis Armstrong, Paris, 1960

Ellen Miller Gallery

Price: $5,000

From: The Analog Enthusiast

Louis Armstrong, Paris, 1960
Herman Leonard
Ellen Miller Gallery

There’s something quite wonderful about seeing Louis Armstrong like this. Not on stage, trumpet raised, nor posing with that signature warm smile, but sitting quietly, a hand resting on his instrument, seemingly lost in thought. I was actually listening to Armstrong’s 1957 album Under the Stars recently, and was reminded how his music can make even an ordinary evening feel magical.

Herman Leonard—who was to jazz photography what Mick Rock was to ’70s rock—took this photograph backstage at the Olympia Theatre in Paris in 1960. Armstrong was in the city performing and filming Paris Blues, which also starred Sidney Poitier, Paul Newman, and Duke Ellington (worth a watch!). I love that it captures a rare moment of pause in the life of someone whose music and energy brought so much joy to the world.

We see the man behind that magic. There’s a warmth to it, despite the black and white, and something deeply human about seeing him in this unguarded moment.

I’d hang it near a record player, or somewhere to unwind with a drink and some good music. For the music lover in your life, it makes a personal and timeless gift.

—Arun Kakar, senior art market editor


Patrick Hughes, Dancing, 2017

Flowers

Price: £600 ($789)

From: The Dopamine Decorator

Dancing, 2017
Patrick Hughes
Flowers

One of my most-played songs of 2025 was Robyn’s dancefloor banger named after the thrill hormone dopamine, so this collection really speaks to my need for a little visual joy. That also applies to the art that surrounds me. Whether it’s Sarah Morris’s massive neon print with a message or a cartoon-quoting aluminum wall sculpture by Andreas Stylianou, it’s hard not to be drawn to works that immediately lift you up and send you on a high.

Patrick Hughes’s “Rainbows” series is all about that high: in screenprints and paintings he rearranges the typical colorful arc from its spot on the horizon into unlikely scenarios. When a rainbow appears, after all, it brings an immediate hit of dopamine, both in the spontaneity of a one-off moment, and the optical pleasure of every color transitioning into a new one. In Dancing (2017), Hughes repurposes two rainbows as legs against a shocking blue sky, with a shiny red high-heel pump on the end of each. I love how they seem to saunter across the cloudless background, sassy and glamorous.

—Josie Thaddeus-Johns, editor in chief


Johanna Seidel, Sweetwater (II), 2026

Galerie Laetitia Gorsy

€3,900 ($4277)

From: The Surrealist at Heart

Sweetwater ( II ), 2026
Johanna Seidel
Galerie Laetitia Gorsy

The end of the year always takes on a strange dimension, with the days blending together into a blur and waves of the year’s memories flooding back to mind. During these long nights of winter, the magical possibilities of talking animals or women floating through the skies don’t seem so farfetched. This collection of Surrealist-inspired artworks taps into my end-of-year reverie in just the right way. From the chimerical, whimsical beasts of French artist Jacques Merle to a delightfully comical snake-like lady by Lebanese artist Annie Kurkdjian, there are more than a handful of works in the collection that I’ve been pining over.

But it’s German artist Johanna Seidel’s Sweetwater (II) (2026) that I kept returning to, with its uncanny depiction of a brown-haired girl submerged up to her neck in water, ringlets of hair haloing around her, and a swan swimming behind her. The sky is a wash of wild pinks and purples of dawn or dusk. The painting is in keeping with Seidel’s hazy, poetic imagery which draws from history, mythology, and dreams. Here, she references the myth of Leda and the Swan, as well as John Everett Millais’s famed painting Ophelia (1851–52), the tragic heroine of Shakespeare’s Hamlet. Sweetwater (II) is both beautiful and dreamy, but also a deeply uncertain image. Is the swan a friend or foe? In that sense, I think the painting captures some of my own amorphous hopes and anxieties as we head into a new year.

—Katie White, senior staff writer

Nourhan Tchelebi, Bouquet de tulipes jaunes, 2026

L’Original

Price: $445

From: The Plant Parent

Bouquet de tulipes jaunes, 2026
Nourhan Tchelebi
L'Original

During the pandemic, while many people were baking focaccia and sourdough, I picked up a different domestic hobby: raising plants. I’d buy them online and have them shipped across the country so I could nurse them back to health on my windowsill. That changed when I adopted my cat, Martini, who quickly decided he was also interested in gardening and began digging up all of my succulents. No more plant adoptions for me.

Now, to bring plants into my home, I have to get creative. This collection reminded me of all the ways I can add shades of green, bright botanicals, and dappled light back into my life. My favorite work from the bunch is Bouquet de tulipes jaunes (2026) by Nourhan Tchelebi. I love the shape of the work (no need to find a frame!), which is bold and clean, contrasting the hazy strokes and soft outlines of the tulips themselves. The colors also stand out—plants are never just green, and the blend of blues, greens, and yellows in the leaves and the backgrounds makes this bunch feel particularly alive. I’m also drawn to the happy, oversized heads of the tulips themselves, forever at full bloom. I’d put this piece by my windowsill (bright indirect light is best, I hear) to mark the start of a new collection of plants that never need to be watered (and can’t poison my cat).

—Sydney Gelman, copywriter

issues.author: Arun Kakar
issues.content_html:
The Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (MFA Boston), will present “Taylor Swift: The Eras Collection” from April 10 through August 15, 2027, marking the institution’s first exhibition dedicated to a musician. Featuring more than 50 costumes, instruments, and objects from the pop star’s personal archive, the exhibition will trace two decades of Swift’s career through 12 vignettes, each dedicated to a different musical era. The MFA will be the only venue for this exhibition.

Highlights will include several costumes from Swift’s record-breaking Eras Tour of 2023–24, including a custom red Alberta Ferretti gown worn during the “Folklore” and “Evermore” sets, a bejeweled bodysuit designed by Zuhair Murad, and a tinsel fringe jacket worn during the tour’s “Karma” finale.

Other objects on view will include a Victorian-inspired dress and typewriter from the music video for “Fortnight,” displayed beneath an installation of swirling paper. Musical instruments will include a Deering banjo from the “Speak Now” world tour, a green Gibson acoustic guitar from the “Reputation” stadium tour, and a gilded pink-and-gold piano shell used during Swift’s performance at the 2019 American Music Awards.

“This is the first exhibition in the MFA’s history devoted to a musician, and we’re thrilled to invite visitors for an up-close look at the fashion and instruments of one of the most influential cultural figures of our time,” said Kristen Hoskins, the museum’s director of public programs.

The exhibition will explore Swift’s evolving approach to songwriting, performance, and visual storytelling, beginning with her 2006 debut single “Tim McGraw” and concluding with “The Fate of Ophelia” from her 2025 album The Life of a Showgirl.

Tickets, priced at $40 including museum admission, will go on sale to the public on December 13th, Swift’s birthday, at 6 p.m. MFA members can reserve tickets ahead of the public sale.

issues.title: Artists Nieves González, Addie Wagenknecht, and Slawn behind Grammy-nominated album covers.

González is nominated alongside stylist Leith Clark for Lily Allen's West End Girl . Wagenknecht shares a nomination with musician Nick Steinhardt for Interpol's This Mirror Weighs a Ton . The cover of 21 Savage's WHAT HAPPENED TO THE STREE
issues.author: Katie White
issues.content_html:
Artists Nieves González, Addie Wagenknecht, and Slawn are the creative forces behind three of the nominations for Best Album Cover at the 69th Grammy Awards.

González is nominated alongside stylist Leith Clark for Lily Allen's West End Girl. Wagenknecht shares a nomination with musician Nick Steinhardt for Interpol's This Mirror Weighs a Ton. The cover of 21 Savage's WHAT HAPPENED TO THE STREETS?, credited to art director Tina Ibañez, also features a painted portrait by Slawn. The category’s other nominees include Rapsody’s God Gotta Afro and Gold Hoops and Mavis Staples’s Sad and Beautiful World.

González, a Spanish painter born in 1996 and based in Granada, works within the tradition of Spanish Baroque masters like Jusepe de Ribera and Francisco de Zurbarán, often depicting women in voluminous puffer jackets that she has described as treating “almost as if it were sculptural.” The West End Girl commission shows Allen in a periwinkle Miu Miu puffer and Valentino boots.

“It seems to me the portrait reflects so many facets of the album—strength, power, vulnerability, determination, and confusion,” Allen has said of the painting, which is now on view at London's National Portrait Gallery. González has since opened “Sacred Hair,” a solo show on Mary Magdalene at Rome's T293 gallery, and will mount her first institutional solo exhibition in November 2027 at Contemporary Gallery Kunming in China.

Wagenknecht, born in 1981 in Portland, Oregon, blends conceptual art, gestural abstraction, and computer hacking into her practice. She was an early adopter of drones as a painting tool in the 2000s. Her past work includes Believe me, a 2017 commission for the Whitney Museum of American Art's artport that layered cracked-screen imagery over political and internet-vernacular images. She has also collaborated with CERN, Chanel, Coinbase, and Google's Art Machine Intelligence group.

Slawn, born Olaolu Akeredolu-Ale in Lagos in 2000, moved to London in 2018 to study graphic design before turning to painting during lockdown. His style mixes graffiti and street art with influences from pop art and Abstract Expressionism. He designed the Britannia statuette for the 2023 BRIT Awards, becoming the youngest and first Nigerian-born artist to do so, and later designed the 2024 F.A. Cup Trophy. His album cover for WHAT HAPPENED TO THE STREETS? was inspired by artist Kerry James Marshall’s A Portrait of the Artist as a Shadow of His Former Self (1980) and included the addition of Slawn’s signature tattoos. It was issued with several numbered alternate covers also made by the artist. At Art Basel Miami Beach 2025, Slawn debuted a large-scale inflatable balloon, inspired by the album cover, in promotion of the album.

Slawn is represented by Saatchi Yates, where he opened his first major London solo show in 2024 and, this past July, his largest exhibition to date, a Nike- and Team Nigeria-themed pop-up in New York.

Winners will be announced at the 69th Annual Grammy Awards ceremony on Sunday, February 7, 2027.

issues.title: When an Anatomy Practical Exam Becomes a Learning Event
issues.summary: In higher education, we often say we want students to move beyond memorization. Yet many of our exams still reward exactly that: recognize the correct answer, write it down, move to the next question. In my own teaching, I began noticing a familiar pattern. Many students were doing well, but the lower-performing tail of the […] The post When an Anatomy Practical Exam Becomes a Learning Event appea
issues.author: Pradeep Malreddy, DVM
issues.content_html:
In higher education, we often say we want students to move beyond memorization. Yet many of our exams still reward exactly that: recognize the correct answer, write it down, move to the next question.

In my own teaching, I began noticing a familiar pattern. Many students were doing well, but the lower-performing tail of the class seemed to be getting longer. These were not students who lacked potential. Many were working hard, but they were struggling to connect isolated facts into usable understanding.

That raised a simple question for me: Was my exam only measuring the gap, or could it help reduce it?

This question led me to redesign one practical exam using a format I now think of as collaborative reasoning with individual accountability. The goal was not to make the exam easier. The goal was to make students’ thinking more visible before they had to answer on their own.

The Problem With “Just Make it a Group Exam”

I did not want to simply turn the exam into a group test. That can create legitimate concerns: uneven participation, stronger students carrying weaker students, and students receiving credit for answers they may not understand.

At the same time, I did not want to ignore the value of peer discussion. Students often learn a great deal when they hear how classmates approach a problem, especially when the task requires reasoning rather than simple recall.

So the challenge became this: How do we let students benefit from discussion without removing individual accountability?

The solution was a two-phase exam station:

  1. Group reasoning first
  1. Individual answers second

Students could talk through the material, but every student still had to answer independently.

How the Format Worked

At each station, students first saw a set of tagged structures. Importantly, they did not see the questions yet.

They had a short period of time to discuss everything they knew about those structures. They could talk about identification, function, relationships, applications, or anything else that might matter.

Then the timer went off. Discussion stopped. Students flipped over the question card.

At that point, each student answered the questions individually. No talking. No group answer sheet. No shared score.

The format was simple:

  1. Students examine the material.
  1. Students discuss as a group.
  1. Questions are revealed.
  1. Students answer individually.

The group phase created the learning opportunity. The individual phase preserved accountability.

What Changed

When we compared student performance on a traditional exam with performance on the collaborative format, overall performance improved. But the more meaningful result was not the class average.

The biggest improvement came from students in the lower-performing quartiles.

That mattered to me. My goal was not to inflate grades across the board. My goal was to support the students who were struggling to make connections. The discussion seemed to give those students access to how their peers were reasoning before they had to retrieve and apply the information themselves.

The strongest students did not show the same level of improvement, likely because they were already performing near the top. But the lower tail moved, and that was the point.

What Students Thought

Student feedback was generally positive, especially around learning. Many students reported that discussion helped them understand the material more clearly and supported their individual answers.

But their feedback was not universally enthusiastic, and that is important.

Some students felt the individual answer period was too short. Others raised concerns about fairness and group dynamics. Some preferred the traditional format. Some preferred the collaborative format. Some had no strong preference.

That tension is useful. It tells us that the format has promise, but the details matter.

In future versions, I would keep the core structure but refine the timing. I would also be more explicit about expectations during the discussion phase:

  • Every student should contribute.
  • The goal is to explain reasoning, not just name answers.
  • Discussion should focus on relationships and applications.
  • Once the individual phase begins, all discussion stops.

This is not a shortcut. It is a structured thinking phase.

Why This May Work in Undergraduate Courses

Although I developed this format in an anatomy practical, the idea is not limited to anatomy or professional programs. It can work in many undergraduate courses where students need to apply concepts rather than simply recall facts.

In biology, students could examine a diagram, specimen, data figure, or microscopy image together before answering individual questions.

In chemistry, students could discuss a reaction mechanism, molecular structure, or lab scenario before individually predicting products or explaining errors.

In physics, students could reason through a diagram, graph, or conceptual problem before each student solves a related question independently.

In engineering, students could discuss a design constraint, system diagram, or failure scenario before individually explaining the next step.

In mathematics or statistics, students could discuss a problem setup, dataset, or model choice before independently completing a calculation or interpretation.

In humanities and social sciences, students could discuss a short passage, case, artifact, primary source, or policy scenario before writing an individual response.

The key is the sequence: Students discuss before seeing the questions. Then they answer individually.

That sequence matters. If students see the questions first, they may simply divide the work. If they discuss the material first, they must activate what they know more broadly. They prepare each other to think, not just to copy.

Why This Matters for Undergraduate Programs

Many undergraduate programs are concerned with persistence, DFW rates, first-generation student support, and performance gaps in gateway courses. Often, the students who struggle most are not unwilling to learn; they may simply lack access to the reasoning strategies that more experienced or confident students are already using.

This format gives them a brief window into those strategies.

They hear how peers identify key features, eliminate wrong ideas, connect concepts, and decide what matters. Then they must answer on their own.

That is the balance I find valuable: support without removing responsibility.

Practical Tips for Trying This Yourself

Faculty do not need to redesign an entire course to try this approach. Start small.

Use it for one quiz, one exam section, one lab practical, or a few problem-solving stations.

I would recommend:

  • Keep groups small: three to five students.
  • Hide the questions during the discussion phase.
  • Use a visible timer.
  • Keep individual answers short.
  • Use mostly foundational questions with a few deeper application questions.
  • Avoid group scores.
  • Collect feedback immediately afterward.
  • Tell students why you are using the format.

The last point matters. Students may assume group work means the exam will be easier. I tell them directly: this is not designed to make the exam easier. It is designed to make the thinking more visible.

Final Thought

Assessment does not have to be separate from learning. With careful design, it can become part of the learning process itself.

The lesson for me was not that every exam should become collaborative. They should not. The lesson was more practical: when students are allowed to reason together before answering individually, struggling students may get the support they need without removing accountability.

That is the kind of assessment worth building.

Dr. Pradeep Malreddy is a Clinical Associate Professor at Kansas State University, specializing in Anatomy and Histology. Holding a DVM from India and an MS from Kansas State, he brings a blend of clinical and academic expertise. He has additional certifications in Medical Education Research and Online Teaching from AAMC and Harvard. Dr. Malreddy has developed a One-Year Master’s Program at K-State and teaches courses in anatomy, histology, and physiology. His research focuses on anatomy education, eye-tracking technology, and active learning. An active member of professional organizations like the American Association of Veterinary Anatomists, he has received accolades for teaching excellence and diversity initiatives. He was recently honored with Fellowship in the United Kingdom’s prestigious Academy of Medical Educators.

issues.title: Reaching Reserved Students in the Back Row: Strategies for Engagement
issues.summary: The First Five Minutes: Traps and Snap Judgments You walk into classroom 531 on the fifth floor, on a missive to deliver your best first lecture of the fall semester. You smile and say hello to your new students, expecting a wave of friendly faces in return. A few look up from their laptops and […] The post Reaching Reserved Students in the Back Row: Strategies for Engagement appeared first on Fac
issues.author: Beverly Wertheimer, PsyD, DMin, LCSW
issues.content_html:
The First Five Minutes: Traps and Snap Judgments

You walk into classroom 531 on the fifth floor, on a missive to deliver your best first lecture of the fall semester. You smile and say hello to your new students, expecting a wave of friendly faces in return. A few look up from their laptops and grin back, and you instantly decide these will be the “easy” students who like you best. You like them best, too. You take your place at the podium when a student texting on their phone catches your eye. A sudden thought flits across your mind: this student may be trouble. Just like that, assumptions are formed before class even begins. First impressions can stick.

From an evolutionary standpoint, this urge to make snap judgments makes you more than just judgy. It is an adaptive survival mechanism rather than a superficial flaw (Zebrowitz, 2017). Our human ancestors had to rapidly assess the lay of the land to detect threats, so gut reactions kept them safe. But in a modern college classroom free from creatures and carnivores, that ancient instinct can lead to a severe misassessment of the terrain. When a student meets your greeting with silence or a blank stare, their quiet response most likely has nothing to do with you.

Deciphering the Blank Stare

A flat expression is not an automatic sign of hostility, an indictment of your teaching, or a sign of personal animosity. In reality, a reserved student is usually dealing with one of a dozen unspoken realities. The quiet one in the back might be a first-generation student who has never stepped foot inside a college classroom. Another might be experiencing imposter syndrome, afraid to stand out. Some students simply land lower on the extroversion or openness scales, while others may be dealing with physical or mental health challenges that make emotional expressions more difficult to muster. It could simply be that they are daydreaming, having a difficult day, or lost in a laptop screen.

While managing screens is a real challenge—one that can be addressed by keeping a room mostly tech-free and offering old-school notebooks and pens as incentives as I do—the main takeaway is simple. An inexpressive or stoic student is not an adversary. But it makes sense why your brain may register them as one. When someone gives you a still face, you instinctively flag the expression as a threat to the relationship. Because humans are meaning-makers, we interpret a blank face as rejection. Inattention and disengagement may be just as damaging as actual conflict because it leaves you stuck in an uncertain state, wondering if you matter to the other person (Tronick, 1989).

The Neural Overlap of Rejection

This connection between social rejection and physical pain is deeply biological. Research from a meta-analysis of over 500 published studies shows that when rejection is powerfully elicited, like having someone who recently experienced an unwanted breakup view a photograph of their ex-partner, the specific brain regions that support the sensory components of physical pain, such as the secondary somatosensory cortex and the dorsal posterior insula, become highly active (Kross et al., 2011).

This means that social heartbreak and physical injury share the same neural real estate. When brain scans look at someone experiencing severe rejection, the areas lighting up are the same ones that register an actual physical injury, like a broken bone or a burn. Your brain does not distinguish between a wounded body and a wounded ego. These results give literal meaning to the idea that rejection hurts! It is no surprise that our language equates social pain and estrangement with words typically reserved for physical injury, like being crushed, shattered, or having a broken heart (Eisenberger & Lieberman, 2004).

From Cooing to Crying: The Psychology of the Blank Face

It is human nature to like people who like us. We tend to withdraw from those who shun us with a still face. This phenomenon traces back to Edward Tronick’s famous psychology experiment, which demonstrated how a mother’s neutral, still face left a baby feeling sequestered and scared.

To visualize this, picture a mother and her baby interacting, facing each other, smiling, and playing. Everything feels warm and connected. Suddenly, the mother goes completely blank. No smile, no reaction, just a neutral, stony expression, like her face just went on pause. At first, the baby tries to get her attention by smiling, cooing, and waving their little arms. When that fails, confusion turns to frustration. Some babies cry or scream before eventually collapsing into a state of helpless withdrawal. From their perspective, the safe emotional connection is gone, and they cannot get it back (Tronick et al., 1978).

The Trap of the Negative Narrative

Babies are hardwired to demand social reciprocity, but professors enjoy no such evolutionary leverage. While it’s hard not to react negatively to a face that seems unwelcoming,

We cannot throw a tantrum, scream, or shake our fists in the air to force a student to pay attention, smile back at us, or put their phone away. Likewise, publicly singling out a seemingly disengaged student with a sarcastic or critical remark is never effective. This can easily fracture the classroom climate and make everyone feel uncomfortable. A successful classroom fosters group cohesion, creating the emotional bond and sense of belonging that transforms a room of individuals into a supportive learning community (Yalom & Leszcz, 2020). Without that foundational safety, trust can evaporate and tension can spread.

I teach in the psychology department, so I’d like to think that my background has helped me foster a more patient, caring perspective toward students. When I walk into a classroom and cheerfully ask, “How was your break?” and am met with indifference by a few students, I am aware of the importance of avoiding snap judgements or viewing the class as an amorphous whole. Teachers who assume a class is distant or chilly will naturally start to pull back to protect their own warmth.

Attachment Styles in the Classroom

Instead of worrying about rejection, instructors can zoom out and recognize that “still faces” may reflect a student’s childhood attachment style. Avoidant and anxious individuals tend to maintain the same behavioral patterns in school as they do in their interpersonal relationships, using attachment as an innate emotion regulation system to modulate stress (Fraley & Roisman, 2019).

When we view the classroom through this lens, we can cautiously seek out the students who may never otherwise visit our office hours. According to research by Gore and Rogers (2010), a student’s childhood attachment style significantly influences how they handle academic goals. Their study found that securely attached students tend to thrive and earn higher grades when their academic motivations are tied to the interests of important people in their lives. In other words, when a secure student knows their parents are proud of them, or when they have a professor who checks in on them, it acts like fuel. They think, “People care about me and want me to succeed,” and that makes them study harder and get better grades.

In contrast, avoidant students may eschew the involvement of others. Even when a professor reaches out with genuine support, offers help, or tries to learn about their goals, an avoidant student may panic. To them, your involvement feels like pressure, control, or a trap (Gore & Rogers, 2010). From the theoretical perspective of Rentzios and Karagiannopoulou (2021), this behavior is an intentional, self-protective strategy used to regulate overwhelming emotions during the learning process. Because avoidant students may view closeness with an authority figure (the professor) as dangerous or unstable, they might keep that bonding instinct firmly turned off, projecting a lack of interest.

In this way, a student’s blank gaze, apparent boredom, or surface-level effort is actually a sophisticated psychological defense mechanism (Rentzios & Karagiannopoulou, 2021). It is a behavioral pattern meant to avoid emotional risk by keeping both the course material and the professor at a safe, non-threatening distance.

Making Space in Room 531

In my classroom, I’m not trying to force an introverted or anxious student to become a bubbly extrovert. I’m just trying to show them that I am a reliable, safe professional. When an avoidant student realizes that their still face doesn’t make me upset, lose energy, or pull back my support, their defense system often slowly begins to deactivate.

I believe the worst thing a teacher can do is give up on a quiet, reserved class by delivering a cold or distant lecture. Instead, we must show up with the same level of enthusiasm, structure, warmth, and clarity every single week. Ultimately, a blank face is not a personal insult or a threat to our authority. Once we drop defensiveness or snap judgments, we create space for genuine connection, setting the stage for a positive classroom culture that supports learning and growth.

Beverly Wertheimer, PsyD, DMin, LCSW, teaches in the graduate school of psychology at Pepperdine University and is winner of the 2026 national Adjunct Faculty Excellence in Teaching Award from the Society for the Teaching of Psychology, a division of the American Psychological Association. Dr. Wertheimer is a child and adolescent psychotherapist, certified life coach, and author specializing in pedagogy and mental health. She has a background in broadcast journalism, including correspondent stints at ABC and NBC affiliates, as well as CNN’s entertainment news programs.

issues.title: Before Coaching Comes Trust: What Every Teacher Leader Needs to Know
issues.summary: “I don’t know what you think you can teach me that I haven’t already tried.” I still remember those words. My first few months as a coach were far from easy. Many of the teachers I was assigned to support were sceptical of my role and did not believe that I could help improve their […] The post Before Coaching Comes Trust: What Every Teacher Leader Needs to Know appeared first on Faculty Focus | H
issues.author: Shellon Samuels-White
issues.content_html:
“I don’t know what you think you can teach me that I haven’t already tried.”

I still remember those words.

My first few months as a coach were far from easy. Many of the teachers I was assigned to support were sceptical of my role and did not believe that I could help improve their instructional practice nor their students’ learning. In hindsight, I believe part of their hesitation stemmed from the fact that I was younger than many of them and had fewer years of teaching experience, which may have affected my credibility in their eyes.

I vividly remember working with one experienced teacher who had 23 years of teaching experience. During one of our first meetings, she looked at me and said, “I don’t know what you think you can teach me that I haven’t already tried.” Given the significant difference in our years of experience, I could understand why she questioned what I could offer. At that moment, I realized that my greatest challenge would not be helping her teach mathematics conceptually; it would be earning her trust. Instead of immediately focusing on instructional strategies, I intentionally invested time in listening, understanding her concerns, and building a genuine professional relationship.

Rather than immediately offering instructional strategies, I chose to listen. I wanted to understand her concerns, learn about her students, and build a genuine professional relationship before suggesting changes to her practice. That experience taught me a lesson I have carried throughout my career: whether we are coaching faculty, mentoring new instructors, leading professional learning communities, or supporting curriculum redesign, our success depends less on our expertise than on the quality of the relationships we build.

Expertise Doesn’t Automatically Create Credibility

Many instructional leaders assume that expertise alone establishes credibility. It certainly helps to have strong disciplinary knowledge and effective teaching practices, but these are rarely enough. Educators are professionals with deeply held beliefs about teaching. When someone enters their classroom as a coach or consultant, they often wonder:

  • Is this person here to evaluate me?
  • Will my weaknesses be exposed?
  • Do they understand my teaching context?
  • Can I trust their intentions?

These questions are often unspoken, but they shape every coaching conversation.

Rather than trying to demonstrate my expertise, I decided to spend time listening. I asked about my colleague’s challenges, her students, and what she hoped they would learn. I resisted the temptation to offer immediate solutions. Those conversations gradually shifted our relationship from guarded to collaborative. Only then could meaningful coaching begin.

Trust Comes Before Instructional Change

As our relationship developed, the teacher became increasingly willing to invite classroom observations, reflect on her instructional decisions, and experiment with more conceptual approaches to teaching mathematics. The instructional improvements did not happen because I introduced better strategies. They happened because she felt psychologically safe enough to examine her own practice. Research consistently shows that effective coaching depends on trust. Teachers and faculty members must believe that feedback is intended to support growth rather than judge competence (Zepeda, 2019). When that belief is absent, even well-designed coaching initiatives can become compliance exercises instead of opportunities for professional learning.

Five Ways Instructional Leaders Can Build Trust

Looking back, several practices made the greatest difference. These lessons apply equally well to teacher leaders, department chairs, instructional designers, and academic leaders.

1. Listen Before You Lead

Resist the urge to diagnose problems during your first meeting. Spend time learning about instructors’ goals, challenges, and experiences. Listening communicates respect far more effectively than offering immediate advice.

2. Separate Coaching From Evaluation Whenever Possible

Faculty are much more likely to engage honestly when they know conversations are confidential and developmental rather than evaluative. Be explicit about your role and the purpose of your feedback.

3. Acknowledge Existing Expertise

Experienced educators bring years of practical wisdom. Coaching should build on that expertise rather than suggest that previous practices were inadequate. Position coaching as collaborative inquiry instead of expert consultation.

4. Demonstrate Consistency

Trust develops through repeated interactions. Following through on commitments, maintaining confidentiality, and providing thoughtful feedback consistently over time strengthens professional relationships.

5. Celebrate Small Wins

Meaningful instructional change rarely happens overnight. Recognizing incremental progress reinforces confidence and encourages instructors to continue experimenting with new approaches.

Professional Learning is Relational Before Structural

Higher education institutions often invest significant time and resources into professional learning initiatives: faculty learning communities, mentoring programs, peer observations, and instructional coaching. These structures are valuable, but they cannot compensate for a lack of trust. Too often, institutions focus on designing programs without paying equal attention to creating the relationships that allow those programs to flourish. Faculty may attend meetings, complete observations, and participate in workshops while remaining reluctant to discuss genuine instructional challenges.

Professional learning becomes performative rather than transformative. My experience as a coach taught me that meaningful professional learning begins long before discussing pedagogy or curriculum. It begins when educators believe they are respected, heard, and supported.

Trust is a Leader’s Most Important Responsibility

My coaching experience also changed how I think about instructional leadership. While principals, department chairs, deans, and faculty developers are expected to lead professional learning, their most important responsibility is not simply organizing workshops or introducing new initiatives. It is creating the conditions in which educators trust the learning process and those leading it.

Too often, professional development is experienced as something done to educators rather than with them. Trust changes that dynamic. When leaders invite educators to identify their own learning needs, contribute to professional learning priorities, and participate in shaping solutions, professional learning becomes a shared journey instead of another initiative to implement.

This lesson is particularly relevant in education systems where ministry or institutional priorities often determine professional development agendas. Although leaders may not control those priorities, they have considerable influence over how they are enacted within their schools or institutions. They can build trust by creating opportunities for dialogue, valuing educators’ expertise, and demonstrating that professional learning is a partnership rather than a mandate.

Building trust also requires leaders to protect time for what matters most. Administrative responsibilities will always compete for attention, but teaching and learning remain the core business of education. When instructional leaders consistently make time for classroom conversations, coaching, mentoring, and collaborative reflection, they signal that professional growth is a priority rather than an afterthought.

Stephen Zepeda (2019) offers three questions that every instructional leader should regularly ask:

  • Do educators trust me?
  • Do they have confidence in my actions?
  • Do my words and actions align?

These questions remind us that trust is earned through consistency, transparency, and genuine respect, not through position or authority. When I first met that experienced mathematics teacher, I believed my role was to improve instruction. Looking back, I realize my first responsibility was much simpler and much harder. It was to build a relationship in which another professional felt respected, valued, and safe enough to learn alongside me. Only after that foundation was established did coaching become effective. Whether we support new faculty, facilitate communities of practice, mentor colleagues, or lead centers for teaching and learning, the lesson remains the same: instructional strategies matter, but relationships matter first. Trust is not simply one characteristic of effective coaching; it is the foundation on which meaningful professional learning and lasting instructional improvement are built.

Shellon Samuels-White is a passionate, results-oriented educator and curriculum specialist, currently serving as a lecturer in the Faculty of Education and University Assessment Officer at The Mico University College – Jamaica. She holds a Bachelor of Science in Secondary Teacher Education and a Master of Arts in Education, specializing in Curriculum and Instruction. Her research interests are centered on curriculum/school reform, 21st-century teaching methodologies, and the interrelationships between curriculum, instruction, and assessment. She is particularly passionate about integrating social-emotional learning into the curriculum to promote holistic development.

As an assessment officer, Samuels-White’s role includes promoting quality teaching and learning experiences by promoting valid and reliable assessment practices. She provides academic assessment guidance and supports institutional quality assurance. Her work supports both students and educators in achieving meaningful teaching/learning outcomes while upholding institutional standards. Committed to advancing curriculum studies and instructional design, she continues to explore progressive teaching models that foster student engagement and success. Through her work, she remains dedicated to fostering an inclusive and transformative education system.

Reference

Zepeda, S. J. (2019). Professional development: What works (3rd ed.). Routledge.
