issues.title: Between Psyche and Cyborg: Carl Jung’s Legacy and the Countercultural Courage to Reclaim the Deeply Human in a Posthuman Age
issues.summary: "A reanimated world is one in which spirit and matter are not just equally regarded but recognized as mutually dependent."
issues.author: Maria Popova
issues.content_html:
“A reanimated world is one in which spirit and matter are not just equally regarded but recognized as mutually dependent.”

“To be a human being among people and to remain one forever, no matter in what circumstances… that’s what life is all about, that’s its task,” the young Dostoyevsky exulted in a letter to his brother just after his death sentence was repealed — death, that great clarifying force for what it means to be alive, what the stakes and sanctities of living are.

In the two centuries since, our understanding of what it means to be human, to be mortal and imperfect and ablaze with feeling, has altered dramatically as we have entrusted the cold logic of computation with answering the soul’s cry for connection, for creativity, for meaning — something Dostoyevsky’s contemporary Samuel Butler anticipated in his far-seeing admonition against the dehumanization of humanity in the hands of our machines, something that has metastasized in today’s technocratic cult of posthumanism.

In Jung vs Borg: Finding the Deeply Human in a Posthuman Age, Glen Slater bridges ecology, depth psychology, systems theory, and various post-Cartesian philosophies to explore how this civilizational cult has effected “a widening divide between fabrication and authenticity, a loss of more self-aware and soulful modes of living, and an increase in anxiety and depression,” and what we can do to rewild the psyche and reclaim the soul.

He begins by drawing an analogy between the catalytic impact of Rachel Carson’s Silent Spring on awakening the modern ecological conscience and the need for a conscious awakening from the dangerous dream of posthumanism into which Silicon Valley has lulled us. Just as the industrial capitalism of Carson’s era commodified our planet’s ecosystems and elemental resources, Slater observes that digital capitalism has “turned our habits of mind into the earth’s most valuable commodity”; just as Carson pioneered the holistic view of ecology that may be our only path to saving Earth, her contemporary Carl Jung pioneered the holistic view of psychology that might, just might, save the human soul from death by commodification.

Slater writes:

Whether or not we have turned the ecological corner, there is more consciousness about the way we relate to the world around us and the actions required to avert a climate catastrophe.

However, the world within us, the inner life of thought and emotion, is another matter. Here integrative understanding has been resisted. The human psyche, the ecosystem of the mind, with its own structures and dynamics, our relation to which is surely as significant as our relation to the outer world, now faces its own significant disruption, one that essentially parallels the syndrome Carson described… The depths of human nature are becoming harder to recognize and protect. Abundant information has furthered scientific knowledge but not human understanding. It has instead left us dazed, confused, and disoriented. Attention, motivation, identity, self-image, and the capacity to reason clearly and imagine deeply are all impacted… While the advantages of digital technologies are impressed upon us at every turn, the rapid entry of these technologies into every aspect of life is evidently impacting our ecology of mind.

With an eye to the urgency of “moving beyond objectification of the earth and of the bodies and minds that inhabit it,” he adds:

The technosphere now overlays the ecosphere and we cannot help but inhale its post-industrial gases. Virtuality has begun to displace reality, making the ground of human existence hard to discern… The human psyche and the nature of the whole person are not only suffering in this technospheric environment, the suffering has itself been given over to technological solutions, resulting in a vicious cycle.

[…]

The penchant for digital ways of relating, expanding faith in AI, and the one-sided education designed to service these things are combining to generate reductive conceptions of psychological life. We are, in particular, discounting the deeply human… the essential qualities of human experience, which extend from the instinctual patterns that shape basic behavior to the timeless values that mold the cultural imagination. The deeply human anchors the vertical axis of inner understanding; it grounds the ecology of mind. It is also what connects us to the more-than-human. In our era, however, an almost exclusive dedication to a horizontal axis of data gathering threatens this verticality and grounding. This is leading to a world drowning in information and thirsting for understanding.

At the heart of this civilizational crisis is the systemic compartmentalization of our experience, evident in the core polarities and dichotomies of Western culture — past and future, inner and outer, matter and spirit. Pulsating beneath it all is our dissociation from the life of the body, which connects us to the life of the Earth and the life of the universe. Everything beautiful that we touch and see and hear — birdsong, a sunrise, a kiss — is a bittersweet reminder that we have a body and are therefore mortal. Dissociation thrives on the denial of death that began with our ancestors’ mythologies of immortality and is culminating in Silicon Valley’s lurid and lucrative dreams of redesigning human nature, of downloading the mind onto disembodied machines and reducing the soul to a datum.

Pointing to Jung’s timeless cosmogony of the unconscious as the antidote to this damaging delusion, Slater writes:

Jung’s comprehension of the depths of human nature constitutes an incisive counterpoint to the assumptions of posthumanism and to the dissociative bubble that presently fosters these assumptions… Jung sheds light on the self-regulating nature of the psyche and the archetypal forms behind this — forms we may choose to overlook but cannot ultimately dismiss. These forms pertain to brain structure, anatomy, and evolved patterns of perception and behavior. But they also reflect the larger rhythms of the cosmos and are seemingly woven into the fabric of life itself. Jung pointedly demonstrates that even as we have embraced reason and science, the archetypal world of non-rational impulses and religious ideas have continued to unconsciously influence our thoughts and actions.

Jung’s crowning contribution was to invite an understanding of the psyche as the foundation of all perception, experience, thought, feeling, and action — the wellspring of our humanity. In exploring the psychology of the unconscious with all of its interlaced convolutions — archetypes and complexes, projections and introjections — Jung illuminated the way our dreams and fantasies unconsciously shape the course of our lives, the way our arts and sciences cohere into a vast collective unconscious that shapes the course of our civilization. With an eye to Jung’s legacy, Slater writes:

It is the psyche that contains the pursuit of the angelic, the claims of the animal body, and the structures and dynamics that join the two. It is the psyche that generates and insists upon the symbolic expressions of culture, which are often based on the transformative and aspirational power of ordinary, even elemental, things — mountains and rivers, suns and moons, fire and rain — thereby reminding us of the inextricable bond between mind and world. If cosmic matter has given rise to consciousness, and we are now called to grasp the nature of consciousness, realizing that thinking about our thinking is the necessary companion of any exploration and understanding of the universe that surrounds us, our grasp of the inner world becomes just as vital as our grasp on the outer world — perhaps even more so.

Nearly a century after the Swiss poet, philosopher, and linguist Jean Gebser made his exquisite case for the evolution of consciousness, Slater reflects on Jung’s legacy and writes:

Godlike power necessitates godlike responsibility. This begins with self-awareness, which is rooted in a sober consideration of the human psyche, the most critical part of which is shedding light on the shadow side of our willful pursuits… Will and reason alone cannot form a seat of wise agency — a far more expansive consciousness is required.

[…]

An expansion of consciousness is imperative if we are to make responsible use of the transformative power in our hands… With divine guidance largely beyond our secular vision, we are left to look within for something deeper than our controlling inclinations and to look without to perceive the guidance of nature’s intelligence. Guidance must ultimately come from dialogue with these marginalized sources of knowledge and from the cultural imagination, which shapes this dialogue. The result will be a “co-creation” — a partnership between innovation, self-knowledge, and a cosmology befitting this age. Such a co-creative process will mitigate and shape our technologies as well as generate opportunities for spiritual renewal.

Such co-creation, Slater argues, demands a reanimated view of existence — one that “counters the commodification of all things that is currently consuming us,” one that “conveys a confluence of spirit and matter — the very means by which a sense of soul is generated.” He writes:

A reanimated world is one in which spirit and matter are not just equally regarded but recognized as mutually dependent. The great task of this late modern era is thus to bring together what the spiritual preoccupations of the old world and the material focus of the new world have torn apart. The psyche shows us this dependency whenever a person or group attempts to embrace one without the other, in the way the neglected side begins to rule the unconscious… But the earth process itself suggests we rediscover nature as spirit as well as understand it as matter — nature as presence, intelligence, and root source of inspiration and imagination… Both mind and earth are calling for perspectives capable of marrying these dimensions of reality.

Countering this fragmentation of reality requires, above all, learning to resist our dissociative tendencies and trust our emotions — for, as philosopher Martha Nussbaum observes in her masterwork on the intelligence of the emotions, “emotions are not just the fuel that powers the psychological mechanism of a reasoning creature, they are parts, highly complex and messy parts, of this creature’s reasoning itself.” Slater considers the building blocks of this self-trust:

Such trust begins with a natural appreciation of emotional intelligence and the guiding potential of this intelligence, which can feel like it emanates from a will of its own. This trust may grow over a long time or it may come as a sudden life-lesson. But few things beyond the contemplation of emotional responses open the door to the deeply human and the awareness of having an inner partner [that] operates apart from conscious, rational direction. To be full of emotion is to be animated by something in spite of ourselves; perhaps this is why we end up regularly conversing with the sadness or anger that grips us. Emotions like these stand in need of negotiation, mollification or perhaps just more attention. Often, when we want to keep moving on, the emotions will not allow it. And sometimes when we would choose to hold back, emotions charge ahead.

Because our emotions are a fundament of our human nature, which is itself a fractal of Nature, they are the raw material for the co-creative process that offers an antidote to the dehumanization of humanity. Slater writes:

We are affected by desire for more satisfying ways of being, outrage about all that is regularly exploited and destroyed, fear of what stresses and overwhelms, and shame about participating in the machinations of it all. To consider the way emotion comes upon us, from a nature we call “ours,” all the while being a branch of Nature itself, calls into question whether these emotions even belong to us or to the sufferings of the world, and we are being directed to feel and respond on its behalf. In other words, our animation may be the world’s way of speaking to us, and thus be an indispensable dimension of the co-creative process. Recognition of the autonomous intelligence of these deep emotional responses may be an invitation to attune ourselves to the presence of the earth’s own intelligence — or intelligences.

It is the psyche that bridges these regions of intelligence, the inner and the outer, the human and the cosmic, death and life. Slater writes:

The psyche, which is obviously grounded in nature, also leads us beyond this ground, into a concern with destiny and leaving some trace of ourselves in service to humanity… We neither have to lean on notions of a spirit that literally departs the body, nor on fantasies of downloading our minds. Rather, we accept that the substance of psychic experience, accumulated over a lifetime, marks everything we do and everyone around us. And such a marking can be dreamed on. Life and death thus intertwine to produce defining qualities of being.

In a passage evocative of James Baldwin’s soulful insistence that “it is necessary… to know that in oneself, waiting to be found, there is a light,” and that “everything in our lives depends on how we bear the light,” Slater adds:

The wonder of psychological life is that this dimming of the ego-light allows the perception of another light, one that has been in the background all along… Posthumanism brightens the ego-light, the light of the intellect and will that blankets the light of natural consciousness the wise ape presents to us. It fails to reconcile our spiritual reach and our instinctual ground. It cracks cultural vessels that have always incubated this reconciliation and truncates rather than extends the human experiment.

Lensing Jung’s legacy through the light of thinkers as varied as Hannah Arendt, William James, Yuval Harari, and Oliver Sacks, Slater goes on to explore and celebrate the countercultural movement in the margins of this techno-trance — ways of seeing and of being that, unlike posthumanism, refuse to exclude beauty, eros, and transcendence from the human story, a story told in the language of the soul, irreducible to data. Complement Jung vs Borg with Iain McGilchrist on how we render reality, James Bridle on rethinking intelligence, and Pierre Teilhard de Chardin on bridging the scientific and the sacred, then revisit Jung himself on the most important paradigm for living.

issues.title: Necessary Losses: The Life-Shaping Art of Letting Go
issues.summary: "We cannot deeply love anything without becoming vulnerable to loss. And we cannot become separate people, responsible people, connected people, reflective people without some losing and leaving and letting go."
issues.author: Maria Popova
issues.content_html:
“The art of losing isn’t hard to master,” Elizabeth Bishop wrote in one of the great masterpieces of poetry. “Every mortal loss is an Immortal Gain,” William Blake wrote two centuries before her in his beautiful letter to a bereaved father.

We dream of immortality because we are creatures made of loss — the death of the individual is what ensured the survival of the species along the evolutionary vector of adaptation — and made for loss: All of our creativity, all of our compulsive productivity, all of our poems and our space telescopes, are but a coping mechanism for our mortality, for the elemental knowledge that we will lose everything and everyone we cherish as we inevitably return our borrowed stardust to the universe.

And yet the measure of life, the meaning of it, may be precisely what we make of our losses — how we turn the dust of disappointment and dissolution into clay for creation and self-creation, how we make of loss a reason to love more fully and live more deeply.

That is what Judith Viorst explores in her 1987 consolation of a book Necessary Losses (public library) — an inquiry into the profound and far-reaching relationship between our losses and our gains, revealing renunciation as a fulcrum of growth. She paints the vast landscape of loss upon which life plays out:

When we think of loss we think of the loss, through death, of people we love. But loss is a far more encompassing theme in our life. For we lose not only through death, but also by leaving and being left, by changing and letting go and moving on. And our losses include not only our separations and departures from those we love, but our conscious and unconscious losses of romantic dreams, impossible expectations, illusions of freedom and power, illusions of safety — and the loss of our own younger self, the self that thought it always would be unwrinkled and invulnerable and immortal.

[…]

These necessary losses… we confront when we are confronted by the inescapable fact… that we are essentially out here on our own; that we will have to accept — in other people and ourselves — the mingling of love with hate, of the good with the bad;… that there are flaws in every human connection; that our status on this planet is implacably impermanent; and that we are utterly powerless to offer ourselves or those we love protection — protection from danger and pain, from the in-roads of time, from the coming of age, from the coming of death; protection from our necessary losses.

These losses are a part of life — universal, unavoidable, inexorable. And these losses are necessary because we grow by losing and leaving and letting go.

As a sculpture is shaped by what is chiseled off from the block of stone, so too are we shaped by what we lose — by choice, with all the complexities and difficulties of letting go, or by the scythe of chance, which takes away as impartially as it gives. Viorst writes:

The road to human development is paved with renunciation. Throughout our life we grow by giving up. We give up some of our deepest attachments to others. We give up certain cherished parts of ourselves. We must confront, in the dreams we dream, as well as in our intimate relationships, all that we never will have and never will be. Passionate investment leaves us vulnerable to loss. And sometimes, no matter how clever we are, we must lose… It is only through our losses that we become fully developed human beings.

We enter the realm of loss the moment the umbilical cord is cut to sever what Viorst calls the “blurred-boundary bliss of mother-child oneness” — the primal loss that sets off the ongoing task of becoming ourselves. From this origin point, she traces the lifelong vector of losses and gains:

Exchanging the illusion of absolute shelter and absolute safety for the triumphant anxieties of standing alone… we become a moral, responsible, adult self, discovering — within the limitations imposed by necessity — our freedoms and choices. And in giving up our impossible expectations, we become a lovingly connected self, renouncing ideal visions of perfect friendship, marriage, children, family life for the sweet imperfections of all-too-human relationships. And in confronting the many losses that are brought by time and death, we become a mourning and adapting self, finding at every stage — until we draw our final breath — opportunities for creative transformations.

In a sentiment the poet Mark Doty would echo — “you need to both remember where love leads and love anyway,” he wrote in his beautiful reckoning with love and loss — she adds:

We cannot deeply love anything without becoming vulnerable to loss. And we cannot become separate people, responsible people, connected people, reflective people without some losing and leaving and letting go.

Complement Necessary Losses, which goes on to explore the many regions of loss in human life and how they can become frontiers of growth, with Hannah Arendt on learning how to live with the fundamental fear of loss, Thoreau on living through a loss, and Alan Watts on learning not to think of gain and loss, then explore two uncommon lenses on loss: fractals and chlorophyll.

issues.title: Your Brain on Grief, Your Heart on Healing
issues.summary: "Grief is a heart-wrenchingly painful problem for the brain to solve… to live in the world with the absence of someone… ingrained in your understanding of the world… For the brain, [they are] simultaneously gone and also everlasting, and you are walking through two worlds at the same time."
issues.author: Maria Popova
issues.content_html:
“Grief is a heart-wrenchingly painful problem for the brain to solve… to live in the world with the absence of someone… ingrained in your understanding of the world… For the brain, [they are] simultaneously gone and also everlasting, and you are walking through two worlds at the same time.”

“‘Tis good — the looking back on Grief,” Emily Dickinson wrote as she calibrated love and loss. But she did not mean that it is good to ruminate and wallow — Dickinson so deftly played with the surface of meaning, so delighted in startling us into a flinch or furrow before plunging us into the deeper truths she fathomed. She meant, I think, that a love lost is grieved forever, whatever the nature of the loss — this she knew, and turned the ongoingness of it into a lifetime of art — but by looking back, we are reminded over and over that the sharp edge of grief does smooth over time, that today’s blunt ache is worlds apart from the first stabs, until grief becomes, as Abraham Lincoln wrote in his stirring letter of consolation to a bereaved young woman, “a sad sweet feeling in your heart, of a purer and holier sort than you have known before.”

And besides, what does it mean to lose a love anyway? We never lose people, not really. I don’t mean this in some mystical sense — let there be no confusion about what actually happens when we die. I don’t even mean it in the poetic sense. I am speaking strictly from the point of view of the mind emerging from the dazzling materiality of the brain — that majestic cathedral of cortex and synapse shaping every thought we have and every feeling we tremble with.

I am speaking of the paradox inside the brain:

On the one hand, we lose people all the time — to death, to distance, to differences; from the brain’s point of view, these varieties of loss differ not by kind but only by degree, triggering the same neural circuitry, producing sorrow along a spectrum of intensity shaped by the level of closeness and the finality of the loss.

On the other hand, no person we have loved is ever fully gone. When they die or vanish, they are physically no longer present, but their personhood permeates our synapses with memories and habits of mind, saturates an all-pervading atmosphere of feeling we don’t just carry with us all the time but live and breathe inside. Or the opposite happens, which is its own devastation — the physical body remains present, but the person we have known and loved, that safehouse of shared memories and trust, is gone — lost to mental illness, to addiction, to neurodegenerative disease.

In both cases, the brain is tasked with the slow, painful work of reconstituting its map of the world, so that the world makes sense again without the beloved person in it. Mapping, in fact, is not a mere metaphor but what is actually going on in the brain, since our orientation in spacetime and our autonoeic consciousness — the capacity for mental self-representation — share a cortical region.

Where the missed and missing person goes on the map, how the remapping actually unfolds, and what it takes to redraw the map in such a way that the world feels whole again are the questions coursing through The Grieving Brain: The Surprising Science of How We Learn from Love and Loss (public library) by neuroscientist Mary-Frances O’Connor — a pioneer in fMRI research since the technology first became available, who has devoted a quarter century to studying the particular neurophysiology of grief. She writes:

The brain devotes lots of effort to mapping where our loved ones are while they are alive, so that we can find them when we need them. And the brain often prefers habits and predictions over new information. But it struggles to learn new information that cannot be ignored, like the absence of our loved one.

[…]

Grief is a heart-wrenchingly painful problem for the brain to solve, and grieving necessitates learning to live in the world with the absence of someone you love deeply, who is ingrained in your understanding of the world. This means that for the brain, your loved one is simultaneously gone and also everlasting, and you are walking through two worlds at the same time. You are navigating your life despite the fact that they have been stolen from you, a premise that makes no sense, and that is both confusing and upsetting.

Making an important distinction between grief (“the intense emotion that crashes over you like a wave, completely overwhelming, unable to be ignored”) and grieving (an ongoing process punctuated by recurring moments of grief but stringing the moments into a larger trajectory), O’Connor adds:

Grieving requires the difficult task of throwing out the map we have used to navigate our lives together and transforming our relationship with this person who has died. Grieving, or learning to live a meaningful life without our loved one, is ultimately a type of learning. Because learning is something we do our whole lives, seeing grieving as a type of learning may make it feel more familiar and understandable and give us the patience to allow this remarkable process to unfold.

[…]

Grief never ends, and it is a natural response to loss. You will experience pangs of grief over this specific person forever. You will have discrete moments that overwhelm you, even years after the death when you have restored your life to a meaningful, fulfilling experience. But… even if the feeling of grief is the same, your relationship to the feeling changes. Feeling grief years after your loss may make you doubt whether you have really adapted. If you think of the emotion and the process of adaptation as two different things, however, then it isn’t a problem that you experience grief even when you have been grieving for a long time.

Although volumes have been written about the psychology, philosophy, and poetics of grief — none more piercing than the Joan Didion classic, none more practical than Seneca’s advice to his bereaved mother — there is something singularly revealing about exploring grief from the point of view of the brain beneath the mind, which must begin at the developmental beginning. Childhood — the brain’s most fertile growth period, when most of its major infrastructure is laid out — is also our training ground for loss. Every time we are separated from our primary caregivers, we experience scale-models of loss; every time they return, we learn that the loss of their presence is not a loss of their person, of their love. (A pause worth taking: every abandonment is a miniature of grief.)

In those formative attachments, we also learn the role we ourselves play in the relationship. Because, in building its relational world-map, the brain is constantly computing our loved ones’ position in three dimensions — time, space, and closeness, also known as psychological distance — we learn the causal link between our behavior and a caregiver’s position in the closeness dimension, just like we learn the causal link between our bodily movements and our position in space. When there is secure attachment, the child learns that throughout various surface disruptions, situational factors, and passing emotional weather patterns, there is a steadfast underlying closeness. O’Connor writes:

Closeness is partially under our control, and we learn how to maintain and nurture this closeness, but we also trust those who love us to maintain that closeness as well.

The obvious — and heartbreaking — corollary is that children who grow up without secure attachment experience the pangs of miniature grief much more readily throughout life, with each departure of a loved one, however temporary, because trusting a continuity of closeness does not come naturally to us. But no matter the formative experience of closeness, human beings are universally undone by the death of someone close — the final abandonment, at once the most abstract and the most absolute absence, in which our brains simply cannot compute the total removal of a person so proximate and important from the fabric of psychological spacetime.

Citing the disoriented devastation of a woman ghosted by a lover, O’Connor notes that “ghosting” is the neurologically appropriate word-choice for such abandonments — studied under fMRI, the brain of a person who has lost a loved one to “ghosting” behaves much the same way as the brain of a person who has lost a loved one to death, the mental map suddenly crumbled and torn to pieces. O’Connor describes the strange yet strangely sensical way in which the brain copes with this incomprehensible disruption of reality:

If your brain cannot comprehend that something as abstract as death has happened, it cannot understand where the deceased is in space and time, or why they are not here, now, and close. From your brain’s perspective, ghosting is exactly what happens when a loved one dies. As far as the brain is concerned, they have not died. The loved one has, with no explanation, stopped returning our calls — stopped communicating with us altogether. How could someone who loves us do that? They have become distant, or unbelievably mean, and that is infuriating. Your brain doesn’t understand why; it doesn’t understand that dimensions can simply disappear. If they don’t feel close, then they just feel distant, and you want to fix it rather than believe they are permanently gone. This (mis)belief leads to an intense upwelling of emotions.

[…]

If a person we love is missing, then our brain assumes they are far away and will be found later. The idea that the person is simply no longer in this dimensional world, that there are no here, now, and close dimensions, is not logical.

Drawing on brain imaging studies, she adds:

The ephemeral sense of closeness with our loved ones exists in the physical, tangible hardware of our brain.

The particular bit of hardware is the brain’s posterior cingulate cortex — our built-in GPS of love. Scanning the environment and processing innumerable bits of sensory information, the PCC is constantly calibrating and recalibrating the psychological distance between us and the people we love, tightening the bond the closer we feel and loosening it when we sense distancing. Death turns the GPS into a crude compass trying to orient to an all-pervading, ever-shifting magnetic field suddenly bereft of its true north. O’Connor writes:

After the death of a loved one, the incoming messages seem scrambled for a while. At times, closeness with our deceased loved one feels incredibly visceral, as though they are present in the room, here and now. At other times, the string seems to have fallen off the board — not shorter or longer than it was before, but simply stolen from us entirely.

This confusion is so fundamental and so primal, so beyond the reach of reason, that it befalls minds indiscriminately along the spectrum of intelligence and self-awareness — a reality most clearly and devastatingly evinced in the extraordinary love letter Richard Feynman wrote to his wife 488 days after her death and 6,994 days before he won the Nobel Prize in Physics.

But O’Connor notes that while Western physicians long believed such continuing bonds across the life-death divide to be a symptom of poor coping with grief that makes for poorer bonds with the living, recent research drawing on various grief rituals and customs from cultures around the world has demonstrated that such ongoing inner dialogue with the dead might actually enrich our relationships with the living and allow us to show up for them in a fuller, more openhearted way. She writes:

Our understanding of ourselves changes as we gain wisdom through experience. Our relationships with our living loved ones can grow more compassionate and resonant with gratitude as we age. We can also allow our interactions with our beloved ones who are gone to grow and change, even if only in our minds. This transformation of our relationship with them can affect our capacity to live fully in the present, and to create aspirations for a meaningful future. It can also help us to feel more connected to them, to the best parts of them… Their absence from our physical world does not make our relationship to them any less valuable.

[…]

Instead of imagining an alternate what if reality, we must learn to be connected to them with our feet planted firmly in the present moment. This transformed relationship is dynamic, ever-changing, in the way that any loving relationship is ever-changing across months and years. Our relationship with our deceased loved one must reflect who we are now, with the experience, and perhaps even the wisdom, we have gained through grieving. We must learn to restore a meaningful life.

The greatest challenge, of course, is the perennial challenge of the human mind — how to integrate seemingly contradictory needs or ideas in such a way that they coexist harmoniously, perhaps even magnify each other, rather than cancel each other out. Without such integration, any new relationship can feel like a threat to this ongoing inner bond with the dead, undamming a flood of grief at the notion of emotional erasure: grief for the grief itself, for that outstretched hand holding on to the gone and to ourselves at the same time, to the map as it used to be. This is a fear so understandable as to cusp on the universal. It is also — and this might be the most assuring part of O’Connor’s research — a neurophysiologically misplaced fear. Within the brain, every person we love leaves a tangible, structural imprint, encoded in synapses that can never be vanquished or replaced by new and different love. Because that bond — like every bond, like every idea, like the universe itself — was “only ever conjured up in the mind,” it is there too that it always lives, unassailable by other minds and other events.

O’Connor writes:

Gaining a new relationship is simply not going to fill the hole that exists. Here is the key — the point of new roles and new relationships is not to fill the hole. Expecting that they will can only lead to disappointment.

The point is that if we are living in the present, we need to have someone who loves us and cares for us, and we need someone to love and care for as well. The only way to enjoy a fulfilling relationship in the future, however, is to start one in the present. If we can imagine a future in which we are loved, then we must start a relationship that eventually will become important to us in a way that is different from our previous relationship, but rewarding and sustaining.

Understood this way, then, the ongoing relationship with the gone is a lavishment to other loves, for it has made us exactly who we are — the person doing the loving, the person being loved, the mapmaker of present and possible worlds. O’Connor offers neural affirmation for this poetic aspiration:

After a loved one dies, they are clearly no longer with us in the physical world, which each day proves to us. On the other hand, they are not gone, because they are with us in our brain and in our mind. The physical makeup of our brain — the structure of our neurons — has been changed by them. In this sense, you could say that a piece of them physically lives on. That piece is the neural connections protected within our skull, and these neural connections survive in physical form even after a loved one’s death. So, they are not entirely “out there,” and they are not entirely “in here,” either. You are not one, not two. That is because the love between two people, that unmistakable but usually indescribable property, occurs between two people. Once we have known love, we can bring it into our awareness, we can feel it emerge and emanate from us. This experience reaches beyond the love for the flesh and bones of the person we once knew on this earthly plane. Now loving is an attribute of us, regardless of who we share it with, regardless of what is given to us in return. This is a transcendent experience, a felt sense of being loving without needing anything in return. In the very best moments together, we learned to love and to be loved. Because of our bonded experience, that loved one and that loving are a part of us now, to call up and act on as we see fit in the present and the future.

Complement The Grieving Brain with a mathematician’s geometric model for living with grief and this soulful animated film of “Dirge Without Music” by Edna St. Vincent Millay — the most beautiful homily on the emotional paradox of loss I know — then revisit Nick Cave’s life-honed wisdom on grief as a portal to greater aliveness.

issues.title: A Van Gogh painting sold for a record $190.4m last night
issues.summary: The sale almost didn’t happen.
issues.author: Matty Merritt
issues.content_html:
Vincent Van Gogh? More like Van Gogh get your wallet. The painter’s “Châtaigniers en fleurs” (“Blossoming Chestnut Trees”) sold for $190.4 million last night at a Sotheby’s auction in New York City after not being seen by the public in over 60 years. The price blew past the artist’s previous auction record of $117.2 million from four years ago.

The sale almost didn’t happen

It proceeded only after the owner selling the painting reached an eleventh-hour deal with the heirs of the previous owners. Anonymous heirs to Samuel Fischer, who bought the painting in 1909, allege the painting was sold in 1936 because of financial difficulties forced upon the family’s business by the Nazi regime:

  • Sotheby’s initially claimed there was no evidence the painting’s 1936 sale was made under duress.
  • On Tuesday, the families reached an agreement so that last night’s sale could take place. Details of the agreement were not released.

The painting was one from a collection of 12 that went on the auction block. Sotheby’s estimated that the dozen would fetch $450 million collectively, but they only sold for $412 million.

The art market is having a legendary week. Total sales at three of the biggest auction houses, Sotheby’s, Christie’s, and Phillips, are expected to hit $2.4 billion this week. That would rival 2025’s sales for the whole year. The houses already brought in $6.8 billion in the first half of 2026, per Bank of America’s recent Art Market Update report.—MM

issues.title: 'Grand Theft Auto VI' is out, and it's the highest-rated game ever
issues.summary: ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ was finally released, in all its alligator-quarreling, canine jet-skiing, and insurance-scam side quest glory.
issues.author: Molly Liebergall
issues.content_html:
Bad news: You can’t say “We got ___ before GTA VI” anymore, because after 13 years of waiting, two delays, and several leaks, Grand Theft Auto VI, the most anticipated video game probably ever, finally came out today at midnight local time.

It’s already the highest-rated game in history: GTA VIscored a site-wide best 99/100 on the review aggregator Metacritic. Bloomberg called the open-world game “a masterpiece,” the New York Times said it’ll “steal your heart,” and IGN’s reviewer described it as “the single most impressive video game I have ever played.”

All those years spent crafting the franchise’s new Bonnie-and-Clyde-in-Florida installment appear to have been worth the wait for publisher Rockstar Games. Amid earth-shattering (and possibly internet traffic-shattering) demand, the company may have already made back its entire development budget, which is believed to be between $1 billion and $1.5 billion:

  • Preorders surpassed $1.5 billion, Sensor Tower estimated, putting GTA VI hundreds of millions of dollars ahead of preorders for other recent big-name video game releases.
  • Some analysts think GTA VI will sell 40 million copies in its first four months, raking in $3 billion in revenue, Bloomberg reported. For context, the highest-grossing movie in the world, Avengers: Endgame, made $2.9 billion.

Expect a ghost town today. Schools around the world anticipated empty classroom chairs, and time-off requests are ~20% higher today than usual, according to the workplace software provider UKG. Logitech gave its 7,000 employees the day off to explore GTA VI in all its alligator-quarreling, canine jet-skiing, and insurance-scam side quest glory.

Even if you don’t plan on playing…

…you’re still living in the GTA VI entertainment economy. According to Sensor Tower, over the next month:

  • Other games could see a 10% collective drop in players.
  • Streaming movies and TV shows might get 6 million fewer hours of playtime in the US.

Meanwhile…food delivery services, music platforms (the game has a 30-song original soundtrack) and livestreamers are expected to cash in.

Farewell, GTA V. In preparation for GTA VI, GTA Online players bid adieu to the franchise’s beloved fifth installment last night with a peaceful “last ride” through Los Santos.—ML

issues.title: What’s causing all the tech outages?
issues.summary: Experts are attributing the recent slew of disruptions to a rush to patch system vulnerabilities.
issues.author: Dave Lozo
issues.content_html:
If you couldn’t log into a Teams meeting or watch Matchbox: The Movie due to tech issues in the past week, experts say it was likely the result of companies and government agencies rushing to make system upgrades to patch vulnerabilities—not a coordinated cyberattack.

It’s AI’s fault…sort of. Anthropic and OpenAI have released AI models that can detect exponentially more bugs than a human could ever find. That’s created a race between organizations trying to close the holes and hackers looking to exploit them. The speed and volume of recent patches have caused some infrastructures—like the ones at Microsoft, Apple, and the NSA—to buckle. Experts believe more disruptions will happen as institutions continue to gain the tools to patch vulnerabilities.

In the case of the infamous ground stoppage last weekend, the FAA said the problem was traced to defective routers in Arkansas and Texas, although experts who spoke to CNET doubted the explanation’s plausibility and pointed to a new AI air traffic control system that rolled out nationwide shortly before the debacle.

Paranoia is understandable. Last month was dubbed “Black October” because of the high volume of cyberattacks—many done by a new AI hacking tool called Artex. On the Friday of the ground stoppage, the FBI released a warning about Artex, but a spokesperson later said that it was just a coincidence.—DL

issues.title: Who’s going to profit from Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO?
issues.summary: As the first major AI lab to go public, the IPO is viewed as a high-stakes stress test for both the AI industry and the entire global economy.
issues.author: Matty Merritt
issues.content_html:
Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO this week really has to work, as investors question the billions of dollars the AI market has hoovered up. A record-setting market debut for the giant could revitalize the sluggish tech sector—and spill into the broader US economy.

The company will officially price its initial public offering today, before trading on the Nasdaq tomorrow under the ticker “ANT.” The IPO will not be very ant-like: Anthropic initially set shares at $70 to $78 apiece, and at the top end of its pricing, it would raise $90.4 billion, with a valuation at $1.4 trillion. As banks closed share orders yesterday afternoon, orders were seven times the number of available shares, according to Bloomberg.

  • Anthropic’s share price could be over $80 today, according to a Wall Street Journal report.
  • That would mean a valuation as high as $1.6 trillion.

As the first major AI lab to go public, the IPO is viewed as a high-stakes stress test for both the AI industry and the entire global economy. A disappointing opening would still net investors huge gains, but it’d also add further fuel to ongoing AI skepticism.

Who’s set to gain?

For starters, the 300 or so investors who threw money at Anthropic, according to PitchBook. Some of the biggest venture capital funds are already preparing the champagne bottles: Menlo Ventures was in for $750 million in 2023. Lightspeed Venture Partners led a $3.5 billion round in 2025, and earlier this year, Sequoia, Greenoaks, and Altimeter joined private equity and corporate buddies to raise Anthropic’s largest funding round of $65 billion.

  • In the first half of this year, AI has snagged $355.9 billion from VC funds. That’s 86% of all US venture capital funding in that time frame, according to Clearstead’s analysis of Pitchbook data.
  • Because so much of AI development is concentrated in San Francisco, the city is taking in a third of all global VC dollars right now, according to PitchBook.

Who else is getting rich? An average Anthropic employee could see their equity balloon to $72 million. The company’s biggest customers, Amazon and Google, are set to own roughly 28% of Anthropic’s stock after the IPO.—MM

  • ⚠️ Using Vite? A critical flaw allows remote code execution on dev servers exposed to the network with --host or server.host. Update to 8.3.7, 8.2.5, 8.1.7, 7.3.8 or 6.4.6.

  • Storybook 11 beta now has an official post. React projects get faster, more accurate component metadata, and there are type-safe stories and official skills for agents. The final release is due in December.

  • React's <form> docs now explain how to keep field values after an Action, and requestFormReset gets a reference page of its own.

UI SDK: Vercel and shadcn's Headless UI Behaviors Library — A low-level library of behaviors, like keyboard navigation, popups, drag and drop, that you compose into your own components. A core idea is to give a solid base for agents to build full components from. In beta, but you can get started now.

shadcn (Vercel)

How X is Rebuilding Its Web App with React, Relay and Vite — X/Twitter is replacing its decade-old client-rendered React app with a stack built around streaming SSR and Suspense. Lab tests show profiles displaying posts much sooner, and the hydration and chunking fixes make this an interesting case study.

Yagiz Nizipli (X)

📊 Six React Chart Libraries vs Hand-Written SVG – The results are close at native speed but with large gaps under CPU throttling or with large datasets. Pavel Gusev

📊 Remix v3 vs TanStack Start: Fast Pages, Thin Ecosystem – Comparing the same site built in React-free Remix v3 and TanStack Start. Jonathan Arnault (Marmelab)

📱 How Five Web Developers Built an iOS Keyboard Extension with Expo Anirudh Coontoor (Supernova)

🛠 Code, Tools & Libraries

Text.js: React Apps That Render in the DevTools Console — Continuing the trend of rendering React apps everywhere, this new framework heads to DevTools as a host environment, supporting App Router-style routing, Suspense, keyboard input and ASCII fonts. Open the console on the page to see it in action!

Anomaly

Exact: A New Rust-Powered App Framework from Expo's Co-Founder — It isn't React as the UI is written in a small, constrained language called Contract that's designed specifically for agents to write and test, but 𝕏 Andrew Clark says it's "eerily similar" to what he thinks React 20 is shaping up to be.

Charlie Cheever

React Shepherd 8.0: Guided Tours for Apps, Now with a Leaner Engine — The React wrapper (React docs here) for Shepherd, a popular library for building step-based on-page tours. Note that it's AGPL, with a paid license for commercial use.

Ship Shape

  • EmbedPDF 3.0 – Powerful PDF viewer with a drop-in React component and a headless library for adding your own UI. (Demo.)

  • react-virtualized 10.0 – The original list and grid virtualization library, modernized. Now in TypeScript, built on function components, and requires React 18+.

  • 📱 React Native Audio API 1.0 – Software Mansion's Web Audio API for React Native goes stable. Adds spatial audio, and FFmpeg is now opt-in.

  • Mantine 9.8 – Adds an emoji picker package, plus new Diff, PhoneInput and week and quarter picker components.

  • BagUI – A shadcn/ui registry of blocks and templates for SaaS landing pages, like pricing and hero sections.

📰 Classifieds

🔍 Can ChatGPT and Claude read your React site? Run a free SEO and GEO scan with Fimo and see what they miss. By the Strapi team.

🎬 Stop approving mobile PRs nobody ran. An agent tests each one on Expo Simulators and puts the recording in the PR.

Build durable AI agents & workflows in TypeScript with Trigger.dev. If steps fail or code deploys, tasks pick up right where they left off.

📢 Elsewhere in the ecosystem

  • Vectoys is a set of React components that render phones, laptops and other small 3D objects as SVG, with interactive HTML inside their screens. Could be handy for mockups or 'in-situ' teasers on your homepage.

  • 🤖 Chrome's Modern Web Guidance 1.0 is a set of skills that steer coding agents toward modern, Baseline-aware HTML and CSS. The team has also listed the 'top 10 things AI gets wrong' when building for the Web.

  • Need a clip of a component or animation for a PR or README? Paul Irish's chrome-capture tool can record a Chrome tab to an MP4 at 60fps with a single npx command.

  • 📊 The State of JavaScript 2026 survey is now open if you want to get involved.

issues.content_html:
#​496 — November 6, 2026

Read on the Web

React Status

Discord Dropping Electron and React Native for a Rust Rewrite — Discord, one of React Native's best-known users, is moving away, with its CTO 𝕏 showing off a Rust desktop client built on GPUI using 290MB of RAM, with mobile keeping native UI over Rust code shared with the desktop client.

Tom Warren (The Verge)

▶️ Just prior to this reveal, Software Mansion interviewed Discord's Chas Jhin about how React Native development works at Discord's scale, in the ominously titled 'Maybe React Native Is Impossible'.

Run AI Coding Models on Your Own Machine — Local models are now good enough for everyday coding. Learn to run them on your own Mac or GPU, wire them into your editor and terminal agents, and keep your code private with no per-token bill.

Master.dev sponsor

A Roadmap for Redux Toolkit v2.x and 3.0 — Mark Erikson has laid out the roadmap for Redux (complete with a neat history lesson) with RTK 3.0 expected in six to eight months, going ESM-only with 'React 19-scale' breaking changes. But a run of 2.x releases will ship the groundwork first, starting with 2.14 this week.

Mark Erikson

IN BRIEF:

  • ⚠️ Update to Next.js 16.4.5 or 15.5.29, as appropriate: the November security release fixes seven advisories. Most are Cache Components bugs, so the post is worth reading.

  • 🤖 TanStack Query maintainer Dominik Dorfmeister says work on Query v6 can start once 'slop PRs' stop coming in and taking up his time, leading to a thread on the effects of AI-made contributions on maintainers.

  • Vercel is folding Next.js's Data Cache into Runtime Cache with bigger allocations but… new per-read and per-write pricing. Hobby teams migrate on November 29, but check the dates and prices for your use case.

  • Vercel builds also now block known-malicious npm package versions before and during install, on all plans and with no configuration needed.

Next.js is Prototyping Go(lang) Route Handlers — A merged experimental PR lets an App Router route be a route.go file exporting GET and friends, compiled by Turbopack and run in supervised Go-powered workers. Tim says Rust could follow along the same path.

Tim Neutkens (Vercel)

Understanding React Internals: A Deep Dive — A seven-part, source-grounded tour of React's internals that, unusually, starts from the server end before getting to fibers, lanes and the commit phase.

Alexandre Trotel

Amazon's React Native-Based Vega OS Hits 2.0 — Vega, the React Native-based OS behind newer Fire TV devices, is out of beta. SDK 2.0 takes apps from RN 0.72 to 0.83, bringing the React Compiler and Hermes v1 into play. The release notes go into more detail than the post.

Barak Schlosser (Amazon)

📄 Why We Finally Left Next.js for TanStack Start – Production memory leaks in two Next.js 16.3 releases were the last straw. Harrison Milbradt

📄 Writable Derived State: Stop Synchronizing State – Using clientData ?? serverData instead of a useEffect that wipes user edits on refetch. Corbin Crutchley

🛠 Code, Tools & Libraries

Skullet: Skeleton Loading States Measured from Your Components — Hand it sample data and it renders your real component invisibly, measures everything, and draws a matching skeleton to reduce layout shifts when data arrives. The docs have a neat How it Works section explaining the technique.

Lochie Axon

Parcel 3 Alpha: A Rust Rewrite with React Compiler, Tailwind and RSC — Parcel's core is now a Rust binary with no Node dependency, and the team reports cold builds up to 100x faster than v2. React Compiler (opt-in), Tailwind and MDX are built in, with RSC support in beta.

Devon Govett (Parcel)

🤖 Reticle: Let Coding Agents Verify Their Changes Against Your Running App — A dev-only SDK and MCP server so coding agents can drive your running app, inspect network requests, application state, and console activity, and return a pass, fail or 'can't tell' verdict with what needs fixing.

Reticle Labs

react-resizable-panels Gets a VS Code-Style Workspace Component — Brian Vaughn's popular panel library now does dockable tabs you can drag to split or merge panes, and moved tabs keep their state rather than remounting. There's a live demo here.

Brian Vaughn

  • Preact 11.2 – Now has a runtime for React Compiler output via preact/compat, plus scoped custom element registries in shadow roots.

  • XState 6.0 Beta – "No further breaking changes are planned" for public APIs, and @xstate/react 7 is in beta alongside.

  • TanStack Redact 0.3 – The lightweight, synchronous-only React / React DOM replacement adds browser SPA plugins for Webpack and Rspack.

  • React Native 0.89 RC – Faster text layout and native module calls, legacy bridge APIs gone. Stable expected in December.

  • Storybook 11.0 Beta

📰 Classifieds

🤖 Fimo gives your marketers a visual editor and AI agents for SEO and GEO. No more tickets for your React devs. By the Strapi team.

QVAC allows you to run any AI capabilities for free, on your phone or laptop, privately. Try the QVAC SDK now on GitHub.

📢 Elsewhere in the ecosystem

  • James Long has been reviving Prepack, Facebook's abandoned JavaScript partial evaluator. There's a React demo where a pretend site is server rendered three ways, by React, by Prepack's output (which essentially 'compiles' React away), and a hybrid, with the render times to compare.

  • Node.js 27 Alpha has landed, the first version using Node's new release process (where a release will spend six months in 'alpha' before going Current), while Node 26 is now the new LTS line.

  • Chrome 157 rolled out this week with HTML-in-Canvas now stable. It provides a way to draw real DOM elements into 2D, WebGL and WebGPU canvases. The demos are striking.

  • Vercel has released Geist Serif, a new serif font that shares metrics with Geist Sans so the two can mix cleanly. It's not on Google Fonts yet, but the geist npm package includes it.

issues.title: TanStack's smaller React for the browser

"Performance belongs on the design system team's priority list, next to accessibilit
issues.content_html:
#​495 — October 30, 2026

Read on the Web

React Status

Putting MUI, Mantine, Ant Design
and React Spectrum Under Load

Den Odell wanted to see how popular design systems cope when you give them real work, so he timed ten of them, including MUI, Mantine, Ant Design and React Spectrum, and profiled the slowest cases. "Performance belongs on the design system team's priority list, next to accessibility," he says. Some highlights:

  • 📊 With the CPU slowed 4x, opening a 249-country dropdown took 84ms in Mantine and 134ms in Ant Design, but over 200ms in MUI and React Spectrum, both of which froze the UI past his 100ms budget.

  • 🔍 React Spectrum's problem was React Aria measuring options one at a time and forcing layout for each. Den filed an issue and a fix is in review.

  • ⚖️ Framework alone didn't decide the results as non-React Ionic was by far the slowest to open (1,266ms) yet was quick at checking 100 checkboxes, while MUI handled them in 70ms compared to Ant Design's 421ms.

  • 🧪 Want to try this on your own components? Den's Playwright tests are available on GitHub.

Agentic Mobile Development Needs Mobile AI Infrastructure — Your agent writes mobile screens fast. Getting them built and into the App Store is where it stalls. Expo is mobile AI infrastructure: native builds, store submits, over-the-air updates and workflows your agent can run. Start free.

Expo sponsor

TanStack Redact: A Smaller React for the Browser — A drop-in replacement for React/React DOM in the browser. Add it to your build config (Start, Vite, Vinext and Next.js are supported) and ship less JavaScript. But it renders synchronously, with no time slicing, so the compatibility guide is handy.

Tanner Linsley

💬 Does Redact pay off? On r/reactjs, commenters pondered who needs it and how it differs from Preact, while one tester found re-renders cost about twice the CPU across two production sites.

IN BRIEF:

  • ⚠️ Next.js has a security release scheduled for November 3, fixing seven medium-severity vulnerabilities. Advisories will be published with the patches.

  • Dan Abramov is fuzzing React's Flight protocol, the format behind Server Components, by streaming random value graphs through the real server and client. It's turned up six stream bugs and three writer bugs so far.

  • TanStack AI 1.0 is stable: a vendor-neutral AI toolkit with React hooks like useChat(), 23 provider adapters and MCP support.

  • 📱 React Native Windows 0.85 completes its move to the New Architecture, and there's more React Native on the desktop with Expo Desktop (an independent project – not by Expo) and Legend Spark for macOS.

React.lazy, Suspense and the Hidden 300ms Startup Delay — A lazy component can suspend on its first render even when its code is already loaded, and React can throttle reveals of suspended content to once every 300ms. Here's how one team traced the delay, and what fixed it.

Matthew Wong (Tab Widgets)

TanStack DB 1.0 RC1, and How 'Oracles' Found Its Bugs — The reactive client data layer is now API stable, but check the migration guide, as mutation handlers, hooks and errors have changed. Kyle explains how agents, checked against simple reference models, found many of the bugs fixed.

Kyle Mathews (TanStack)

🤖 Ship Less JavaScript in Next.js with Your AI Agent – A new skill hunts bundle bloat using Turbopack's module graph. Will Binns-Smith (Vercel)

📄 Porting 287,000 Lines of React to Foldkit in 3 Days – Focuses on how they built a harness to ensure visual and behavioral parity. David Granzin (Maple)

📄 Async React and Progressive Server Actions – How to keep server action forms working before hydration, even with optimistic UI. Jacob Ebey

📊 React Compiler in Next.js 16.4: Babel vs Rust, Benchmarked Waseem Anjum

🛠 Code, Tools & Libraries

Puck 0.24: The Visual Page Editor for React — A drag-and-drop page editor you embed in your own app, using your own components. 0.24 lets you lay out a component's settings panel as you wish, improves drag and drop, and more. GitHub repo.

Fede Bonel Tozzi

react-window 2.5: Virtualized Lists That Scroll with the Page — Brian's long-standing virtualization library adds a scrollElement prop, so lists/grids can scroll along with the page or an ancestor, plus a headless useVirtualizer() for building your own virtualized layouts. Docs and demos.

Brian Vaughn

Vinext 1.4: The Vite-Powered Next.js Reimplementation Gets Faster — A Vite plugin that reimplements the Next.js API so you can deploy anywhere. 1.4 focuses on performance, with a Hacker News clone example now using 43% less server CPU per request vs 1.3, putting it slightly ahead of Next.js in that test.

James Anderson

  • OpenTUI 0.8 – Terminal UI library with React bindings that powers OpenCode. Now repaints only what changed each frame.

  • React Hook Form 7.91 – Lots of useFieldArray and async validation fixes, plus fewer re-renders. v8 is also now at beta 5.

  • React-Toastify 11.2 – Popular toast notification library. Now with theme="auto" to follow the OS color scheme.

  • emoji-picker-react 5.1 – Full-featured customizable emoji picker. Live demo.

🎃 And finally…

Halloween is almost upon us, so how about a round of Graveyard Pinball? It's built with React Three Fiber, with skulls, cauldrons and a skeleton mage. Its creator explains more about how it works here, including how the 3D table actually uses 2D physics.

issues.content_html:
#​494 — October 23, 2026

Read on the Web

React Status

TanStack Start Reaches 1.0

After a year as a release candidate, TanStack Start 1.0 is officially stable. Tanner Linsley explains how it grew out of TanStack Router, and is candid about RSC, which felt like "this box we had to check to be taken seriously as a React framework", and which tanstack.com itself no longer uses. Plus:

  • 📊 The same app in Start and Next.js 16.4, benchmarked – Start handled 2.9x-8.6x more dynamic requests and built ~1.7x faster with type-checking included.

  • 🚚 Moving over? There are official guides for migrating from Next.js and from the RC. Sarthak Mishra moved his site over from Astro (and explains why) and Lovable offers older projects a migration option (here's how one went).

  • 💬 Ryan Carniato called it "a React metaframework with an architecture I can get behind", while in the r/reactjs thread Tanner explained why '1.0' is listed as 1.169 on npm.

TypeScript in the Age of AI — Knowing TypeScript deeply is how you get better code out of AI. Adam Rackis of Spotify shows you how to steer AI toward simpler, correct types and catch the mistakes it slips in.

Master.dev sponsor

IN BRIEF:

  • ⚠️ Last week, Next.js patched two critical RCEs, one rooted in React Server Components, and a public PoC is now out. Update Next.js to 16.4.1 or 15.5.28; for other RSC setups, update the react-server-dom-* packages to 19.3.1 (or 19.2.9/19.1.10/19.0.9).

  • React DevTools for agents now has official docs, covering how it exposes profiling and component data to coding agents through Chrome DevTools MCP.

  • 📱 Expo SDK 58 is out, using the new React Native 0.88, targeting iOS 27 and ready for the iPhone Duo on day one.

  • React Native for Web has active maintainers again and is moving to the React Foundation's GitHub org.

  • TypeScript 7.1 is now in beta, adding a programmatic API and more speed. Type-checking MUI's docs is 1.9x faster and uses half the memory.

Improving Navigation Experience in v0 with Next.js 16.4 — How the Next.js team used Partial Prefetching, intent-based prefetching and the new navigation() API to cut loading skeletons across its v0 AI app builder.

Aurora Scharff (Vercel)

React Only Where Needed: Owner's Next.js to Astro Move — Owner's 10,000+ restaurant sites now run on Astro and Cloudflare Workers, keeping React for interactive islands. Menu-page p75 LCP went from 5.4s to 0.7s.

Selden and Hanford (Owner)

Dead Code Shouldn't Exist — The slides and transcript from a popular talk Dominik has given at several conferences this year on how Sentry removed 28K lines of unused code with Knip.

Dominik Dorfmeister

🤖 Testing AI-Generated Code: Lint the Pattern, Test the Decision – Structural lint rules and shared harnesses beat a test beside every component. Robin Wieruch

📱 Apple Didn't Invent the Foldable. It Might Make You Support One. – Getting a React Native app ready for the iPhone Duo's three compatibility tiers. Sean Barker (Infinite Red)

📄 Loading a 9MB WebAssembly Module Earlier Made Recraft's Editor 17% Faster – Suspending components left the module's download waiting its turn in the React tree. Sergey Patrakeev (Recraft)

🛠 Code, Tools & Libraries

Pixel: Build Graphical Applications in the Terminal — Like Ink, but with "pixel perfect" graphics. It's a React renderer that draws rounded corners, gradients and proper fonts in terminals that support the Kitty graphics protocol, and that can even embed Chromium WebViews to run web apps in a pane(!)

Rob Pruzan (Zenbu Labs)

TanStack Hotkeys Beta: A Type-Safe Library for Keyboard Shortcuts — Hotkeys takes care of the fiddly, cross-platform edge cases of keyboard shortcuts, sequences, and user-recorded hotkeys. The beta adds scopes, so that, say, a dialog's Escape doesn't close the panel behind it. Try the demo on the homepage.

TanStack

React Router 8.5 Hands View Transitions Over to React — Its own view transition APIs are deprecated in favor of React 19.3's <ViewTransition>. Migrating starts with wrapping an <Outlet> and removing the old props and state styling. There's also an unstable 'API-only' mode that serves static HTML but keeps a server for loaders and actions.

Remix Team

env.style: Style Every Environment with Colors or Custom Icons — A utility that wraps your Next.js config or Vite setup to tint the favicon per environment at build time, so you can see at a glance where you are.

Ryan George

Tamagui 3: One React UI Codebase for Web and Native — A styling system and UI kit for sharing one codebase between React web apps and React Native. v3 adds an opt-in (beta) C++ native runtime that applies theme changes without re-rendering, plus React Strict DOM and Tailwind-style syntax.

Nate Wienert

  • Hydrogen 2026.10 – Shopify's commerce toolkit is now a library you can drop into existing Next.js or React Router apps.

  • Morphicons 2.0 – Spring-physics morphing between SVG icons. Now filled icons morph too, not just stroked ones. See it in action on its homepage.

  • Unistyles 3.6 – High-performance React Native styling library. Now with an experimental zero-config Metro integration instead of the Babel plugin.

  • Motion 14.6 – Adds keyboard grab-and-move to Reorder lists, plus stepFrames for deterministic animation testing.

📰 Classifieds

Build and deploy durable AI agents in TypeScript, without managing your own infrastructure. Ship your first agent with Trigger.dev.

Expo is mobile AI infrastructure: Your agents build, test and ship iOS and Android apps, and you approve what goes out. Try it.

🎶 And finally… make a little noise

Fancy making a little music with React? Strudel Flow 2 is an open source React app built with React Flow and shadcn/ui. Connect instruments and effects to generate Strudel code, or load a community patch and start turning knobs.

The source code offers a neat extension point: define an instrument or effect in a small .node.ts file, then supply a React component for a custom interface. As the team says, "coding is a fun thing to do for its own sake." 🤘

issues.content_html:
Claude Code + Obsidian: My family’s AI brain | Scott Farrar

Listen now on YouTube • Spotify • Apple Podcasts

Brought to you by:

  • WorkOS—Make your app enterprise-ready, with SSO, SCIM, RBAC, and more

  • Jira Product Discovery—Prioritize with insights, build with confidence

Scott Farrar is a math educator and parent who built a shared household brain using Claude Code and Obsidian. In this episode, he shows how the system tracks appliances and warranties, compares insurance quotes, organizes family projects, and keeps household tasks moving through a shared to-do list and wall display. He also explains why persistent files work better for him than long AI chats, and how the same philosophy shapes his approach to using AI without taking the thinking away from students.

Biggest takeaways:

  1. The problem with chat is not intelligence, but memory drift. Scott moved to Claude Code because it stores context in Markdown files he can inspect, correct, and reuse across sessions. His memory is no longer trapped inside an opaque conversation.

  2. Let the AI tell you what context it needs. When Scott asked Claude how to document his home, it suggested photographing every appliance. Those photos became a searchable inventory of model numbers, serial numbers, and warranty details.

  3. Unstructured input is fine when the system handles the organization. Scott gives Claude raw information and lets it maintain the underlying files. A custom linter prevents verbose agents from bloating documents such as his household to-do list.

  4. Better context helps people ask better questions. Claude compares insurance quotes with detailed information about Scott’s home, identifies potential coverage gaps, and prepares specific follow-ups. He no longer has to rely entirely on the agent selling him the policy.

  5. One master list can eliminate a house full of mental clutter. Scott and his wife captured every household task they could think of, then Claude organized them by priority, cost, and supporting information. The system now surfaces overdue work before it becomes another fire.

  6. Multiplayer household systems require practical compromises. Claude recommended GitHub to avoid file conflicts, but that added more complexity than Scott’s wife wanted. They settled on GitHub for shared scripts and Dropbox for everyday files, matching the tools to how they actually work.

  7. A household system becomes more useful when it leaves the laptop. Scott’s wall display shows upcoming trips, open tasks, recent wins, and small daily suggestions. It turns a private collection of files into something the whole family can see and use.

  8. Scott rebuilt his father’s file cabinet as an AI system. His dad saved every receipt and warranty and could explain repairs from decades ago. Claude now gives Scott that same dependable household memory, only searchable through conversation.

  9. AI should help children think, not think for them. Scott prefers tutors that ask students to explain their reasoning and work through productive struggle. He also believes some children may share unfinished ideas more comfortably with AI than with another person.

  10. Infinite patience is not always good teaching. Scott wants AI to act as a “warm demander” that encourages students without doing the work for them. When his own agent goes off track, he starts fresh or investigates its reasoning before incorrect information reaches his memory files.

How I fight token fraud as a solo founder

Listen now on YouTube • Spotify • Apple Podcasts

Brought to you by:

  • WorkOS—Make your app enterprise-ready, with SSO, SCIM, RBAC, and more

  • Auros—The human network behind AI

In this solo episode, Claire explains how token fraud cost ChatPRD tens of thousands of dollars and consumed much of her engineering time. She walks through six forms of abuse, including farmed free trials, resold promo codes, card testing, product relays, and a custom MCP running as a 24/7 compute worker. She also shares the business and technical defenses she built, how Jev classifies suspicious activity in real time, and why she ultimately eliminated free trials.

Biggest takeaways:

  1. Token fraud is a business risk most AI founders underestimate until the bill arrives. Unlike traditional SaaS abuse, every fraudulent model call costs real money. It cost Claire tens of thousands of dollars despite ChatPRD being SOC 2 compliant, regularly penetration-tested, and run by an experienced technical founder.

  2. Free trials may no longer work for AI products. Fraudsters automated account creation and used ChatPRD’s most expensive models for unrelated work. Claire ultimately removed free trials, sacrificing a valuable source of product-led growth and enterprise leads after credit-card gates and paid trials also failed.

  3. Promo codes have become a serious attack vector. Codes intended for partners were stolen, resold, and used to power other AI businesses. After discovering that roughly half of her promo codes had reached resellers, Claire stopped issuing them entirely.

  4. MCP access creates a new category of abuse. One fraudster turned ChatPRD’s custom MCP support into a compute worker that ran around the clock. Claire responded by restricting approved hosts and blocking free tunnels and infrastructure that did not appear connected to legitimate companies.

  5. Cheap decision models can classify fraud in real time. When a session crosses ChatPRD’s abuse threshold, a zero-data-retention Jev loop categorizes the activity. Confirmed fraud results in either a ban or a silent downgrade to a less expensive model.

  6. AI support agents need firm boundaries around fraud. After mass bans, ChatPRD received both clumsy appeals and polished messages written by AI. Claire equipped her support agent with fraud tools and explicit rules preventing it from restoring accounts or distributing promo codes.

  7. Blunt defenses are sometimes the most effective. Blocking traffic from certain countries using Vercel Firewall significantly reduced abuse and forced Claire to reconsider ChatPRD’s international strategy. Her new default is simple: trust must be earned rather than assumed.

  8. Token fraud is affecting companies of every size. Claire found the same people abusing ChatPRD through rotating proxies across several major AI products. She has started discussing the problem publicly and filed FBI cybercrime reports with help from Codex.

  9. If a company sells AI, it is ultimately selling compute. Founders should track dollars instead of requests, monitor model spending continuously, close every free entry point, and verify the client rather than only the account. Claire also learned that fraud disappears quickly when expensive models are no longer available to steal.

↳ Detect Automated Abuse on AI Routes with Vercel BotID: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/detect-automated-abuse-ai-routes-botid
↳ Use an AI Assistant to Create Payment Fraud Rules: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/use-an-ai-assistant-to-create-payment-fraud-rules

I was a Claude hater. Fable 5.2 changed my mind.

Listen now on YouTube • Spotify • Apple Podcasts

In this solo episode, Claire tests Claude Fable 5.2 to see whether Anthropic has finally built a model she enjoys using. She turns a tweet into an animated marketing video, creates assembly instructions from photos of unboxed furniture, reworks a complex ChatPRD pipeline, and builds a fully functional 3D typewriter. She also explains where Fable fits alongside Opus 5.5, why its creative work impressed her, and why she still would not trust it to design a website on its own.

Biggest takeaways:

  1. Fable 5.2 turned Claire from a Claude skeptic back into a fan. She found the original Fable difficult to understand and unpleasant to use, with Opus 5 offering little improvement. Fable 5.2 feels fast, capable, creative, and dramatically easier to work with.

  2. Fable 5.2 complements Opus 5.5 rather than replacing it. Opus remains the better default for most coding and knowledge work. Fable is the model Claire would choose for greater complexity, broader scope, or tasks that demand more creativity.

  3. Its speed changes how the model feels to use. Many benchmark tasks finished in under a minute, and even a complex animation took only 16 minutes. Fable also communicates sparingly during autonomous work, surfacing only the moments that require input.

  4. Fable 5.2 made AI video feel animated instead of assembled. From one tweet and the CXO.dev brand guidelines, it created a narrated story featuring custom invader-bot sprites that walk, jump, and cheer. No other model Claire tested produced anything comparable, so the task is becoming a permanent benchmark.

  5. Its spatial reasoning solved a real-world problem every other model failed to. Claire gave Fable low-resolution photos of an unassembled piece of furniture with no instructions. It identified the parts, created a diagram, and produced the correct assembly sequence, which her household successfully followed.

  6. Fable 5.2 is unexpectedly funny. It designed a bug-fighting game around real engineering tradeoffs, then made a trailer in which finance sees the token bill and downgrades the team to a cheaper model. The humor felt intentional enough to make Claire genuinely laugh.

  7. It also holds up on serious engineering work. Fable created a sensible migration plan for ChatPRD’s messy product-intelligence pipeline and aligned closely with Claire’s own roadmap. It worked autonomously and paused at appropriate moments, though the migration is still underway.

  8. Fable needs strong direction for visual design. It follows an existing brand system well, but its unguided web and storybook designs were unattractive. Claire expects to pair it with Opus 5.5 for frontend work and use a separate image model when original visuals are needed.

  9. The 3D typewriter was Claire’s “AGI moment.” Fable built a working keyboard in one shot, then added white-out, music, weather, timers, writing prompts, and multiple immersive settings. It turned an idea Claire never imagined building into a tool she wants to use every day.

  10. Fable 5.2 is available now, with an even faster mode coming. It is launching across the Claude API, cloud platforms, Claude apps, and Claude Code. Claire plans to compare it with the other new models in a full How I AI benchmark.
