issues.title: Obituaries
issues.summary: The demise of Jensen Huang was the end of a great many things, including Nvidia's long-term prospects, the AI bubble, and the exceptional way in which the U.S. viewed itself in the world.
issues.author: Ben Thompson
issues.content_html:
Listen to this post:

Dearly beloved, we are gathered here today to get through this thing called life.
― Prince

Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, 1993–2026

Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Thursday, November 12, 2026. He had been CEO of the company ever since he founded it on April 5, 1993. Nvidia started out as a graphics card company; Huang’s exit — nominally because of affairs with a buyer who may or may not have been a Chinese spy, as well as at least two company employees — was ultimately because Nvidia was, by the powers that be, considered a defense contractor, and Huang never adjusted.

In this, Huang was the ultimate victim of his own success. Nvidia’s first graphics cards simply translated triangles into pixels. The 2001 GeForce 3 introduced a programmable pixel shader, which meant a video card’s functionality was no longer pre-defined. The killer move, however — which almost killed the company — was the 2006 introduction of CUDA, which was an API for programming those shaders. For much of the next 16 years Huang sold the gospel of CUDA, convinced it was the platform for a future of accelerated computing; then, in 2022, came ChatGPT.

ChatGPT made clear what GPUs were most useful for: large language models, and Nvidia made the best GPUs. More than that, Huang had realized that the future of accelerated computing was not just chips, but rather systems; that drove the purchase of Mellanox in 2019, which provided the technology for Nvidia to scale out from chips, setting it down the road to being the best option for the sort of large scale training that made large language models possible. For this Nvidia charged very high prices, with margins exceeding 70%, because they could: they had the platform, the technology, and, over the past few years as others sought to make their own chips, the supply chain.

Huang’s impact on the Asian supply chain in particular cannot be overstated. Byrne Hobart, in his book Boom: Bubbles and the End of Stagnation, notes that one of the benefits of bubbles is that they provide a coordination function, as the fear of missing out incentivizes multiple entities with interlocking dependencies to all commit to building at the same time; Huang was, in many respects, a one-person coordination function. Huang gave multiple keynotes a year, which he explained as how he communicated with the ecosystem broadly, and was famous for eating and drinking his way across Asia in particular, convincing reluctant suppliers that the AI boom was real, and locking up the lion’s share of their output for Nvidia and its stunning commitment to a yearly release cycle.

Huang, who had toiled for decades in relative obscurity, known primarily to gamers, and only barely to the tech industry, became a rock star, swarmed wherever he went, always in his black leather jacket. He also, to his ultimate detriment, became a political figure. Nvidia had long had no presence in either Washington D.C. or Beijing, and was blindsided by the Biden administration’s imposition of chip controls in 2022. Nvidia’s immediate reaction to those initial controls, which restricted exports based on interconnect speed, was to immediately release the A800 in China, which was an A100 with a third of its interconnects disabled. That set the tone for the conflict that I believe was the true cause of Huang’s downfall: Huang strenuously disagreed with the various iterations of the chip ban, and Nvidia only bothered to do the bare minimum to abide by the letter of the law, never the spirit.

That approach, in all likelihood, extended to Nvidia’s oversight (or lack thereof) of Singaporean entities that were alleged to be fronts for chips for China. Some of these were legal: Chinese companies are allowed to access cloud computing facilities outside of China that house leading edge Nvidia chips, although chip control advocates are seeking to close that loophole; some were not legal, in that the chips were ultimately ferried to China. Megaspeed, whose executive, Alice Huang, was the first person Huang was alleged to have an affair with, was officially in the former business, and alleged to actually be in the latter. There are whispers that Megaspeed’s ultimate customer was not, or not just, Alibaba, but also the Chinese military. These are whispers, to be clear; it was the affairs that were enough, at least publicly, to lead to Huang’s resignation.

Nvidia, Most Valuable Company in the World, 2024–2026

Nvidia’s durability — at least that of their margins — was already an open question. Start with CUDA: when the market was software written for GPUs, a platform — including not just an API but a huge set of libraries targeting every conceivable market for accelerated computing — was a nearly impenetrable moat. That is why LLMs like GPT were written using CUDA.

LLMs, though, both brought Nvidia its incredible success, and also seeded its greatest risks. The first is that the vast majority of developer energy moved up the stack, using the LLM’s API as a platform; for most companies, CUDA didn’t matter. The second is that Anthropic, which found funding from Amazon and Google, originally also-rans to the Microsoft-OpenAI partnership, had to learn how to use Trainium chips from Amazon and TPUs from Google; this was difficult, but ultimately meant that the leading LLM did not have any Nvidia dependency at all (Anthropic runs on Nvidia chips, because they learned how to run on anything). The third is the most devastating: LLMs are so effective at writing software that any software-based moat will inevitably dry up.

Nvidia’s second moat, its networking and systems approach, is more durable, although challenged by Google (and by extension, Anthropic) in particular. Nvidia’s systems approach is also the easy answer for enterprises and governments seeking to own their own hardware, and neoclouds seeking to build data centers that are independent of the hyperscalers. The latter market rents chips to both hyperscalers and frontier labs, as well as individual companies, but is challenged as obvious sources of power and political permission disappear. They also need money to afford Nvidia’s systems, which has increasingly come from Nvidia itself.

Nvidia’s third moat is its mastery of the supply chain, and this is the moat that suddenly looks much more tenuous. Huang has bragged about the fact that he has never signed a contract with TSMC over their three decades of partnership; it’s a relationship built on a handshake and mutual trust with Huang specifically. This is, per the point above, a very Asian way of doing business, and Huang was the master of that. It’s questionable whether or not that trust and willingness to commit will persist when the handshake is no longer there.

Nvidia’s most important moat, however, was the degree to which it was not a normal company. Huang organized Nvidia as an exoskeleton around one man: himself. There is very little management at Nvidia — Huang famously has 60 direct reports — for the same reason that there was no succession plan: Nvidia could move so quickly and so aggressively because the company still behaved as if it were a startup. Indeed, lots of established companies — including those still led by founders — claim to still be a startup, but only one, Nvidia, really was organized that way. That paid off with all of those successful bets; it also created an environment where there were no checks on Huang. And, now that he is gone, the exoskeleton is much more poised to collapse than you might expect.

The AI Bubble, 2025–2027?

The first part of the AI buildout was funded by free cash flow, particularly from the hyperscalers. Then, during the second half of last year, nearly everyone started turning to debt. Now — starting with Google this past summer — the primary funding mechanism is equity. In the long run, this should come full circle, and future build-outs will once again be funded by free cash flow, generated from the infrastructure that is being built now.

The problem for Nvidia is that the companies most able to navigate this progression are the hyperscalers, which have the resources to challenge Nvidia’s hold on the chip market. To that end, Nvidia has been very eager to ensure that it is selling not only to the hyperscalers, but to other would-be competitors, like the neoclouds; there will likely, at some point, be serious questions raised about exactly how Nvidia went about allocating compute in pursuit of this goal.

The neoclouds, however, are at a meaningful disadvantage when it comes to funding. First, their debt is significantly more expensive, given that their only business is renting GPUs (as opposed to, say, running the most valuable advertising businesses in the world, or the world’s largest e-commerce platform, or dominating enterprise software). Second, their equity is increasingly worthless, given the significant risks attached to that credit. If a neocloud can’t pay, it’s the equity holders that get wiped out first.

This led to what I termed Nvidia’s Risky Business: Nvidia increasingly used its cash flow and credit rating to backstop and fund the companies who were buying its chips. Bears called this circular financing; bulls called it a necessary bridge to a future where AI revenue paid down these companies’ debt and drove massive upside. What is undoubtedly true is that this was the sort of risky business that is uniquely possible for a multi-trillion dollar company that is completely controlled by one man, who has made an entire career of pushing the limits and making risky bets — and seeing them pay off.

It’s also a series of bets that are unlikely to continue. The neoclouds should be very nervous about losing their patron, along with their creditors and equity holders. The other problem is that the revenue necessary to make all of this build-out work is something on the order of a trillion dollars industry-wide, and it needs to materialize sooner rather than later; if it falls short, it’s the hyperscalers who will prioritize their own compute first, and they will likely be seen as a safe haven for everyone committing to spending. In that world, Nvidia’s neocloud hedge — absent Huang’s willingness to shore the ecosystem up — is liable to turn into a millstone, with their assets flooding the market even as the supply chain ramp-up brings ever more supply to market.

AI as Normal Technology and the U.S. Semiconductor Industry, 1947~2047

Perhaps because he had been preaching the gospel of accelerated computing for so long, Huang was the leading figure pushing back against the doomer narrative surrounding AI. Yes, AI was a massive business opportunity, but it was still normal technology; the safety issues presented were engineering challenges to be solved. What required consideration was not just the next five years, but the next fifty. It’s a view that I am, in full disclosure, generally aligned with.

Many others are not. On one hand there are the aforementioned doomers, certain that fast takeoff is imminent — or has already started — as AI increasingly builds better AI in a recursive loop. The end state is an AI that is massively more capable than humans, and uncontrollable by them; the only hope is to ensure that AI is aligned with humanity, by which adherents to this viewpoint mean aligned with them and their view of the world. This contingent is, broadly speaking, represented by Anthropic. And, in this view, actively working to enable and accelerate uncontrollable open weights models is a threat to humanity.

On the other hand there are the China hawks, who view AI as a national security issue, and the key to U.S. military dominance in a world where China owns the means of production of most militarily relevant hardware. In this world giving China access to chips is effectively treason against the United States.

For both of these groups, Huang was public enemy number one, because of his determination to do what was best for Nvidia’s business, which was to sell chips to China. This made sense for Nvidia for multiple reasons:

  • The first and most obvious reason is that it is good for a company to be able to sell to everyone, including the second largest market in the world (China has traditionally made up about a quarter of Nvidia’s sales, long before AI was even a thing).
  • The second is that China is a large enough market, with sufficiently motivated and capable developers, that it can actually create a meaningful CUDA alternative; furthermore, such an alternative would, in the long run, not be constrained to China, but rather compete with Nvidia all over the world.
  • The third is that China’s AI ecosystem, unconstrained as it is by such niceties as terms of service, distills frontier lab models and releases them as open weights models; those models, meanwhile, are tuned to run on Nvidia chips. These models give Nvidia leverage versus the frontier labs all over the world, including in the West.
  • The fourth is that China is uniquely positioned to create a fundamentally different approach to systems design using optical interconnects to scale out training clusters. This is much more inefficient in terms of power usage than Nvidia’s more elegant designs, but China is also much more capable of manufacturing excess amounts of power to make it work.
  • The fifth is that, in the very long run, China can create an entire alternative supply chain for semiconductors broadly, rendering Nvidia’s mastery of the Western-aligned supply chain much less important.

This last point is worth dwelling on. The chief objection that China hawks in particular make to the idea that it is a good idea to sell China chips in order to prevent them from surpassing the U.S. is that China is already heavily invested in building their own ecosystem. This is certainly true, but I think it underplays the complexity of chips and what is necessary to actually compete with the West.

Specifically, the Chinese government can only control the supply side, by spending money and making top-down imperatives; building an ecosystem, however, whether that be for AI specifically, or semiconductors broadly, requires demand as well. Progress in models and systems and chips depends on a feedback loop between the user and the developer, or the customer and the manufacturer. The demand side, however, is much more short-term oriented than the Chinese government might prefer. The model companies’ concern is the other model companies: that means if they are distilling, we must distill too. If they are using Nvidia chips, then we must too. This matters up and down the stack, just as it has always mattered in technology, which really is different in this regard from almost every other industry.

A useful analogy is to consider the Internet. Why is it that country after country can profess a desire to have an indigenous alternative to the American tech giants, yet miserably fail in every attempt to generate it? It’s because the tech giants are only a click away! In this regard, China’s Great Firewall was one of the most brilliant geostrategic moves ever: by virtue of cutting off access to the American tech companies, China created the demand that pulled China’s own tech giants into existence. You need demand, not just desire.

This is why China itself is currently banning the import of Nvidia’s two-generations-behind H20 chips, after the Trump administration foolishly banned their import, only to reverse themselves while bragging about the reason to do so — i.e. keep China addicted to Nvidia. China is replaying the Great Firewall playbook: force its internal demand to use its much worse alternatives, because that is the only way those alternatives become better. And, in the long run, those alternatives, and the entire ecosystem that supports them, will flood the world.

Huang was, to be perfectly clear, talking his book when it came to his insistence on selling chips to China, or, in the case of the current controversy, allegedly turning a blind eye towards nominally legal buyers who were intent on violating the chip ban; that doesn’t mean, however, that he was wrong about the long-term effects, at least if AI is a normal technology (and I haven’t gotten to the risks this imposes on the Taiwan Strait). What is clear now, however, is that the doomers and the hawks have won: AI, at least in terms of policy, will be treated as anything but normal, and in the fullness of time, it is the U.S. chip ecosystem that will pay the ultimate price.

Tech Company Independence, 1968–2026

The birth date for the last obituary was the invention of the transistor; the birth date for this one is the founding of Intel. Robert Noyce and co-founders had spent the last decade at Fairchild Semiconductor, but were constrained by their parent company’s fundamental conservatism and chafed at their lack of upside. Arthur Rock effectively created the venture capital industry in Silicon Valley through his financing of Intel; Noyce created the concept of the commercial-market-led technology company that made it up in volume. At that time the largest single purchaser of chips was the U.S. government; Noyce realized that the fastest way to progress was to make chips for everyone, including the government, and on his terms, not theirs.

From that point on, tech as an industry operated with the assumption that the world was its customer, and that their own executives defined the route to progress. Government was free to buy their products, but not to define them, and if they wanted the best products, then they best not restrict who they could sell them to either. That’s how important volume was, and, over time, it became clear how powerful and essential ecosystems were.

Other industries operate differently; I thought this article in the Financial Times was striking, and not just because of the headline: Bessent says Nvidia needs ‘shake-up’ with external CEO:

Bessent said that it is important “to examine whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the US export restrictions” and whether its top executives knew they were being skirted. “Was it a low-level fail? Was it in the middle, or was it up in the C-suite? And who knew? These shell companies were obvious, they were being investigated, and did Nvidia use them as a workaround to sell chips to the Chinese?” he said. “Were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?” The Treasury secretary added that Nvidia needs to provide answers within a matter of days: “I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel”. He added that “we will see if Nvidia intentionally ignored the warning signs of these shell companies, many of them in Singapore”.

Bessent has pointed the spotlight on Howard Lutnick’s commerce department for failing to ban exports of Nvidia’s chips to Megaspeed, the Singaporean company linked to the alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Huang. US authorities have been investigating whether Megaspeed, which builds AI data centres in Asia, has been involved in smuggling high-end Nvidia chips, which are powering the AI boom, into China. Bessent has blamed the commerce department more than once this week for failing to ban exports of Nvidia’s chips to Megaspeed. Commerce delayed efforts to add Megaspeed to Washington’s blacklist of companies the US considers a risk to national security. “Many other departments were pushing for this, and commerce had the pen,” Bessent repeated on Sunday. “We have all the rules we need. We just need them enforced.”

Lutnick is under mounting pressure from within the administration and from Congress, which has demanded that he explain how he allowed chips to be exported to a company linked to an alleged Chinese spy. US lawmakers are also accelerating efforts to crack down on advanced AI chips reaching China. If Nvidia “were a bank and they hadn’t complied like this, the [Treasury’s Office of the Comptroller of the Currency] would be in there right now, and a lot of the executives would be removed”, Bessent said.

Scott Bessent is the Treasury Secretary, which is to say that he operates an apparatus that is arguably just as, if not more, powerful than the U.S. military. Treasury controls the flow of money around the world, and its soldiers are the banks; if Treasury has sanctioned an entity, then it is up to banks to ensure those sanctions are enforced. They need to know their customers, and they need to analyze every dollar flowing through their systems; if they do not, they are breaking the law. Ignorance is not a defense.

Ignorance, on the other hand, has been tech’s defense basically forever. Yes, there are bad people in the world, which means that if the whole world is using your products, they will be used to do bad things. That was considered an acceptable trade-off, however, because most people are good and the benefits that come from scale — and an avoidance of the friction that comes from trying to track the activities of billions of people — were worth the risk.

This was certainly what Huang believed, and, to his detriment, he aggressively belittled anyone who dared disagree (the extent to which Huang is despised in Washington D.C., as evidenced by the giddiness and bloodlust online last week, is extraordinary). In Huang’s view, as long as the Commerce Department said that it was ok to sell to Megaspeed, then it was ok to sell to Megaspeed — and to sleep with one of its executives.

Bessent views the matter entirely differently: he thinks that Nvidia should operate like a bank. It’s not just their job to abide by the letter of the law, but the spirit of it. It’s not the government’s job to enforce the chip ban, but the company’s. An attestation from a Singaporean customer that chips aren’t going to China isn’t worth anything; actually putting boots on the ground and ensuring compliance is the only way Nvidia cannot be in violation of the U.S. government’s dictates.

Again, for tech, this is extraordinary, even if it is normal in banking. Extraordinary enough, in fact, that Huang is being labeled by many — not just in Washington, but also in the finance world — as a traitor. Huang, in my estimation, is just a businessman who cares about nothing else other than Nvidia; that worked out great when he made GPUs for gaming that no one in government cared about or understood. That’s just a normal technology; when AI was deemed to be anything but normal, however, business as usual wasn’t just over: it was a crime, and it cost Huang his job — and maybe more.

It’s worth pointing out that while this episode was shocking, I should not, in retrospect, have been surprised. Earlier this year, when Anthropic faced off against the U.S. government, I wrote in Anthropic and Alignment:

At the same time, what is the standard by which it should be decided what is allowed and not allowed if not laws, which are passed by an elected Congress? Anthropic’s position is that Amodei — who I am using as a stand-in for Anthropic’s management and its board — ought to decide what its models are used for, despite the fact that Amodei is not elected and not accountable to the public.

And, on the second point, who decides when and in what way American military capabilities are used? That is the responsibility of the Department of War, which ultimately answers to the President, who also is elected. Once again, however, Anthropic’s position is that an unaccountable Amodei can unilaterally restrict what its models are used for.

My point in that Article was that if AI is as exceptional as claimed, then the government will demand a say in how it is used, whether or not private company executives agree; moreover, that was a good thing, or at least a least-bad thing. The same analysis applies to Nvidia and Huang: Huang may have fundamentally disagreed with the chip ban, but at the end of the day, it was his duty to accept that it was the law of the land. To the extent he did not do so is ultimately his responsibility.

American Exceptionalism, 1776–2026

Perhaps the most tragic aspect of the Huang affair is the extent to which he was the personification of The American Dream. Huang was sent to America as a nine year old who didn’t speak a lick of English, and somehow ended up at a boarding school in rural Kentucky for misbehaving youth, where he would trade help on homework for protection from bullies. From there he went to a state school in Oregon, became an engineer, before famously ending up at a Denny’s diner where he and his co-founders decided to start Nvidia. Then, over the following 33 years, he took risk after risk, created innovation after innovation, until he became a hero not just in the United States, but across the world.

And then, you might say, he flew too close to the sun. Certainly he did so in his private life: it’s not just the affairs, which may be par for the course for rich and powerful men; rather, it’s notable just how reckless the affairs were. The ones that were revealed last week were with a customer and potential Chinese spy, and two of his own employees; both are fireable offenses. Meanwhile, the way in which Huang treated his opponents — including actively seeking to get people fired who he felt stood in the way of getting his way — bore the marks of a man who has constructed a life, and a company, where no one can or will stand up to him. That is a recipe for disaster, and here we are.

At the same time, it really does bum me out that what ultimately doomed Huang was a set of rules that really are a big departure from the status quo — and, in my opinion, misguided. Huang’s actions — or lack of actions, in terms of enforcing compliance with the chip ban — are treated as if they are an obvious crime, when in fact this is a dramatic shift in expectations from a short time ago (although there is certainly a callback to previous controversies around selling advanced computing to adversaries). Huang should have adjusted and accepted the new reality, make no mistake; I’m sympathetic to the fact he couldn’t, and recognize the failure in not having structures in place that could have warned him about the dangerous road he was embarking on, even as I realize Huang’s willingness to navigate dangerous roads is precisely why he was an American success story.

Beyond Huang, however, there is the question of how we compete with China, and I am disappointed, although not surprised, that we are pursuing the route of bans and forced compliance, instead of innovation and openness. Make no mistake, I am no China dove, and I have been very early to the argument that we erred greatly in willingly exporting entire industries to the communist state. That, however, makes it even more imperative that we sprint in the opposite direction of China, towards more freedom in a bet on inventing new industries, not more control and a focus on gatekeeping what we have. I get the logic, particularly in the case of AI, which is extraordinary; I lament the implications of what it says about our belief in ourselves and our ability to stay ahead.

Presented by

As AI models improve, you might expect the market will consolidate around a handful of providers. But user data tells a different story.

Among OpenRouter customers spending at least $100 a month, the median number of AI model families in use has doubled over the past year, from three to six.

Even as AI models become more capable, businesses are using more models, not fewer. This makes sense when you consider that intelligence isn’t one-dimensional. A model that’s exceptional at writing code may not be the fastest at answering customer questions, or the most economical at processing millions of documents.

The question is shifting from “which AI model should we build on?” to “which model should handle each task?” The answer, increasingly, is ‘it depends.’ Which is great for flexibility, less great for simplicity.

issues.title: 🔮 What Anthropic is really listing
issues.summary: Tithes, not tokens
issues.author: Azeem Azhar
issues.content_html:
Azeem’s sketchbook is an experimental format we’re trialing for paying members, where we share raw research notes, early frameworks, and unfinished ideas. They are the earliest indication of what I’m thinking through.

It’s Anthropic’s big week. It will become the first real AI company in the West to list on a public market.

Anthropic has an extraordinary market opportunity. The battle hangs on the sustainability of its business model – whether falling token costs or competition from open-weight models won’t simply erode its margins. These forces, no doubt, exist. The bear case claims the company is merely a peddler of progressively devalued tokens. This misses the point.

Anthropic is building an ever-improving system that produces machine intelligence. That machine intelligence is valuable because of the nature of modern economies. Most value in our economies now comes from intangibles, scientific knowledge, patents, software, brand, and data. If Anthropic’s machine intelligence can create intangibles like these – breakthrough science, information, or software – then it should be able to create extraordinary value.

Over the past fifty years, value in the S&P 500 has shifted from tangibles, things you can count in warehouses or can stub your toe on. Most value now resides in that ethereal flim-flam of the intangible: brand, customer lists, patents, and software.

Put another way, Anthropic’s machine intelligence lets it compete for 92% of the value of the S&P 500 before it needs to deploy a single robot.

That is the big macro-level survey that paints the opportunity. But I’ve been digging deeper. My conclusion is that AI companies in general, and Anthropic, are in a unique position. Look at the chart below. Each time Anthropic announced a new product feature that encroached on a given sector, the stock prices of firms in that sector responded as you’d expect.

AI companies might be able to extract a permanent tithe on the economy. Anthropic, as the leading player, is best positioned to do that.

The following are my sketches. They’ll give you a sense of the direction that I think merits further exploration.

Capturing the intangible

Anthropic has three approaches to capturing value in an intangible economy:

  1. It can ask companies to pay to defend their assets. As I wrote in The Internet’s Wuhan moment, AI has laid bare the software’s non-existent security model. Anthropic’s Mythos is the world’s most powerful security-oriented AI.

issues.title: 🔮 The $22 billion question about AI self-improvement #610
issues.summary: Plus: Cheap solar, who pays for Claude & DNA immunotherapy++
issues.author: Azeem Azhar
issues.content_html:
It’s simply the best, data-rich source for the money on how AI is reshaping the economy. — Matt G., a paying member

Subscribe now

My AI agent bought an iPhone for me this week. For an Uber, I’d still reach for the app.

That’s where we start today – I look at which jobs are worth handing over to AI, and why more Brits are paying for Claude. We’ll also look at what cheaper renewable power still needs and whether AI self-improvement owes more to intelligence or a massive research budget.

If you’re a member of Exponential View, join me in the subscriber chat:

Claude Britannia

Brits are spending more and more on AI. One in twenty adults in the UK pays for AI, spending more than $1.3 billion a year. Five percent is early days, but it is a fast ramp – it was 1% two years ago, and 2.5% a year ago. London is the hotspot; the professional skew is predictable, with those involved in tech, finance, education, and PR. And we are increasingly falling for Claude. Its share has quadrupled in a year.1 Was the trigger the improved harness on Claude Cowork?

Separately, made his first purchase using his Instinct agent, sweaters for winter. My Instinct agent secured my iPhone Duo for me on Tuesday. ’s agent booked a squash court for a showdown with . We’re playing around with them and finding them quite useful.

But in general, agent-based shopping is still early. Uber says four rides out of 320 million during Halloween week were booked by agents. I’m not sure I’d use an agent to book an Uber yet; hitting the app is easier. But getting an iPhone Duo, which involved checking Apple’s website every few minutes from 7 am, is a perfect job for them. So is finding finicky, complicated products like surge-protected power extensions, medicine pouches, or, in Will’s case, woolly jumpers.

Subscribe now

Fair-weather friends

The technology is doing its bit. Adding wind to solar and batteries cuts the median cost from $105 to $86 per MWh. North of Milan and Montreal (yes, they are on the same latitude), it falls from $164 to $99. Based on hourly modeling over ten years, and reckon that sun and wind mostly cover for each other – except for a difficult combined lull for about a week every four.

Ember also finds that 83% of the 750GW of fossil plants being planned sit where reliable renewables (with a bit of gas backup) cost under $100/MWh (which is roughly implied with oil at $60 a barrel).

My take is that technology costs will keep falling, and those that haven’t yet benefited from reductions (like panel installations) will start to yield as robotics improve. But redesigning the grid into a largely renewable-based one also requires more than better technology. It’ll need both a better cost of capital (gas plants still find capital cheaper than solar) and financial instruments that match energy prices to the volatility renewable-based energy brings.

  • Our team’s solar supercycle modeling and analysis.

issues.title: 🔮 What does it cost to make a worker?
issues.summary: Some early sketches of the economics of manufactured intelligence
issues.author: Azeem Azhar
issues.content_html:
Azeem’s sketchbook is an experimental format we’re trialing for paying members, where we share raw research notes, early frameworks, and unfinished ideas that haven’t been fully polished. They are the earliest indication of what I’m thinking through.

Here is another peek into my sketchbook. I’m trying to understand the economic trade-off between getting work done by an AI or a human. One way of doing this is to look at tasks in the economy and see how much it costs a human to do them compared to a machine.

Another way is to view the worker as an entity the economy needs, and to consider the minimum cost of creating one. (Of course, humans are much more than that, but I’m limiting the frame purely to economics here.) Those costs include the parenting, educating, and feeding from bairn to adult. We can then compare that to the cost of bringing in a machine capable of doing the same types of work using AI.

AI is manufactured intelligence. That is not the same intelligence that we humans have, but it’s clearly something that looks like intelligence.

While it is being manufactured, it’s highly replicable and follows the classic learning curve I described in my first book. And in my forthcoming second book, I extend these ideas.

Economically useful human intelligence is created very differently. It takes much longer than making a chip, and you don’t know the outcome for a long time.

issues.title: 🔥 Jensen Huang and the future of the AI boom
issues.summary: Good news for some, not so good news for others
issues.author: Azeem Azhar
issues.content_html:
Jensen Huang has resigned.

The company is in an awkward position, having refused to put a succession policy in place. Colette Kress, the CFO, will step in until it finds a replacement.

Company scandal aside, and there has been a lot, it’ll have a big impact on the AI boom.

Nvidia has been, without doubt, the linchpin of that boom. In the five years to 2026, the firm sold nearly 14 million flagship AI chips. They account for 85% of the market. The company has provided financial guarantees to the constellation of upstart AI infrastructure companies, the so-called neoclouds, so they can get their business moving. It has been a substantial venture capital backer of AI companies, with nearly $10 billion across Europe in the last year – the biggest investor there.

The numbers don’t do justice to how important Jensen himself has been. This isn’t like Apple without Steve Jobs. When Steve Jobs relinquished the CEO role in 2011, shortly before he passed away, he left a well-briefed successor and a management team known to customers and the market alike. And if Nvidia has been the linchpin of the AI boom, Jensen has been the linchpin of Nvidia.

I thought of him as the person with the best visibility into what was going on in AI, simply because everything ran on his chips. He advocated open-source models, including, uncomfortably now, Chinese ones. And pushed for a more accommodating approach to China.

I’ve seen him in London a couple of times. Once, he arrived on stage from down the street with then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer in tow. He brings energy and hands out billions of dollars. Calling out a startup’s name, followed by “I’m backing you with $500m” or whatever the number was. He returned a printout of our State of the AI Economy report, his signature across the front in gold marker, telling me it would be worth more now. Maybe even more after today.

The linchpin seems to be made less of solid steel and more of a well-worn leather. Will the ecosystem that depends on it stay on the road?

The current wave of AI investments, in model makers and infrastructure, is predicated on massive customer demand, not rampant oversupply. The industry’s common refrain over the past two years has been consistent: we are short on capacity. Not tomorrow, but today. That is why the spot prices for AI chips stay high even as they age. It’s why Anthropic has lined up $900bn of computing supply over the next 15 to 20 years – to make sure they don’t run short.

We’ve estimated that in the last 12 months, total revenues in the AI sector (outside of China) came to $188bn, growing faster than 4.2x a year. About 75% of that ends up at the infrastructure layer: the companies that own and operate the chips that do the calculations that make ChatGPT run for you.

The vast majority of revenue comes from chips made by Nvidia.

And the lack of capacity is what has created opportunities for new infrastructure companies, the so-called neoclouds. These young pups don’t have the track record of Microsoft or Google, so they have had to lean on Nvidia, their main supplier, for various kinds of guarantees. These guarantees range from the reasonably above-board to things that smell circular. While the numbers are large, for some companies (like Anthropic or XAI), Nvidia’s contribution is not a do-or-die proportion. But the man behind it all is leaving the building.

Demand stays

issues.title: ‘Anyone forecasting 2027 is forecasting data centers’: The Fed is about to hike into an AI boom it can’t cool, and Main Street gets the bill
issues.summary: Voters rejected data centers, giving the Fed a problem: "AI is the number one source of growth for the U.S. economy."
issues.author: Nick Lichtenberg
issues.content_html:
The Federal Reserve is getting ready to raise interest rates again, after a hike in September. This time it’s pinning part of the blame on artificial intelligence.

Minutes from the Fed’s late-October meeting, released Wednesday, show “almost all” officials thought more rate hikes “would likely be appropriate.” The usual suspect was there: the “vast majority” said high energy prices were still feeding inflation. The new one was AI. “Many participants observed that demand for products associated with the AI buildout was continuing to strain supply and raise prices of technology-related consumer goods,” and several said the price pressure was spreading “beyond industries directly affected by data center construction.”

That meeting was held a week before the midterms. Measures restricting data centers passed in 44 places, from Ohio to Nevada, according to a Redbud Consulting count reported by U.S. News & World Report.. In Ohio, Sherrod Brown’s campaign ran an ad calling his opponent “the face of data centers.” Brown won. The governors-elect in Texas and Georgia have both talked about pausing new projects. In a Pew Research Center survey this summer, 60% of U.S. adults said they’d be not too or not at all comfortable with a new data center in their area.

Put those together and many Americans end up squeezed from both sides. Where data centers were on the ballot, voters rejected them.The Fed is now lining up to raise their borrowing costs, partly because of data centers. And those same data centers are still the biggest thing holding up the economy heading into next year.

Torsten Slok, chief economist at Apollo, estimated Thursday that AI investment accounted for roughly 65% of U.S. economic growth over the past three quarters. He said the true figure is “likely somewhat smaller” once you subtract chips and equipment bought from overseas, but “AI is the number one source of growth for the US economy.”

Anyone forecasting stocks and credit for 2027, he wrote, “is implicitly making assumptions about the pace and magnitude of the AI data center buildout,” according to Slok.

Other analysts have similar questions. “How much of this new dent in the GDP growth outlook is going to factor into the Fed’s thinking?” David Rosenberg of Rosenberg Research asked after the election. The Fed hasn’t met since. Its next meeting, Dec. 8-9, is its first chance to answer.

Why your car loan is paying for their chips

The problem with fighting AI inflation using interest rates is that the AI spenders barely feel them. Paul Donovan, chief economist at UBS Global Wealth Management, said in his Thursday morning commentary that the Fed’s inflation worries center on oil prices, “which the Fed cannot influence,” and “perhaps AI-related demand,” which he called “largely beyond the Fed’s reach.” The only way to offset those, he said, would be to create “near-recessionary conditions in the parts of the economy that respond to Fed action.” That means people with mortgages, car loans and credit card balances, and small businesses borrowing to make payroll.

Most Fed officials judged that wage growth “was broadly consistent” with their 2% inflation target. Donovan reads that as wages falling behind prices. Higher rates would land on households whose paychecks are already losing ground.

The Fed held rates at 3.75% to 4% in October. Bank of America Research analysts wrote last week that “the Fed seems to be falling behind the curve on inflation.” Fed Governor Christopher Waller said he was leaning toward a quarter-point hike in December, but a double-size hike “should be considered” if inflation ran hot, because a normal one “would put our credibility at risk.” Traders put about 96% odds on a quarter-point hike in December, with the rest on a half point, according to 24/7 Wall St.’s read of CME data on Nov. 18.

The voters may cool what the Fed can’t

The vote could do what interest rates can’t: slow the buildout itself. Jefferies called the election “the Worst-Case Near-Term Scenario” for data centers and cut its forecast for new capacity through the end of the decade to 112.8 gigawatts from 122.4. Goldman Sachs economists expect “conditional moratoria” in Texas, Georgia and Michigan, but project they won’t be long-lived if enacted, because data centers actually ranked low on voters’ priorities this election. JPMorgan strategists see no “material changes” to 2027 spending, but “some impact” in 2028 and beyond. Morgan Stanley estimates about 5 gigawatts of capacity slips from 2028 to 2029, according to a summary of its Nov. 9 report.

Oxford Economics wrote that “slower construction in the medium to long term wouldn’t necessarily be a bad outcome for the macroeconomy.” Less AI demand would mean less pressure on prices, after all.

But then there’s the debt question. The buildout runs partly on borrowed money, and the Fed’s own minutes are worried about it. “Most participants observed that AI-related debt had grown rapidly and that much of this growth had taken place through complex and opaque financing structures.” Junk bonds sold to build data centers saw “an especially notable widening” in their borrowing costs during the period.

Credit rating agency Moody’s said in a report this week that data-center financing is moving out of construction loans and into long-term debt, and that recent “market volatility” suggests the shift “may require stronger protections,” including more equity and paying the debt off within the first lease term. In plain terms, the bet has moved from “will they build it” to “will the tenant still be paying in 10 years.” A town vote against a project, or a Fed hike, makes that bet harder to refinance.

That’s why this reaches people who will never live near a data center. Your 401(k), your company’s hiring plan and next year’s raise all sit downstream of Slok’s assumption about the buildout. The midterms made that assumption shakier. The Fed is about to make money more expensive anyway.

The Fed meets Dec. 8-9, for the first time since voters said no. How much growth is the central bank willing to give up to chase prices driven by a boom the voters just tried to stop?

This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

issues.title: Anthropic set to begin trading any moment. Reports suggest stock could pop 20% or more in biggest IPO ever
issues.summary: Anthropic’s debut is a stress test of whether public markets still believe in the AI boom.
issues.author: Beatrice Nolan
issues.content_html:
Wall Street is bracing for what could be the biggest IPO ever, with Anthropic set to begin trading on the Nasdaq exchange on Thursday morning and some reports suggesting the shares could pop by more than 20%.

Anthropic priced the offering Wednesday night at $83 a share, above its marketed range of $70 to $78, and giving the company a $1.5 trillion valuation. Demand was strong enough that it raised the deal to 980 million shares from 825 million.

Shares of Anthropic, under the ticker symbol “ANT,” will likely begin trading a couple of hours after the stock market’s opening bell. The Nasdaq was up 241 points in early trading Thursday. Bloomberg news reported that pre-trading pricing indications suggest that Anthropic’s stock could jump as much as 25% when it begins trading.

There had been endless speculation about whether Anthropic would top SpaceX as the largest IPO of all time. At a $1.5 trillion valuation, Anthropic would be the second most valuable IPO of all time, behind SpaceX’s $1.77 trillion IPO in June. Measured by capital raised however, Anthropic’s $79 billion ($81.4 billion, if stock sold by insiders is included) would top the $75 billion raised by SpaceX.

Seven strategic partners, including Google and Nvidia, have also agreed to buy $26 billion of non-voting Anthropic stock at the IPO price. And the deal’s underwriters have an option to purchase an additional 147 million shares, meaning that, all told, the Anthropic could IPO could generate a stunning $118 billion in proceeds.

Anthropic’s debut comes at a tenuous time for the AI industry. It’s been barely a week since the AI industry lost one of it’s most powerful figures. Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO last Thursday following reports that he had engaged in two extramarital affairs: one with a customer suspected by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese intelligence asset, and one with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. His exit added fresh pressure to a listing that was already seen as a stress test of investors’ appetite for AI.

Analysts and investors told Fortune they didn’t expect the Nvidia shock to derail the offering or touch Anthropic’s core business. The bigger risk, they said, may come later. Seaport Research Partners analyst Jay Goldberg warned that turmoil at Nvidia could bring Anthropic “much tougher questions” once it starts reporting quarterly results as a public company. Georgetown’s Jason Schloetzer predicted closer scrutiny of Anthropic’s ties to Nvidia and to customers associated with the chipmaker.

The stakes reach well beyond one company. Anthropic has more than 400 backers, and nearly every major venture firm owns a piece of it, so the IPO is effectively a liquidity event for the AI boom itself. A strong debut and a stable stretch of trading afterward would suggest the boom has more runway. A stumble would be read as a sign the bubble is near its peak. At least one investor argued that Huang’s departure could even help Anthropic: CEO Dario Amodei had clashed with Huang over chip exports to China and over AI regulation.

issues.title: Anthropic’s IPO is set to make the average employee worth over $40 million—and at least 400 early hires will be worth $100 million or more
issues.summary: Anthropic is expected to have hundreds of multimillionaires. The company's seven billionaire cofounders have pledged to give away 80% of their equity.
issues.author: Preston Fore
issues.content_html:
Anthropic’s long-awaited IPO, which values the company at $1.5 trillion, marks a major milestone for the AI industry and its investors. But for the company’s 5,300 employees, the public listing could prove just as lucrative.

With shares priced at $83 apiece, Anthropic employees now hold an estimated $232 billion in combined wealth—equivalent to roughly $44 million per employee.

The gains are particularly pronounced for employees who joined the San Francisco-based company early: at least 400 early hires will be worth $100 million or more, according to CNBC, and several could join Anthropic’s seven cofounders in becoming billionaires.

If there’s a desire to cash out, non-founder employees can sell up to 10% of their stock on the first trading day, with another 35% becoming eligible for sale after the company’s 2026 earnings. This would add to the fortunes that have likely already soared in recent years thanks to highly competitive pay packages for AI talent.

The IPO will put Anthropic in the exclusive club of trillion-dollar companies, a group currently led by Apple, valued at $5.12 trillion. By valuation, Anthropic’s $1.5 trillion offering would rank as the second-largest in history, behind SpaceX’s $1.77 trillion IPO. But measured by capital raised, Anthropic comes out ahead: Its $81 billion surpasses the $75 billion SpaceX raised.

Anthropic’s new class of millionaires and billionaires could fuel Amodei’s fears of wealth concentration that could ‘break society’

Anthropic’s seven cofounders, including CEO Dario Amodei and President Daniela Amodei, hold relatively equal stakes in the company and are expected to see their fortunes roughly double to about $19.9 billion each.

But even as Anthropic celebrates a landmark milestone in its five-year history, Dario Amodei has warned that the extraordinary wealth being generated by AI could come at a broader societal cost.

“The thing to worry about is a level of wealth concentration that will break society,” Dario Amodei wrote in a letter released in January.

He compared the emerging AI boom to America’s Gilded Age, when rapid industrialization in the late 19th century created enormous fortunes for a handful of business magnates. At the height of his wealth, oil tycoon John D. Rockefeller’s fortune was equivalent to roughly 2% of U.S. GDP. A similar fraction today would be roughly $600 billion—a net worth already exceeded by Elon Musk’s $900 billion net worth.

Amodei argued that AI leaders of today could benefit from studying Rockefeller, who credited society for his success—and thus felt a need to give back.

“That spirit seems to be increasingly missing today, and I think it is a large part of the way out of this economic dilemma,” Amodei said. “Those who are at the forefront of AI’s economic boom should be willing to give away both their wealth and their power.”

For their part, each of Anthropic’s cofounders have pledged to give away 80% of their personal equity in Anthropic to philanthropic causes, which could total over $100 billion.

And even when it comes to staff, Anthropic has increasingly tried to prioritize hiring people who are motivated by the work, not the money. Anthropic reportedly introduced a question into its culture interviews asking candidates how they would feel if the company abandoned its AI ambitions for safety reasons—and that decision caused its stock to fall to zero.

Are you an Anthropic employee or investor, and have plans for your newfound wealth? Reach out to Fortune to share: preston.fore@fortune.com

issues.title: Bank of America CPO Sheri Bronstein: ‘The traditional definition of a working parent is too narrow’
issues.summary: Eighty-three percent of parents at Bank of America say the company offers special and unique benefits, compared with 59% of parents at a typical U.S. workplace.
issues.author: Roula Amire, Great Place To Work
issues.content_html:
For years, the conversation about working parents has focused on childcare.

But the reality is much more complicated.

A parent may be raising children and caring for an aging parent while juggling the demands of a full-time job.

“The traditional definition of a working parent is too narrow,” says Sheri Bronstein, chief people officer at Bank of America.

More than half of Americans in their 40s are part of the “sandwich generation,” balancing the responsibilities of raising children while supporting aging parents.

“Teammates tell us that caregiving is often one of the most meaningful roles they will ever have, but it can also be difficult,” Bronstein says.

That reality is reshaping what support for working parents looks like at Bank of America. The bank jumped 23 spots, from No. 33 to No. 10, on the 2026 Fortune Best Workplaces for Parents™ list in 2026.

Caregiving needs are changing

For many organizations, support for parents starts and ends with parental leave.

At Bank of America, the approach is built around the reality that employees may be caring for different people at different stages of their lives, sometimes at the same time.

“Life is not one-dimensional,” Bronstein says. “At any given time, a teammate may be raising children, caring for an aging parent, dealing with a health issue, or navigating a major life change, and sometimes a number of these at once.”

Employee feedback has played an important role in how Bank of America has responded.

“Listening to our employees is one of the most important ways we understand how to better support them,” she says. “People’s lives, responsibilities, and challenges evolve over time, so it is essential that our programs evolve with them.”

That listening is reflected in the employee data: 79% of parents at Bank of America say management genuinely seeks and responds to suggestions and ideas, compared with 59% of parents at a typical workplace.

One example is the company’s Parents and Caregivers Network, which expanded as employees shared that they were increasingly balancing caregiving responsibilities.

The bank also expanded its support to include back-up care for both children and adults, and personalized guidance through its Life Event Services team.

What leaders often miss

Bank of America offers 26 weeks of parental leave for birth or adoption, including 16 weeks fully paid for eligible employees; up to 50 days of backup care annually for both children and adult dependents; and up to $20,000 in reimbursement for adoption, surrogacy, or fertility treatments.

Eighty-three percent of parents at Bank of America say the company offers special and unique benefits, compared with 59% of parents at a typical U.S. workplace.

But benefits alone aren’t enough.

“Benefits and resources only make a difference if employees know about them and feel comfortable using them,” Bronstein says. “A manager who listens, shows empathy, and helps connect a teammate to available support can have a meaningful impact during a challenging time.”

That starts with changing how leaders think about caregiving.

1. Caregiving is not a temporary challenge. “Caregiving is a part of life, not a reflection of someone’s commitment to their job,” she says. “Employees can be deeply dedicated to their work while also carrying significant responsibilities at home.”

2. Employees aren’t looking for employers to solve every challenge.”What matters most is knowing they are understood, that support is available when they need it, and that they can reach out for help without feeling alone or judged,” she says.

3. Leaders don’t need to have all the answers. “Our role as leaders is not to have all the answers or solve every challenge,” Bronstein says. “It is to listen, create an environment of trust, make people aware of the support available to them, and respond with empathy.”

“When employees feel supported both inside and outside of work, they are better positioned to do their best work and deliver for clients,” Bronstein says.

Roula Amire is the senior content director at Great Place To Work. Follow her on LinkedInand sign up for the Great Place To Work LinkedIn newsletter to get the latest research on what drives business success.

issues.title: Comrades No More: Thoughts on Russia’s Invasion of Ukraine
issues.summary: Today is a profoundly sad day. Russia’s aggressive action is heartbreaking for the death, suffering, and economic turmoil it will cause in Ukraine and, indirectly at least, beyond. Here at Rick Steves’ Europe, we hope that a diplomatic solution can be found and peace will return to that fragile and long-suffering part of our … Continue reading "Comrades No More: Thoughts on Russia’s Invasion of Uk
issues.author: Rick Steves
issues.content_html:
Today is a profoundly sad day. Russia’s aggressive action is heartbreaking for the death, suffering, and economic turmoil it will cause in Ukraine and, indirectly at least, beyond. Here at Rick Steves’ Europe, we hope that a diplomatic solution can be found and peace will return to that fragile and long-suffering part of our world.

Our mission at RSE is to help Americans better know and understand our neighbors through travel. But when we bring travelers to another country, we also bring their dollars — dollars that would support Putin’s aggression. Therefore, as of today, we have canceled all 2022 tours that include a stop in Russia.

Of course, we will keep a close eye on unfolding events and monitor any travel impacts through the rest of Europe. But it is important to keep geographic realities in mind and remember that a war in Ukraine is as far from our European vacation dreams as a war in Guatemala would be from Texas or Florida. For 40 years now, we have lived, worked, and traveled through many periods of tragic warfare in lands far from where we lead our tours (and some closer). And at this time, we see no reason to change the rest of our travel and touring plans.

The tragic reality unfolding in Ukraine only reminds me how important it is for Americans to keep on traveling and to do so in a way that makes us better and more engaged citizens of our world. I’m flying to Europe next month for a 40-day trip through a dozen great cities from London to Athens — and I’m proud that thousands of my fellow travelers will experience the European trip of their dreams while having rich learning experiences far from home on a 2022 Rick Steves tour.

In the meantime, let’s be thankful for our blessings, support our nation’s leaders as they do their best to navigate this crisis, and keep the troubled corners of our world (Ukraine, Russia, Afghanistan, and more) in our thoughts and prayers.

—Rick

issues.title: The Tour du Mont Blanc: Some Tips I Learned Along the Way
issues.summary: At 66, I felt a bit like the father of the hiking community when I hiked around Mont Blanc earlier this fall. But the Tour du Mont Blanc is doable for any reasonably fit hiker, and there were plenty of people on the trail who were older than me. For total novices like Shelley … Continue reading "The Tour du Mont Blanc: Some Tips I Learned Along the Way"
issues.author: Rick Steves
issues.content_html:
At 66, I felt a bit like the father of the hiking community when I hiked around Mont Blanc earlier this fall. But the Tour du Mont Blanc is doable for any reasonably fit hiker, and there were plenty of people on the trail who were older than me.

For total novices like Shelley and me, it’s wise to be proactive about health and safety. Here are some tips I learned along the way:

Good boots, liner socks, slippery powder, and moleskin for tender skin are essential. We kind of became gear geeks — investing in good day bags (Osprey), woolen clothes (socks, underwear, shirts), and great hiking shoes. I was never so thankful for a wool cap in Europe.

I was skeptical about a lot of “good ideas,” but two things I eventually appreciated were a daily baggie of trail mix and my metal water bottle. (I complained about its steep $40 price tag…but soon came to recognize it was a great value).

I must say, if the weather turned bad and it rained hard, I think much of the trail would become no fun at all. In fact, it would be dangerous. Hiking poles are essential, and even in perfect weather, I would have been worried about a stumble without my own trusty set.

Eat a solid breakfast. The one day we had breakfast with no protein, climbing was tougher.

Put on sunscreen, even if the weather’s bad.

After learning my lesson on other long hikes, I decided to be religious about stretching on the Tour du Mont Blanc from the start. I had a routine of six stretches and spent time throughout the day making sure I didn’t tighten up. Very important!

Don’t be a hero. If skin is getting hot, wrap it up. I did the entire TMB hike without a blister — and then just got one on purpose in the last two hours.

Good gear, smart and proactive ways to stay healthy, stretching, and taking it easy… it all worked just great.

issues.title: Taking it Easy on the Tour du Mont Blanc
issues.summary: While the Tour du Mont Blanc is demanding, it’s not a particularly difficult hike. It’s just long, with lots of altitude gain and loss, and always scenic. On my recent trek around the mountain with three friends, it seemed each of us had a weak spot: knees, toes, or lungs. For some, the challenge was … Continue reading "Taking it Easy on the Tour du Mont Blanc"
issues.author: Rick Steves
issues.content_html:
While the Tour du Mont Blanc is demanding, it’s not a particularly difficult hike. It’s just long, with lots of altitude gain and loss, and always scenic. On my recent trek around the mountain with three friends, it seemed each of us had a weak spot: knees, toes, or lungs. For some, the challenge was the uphill part, and for others (with weak knees), it was going downhill. We just took it easy, with lots of little breaks.

For long climbs, steady, smaller steps are best. The trail could be really rocky, and I can’t imagine doing it without hiking poles. The trail signs were great, and apps made staying on the trail easy: Just follow the blue dot. And I got good use out of a top-quality printed map. (I’d spend time the night before reading up on the hike and familiarizing myself with the trail on the map.)

While the weather forecast looked threatening, we hiked six days (in September, during the last week of the season) and, thankfully, had only one hour of rain. Still, each day we’d pack rain gear, and we’d add on and take off layers as we gained and lost altitude. After four days, we had it sorted out, and it occurred to us rank beginners, “We’re getting good at this.”

As we were hiking in a big circle around a big clump of mountains and sleeping in charming towns each night, every day seemed to be up and over a daunting mountain pass. A nightly treat was a stroll under a milky blanket of stars.

As nearly everyone hikes in the same direction (counter-clockwise), you become friends … Continue reading
issues.author: Rick Steves
issues.content_html:
Hiking Europe’s Tour du Mont Blanc was a totally different slice of European culture for me: Coming upon a remote farmhouse-turned-thriving-cafe serving wonderful lunches…flowers and cows (with classic bells) scenically sprinkled throughout…and an esprit de corps where everyone is like family.

As nearly everyone hikes in the same direction (counter-clockwise), you become friends with fellow hikers. It seemed like half the people on the trail were from the US, and I met lots of Seattleites.

And in the interest of hiking light, lunches were very simple — just a sandwich from the hotel, maybe a carrot, a piece of fruit, and water. But upon reaching the mid-day summit, lunch was a marmot’s banquet. (Speaking of marmots, we saw no wildlife except a couple of mice that had been squished under hiking boots on the trail.)

issues.title: New Godflesh & Jesu with Phoebe too
issues.summary: Some of the many reasons it’s been a great year for post-metal.
issues.author: Jeff Bergstrom
issues.content_html:
The great Jon Wurster (The Mountain Goats, The Bob Mould Band, Superchunk, The Best Show with Tom Scharpling) is a prolific drummer and one of the funniest people on earth. One of my favorite Wursterisms™ is that he utilizes the hashtag #rocknrollweirdness on Instagram when posting images of incongruous moments in rock n’ roll. Whether it’s a picture of The Who holding their Who Are You release party on the Hollywood set of the TV show Battlestar Galactica, Oasis hanging with Wesley Willis, or Motörhead drummer Philthy Animal Taylor and W.A.S.P. guitarist Chris Holmes having ice cream on a nice day, Wurster is a master curator of singular images of #rocknrollweirdness.

It’s rare for an instance of #rocknrollweirdness to land so profoundly with me that it gives me the energy to take finger-to-keyboard for the first time in years. Yet it recently came to my attention that master of heviosity Justin K. Broadrick was recently tapped by mainstream indie icon Phoebe Bridgers to play guitar on two tracks of her August 14, 2026 release Lost Weekend. Justin performs on track #5, “Bobby,” as well as on the ‘hidden’ track “Best Dressed” (track D17 on the vinyl and Track 00 on CD). Broadrick is involved with many different personal projects, each with their own particular signature sonic qualities, so it is important to note that he performs on these tracks under his Jesu moniker. And although I find his contributions to be buried under too many layers of over-production, the Broadrick aficionado can immediately recognize Jesu’s signature guitar sound in the first 15-seconds of “Bobby.” Lost Weekend was the Number 1 album in the UK and debuted at No. 2 on the Billboard 200. This is almost definitely the first time Justin has been that high in the charts.

But there was more! Phoebe Bridgers then released “On Video,” her song from the new A24 film Primetime. You can listen to it below. Oh and guess what? Justin Broadrick played bass and guitar on that song. As you probably know by now, Phoebe is also in the movie, and has been playing the song on tour.

These aren’t the first instances that Justin and Phoebe’s careers have intersected. Back in 2021, again under the Jesu moniker, Justin remixed Phoebe’s Boygenius bandmate Julien Baker’s track “Favor.” Justin not only executed the remix, but he also played guitars on the track which also features Phoebe Bridgers (and Lucy Dacus) on backing vocals. Check that track out below.

In other Justin K. Broadrick news, we’ve had a few months to let it sink in that the mighty Godflesh has retired from touring due to ongoing health issues plaguing Justin. The good news is that prior to his tour-ending surgery, Justin and Benny had an entire new Godflesh album pretty much already in the can. The album, entitled Decay, dropped on September 25 via Relapse Records and is available in all the formats, including vinyl in all kinds of colors and patterns.

Fortunately, all of the recordings for Decay were completed long before the surgery, vocals included… although the back end of a couple of songs were recorded with the hernia itself, and that was a struggle. I was already aware that the GODFLESH shout, so to speak, was exacerbating the hernia greatly, as was every GODFLESH performance in the lead-up to the surgery once the hernia appeared, and the hernia was mostly caused by year upon year of shouting in GODFLESH. The album was mixed post-surgery, and while I was still in some pain and considerable discomfort, but fortunately GODFLESH is generally me expressing my pain, albeit [usually] mental, philosophical and existential, whereas this was physical pain.

You can listen to “Living/Ending” below and do some heavy duty ordering of the vinyl.

I interviewed Justin back in 2014 and would love to interview him again someday to discuss all of his projects BUT Godflesh. Until that happens, both Guitar World and The Guardian have published very good interviews with him that do a great job bringing fans up to speed with the current state of Justin’s world.

See also: it’s been a great year for post-metal.

issues.title: 5 Artists We Want to See at Louder Than Life 2026
issues.summary: Louder Than Life’s 2026 edition is coming. Check out who we’re excited to see.
issues.author: BrooklynVegan Staff
issues.content_html:
Louder Than Life‘s 2026 edition is this weekend: September 17-20 at Kentucky Expo Center in Louisville, KY. As always, we’re figuring out who we most don’t want to miss. We’ll of course be sticking around for big headliners Tool, Iron Maiden, and My Chemical Romance, but the variety of acts we’re excited about across punk and metal genres this year is vast. Here are five artists that we’re especially looking forward to:

Circa Survive

As Andrew Sacherwrote when the band first announced their return:

Circa Survive went on “indefinite hiatus” in 2022, which came as bummer news considering they had just released some of the best music of their career, and the prospect of a reunion didn’t look very good after singer Anthony Greensaid on HardLore in December that what happened in 2022 was more of a “breakup” than a “hiatus” and added, “I don’t know if the band is ever going to do anything ever again… And even if it did, it wouldn’t be the same. It just wouldn’t.” So, it comes as a nice surprise that Circa Survive just announced their first show in nearly five years! They’ll be playing Louisville’s Louder Than Life festival in September, and Anthony Green will be pulling double duty at that fest, as L.S. Dunes are playing too. (Everyone in L.S. Dunes will be pulling double duty at that fest, as My Chemical Romance, Coheed & Cambria, and Thursday are playing too.

We can’t wait!

Haywire

Boston punks Haywire are one of the most exciting, most fun, and fastest rising hardcore bands of recent times, with banger after banger, and with more on the way soon, as they recently announced their second full-length album, I Don’t Wanna Say Goodbye, due October 2 via their new label home, Roadrunner Records. Their raucous live shows continue to be unmissable, whether in a basement, a boxing ring, a club, or at a fest. See you in the pit.

Missing Link

Staying on the fest’s Friday hardcore stage for a second: playing before Haywire and the recently-announed, no-longer secret guest Knocked Loose, we want to highlight NY heavy hardcore band Missing Link whose intesity blows us away every time we get the chance to catch them (including sometimes with Haywire). Great live show. Don’t mess up and miss them in Louisville.

Hot Mulligan

Louder than Life also brings the pop punk, and the post-hardcore and emo-leaning Lansing, Michigan band Hot Mulligan are doing it better than most right now. Now four full lengths into their career, the band has become a festival staple, somtimes a rare mosh pit-inducing band on a lineup (like when we saw them at Gov Ball and Lolla), and sometimes right where they belong like in between Alkaline Trio and Jimmy Eat World in Louisville in Thursday. Always a super fun time, we can’t get enough of their energy, their humor, and their infectious hooks.

Danzig

The man, the myth, the legend. Danzig on this year’s fest officially brings it over the top for this Danzig-obsesed writer.

Check out the entire lineup HERE, and have fun this weekend.

Citizen‘s Mat Kerekes produced the album. Taylor Young mixed it at The Pit. We’ve teamed up with the band for a BrooklynVegan-exclusive vinyl variant of I Don’t Wanna Say Goodbye, limited to just 300 copies. Pre-order now in the BV Shop.

The first single from I Don’t Wanna Say Goodbye is “Interstate Love Affair,” which comes with a Luis Hernandez-directed video. Watch it below.

It follows Haywire’s 2024 great releases, the Conditioned for Demolition LP and For Better or for Worse EP, and 2025 splits with No Guard and Dropkick Murphys ( “Citizen I.C.E.” included).

Constantly on the road (and in our feeds), last year Haywire completed a goal of playing all 50 states, and played an amazing tour with Drain, No Pressure and Secret World. They’re taking a short unexpected break though. They announced this morning that their Australia tour this week is postponed till later in the year, but they’ll be touring again in the US in September, including a Milwaukee show supporting Turnstile, a run opening for Circle Jerks, and appearances at Louder Than Life, Riot Fest, Four Chord Music Festival and CBGB Fest. issues.title: Mouse fight club might explain why we like to watch violent things
issues.summary: Watching fights wasn't as good as practical experience, but it got the mice halfway there.
issues.author: Jennifer Ouellette
issues.content_html:
There's something about watching violent events that broadly appeals to us, whether it's the latest John Wick movie, a video game, or a live UFC bout. Scientists have debated whether watching violent things could make us more aggressive, but it could also be an adaptive survival strategy. Male mice, for instance, who watch other mice fighting learned enough about how to fight to better protect themselves (compared to mice who didn't watch fights) when pitted against stronger, more aggressive opponents, according to a paper published in the journal Nature.

The team assigned male mice randomly to three different groups—fighters, spectators, or novices—and then subjected each group to eight days of training involving three 10-minute sessions per day. The novices played with stuffed mice in isolation, while the spectators watched various pairs of fighter mice battle it out from a raised platform behind a transparent barrier—a set-up chosen to let them smell and listen to the fights as well as observe them.

The ninth day was "fight night," when all the mice had to face a daunting opponent in three 4-minute rounds. Each fight was filmed from above so that the mouse behavior could be analyzed. To monitor corresponding changes in brain activity, the team engineered the rodents' excitatory brain cells to glow green whenever they were activated, while inhibitory brain cells glowed red. They also implanted tiny optical fibers into 12 interconnected brain regions so they could track changing activity in every brain region simultaneously.

issues.title: NASA's new Moon plans have a problem: Orion wasn't designed to fly this way
issues.summary: "We also have a responsibility to not go too fast and cut too many corners."
issues.author: Eric Berger
issues.content_html:
NASA recently announced a significant shakeup to the Artemis program that will land humans on the Moon.

The moves were designed to give the agency's lunar lander providers—SpaceX with its Starship vehicle, and Blue Origin with Blue Moon—more flexibility in reaching the Moon. For Starship, this means docking with Orion in Earth orbit, and then traveling to the Moon in tandem. For Blue Moon, it shifts the rendezvous with Orion all the way to low-lunar orbit.

These changes benefit the lunar landers, but in turn impose more of a burden on the Orion spacecraft, which is built for NASA by Lockheed Martin. To understand the implications for the spacecraft, Ars spoke with Kirk Shireman, Human Spaceflight Exploration and Orion program manager at Lockheed.

issues.title: How to tell a cyberattack from a plain old outage
issues.summary: When everything goes down, don’t assume it’s a cyberattack.
issues.author: Andy Greenberg, wired.com
issues.content_html:
Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV–style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US.

Across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies, a Federal Aviation Administration tech screw-upgrounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a US war with Iran and rising fears of AI-enabled hacking, this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence.

Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack.
