issues.title: Think It, Say It: A Two-Step Guide To Writing
issues.summary: Everyone has the ability to write, especially when called into service, whether to pen a novel or an important press release.
issues.author: Andrew Welsh-Huggins
issues.content_html:
Today’s guest post is by author Andrew Welsh-Huggins.

Good writing advice can come in the most unexpected ways, as I learned recently at an event where I was the one who was supposed to be doling out ideas.

The forum was a “meet the author” event at a bookstore in our neighborhood on the West Side of Columbus, Ohio, during which I talked about my writing journey, followed by Q&A and a book signing.

After my presentation, rather than ask a question, an audience member related his own experience writing many years ago. A supervisor had asked him to draft a press release, striking terror in this non-writer’s heart.

“How do I do that?” he asked.

The supervisor responded: “Well, think about what you want to say, then say it.”

The story elicited a chuckle from audience members. But the more I thought about it, the more I realized how sound the advice was, and how succinctly it encapsulated a writing philosophy to live by.

Here are three things the remark brought to mind:

First off, unbeknownst to the person relating this anecdote, he waded perfectly into the plotter vs. pantser debate. As someone who has tried both pure pantsing and extensive plotting, and now straddles the line between the two approaches, I value the idea of thinking about what I’m going to write before I pen a single word. In my case, the “thinking” that comes before beginning a new book involves an outline that covers around 75% of what I expect to happen, leaving me plenty of wiggle room as unexpected characters and plot twists emerge during the “say it” portion of writing.

While not an outliner, crime novelist Karin Slaughter, in a 2023 interview, captured what I consider an ideal way to think about plotting and writing:

Before I start a book, I think about it a lot, and I get some idea of the story. Then I sit down with my editor, and we talk it through. And she’s like, ‘Okay, this sounds good’ or ‘Well, you’ve killed everybody in the first chapter.’ And I’ll be like, ‘Oh, maybe I should kill someone in the fifth chapter.’ That kind of thing. We don’t outline. It’s more like this happens, this happens, this happens. And that’s a good scaffolding for me to follow.

Secondly, the “first this, then that” structure of the audience member’s advice is a reminder that, having conceived of an idea, it’s important to get the work done. As crime writer Susan Isaacs has noted, “Writing may be an art. It is certainly a craft. But also it’s a job. You have to put in regular hours and go to work whether you feel like it or not.” Similarly, you can’t just think about what you want to say. At some point, you also have to say it however you best work: pen on paper, fingers on keyboard, dictation app primed and ready to go.

Finally, the audience member provided a valuable lesson in how we define writers. One of my least favorite words is the adjective-turned-noun “creative,” as in, “Of course he’s a good writer—he’s a ‘creative’.” A creative, the implication being, as opposed to the rest of us mere mortals. I couldn’t disagree more. Everyone is a creative in some form or fashion, whether they’re a gifted artist, baker, or car mechanic. And within the context of this essay, everyone has the ability to write, especially when called into service, whether to pen a novel or an important press release. As novelist Phoenicia Rogerson has said:

It’s quite common, I think, to have this idea of what a real writer is, and to go chasing after that, rather than letting yourself be who you are. If you write, you’re a real writer, and there’s no superiority in writing one genre over another.

“Think about what you want to say, then say it.”

I couldn’t have put it better myself.

issues.title: Celtic silver coin hoard found in Hungary

Less than 40 cm (16 inches) under the surface, the … Read the full post → "Celtic silver coin ho
issues.author: livius drusus
issues.content_html:
A hoard of more than 200 Celtic silver coins has been discovered during construction of an electrical substation in Szombathely, Hungary. The new substation is being built on a site where archaeological remains have been found in the past, triggering a professional excavation before construction began. Less than 40 cm (16 inches) under the surface, the team from the National Archaeological Institute of the Hungarian National Museum Public Collection Center uncovered a few silver coins that had been scattered by agricultural work. Metal detectors then located the core of the hoard.

They were cached in a pit, some loose, some inside a small earthenware container. The coins are all Velem-type tetradrachms dating from the late 2nd century B.C. to the beginning of the 1st century B.C. On the obverse of the coins is a Celticized head in profile facing right bearing a pearl diadem and necklace. On the reverse is a stylized horse and rider wearing a crested helmet. They were probably minted in the Velem-Szentvid area, less than 10 miles from the find site.

Worth four drachmae a piece (hence “tetradrachms”), the denomination was widely used as trade coin and for state expenses throughout the Greco-Roman world. Their high silver content and large value made them unsuitable as a daily currency for individuals to spend, but perfect for them to store their wealth. The number of tetradrachms found in hoards attest to this usage.

The coin hoard is not the only significant find made in the two years since excavations began. Archaeologists have found material remains and thousands of artifacts covering almost 7,000 years of history. The oldest object is a polished stone axe used to fell trees and work wood. Another stand-out piece is a peacock-eye glass bead from the Early Iron Age (7th-6th century B.C.). From the remains of a Roman building, archaeologists recovered a fragment of a brick with a dog pawprint. It’s a flat tile, perhaps from a pilae stack that raised the floor over a hypocaust heating system.

A selection of the finds from the excavation will be exhibited at the Savaria Museum in Szombathely.

Similar to a modified mace, the scepter is decorated with swirl patterns on the top and eight flattened blades. It was a symbol of royal power from a time when Armenia had vassal kingdoms under the central monarch. It dates to the … Read the full post → "Copper scepter head found in Armenia"
issues.author: livius drusus
issues.content_html:
A rare medieval copper scepter head has been discovered in Kapan, southeast Armenia. Similar to a modified mace, the scepter is decorated with swirl patterns on the top and eight flattened blades. It was a symbol of royal power from a time when Armenia had vassal kingdoms under the central monarch. It dates to the 10th or 11th century.

The Kapan area was part of the territories of the princely Siunia dynasty. There was a small settlement at the site of what would become Kapan by the 5th century, and a fortress was built nearby in the 4th century. Kapan rose to major prominence in the 10th century when it became the capital of the self-style Kingdom of Kapan. It was a vassal of the Bagratid dynasty rulers of Greater Armenia, and survived a little more than 100 years, from 987 to 1170.

According to Stepanos Orbelian, a medieval Armenian historian, bishop, and a prominent member of the noble Orbelian dynasty, the capital of the Kingdom of Syunik was destroyed in 1126 under the command of Amir Harun as a result of Seljuk invasions, but the kingdom, thanks to the already impregnable fortress of Baghaberd, survived until 1170, being the last independent Armenian kingdom of Greater Armenia.

The first systematic archaeological investigations at the site of Old Kapan an environs began only in 2024. They found evidence of powerful fortifications, double-layered walls and a larger defensive tower near the entrance to the fortress.

Last year’s excavation uncovered the remains of foundations and column bases from a three-aisled basilica dating to the 4th or 5th century. Near the church, archaeologists found a stone oil press four feet in diameter. This year the team uncovered a furnace of polished stone that likely heated the water of a public bath at the site.

The scepter has been transferred to the Kapan Geological Museum for conservation and display.

issues.author: livius drusus
issues.content_html:
A larger-than-life-sized gilded bronze leg discovered in 1820 has been newly identified as a fragment of a monumental statue of Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius erected in the Scottish Borders. Since its discovery, the leg was believed to have come from England, likely the urban center of Eboracum, modern-day York.

The leg was found in a bog in Milsington near Hawick. It was exceptional for its great size and condition, with much of its original gilding still intact. It is a lower leg below the knee wearing with straps crossed the top of the foot, wrapping around the ankle and tied in front knot. It dates to 140 A.D.

Scholars initially thought it came from northern England because its high quality and rich gilding suggested close proximity to expensive craftspeople and materials, but more recent studies of Roman statue fragments has found that in fact, frontier forts on the Scottish border did erect bronze statues of the emperor, even equestrian ones.

In addition, the cut line where the leg was removed was handled very gently. There are no cut marks on the top. It was taken down as cast. Had the statue been dismembered by angry locals after the Romans withdrew from southern Scotland in 160-180 A.D., it would have been hacked off, not carefully removed, and chopped up for scrap.

Once curators had established that the statue was likely to have been erected in Scotland, they looked to answer the question of who it depicted. Just one emperor paid particular heed to his Scottish victories – Antoninus Pius. His conquest of southern Scotland was the only foreign adventure that he commemorated with the title Imperator, a battle-honour meaning ‘commander’ which marked an emperor’s victory.

Dr Fraser Hunter, Principal Curator of Prehistoric and Roman Archaeology at National Museums Scotland said:

“This really turns on its head our understanding of Rome’s second attempt at conquering Scotland. This was a big deal for the Emperor, something which was worth celebrating. It offers us a tantalising glimpse into the kind of grand monuments which once stood in southern Scotland and shows the importance Pius placed on his victories in Scotland. But it begs the question … where is the rest of the statue?”

Mounted to a model of an equestrian statue like the iconic Marcus Aurelius in the Capitoline Museums in Rome, the leg is now on display in Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire, alongside a wealth of other priceless Roman-era artifacts, including the incredible Mithraic altar with the cutouts of the sun god Sol so it glowed when lit from behind found at Inveresk. The exhibition opened Saturday and runs through April 18th, 2027.

issues.title: In Search of the Deep Life
issues.summary: Early in the coronavirus pandemic, as I sat at home channeling my anxiety into publishing daily essays on this newsletter (a streak I kept up ... Read more The post In Search of the Deep Life appeared first on Cal Newport .
issues.author: Cal Newport
issues.content_html:
Early in the coronavirus pandemic, as I sat at home channeling my anxiety into publishing daily essays on this newsletter (a streak I kept up for six weeks), I had a revelation: none of my advice, ideas, or systems really mattered if you didn’t build them on the foundation of a meaningful life.

Who cares about losing yourself to social media or letting work devolve into email whack-a-mole if the world outside of your phone and inbox isn’t that compelling?

On March 17th of that infamous spring, I captured these notions in an essay titled ​“The Deep Life: Some Notes.”​ As I explained:

“To me, the deep life is about focusing with energetic intention on things that really matter — in work, at home, and in your soul — and not wasting too much attention on things that don’t.”

In the weeks that followed, I wrote ​several​​more​​essays​ on pursuing the deep life. Later that summer, when I ​launched my podcast​, I dedicated a third of my inaugural episode to this concept. (My original tagline: “a show about work, technology, and the deep life.”)

Two years later, as we returned to normalcy, I convinced my publisher to let me try writing a book on these ideas. I then set out on the long, patient process of elaborating and developing my thoughts into a coherent system.

All of this brings me to the current moment. I’m proud to finally announce that my next book, ​The Deep Life: A Structured Approach​, is now ​available for pre-order​.

The Deep Life brings together and significantly expands on my past thinking on this topic. It presents a step-by-step approach to achieving the intentional-living goal laid out in that original March 2020 post. It’s less an idea book than a classic-style advice guide, offering practical details on how to identify what resonates, refine it into an actionable vision, and then move toward that vision systematically.

My friend ​Oliver Burkeman​, to whom I sent a proof copy of the manuscript, had the following reaction:

“It’s hard to imagine a more timely or inspiring manual for a life of sanity and accomplishment, or a better guide than Cal Newport. This is a profound book, but just as importantly, a profoundly practical one: it shows that depth is something we can do.”

I believe that this book is thekey that unlocks the value in almost everything else I write about. If you’ve followed me this far, then you need to read this one.

With this in mind, here are some of the places where you can pre-order the book right now in advance of its March publication date:

  • ​Amazon​
  • ​Barnes & Noble​
  • ​Bookshop.org​
  • ​Amazon UK​
  • ​Waterstones ​

You can also pre-order ​a signed copy​ from my local bookstore here in Takoma Park.

If you think you’ll eventually read this one, I humbly ask that you consider pre-ordering it, as these early purchases signal to booksellers that the book is worth stocking on their shelves. (And if you do pre-order, hold on to your digital receipt, as I’m working on a pretty cool bonus that I’ll announce soon.)

Most of all, however, I want to extend my thanks for your support over all these years as I’ve explored these fundamental ideas. We only get one life. Why not make it deep?

The post In Search of the Deep Life appeared first on Cal Newport.

issues.title: The Good Thing About Hard Things
issues.summary: A new research paper titled “​AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance,”​ which was recently presented at the ​Conference on Language Modeling​, has been ... Read more The post The Good Thing About Hard Things appeared first on Cal Newport .
issues.author: Cal Newport
issues.content_html:
A new research paper titled “​AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance,”​ which was recently presented at the ​Conference on Language Modeling​, has been attracting attention.

It explores an obvious question: do AI tools negatively affect your ability to think? It does so with a simple experimental design: participants were divided into two groups tasked with solving a series of math problems involving fractions. One group had to find answers on their own, while the other used ChatGPT to help.

At first, the ChatGPT group performed better, which is not surprising because LLMs are good at solving math problems. But then the researchers turned off the chatbot. Not only did the AI group’s accuracy fall below the control group, but many participants in the AI group gave up and started skipping questions altogether.

The researchers repeated the same experiment several more times, including one instance where math problems were replaced with an SAT reading comprehension prompt. They kept finding the same drop-offs in accuracy and persistence.

Here’s how ​a press release​ about the paper summarized these results:

“The findings backed up what anecdotes and surveys have increasingly found in recent years: An overreliance on AI for answers erodes our cognitive fitness. When AI produces answers in seconds, we get used to that speed; anything that takes longer feels inefficient.”

Brian Christian, one of the paper’s authors, put it plainly: “You almost couldn’t ask for a clearer story.”

I’ve spent the last decade thinking and writing about how technologies might accidentally degrade our ​cognitive fitness​, and how this might in turn degrade not only our economic productivity, but also the quality of the human experience more generally.

In this sense, these LLM findings aren’t revealing something new.

What is new, however, is the jaw-dropping speed of these impacts. We’re accustomed to slow-moving techno-cognition trends such as the negative effects of ubiquitous smartphone usage, which took years to emerge in the data.

With chatbots, the negative impact is immediate. The high generated by side-stepping mental effort using LLMs is so compelling that, with only a short exposure, hard thinking quickly becomes intolerable.

The good news is that we don’t yet know if these effects are permanent. Presumably, the research participants who struggled immediately after ChatGPT was turned off might do much better on the same type of test if they tried again later in a setting where AI help was clearly not an option.

But we cannot ignore the warnings that these early studies are generating. When it comes to our cognitive fitness, we’re playing with a powerful new force that we don’t yet fully understand.

A key theme of my work in the technology critic space is that a life without serious, sustained, intentional thought is impoverished. Thinking is how we make sense of ourselves and the world, and is how we imagine new horizons and create the key elements of our future. It’s at the heart of philosophy, theology, and human empathy; the ability that separates our species from all other animals.

Silicon Valley is good at creating tools, but terrible at figuring out how we should use them. The latter step is still up to us — but it requires us to care.

The post The Good Thing About Hard Things appeared first on Cal Newport.

issues.title: It’s Time to Investigate the AI Labs
issues.summary: Over the last several months, the two leading frontier AI labs have shown some brazen behavior. It started with a series of​ carefully planned announcements​ ... Read more The post It’s Time to Investigate the AI Labs appeared first on Cal Newport .
issues.author: Cal Newport
issues.content_html:
Over the last several months, the two leading frontier AI labs have shown some brazen behavior.

It started with a series of​ carefully planned announcements​ and reports from OpenAI that try to establish how unnerving and powerful (not to mention ​felonious​) their LLM-powered agent systems have become.

They then handed the baton to Anthropic, whose employees began ​publicly debating​ the exact probability that these technologies would lead to human extinction. They delivered this all with an eerie calmness that conveyed a nihilistic inevitability about their work.

The ground suitably softened, the campaign crescendoed with Anthropic CEO Dario Amodi releasing a letter, titled ​“We Must Pace the Frontier,”​ in which he enumerates all the harms his own company’s research might cause, and then, instead of apologizing and promising to stop, concludes that catastrophe can only be avoided if we “build the technology in the right way,” which involves – surprise, surprise – the government slowing down potential competitors and allowing the labs to take the lead in advancing the relevant tech. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman quickly ​tweeted his support​ for this brave plan.

Internally, these labs have long embraced this style of messianic thinking, casting themselves as humanity’s only hope against the defied powers of superintelligent AI. This summer, in some sense, was their attempt to induct the rest of us into this long-held ideology.

It didn’t work.

Instead of inspiring the masses to stand up and applaud these engineers’ heroic rationalism, it made us instead start to ask, “What the hell is going on over in those labs?”

To that end, last Thursday ​I published an op-ed in TheNew York Times​ calling on Congress to begin a public fact-finding mission to uncover what research projects OpenAI and Anthropic are conducting, how they’re conducting them, and for what purposes.

I suggested three key areas to explore with this questioning:

  1. We must move past vague discussions of “AI” and instead isolate the specific types of systems that are creating problems. The frontier labs want us to think of AI as a singular technology on an inevitable, fixed trajectory. In reality, most of the problems in recent months result from a​ narrow band of incautious experiments​, conducted mainly by the frontier labs. They need to justify why they’re running them.
  2. We must examine the internal safety procedures surrounding these research efforts. ​OpenAI revealed​ a long series of unauthorized hacking attacks by their autonomous agents. Why weren’t these efforts stopped after the first such incident was revealed? Why not pursue criminal liability for them running systems they knew would likely commit crimes?
  3. We have to investigate the role of apocalyptic futurist ideologies in the decisions being made by the frontier labs, both about what research to pursue and how fast to pursue it. I’m increasingly concerned that OpenAI and Anthropic, in particular, are becoming increasingly reckless because they believe collateral damage is justified in a race to redeem humanity. (For more on these beliefs and their connections to the labs, see: ​this​ and ​this​ and ​this​, all published in the Times in just the last several weeks.)

“We need to stop letting a small number of private companies, acting and talking in increasingly erratic ways, dictate how we’re supposed to feel about A.I.,” I concluded. “We’ve heard what they want to say; now it’s Congress’s turn to step in on our behalf to find out what’s really going on.”

The post It’s Time to Investigate the AI Labs appeared first on Cal Newport.

issues.title: Superintelligence is a Fairy Tale. But Chasing It Can Still Cause Harm.
issues.summary: Yesterday, multiple Anthropic employees casually announced online that they thought the types of AI they’re building could kill billions of people. Not in some distant ... Read more The post Superintelligence is a Fairy Tale. But Chasing It Can Still Cause Harm. appeared first on Cal Newport .
issues.author: Cal Newport
issues.content_html:
Yesterday, multiple Anthropic employees casually announced online that they thought the types of AI they’re building could kill billions of people. Not in some distant hypothetical future, but in the next few years. Understandably, this created a tsunami of media attention and anxious discussion.

I added to this debate with a ​brief essay​ of my own. I fear, however, that in the Sturm und Drang of that charged news cycle, some of my conclusions might have been hard to follow. So, I thought it would be useful to publish three short follow-up points that summarize my core claims more directly…

Point #1:Anthropic and OpenAI arenotable to create superintelligent AI.

The Anthropic employees who spoke out yesterday believe the force that might wipe out humanity will be “superintelligent” AI systems that are much too capable for us to control. Let me be clear: We have no idea how to create such machines. We don’t even know if they’re possible. And if they are possible, we are many, many key technical innovations away from getting there. (Simply scaling LLMs won’t be nearly enough.)

The LLM labs attempt to sidestep this reality ​by claiming​ their models will figure this all out on their own, programming better versions of themselves that will be far more capable than anything us measly humans can conceive. But this is just a warmed-over version of the recursive self-improvement trope that Silicon Valley futurists have been peddling ​since the 1960s​; a rhetorical crutch that lets you somberly discuss sci-fi scenarios without actually engaging with relevant technical details.

Point #2:But their obsession with superintelligence can still create real harm.

When you believe,​ as many at OpenAI and Anthropic reportedly do​, that humanity’s fate rests on winning a race to create the most powerful technology ever, you tend to care less about the damage you inflict along the way.

This is what happened with the HuggingFace hacking attacks from this summer. The experiments OpenAI ran were reckless. They took a relatively common technology called an LLM-powered agent, which is used with minimal issues by millions of software developers every day, and ​then added​ a bunch of dangerous features, removed restrictions, and released a whole mess of them into poorly fenced digital wilds. Why? They were desperate to make as much progress as quickly as possible on a hacking test that they felt was an important milestone en route to superintelligence.

This is the equivalent of deploying a fleet of experimental self-driving cars onto the interstate, hoping that at least one will avoid crashing long enough to win a navigation challenge.

In other words, this behavior was negligent. But they likely justified it because it served the far grander goal of summoning a digital God. (Clearly, there may be additional motivations at play here as well. Given OpenAI’s interest in an IPO, for example, there might have been pressure to do well on this particular benchmark to establish their model’s power. But the more I talk to sources connected to these companies, the more I’ve come to believe that their commitment to futurist ideas is what really drives a lot of their more irresponsible behavior.)

Ultimately, I think the HuggingFace attack is a good representation of the types of near-future harm we should actually be fearing if the LLM labs continue to operate as they currently are: that is, more cyber mayhem than catastrophic risk.

But just because these impending harms aren’t nearly as scary as the extinction events touted by the true believers, they’re still plenty worrisome. More importantly, they’re entirely avoidable!

Which brings me to my final point…

Point #3:AI progress does not have to be this scary or dangerous

First things first, it’s important to emphasize something that many media figures and commentators seem to be missing: AI is not the same thing as LLMs. Many of the most impressive AI systems that exist today – including those that beat humans at games, win Nobel prizes for studying proteins, and self-drive cars through crowded city streets – have very little to do with LLMs. Slowing down OpenAI and Anthropic doesn’t mean that you’re stalling AI progress in general. You would only be impacting the subset of AI research that focuses on hyper-scaled LLMs as a central component.

But even when we do focus specifically on LLM-based AI research, none of the harms I described above are unavoidable. They’re instead side effects of reckless experiments motivated by the pursuit of superintelligence.

If the LLM labs simply acted more responsibly, focusing on producing useful products instead of summoning an AI messiah, and following common-sense research safety protocols instead of racing haphazardly toward some imagined utopia, we could be enjoying a steadily advancing AI industry promising tools that excite us, all without having to endure regular doses of dread and fear.

But due to their ideological commitments to superintelligence, these labs seem incapable of such reforms.

This last observation is what’s driving me to advocate for intervention. Those Anthropic employees absurdly implying that they’re willing to risk a digital holocaust to realize their futurist vision was my last straw. They’re far too weird for us to expect them to ever act reasonably.

Please don’t take this as a call for abandoning AI research or somehow ceding AI supremacy to China. Our problem is not with AI progress, but instead with the eccentric way this small group of companies is trying to achieve it. Fix that, and AI innovation can continue, free from all the doom and with much less potential for collateral damage.

The post Superintelligence is a Fairy Tale. But Chasing It Can Still Cause Harm. appeared first on Cal Newport.

issues.author: melissa
issues.content_html:
• How Does Ozempic Work for Sleep Apnea?

  • Will Insurance Cover Ozempic for Sleep Apnea?
  • How to Check Your Insurance Coverage
  • Alternatives if Insurance Won’t Cover Ozempic
  • Frequently Asked Questions
Key Takeaways
  • Most insurance plans don’t cover Ozempic for sleep apnea, but some partially cover costs of another GLP-1, Zepbound, that’s prescribed for sleep apnea.
  • In 2024, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved Zepbound for the treatment of moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in adults with obesity. Currently, Ozempic is only approved to treat type 2 diabetes.
  • You can find out if your insurance covers weight loss medications for sleep apnea by checking their online directory or calling your insurer directly.

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1s) like Ozempic can help with weight loss, which may assist with sleep apnea symptoms. If your sleep apnea has worsened with weight gain or you have other medical conditions that warrant the use of GLP-1s, your healthcare provider may prescribe one, Trusted Source National Association of Insurance Commissioners View Source but they can be pricey. Monthly out of pocket costs often reach several hundred dollars, and some plans require you to try CPAP or a weight-loss program before approving the medication.

So, will insurance cover Ozempic for sleep apnea? The short answer is no, but some insurance plans may cover other GLP-1s for sleep apnea, especially if you also have other health conditions like high blood pressure or diabetes.

Even if your insurance won’t cover a GLP-1, you still have options. Your provider can document medical necessity, which strengthens insurance approval attempts for weight loss medications. Below, learn how weight loss drugs may improve sleep apnea, how to check your insurance coverage, and what other options exist.

Get a Home Sleep Study for as Low as $0

Based on claims data, eligible insured patients may pay as little as $0 for the home sleep study and related consultations. Actual out-of-pocket costs vary by insurance plan, deductible, coinsurance, and coverage. We will provide your out-of-pocket cost prior to your first consultation. Cost does not include any post-diagnosis medication or treatment, if and when prescribed.

Take a one-night sleep study in your own bed, review results with a certified sleep expert, and get a personalized treatment plan for as low $0 with most major insurance plans.

Check Your Coverage 4.8 60,000+ patients

How Does Ozempic Work for Sleep Apnea?

Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) happens when your airway gets blocked during sleep, causing a pause in breathing. These episodes can happen many times throughout the night and last anywhere from 10 to 30 seconds.

Carrying extra weight around the neck is a major risk factor for OSA, as excess tissue can crowd your airway while you sleep Trusted Source MSD Manuals First published in 1899 as a small reference book for physicians and pharmacists, the Manual grew in size and scope to become one of the most widely used comprehensive medical resources for professionals and consumers. View Source . About 31% of people with obstructive sleep apnea have obesity while 44% are overweight Trusted Source National Library of Medicine, Biotech Information The National Center for Biotechnology Information advances science and health by providing access to biomedical and genomic information. View Source . Because of this connection, experts have started researching to see if GLP-1s like Ozempic can also improve symptoms of OSA Trusted Source Journal of Translational Medicine View Source .

A clear relationship exists between weight loss and better sleep apnea outcomes. A study review found that a 20% decrease in BMI led to a 57% reduction in sleep apnea symptoms Trusted Source National Library of Medicine, Biotech Information The National Center for Biotechnology Information advances science and health by providing access to biomedical and genomic information. View Source .

Other research confirms GLP-1s may improve sleep apnea symptoms through weight loss, a lower BMI (body mass index), and a smaller waist size. But not all GLP-1s offer the same benefits. For example, another study review found that tirzepatide (Zepbound) improved OSA symptoms more than liraglutide (Saxenda). Trials also show that tirzepatide improves daytime sleepiness and blood pressure, two issues that often accompany sleep apnea.

Is Ozempic Approved for Sleep Apnea?

Currently, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has not approved Ozempic to treat sleep apnea or weight loss. Ozempic is only approved by the FDA to treat type 2 diabetes. The only FDA-approved GLP-1s for weight loss are semaglutide (Wegovy), liraglutide (Saxenda), and tirzepatide (Zepbound).

Among these, only Zepbound has FDA approval for sleep apnea. In 2024, the FDA approved Zepbound for the treatment of moderate to severe OSA in adults with obesity Trusted Source U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) The FDA is responsible for protecting the public health by ensuring the safety, efficacy, and security of human and veterinary drugs, biological products, and medical devices; and by ensuring the safety of our nation's food supply, cosmetics, and products that emit radiation. View Source . This approval was based on a large clinical trial showing significant reductions in apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) or sleep apnea severity after weight loss.

Will Insurance Cover Ozempic for Sleep Apnea?

Insurance typically won’t cover Ozempic for sleep apnea since the FDA hasn’t approved its use for that condition. Sometimes, providers will prescribe medications “off-label,” meaning they offer them because they may help with a condition not listed in the approved indications. But insurers typically won’t cover a drug for off-label use.

However, if you have another health condition alongside OSA, you may still be eligible for GLP-1 coverage. For example, Ozempic is FDA-approved for type 2 diabetes, so if you have this condition, your insurance may pay for it. Weight loss and improved sleep apnea become added benefits. Trusted Source National Association of Insurance Commissioners View Source .

Some insurance plans also cover GLP-1s for obesity-related health conditions like high cholesterol or high blood pressure, but each company sets its own criteria. If you have one of these health conditions plus a high BMI and obstructive sleep apnea, you may get insurance coverage for GLP-1s.

Now that Zepbound has been approved to treat OSA, more insurers may cover this medication. Many payers are adding Zepbound to formularies, although prior authorization is common. Requirements often include a BMI threshold, documentation of CPAP intolerance or failure, and proof of structured weight loss attempts.

How to Check Your Insurance Coverage

Every insurance company has a range of coverage plans and each covers different drugs. The first place you can look is your insurance provider’s website. Most insurers have a formulary listed under each of their plans, so you can see exactly what’s covered and how much you can expect to pay.

Medicare and Medicaid have a similar list available online. If your insurance company’s online formulary is confusing or difficult to use, you can call the customer service number on the back of your insurance card to ask for copay information on any medication.

You can also submit an appeal if your provider submits a GLP-1 request for approval and insurance says they won’t pay. Appeals can push insurers a little harder if they have denied payment for your weight loss drug or if it’s not on their list of approved medications. You may be able to get it covered with an appeal if your provider can prove it’s medically necessary.

For most plans, you have six months to file an internal appeal with your insurer. If that appeal is denied, you can request an external review for a third-party to weigh in. Typically, appeals are submitted through your insurer’s website, but you may also request more information through their customer service.

Alternatives if Insurance Won’t Cover Ozempic

If your insurance plan won’t pay for Ozempic, you can ask about Zepbound or another GLP-1 medication. If no weight loss medication is covered, you still have options. Exercise and diet changes are encouraged for people on GLP-1s, and these changes improve sleep apnea symptoms on their own Trusted Source UpToDate More than 2 million healthcare providers around the world choose UpToDate to help make appropriate care decisions and drive better health outcomes. UpToDate delivers evidence-based clinical decision support that is clear, actionable, and rich with real-world insights. View Source .

To lose weight through diet, create a calorie deficit: take in fewer calories than you use daily. Trusted Source National Library of Medicine, Biotech Information The National Center for Biotechnology Information advances science and health by providing access to biomedical and genomic information. View Source .

Cutting foods like sweet and alcoholic beverages, may also help you lose weight faster. However, everyone responds differently to diets, so you may need to try more than one approach. Trusted Source National Library of Medicine, Biotech Information The National Center for Biotechnology Information advances science and health by providing access to biomedical and genomic information. View Source . You should also talk to your doctor before making any big lifestyle changes, especially because they may be able to make medically-sound suggestions based on your history or refer you to a nutritionist.

You can also boost your calorie deficit by exercising.. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services recommends getting 150 to 300 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous exercise each week. They also suggest you include muscle strengthening exercises at least two days per week . Adding resistance training is especially helpful because increased muscle mass improves metabolic rate.

Beyond lifestyle changes, your provider can recommend sleep apnea treatments like Trusted Source MSD Manuals First published in 1899 as a small reference book for physicians and pharmacists, the Manual grew in size and scope to become one of the most widely used comprehensive medical resources for professionals and consumers. View Source :

  • CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) therapy, which keeps your airways open while you sleep.
  • Oral appliances that reposition or retrain your tongue to stay clear of your airway and prevent blockage.
  • Surgical options like nerve stimulation, tonsil removal, and excess tissue removal to improve OSA symptoms through a variety of methods.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Medicare cover Ozempic for sleep apnea?

Medicare does not cover Ozempic for sleep apnea, but partially covers another GLP-1, Zepbound, for this diagnosis. Under Medicare, patients are expected to pay $50 per month for Zepbound.

How much is Ozempic without insurance?

Ozempic costs $499 per month without insurance. Some pharmacies offer discount programs, but costs still remain high.

How much is Ozempic with insurance?

The cost of Ozempic with insurance depends on your plan, but you may pay as little as $25 per month on some plans. To get a better idea of how much Ozempic can cost with your insurance plan, you can contact a representative from your insurance network to talk through any out-of-pocket costs.

How long will insurance cover Ozempic for sleep apnea?

The length of Ozempic coverage depends on your plan and health history. Typically, an initial authorization lasts for six months, but some plans cover this medication for 12 months at a time [/ocm_reference] . Renewals often require documented weight loss progress or updated provider notes.

Medical Disclaimer: The content on this page should not be taken as medical advice or used as a recommendation for any specific treatment or medication. Always consult your doctor before taking a new medication or changing your current treatment.

Still have questions? Ask our community!

Join our Sleep Care Community — a trusted hub of sleep health professionals, product specialists, and people just like you. Whether you need expert sleep advice for your insomnia or you’re searching for the perfect mattress, we’ve got you covered. Get personalized guidance from the experts who know sleep best.

issues.title: The Top 10 Metrics in Anthropic’s S-1 for B2B Execs: $33 Billion in Nine Months, 900% NRR, and 12x More $100K Customers in a Year
issues.summary: Anthropic’s revenue went from $41M in 2023 to $386M in 2024 to $4.585B in 2025. Then it did $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year. No B2B company is going to copy that growth rate. The operating metrics underneath it are a... Continue Reading
issues.author: Jason Lemkin
issues.content_html:
Anthropic’s revenue went from $41M in 2023 to $386M in 2024 to $4.585B in 2025. Then it did $33.24 billion in revenue for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year.

No B2B company is going to copy that growth rate. The operating metrics underneath it are a different story, and most of them apply to any B2B + AI company at $10M or $100M in ARR.

Below are the 10 I’d pull out of the filing.

1. Net Revenue Retention of ~900%, Excluding Flat-Fee Plans

Anthropic reports roughly 900% net revenue retention: existing customers collectively generated about nine times as much revenue in the September quarter as they did a year earlier. Snowflake was at 158% when it filed and GitLab was at 152%, and people thought those were crazy.

The definition in the filing matters here. The number reflects how much a year-old cohort now spends, excluding Pro and Max subscribers. All of that 900% comes from metered accounts. The flat-fee subscriptions aren’t in it.

A seat-priced product tops out somewhere around 120-130% NRR, because a customer can only add so many seats. The 900% happens when the bill grows with the work the product does.

2. $100K+ Customers Went From 950 to 11,900 in One Year

As of Sept 30, more than 11,900 customers were at $100K+ in trailing-12-month revenue, up from more than 950 a year earlier. Further up: 1,900+ above $1M and about 250 above $10M.

The filing also discloses about 40 million customers below $100K. Anthropic leads with the $100K count because that’s the number that shows enterprise traction. If you’re selling to the enterprise, that cohort belongs at the top of your board deck too.

3. Gross Margin of 85.5%, Up From 29.4% a Year Earlier

The amended prospectus puts cost of revenue at $4,812 million against $33,242 million of revenue for the first nine months of 2026, an 85.5% gross margin by FourWeekMBA’s arithmetic, up from 29.4% a year earlier.

Two caveats. Anthropic moved gross margin off the income statement, so this is derived from the footnotes. And per The Information, the ~85% excludes the cost of developing its models.

Still, a year ago this business kept 29 cents of every revenue dollar after serving customers, and now it keeps about 85. If your AI product runs at 50% gross margins today, that’s where you are now, not where you’ll end up. It’s a bad reason to set prices at cost-plus.

4. Compute Went From 48% of Revenue in Q2 to 58% in Q3

In the first half, revenue outran compute badly. In Q2 2026, revenue rose 1,368% year over year while compute costs rose 300%.

Then Q3 reversed part of that. Compute as a share of revenue went from 48% in Q2 to 58% in Q3. And Anthropic disclosed purchase commitments of $895.4 billion.

Inference cost per dollar of revenue doesn’t go down every quarter. It moves with model mix, agent workloads, and how much heavier usage gets. Track it quarterly, next to gross margin, so a bad quarter shows up before your board asks about it.

5. Sales & Marketing at 23% of Revenue (First Half)

First-half 2026 sales and marketing was $3.808B, about 23.4% of revenue. That’s at 1,000%+ growth. Plenty of B2B companies growing 30% spend twice that ratio.

When the product is pulling, S&M grows slower than revenue. If your S&M ratio is flat or rising while you grow, you need to fix the product and the pricing before you add AEs.

6. 79% of Revenue Is Consumption-Based

In the first nine months of 2026, consumption brought in $26.3 billion, or 79% of revenue, and subscriptions $6.9 billion, or 21%. The Pro, Max, and Team plans everyone sees are the smaller business.

The filing also shows the cost of consumption pricing: customer spending fell about 20% in the two weeks ended Jan 2, 2026, vs. the two weeks ended Dec 19, 2025. Usage revenue drops when customers’ engineers go on vacation. Committed-spend contracts are what keep a usage forecast intact through December.

7. 48% of Revenue Came Through Cloud Marketplaces (First Half)

48% of H1 2026 revenue came through cloud marketplaces, reported gross. Marketplaces also account for 58% of receivables.

So nearly half of Anthropic’s revenue gets bought through AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure, because enterprises have committed cloud spend they need to draw down. If you sell to the enterprise and aren’t listed there, procurement takes longer than it has to.

8. Under $1 of Every $1,000 in Fortune 500 Spend

Anthropic already counts more than half the Fortune 500 as customers generating at least $100,000 in annual revenue. Among the publicly traded companies in that group, spending with Anthropic still averages less than one dollar for every thousand dollars of total expenses. The ten largest Fortune 500 customers spend more than 8x the group’s average share of expenses, but still below 1%.

The denominator is total expenses, not the IT budget. Anthropic is going after spend on headcount, services, and operations, not just the software line.

I use this exact test for agentic B2B deals in Fund II. I won’t invest unless the company unlocks budget beyond software, and the proof is deal sizes at least 2x what pre-AI competitors get.

9. More Than Half of $100K+ Customers Use Two Products, Up From 30%

More than half of $100K+ customers used both Claude Platform and at least one Anthropic application in the September quarter, up from about 30% in Q4 2025.

That’s the second-biggest NRR driver in the filing, after pricing. API customers picked up Claude Code and the apps, and app customers started building on the API. If you have a second product, report its attach rate in your top cohort every quarter.

10. Customers Outside the Top Five Went From 64% to 79% of Revenue

The top five customers were about 25% of revenue for the first nine months of 2026. But customers outside the top five supplied about 79% of September-quarter revenue, up from about 64% in the March quarter. One customer, “Customer C,” went from 43% of revenue in 2023 to 11% in H1 2026.

The top five didn’t shrink to get there. Each top-five customer hit a revenue record in the September quarter. The rest of the base grew faster. Early concentration is survivable if the trend line looks like this, and that trend line is what to show your board.

5 More Numbers From the Filing

  • Q3 growth slowed, from a very high base: Q3 revenue was $17.0bn, up 46.7% on Q2, after Q2 had grown about 140% on Q1.
  • Operating income moved back and forth: Q3 was a $567M operating loss, after Q2’s $974M operating income.
  • The net loss is mostly accounting: Of the $80.7B first-half GAAP net loss, $72.4B is a fair-value change on convertible notes and SAFEs.
  • Revenue per employee: over $6.6M on a trailing basis. Strong public B2B companies typically land somewhere around $300K-$500K.
  • The most regulated buyers are already in: The customer list includes all ten of the largest banks and nine of the ten largest pharma companies.

Five Numbers to Add to Your Next Board Deck

  • NRR on usage-based accounts, reported separately from seats
  • $100K+ customer count and its year-over-year growth
  • Inference cost as a percentage of revenue, by quarter
  • Second-product attach rate in your top cohort
  • Your spend as a share of your customers’ total expenses, not just their software budget

Anthropic grew 12x in a year while gross margin went from 29% to 85% and S&M stayed under a quarter of revenue. Your numbers will be smaller, but you can track all five of these metrics at your scale.

issues.title: KeyBanc’s 2026 AI x Software Survey: 24% Median ARR Growth, Only 6% at the Rule of 40, and 43% of Vendors Watching Customers Vibe Code Their Product
issues.summary: KeyBanc Capital Markets just published the 17th edition of its private software benchmark. For years it has been one of the better sources of private B2B data. This year KeyBanc added a large AI section covering pricing, AI costs, agents, internal adoption, and whether customers are building their own replacements. The survey ran from July... Continue Reading
issues.author: Jason Lemkin
issues.content_html:
KeyBanc Capital Markets just published the 17th edition of its private software benchmark. For years it has been one of the better sources of private B2B data. This year KeyBanc added a large AI section covering pricing, AI costs, agents, internal adoption, and whether customers are building their own replacements.

The survey ran from July through September 2026. 81 companies took part, and 62 of the answers came from CFOs and CEOs. Median ARR was $22M in 2025, so most of the sample is $10M-$50M B2B companies.

The sample is small. Some of the cuts below rest on 4 to 15 answers, so read the medians as directional.

The top takeaways:

  • The median company grew 24% in 2025, plans 23% in 2026, and plans 40% in 2027. Only 6% met the Rule of 40 in 2025. 62% plan to meet it in 2027.
  • 43% of vendors say customers are already using AI coding tools to rebuild their product or features. At companies under 100 employees, it’s 55%.
  • Only 41% charge for AI. The most common model is bundling it into the core price. Where it is charged, the median premium is 20%.
  • Only 8% report seat compression from AI.
  • 30 of 68 companies are over budget on AI spend, mostly because token usage beat the plan. Companies spending more than 5% of revenue on AI run 66% gross margins. Light spenders run 78%.

1. The Median Plan Goes From 23% Growth in 2026 to 40% in 2027

The median trajectory, using management’s own forecasts:

  • ARR growth: 24% (2025) → 23% (2026E) → 40% (2027E)
  • EBITDA margin: -3% → 1% → 8%
  • Rule of 40: 16% → 20% → 44%
  • Share of companies at Rule of 40: 6% → 18% → 62%

The median company plans to speed growth up by 17 points and add 7 points of EBITDA margin in the same year. That would follow a 2026 with flat growth.

These operators did beat their own plan last year. Last year’s survey forecast 20% growth for 2025, and the actual was 24%. EBITDA was planned at -4% and came in at -3%. A 4-point beat is still a long way from a 17-point acceleration.

The 12 companies with “very high” confidence in their forecast plan about 30% growth for 2027. The companies with “moderately high” or “average” confidence plan 40-41%.

The GTM side of the plan assumes every efficiency metric improves together:

  • New-customer ARR per AE: $411K → $450K → $487K
  • Quota attainment: 70% → 75% → 80%
  • Gross magic number: 0.76 → 0.79 → 0.97
  • CAC payback: 21 → 19 → 17 months

Meanwhile, 84% say AI has had no material effect on how long deals take. 9% say cycles got shorter, and 7% say they got longer. Median cycles are 2 months in SMB, 3 in mid-market and 8.5 in enterprise. KeyBanc titled that slide “Buyer Process, Not Vendor Efficiency, Sets Deal Pace.”

On one of these boards, I’d underwrite the 30% the high-confidence operators plan. Then I’d ask management for a quarter-by-quarter bridge to the other 10 points.

2. 43% of Vendors Say Customers Are Rebuilding Their Product With AI Coding Tools

43% of respondents report customers using AI coding tools to recreate their product or features. Exposure falls with company size:

  • Under 100 employees: 55%
  • 100-249 employees: 40%
  • 250+ employees: 25%

By sector, vertical software is the most exposed at 48%. Horizontal and infrastructure are both at 39%. KeyBanc analyst Jackson Ader noted that 43% is far more than the share of customers building their own versions 5 years ago.

When asked for their single biggest AI threat, respondents ranked:

  1. Incumbent competitors shipping AI features faster (15)
  2. AI reducing the need for the product (12)
  3. Customers vibe coding (11)
  4. AI-native startups (10)
  5. Hyperscalers (5)

AI-native startups ranked fourth, behind customers needing the product less and customers building it themselves.

The churn data points the same way. In 2025, the median company lost 10% of revenue: 7 points from customers leaving entirely and 3 points from downsell. Ader ties part of that full-logo churn to customers trying AI-native alternatives or building their own.

Contract length has the biggest effect on churn in the data. Median gross dollar churn by initial contract term:

  • 12 months: 9%
  • 24 months: 7%
  • 36+ months: 4%

I use Replit every day and have built production apps on it without an engineering background. A decent internal version of a $20K/year point tool takes a weekend now. The vendors that are hard to replace hold proprietary data, run deep inside workflows, or own integrations nobody wants to rebuild. 64% of vendors in the survey build on proprietary or permissioned data. KeyBanc tells investors to focus diligence on “difficulty of replicating core functionality.”

3. Companies Charging for AI Grew 27%. Companies Bundling It Grew 17%.

How AI is monetized today:

  • 41% charge for AI products
  • 29% are testing or piloting monetization
  • 30% don’t charge for AI separately

The main pricing model, out of 69 respondents:

  • Included in core product price: 31
  • Add-on / separate product: 16
  • Hybrid: 12
  • Usage or consumption: 4
  • Outcome-based: 1

The AI price premium has a median of 20%, a 25th percentile of 4%, and a 75th percentile of 26%. KeyBanc’s summary: “customers have not settled on what AI is worth.”

Growth by monetization stage:

  • Charging for AI: 27% growth in 2025, 30% planned for 2026
  • Testing / piloting: 24% → 22%
  • Not charging separately: 17% → 21%

AI-driven ARR shows the same split. Companies with no AI-driven ARR grew 11% in 2025. Companies with up to 25% of ARR from AI grew 31%.

Net retention sits at roughly 100-104% in all three groups, so charging for AI hasn’t moved retention yet. Some of the growth gap is likely selection: companies with AI good enough to charge for probably had stronger products to begin with.

AI-driven ARR was 4% of total ARR in 2025. The plan is 12% in 2026 and 17% in 2027. Planned 2026 growth in AI ARR is 128%, up from 74% in 2025. Only 21 companies answered that question, and KeyBanc tells investors to “diligence how AI-driven ARR is defined.”

4. Only 8% of Companies Report Seat Compression From AI

I’ve argued all year that seat-based pricing is under pressure. This group doesn’t show it yet.

  • 92% report no seat compression from AI. 8% do.
  • Fixed seat-based is the most common model in use (33 of 64 companies). Usage/consumption is close behind at 30.
  • Of the 30 companies moving to usage-based pricing, 53% are piloting, 27% have partially moved, and 20% have fully moved.

Ader again: “‘Consumption’ can be a scary word for a CIO or CFO.”

This is a mid-market group with a $22M median. Seat compression shows up first at large platforms with very large seat counts in support, sales and service, where one agent can replace a team. A $20M ARR vendor selling 40 seats to a mid-market customer hasn’t seen those cuts yet. Most companies are adding usage pricing on top of seats while keeping the seat base.

Companies whose core product is AI lean further toward usage: 38% of their pricing models are usage/consumption, against 25% for companies embedding AI.

5. 30 of 68 Companies Are Over Budget on AI Spend. Only 4 Are Under.

Year-to-date AI spend against budget:

  • More than 20% over: 16
  • 0-20% over: 14
  • Roughly in line: 34
  • Under: 4

Of the 33 companies that explained their overruns, 25 cited higher-than-expected token usage and 16 cited more adoption of AI features. Per-unit inference cost was flat for 47 of 67 companies. The overruns came from volume.

AI spend intensity against the P&L (2025 medians):

AI spend as % of revenue Under 2% 2-5% Over 5% ARR growth 24% 23% 17% Gross margin 78% 72% 66% ARR per FTE $205K $174K $159K Opex per FTE $171K $166K $83K

The over-5% group is only 4 to 7 companies. In 2025, its AI spend showed up as a 12-point gross margin gap without a growth payoff. Those companies also run at half the opex per employee of everyone else, and still produce less ARR per employee.

Companies selling AI as their core product compared with companies embedding AI in a broader product:

  • Growth: 34% vs 22%
  • EBITDA: -12% vs -1%
  • ARR per FTE: $117K vs $201K
  • Spending more than 5% of revenue on AI: 38% vs 17%

Half of the Core AI companies report a last valuation of 16x revenue or more. Under a third of all other companies do.

On gross margin overall, 16 of 56 companies say AI has hurt it, 22 say no effect, and 18 say it improved. We’ve seen the same split in public companies this year. Figma took the AI cost in gross margin. Box, which sells the content layer underneath the AI rather than buying inference, barely moved.

6. 91% Use AI in Engineering. 65% Have Cut Zero Headcount Because of It.

Internal AI use by function:

  • Engineering 91%, customer support 63%, sales 63%, back office 61%, IT 56%, marketing 54%
  • 24 of 40 companies say AI writes half or more of their new code (2 say all of it)
  • 92% say AI has shortened development cycles
  • R&D as a share of revenue is planned to fall from 29% in 2025 to 24% by 2027

65% report no AI-related headcount reduction or reallocation. Planned cuts over the next 12-24 months are concentrated in R&D (45%), customer service (37%) and marketing (21%). 16% expect cuts in sales.

Jason Celino at KeyBanc says companies are putting the engineering savings into shipping faster, and few are taking them to the bottom line.

32% have no formal way of measuring AI productivity, and fewer than a third track any financial metric. Companies running 6+ internal AI use cases had $188K ARR per FTE in 2025, against $141K for companies with 0-5. They plan $295K by 2027.

We run SaaStr with 3 humans and 20+ agents in production, across events, sales, marketing and support. Most of our leverage came from agents outside engineering.

7. Bootstrapped Companies Posted a 36% Rule of 40. VC-Backed Companies Posted -3%.

The bootstrapped group is only 7-9 companies. The 2025 numbers:

VC-backed Bootstrapped ARR $19M $24M ARR growth 25% 24% EBITDA margin -13% 13% Rule of 40 -3% 36% Gross magic number 0.73 1.08

Growth was nearly identical. EBITDA margin differed by 26 points. The bootstrapped companies added about 48% more net new ARR per dollar of sales and marketing.

The financing data is tough. 16 of 38 companies had less than 12 months of runway at their last VC or growth raise, and 27 of 38 had less than 24 months. Recent raises cluster at modest multiples, and much of the 16x+ group still rests on 2021-2022 marks. 27% say they’re open to being acquired. Active acquirers are mostly in the >$50M ARR group.

5 More Interesting Learnings

  • New logos carry the growth plan. New customers were 56% of net new ARR in 2025 and are planned at 63% in 2026. Median NRR is 102%, planned at 101% in 2026.
  • Infrastructure software is accelerating. It grew 33% in 2025 and plans 54% for 2026. Horizontal software went from 19% to a planned 17%. KeyBanc’s Eric Heath credits data-stack and cybersecurity spending pulled along by AI.
  • Customer-facing agents are mostly supervised. 48% of vendors offer semi-autonomous agents, 33% copilots, and 20% fully autonomous agents. 43% require human approval for agent actions.
  • 57% of vendors use multiple models for customer-facing AI. Model strategy made almost no difference to net retention.
  • 8% of vendors report broad, scaled customer deployment of their AI features. ROI uncertainty and data privacy tie as the top adoption barriers (24 each), with budget next (22).

But we’re going to do what almost no event organizer does: show you... Continue Reading
issues.author: Jason Lemkin
issues.content_html:
Most B2B + AI companies are locking their 2027 event budgets between now and January. Most will spread that budget across too many events, picked off lists built from organizer press releases.

We run SaaStr AI Annual, so discount this post accordingly. But we’re going to do what almost no event organizer does: show you the actual numbers from 2026, name the sponsors, and tell you to call them.

SaaStr AI Annual 2027 is May 11-12, 2027 at the San Mateo County Event Center in the SF Bay Area. Here are 22 reasons to be there. Leads are the first few. Most of the rest are about what happens after the badge scan.

The Leads

The Audience

11. The person in front of you owns the budget. Our core attendees are founders and CEOs at $5M to $100M ARR companies, plus CROs, CMOs, and CCOs at $25M to $1B ARR companies. A CRO at that scale typically owns a seven-figure tool budget. A single conversation with the right one is worth more than a thousand webinar signups.

12. The rooms are senior. Replit’s 2026 session drew 987 people from 715 companies, and 76% of that audience was senior. That was one session at a 10,000-person event.

13. These are the buyers spending on AI right now. We lost about 75% of our pre-AI sponsor base in 12 months and still grew SaaStr AI Annual 2026. The buyers changed, and the sponsor base changed with them. The companies writing $50K, $100K, and $250K sponsorship checks now are doing it because their customers are at SaaStr AI Annual. The incremental budget in B2B is going to AI, and the people holding it are here.

14. 10,000+ B2B + AI leaders in one place for two days. Getting 20 meetings with this audience through outbound can take a year of sequences. At SaaStr AI Annual, all of them are in the same building on the same two days.

15. VCs are in the room too. One good conversation with a partner can turn into intros across an entire portfolio, and those intros keep coming for months after the event ends.

The Format

16. 3,000+ scheduled 1-on-1 meetings. Our “Who Do You Want to Meet” matchmaking app is targeting 3,000+ scheduled 1:1s for 2027. Sponsors who load their target account list before the event show up with a full meeting calendar on day one.

17. Dedicated CRO, CMO, and CCO Summits. These are concentrated rooms of the exact executives most sponsors want to reach, organized by the budget they own. If you sell to revenue leaders, marketing leaders, or customer leaders, there’s a summit built around your buyer.

18. 200+ speakers and 100+ deep-dive workshops. The sponsors who teach get remembered. Artisan’s live main stage demo is a big part of why their leads converted. A workshop that shows real numbers from real deployments does more for you than any booth graphic.

19. A full week of side events across the Bay Area. Host a dinner for 20 target accounts the night before doors open, and your booth conversations the next day start with people who already know you.

20. The reach goes well beyond the floor. Replit’s 2026 presence drove 5.9M+ social impressions. The content, clips, and posts from the event keep working for you through the summer.

The Timing

21. May leads become Q3 bookings. SaaStr AI Annual lands mid-Q2. The pipeline you build on May 11-12 has a full quarter to close before H2 planning, which is when most of your customers finalize budgets for the back half of the year.

The best booth locations, the Diamond slots, and the main stage spots go first. The sponsors who get the most out of this event commit early and spend the months before May preparing to use it.

issues.title: Anthropic Will Get to $100B in Revenue with ~7% of the Headcount Google and Meta Needed
issues.summary: Jon Ma posted Brad Gerstner’s Anthropic thesis from TomorrowX this morning. Google needed about 100,000 people to get to $100B in revenue. Anthropic will get there with about 5,000. The money Google spent on people, Anthropic spends on compute. Brad $ANT Thesis: – Google had 105k people to get to $100B revenue– Anthropic needs 5k... Continue Reading
issues.author: Jason Lemkin
issues.content_html:
Jon Ma posted Brad Gerstner’s Anthropic thesis from TomorrowX this morning. Google needed about 100,000 people to get to $100B in revenue. Anthropic will get there with about 5,000. The money Google spent on people, Anthropic spends on compute.

Brad $ANT Thesis:
– Google had 105k people to get to $100B revenue
– Anthropic needs 5k people to get to $100B revenue
– the 100K people Google had, Anthropic can allocate the human cost to compute

cc @altcap@AltimeterCap@TomorrowXSummit

— Jon Ma (@jonbma) November 17, 2026

The exact figures in the post are a bit off. Anthropic’s S-1 supports the thesis anyway, and Meta’s numbers back it up too.

Google Had 80,110 Employees at $100B. Meta Had 71,970.

Alphabet did $110.9B in revenue in 2017, the first year it passed $100B. It ended that year with 80,110 employees.

Meta passed $100B four years later. It did $117.9B in 2021 and ended the year with 71,970 employees.

Those were two of the most efficient large companies ever built, and each still needed 70,000 to 80,000 people to get to $100B.

Anthropic Has 5,300 Employees and an $81B Run-Rate

Anthropic’s S-1/A shows about 5,300 employees as of September 30, 2026, and an $81B run-rate as of October 31. It added $10B of run-rate in October alone.

At that pace, Anthropic passes a $100B run-rate around the end of the year with fewer than 6,000 people. That’s about 7% of Google’s headcount and about 7% of Meta’s at the same milestone.

$15M in Revenue per Employee vs. $1.4M at Google and $1.6M at Meta

Google did about $1.4M in revenue per employee in 2017. Meta did about $1.6M in 2021.

Anthropic does about $15M per employee on a run-rate basis, roughly 10x either company at the same scale. On trailing twelve months, the S-1 says $6.6M per employee, up from $1.4M a year earlier. Over that year, revenue grew about 1,200% and headcount grew about 170%.

Q3 2026: Compute Was 58% of Revenue, People Were 10%

Anthropic’s Q3 2026 numbers:

  • Revenue: $16.96B
  • Compute and infrastructure: $9.86B, or 58% of revenue, up from 48% in Q2
  • Personnel: $1.71B, about 10% of revenue

Anthropic spent almost 6x as much on compute as on people. Year over year in Q3, personnel costs grew about 3.5x, from $489M to $1.71B. Quarterly revenue grew more than 12x.

Google Had a 23.5% Operating Margin and Meta Had 40%. Anthropic Lost $567M in Q3.

Google earned $26.1B in operating income in 2017. Meta earned $46.8B in 2021. Anthropic posted a $567M operating loss in Q3 2026.

Anthropic didn’t eliminate the cost of 75,000 people. That money now goes to Google, Amazon, Broadcom and the other compute providers. On Q3’s numbers, it costs more than the people did. That could change as inference gets cheaper per token and pricing matures. For now, the small headcount is driving growth, not profit.

What Changes for B2B Founders

The operating plan used to be built around headcount. Revenue per rep, ramp time and quota capacity set how fast you could grow, and the hiring plan sat in the middle of the board deck.

Now the plan gets built around how much work your agents can do and what that work costs. Three things follow:

  • Revenue per employee tells you less than it used to. Anthropic does $15M per employee and still lost money in Q3. Gross margin after inference and cost per unit of output tell you more.
  • Compute spend grows with usage. A hiring freeze does nothing to it, so it needs the same monthly review headcount used to get.
  • Customers are moving payroll money into AI spend. B2B AI companies that charge 2x what pre-AI competitors charge are being paid out of salary budgets.

SaaStr Runs on 3 Humans and 20+ Agents

We see the same thing at SaaStr on a much smaller scale. We run the company with 3 humans and 20+ AI agents in production, and our fastest-growing cost is the AI tools those agents run on.

Google needed 80,000 people to get to $100B, and Meta needed 72,000. Anthropic will get there with about 5,300 people, and in Q3 it spent $9.86B on compute.
